*Silvester* also disputes (as I heard above), *in his 3 De adopt.*: *the Pope can dispense, so that it is licit for a monk, casting off his cowl for a time, to take a wife, namely as long as it takes for the procreation of offspring*.

Others dispute whether in dispensation or relaxation of a vow *just cause* is to be attended. Some deny — that indeed the Pope over a vow without rational cause can dispense sufficiently. And for *rational causes* they hold: **1.** difficulty or precipitation in vowing; **2.** weakness of the one bearing the vow; **3.** necessity or utility, either public — great necessity, great utility private; **4.** every event, from which the fulfillment of the vow becomes useless or noxious, or impediment of a greater good; **5.** every other cause, which the superior has judged sufficient for adding.

*Others hold*: to rescind a vow *just cause is not needed*, but the mere will of him who has power over it suffices. And this opinion *Silvester* names truer (*i q. 3*), since vows are made under tacit condition — *if they should please the superior*.

Then they dispute, whether one can *privately commute one vow into another*, and most conclude that he can, when it is changed into an evidently better good — as *Aquinas* says: *no proposition, or thing promised, obliges, when it is changed into a better* (as Gregory said). But when it is doubtful whether some good is better, then the authority of the superior is needed.

And indeed penes the Pope they say is *the power of commuting* all vows of Christians wherever they live; but under bishops is the power, of commuting at least those, whose commutation is not reserved to the Roman Pontiff. But they say the power of commuting is held by him who has power of dispensing. Then commutation is made: **1.** when the thing which is vowed was useless; **2.** when difficulty arises in performing; **3.** the vow is made from sudden consternation. And this commutation is made with consideration of the qualities of the person. For one about to commute a vow of pilgrimage into a divine service, or of poor labor, indeed he will change certain days into fastings and prayers, and the expenses which he would have made, besides those he would have made at home, into alms — so that on the rich he imposes greater burdens than on the poor. If however anyone is impeded in the fulfillment of a vow at some certain time, then they say it suffices, if the commuter does not remove the vow itself, but grants only a delay of time.

These disputations of the Papists flow from that *spurious empire* which they attribute to prelates, especially to the Pope, over the consciences of men — which is tyrannical and altogether contrary to the Word of God, which recognizes only God as *Lord of consciences*.

No exemplum of such dispensation or rescission exists in the *sacred Bible*. What if the same Pope, thinking he can rescind a vow without any cause, when only his will suffices? Since God, not to the will of the Pope or to the reasoning of the church rules his Church, it is rash to expose consciences to the will of one man without just cause.

Therefore it is to be experienced, how consciences are burdened, when the Pope gives power to monks of transferring from one order into another — which is nothing else than to rescind the vow of the prior order (by which nevertheless they thought consciences bound), and to impose a new yoke by a new vow. From which entanglements the wretched cannot emerge before recognizing that Papal power of imposing and rescinding vows to be null.

But rather: **1.** if the *matter of the vow* was illicit, the vow is by that very fact null, and needs no peculiar dispensation.

**2.** If the vow was *licit and legitimately made*, then it admits no dispensation. For God's mandate of *rendering* vows freely and licitly made is clear (Deut 23:22, Ps 50:14, Eccl 5:5).

Impious therefore is the voice of *Lorichius* (*Institut. cathol.* c. 15): *some impediment supervening to the fulfillment of a vow, the Pope declares that the vow does not oblige: therefore he does not remove divine right, but only explicates*.

But it is licit to no man to dispense against divine right, and where God has not added explication, at our arbitrament divine precepts are not to be explicated. No impediment can there be, which either can remove our obedience to divine mandates, or can suspend it.

The vow of perpetual continence, of religion, of pilgrimage to Jerusalem &c. to fulfill — is not of divine right; therefore it does not need dispensation, but by that very fact is null and illicit, on the causes above indicated.

*So much of vows.*

— ❦ —

## Chapter IX. On Cases of Conscience Concerning Oaths

*De casibus conscientiae circa iuramenta.*

*Iuramentum* by the ancient Latins was the same as *sacramentum*. For as *Festus* and *Isaac Casaubon* remark, it is called *iuramentum* because it is transacted with a *ratio* of swearing (*iure iurandi ratione*) interposed — whence they were said to be *interrogated by oath*, who were compelled by an intervening *ratio* of swearing to speak the truth.

Now the *oath* is a *religious and necessary confirmation of a doubtful thing, in which God himself is invoked as witness of what is spoken, and also as avenger of a false oath*. It is called *confirmation* because it is not a bare promise or assertion but a *stabilizing* of what is promised or asserted; therefore the Apostle writes: *For men verily swear by the greater: and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife.* (Heb 6:16). By this word it is distinguished from a *vow* (which is a promise made to God), for an oath is a *confirmation of any promise whatsoever*. *Religious*, because it is a part of the divine cult, whereby the name of God is exalted, and he is called upon that he may testify of some certain thing, and punish the deceiver. *Necessary*, because oaths ought not to be admitted except when great necessity requires and otherwise our assertion would not be trusted — opposed to the *temerity* of those who swear where simple assertion would suffice.

In an oath *the testimony of witnesses of things said or done is sought from heaven*, which ought not to be done unless witnesses on earth fail. And it is added that it is a *confirmation of a doubtful thing*: for what is certain and in confession needs no oath. The *form and quasi-soul* of the oath is that *God is invoked as witness of things said or done, and as avenger of the deceiving* — which in bare promises, assertions, or obtestations does not occur.

Three things therefore pertain to the form of an oath: **(1)** the bare asseveration of the business; **(2)** the testimony of the divine numen who cannot deceive; **(3)** the execration, or *evocation of the divine avenger*, if the one swearing deceives.

The oath is distinguished into various species. There is the *oath of truth* (*veritatis*), which the magistrate imposes upon one or another party when truth cannot otherwise be sought. There is the *oath of good faith* (*fidei*), used in contracts, treaties, and pacts, when contracting or covenanting parties bind themselves mutually and reciprocally to keep faith. There is the *military oath* (*militare*), which is also called *sacramentum militare*, by which after election each soldier swears that he shall not depart from his rank (*malitia*) except after his stipends or times of service are completed — as is in *Isidore*, *Origin.* lib. 9 c. 3. [So *Cicero* calls soldiers *obstricted by the sacrament*, that is, by the military oath, to render faith to the emperor.]

Three genera of oaths are commonly constituted. One is **voluntary** (*voluntarium*), which *Suidas* calls *αὐθαίρετον*, and has place in pacts and contracts, and is deferred and prostrated by private persons, therefore to anyone is free either to render or to reject. Under it is included the **promissory** (*promissorium*) and **assertoric** (*assertorium*) — the former of future things, whose promises are confirmed by oath; the latter of past or present things. There is the *oath of religion*, by which one binds himself to a certain religion; there is the *oath of fidelity*, by which magistrates and subjects bind themselves mutually to render fidelity, as in homages. Another is **necessary** (*necessarium*), which *Suidas* calls *ἐπάναγκες* — enjoined and commanded: for by a magistrate or judge from most grave causes it is deferred, and therefore cannot be rejected. To which genus pertains the *judicial* oath, which one party of the litigants owes to the other; which when deferred from the challenged to the challenger, is necessary, otherwise it can be rejected. The third is **spontaneous** (*spontaneum*), which *Suidas* calls *ἐπίορκον*, when someone, no one deferring, confirms his assertion by oath.

But as the matter of oaths is subject to many disputations, so various doubts here arise which make pious consciences solicitous, whose chief ones we shall now untangle, so that the studious of truth may acquiesce.

### Case I. Whether oaths are at all licit, since Christ seems to prohibit them, saying *But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.* (Matt 5:37), which the Apostle James repeats (Jas 5:12)

**Respondeo.** Not only the *Anabaptists* today, but also the ancient heretics — *Esseni*, *Bardesanes*, *Barchochba* — established that oaths are entirely illicit for Christians (as is in *Eusebius*, *Praeparat. evang.* lib. 3 c. 12, and *H.E.* c. 4), to which opinion also some of the Fathers seemed to favor, when they saw the temerity and levity of many in swearing.

But rightly wrote *Augustine* (Ep. 154): *not to swear, but to perjure oneself, is a sin*. For that oaths are licit in themselves — whether they are voluntary, necessary, deferred, or enjoined, provided otherwise legitimate — appears from the following arguments:

**(1)** *Because God himself swears*: *he swore by himself* (Gen 22:16); *he swore by his soul* (Jer 51:14; Amos 6:8); *by his life* (Num 14:21; Deut 32:40; Ezek 33:11); *by his sanctity* (Ps 89:36; Amos 4:2) — which the Apostle interprets in the Epistle to the Hebrews (6:13): *God swore by himself*. For life and sanctity are God himself.

**(2)** *Because God enjoins oaths* in certain cases through the magistrate (Exod 22:11); *that by his name we should swear* he expressly commands (Deut 6:13; 10:20); and thus even in the NT the Prophet foretold (Isa 65:16).

**(3)** *Christ himself swore several times* (Matt 26:63 and 27:14; John 5:19; 6:26; Mark 8:12), in which places he uses the particle *Amen*, which notes affirmation with interposed oath, as it is written: *he who blesses in the earth shall be blessed in God Amen, and he who swears in the earth shall swear in God Amen* (Isa 65:16).

**(4)** *Angels swore* with lifted hand attesting heaven and earth (Rev 10:5, 6), by which gesture the one swearing swears.

**(5)** *Patriarchs and Apostles swore and demanded oaths of others* (Gen 14:22–23 Abraham; Gen 24:3 Isaac; Gen 47:29 Jacob; Rom 1:9; 2 Cor 1:23; 1 Thess 2:5 Paul).

**(6)** *Reason too convinces* oaths are not illicit. For they arise from *right faith in God, who as more excellent none is* (Heb 6:13,16), who gives testimony that things are as spoken; who indeed is truth's lover and avenger of the false, and can punish perjurers. Utility too both to ourselves and to the neighbor is served by those who swear — to ourselves, because more credit is granted to the one swearing than the simple asserter, whence *commonly it is called the "act of confirmation"*; to the neighbor, because innocents by oaths are freed from perils, and controversies are ended (Heb 6:16), and occasion of deceiving others is removed. Nay, the oath is part of divine cult, whereby the name of God is exalted, and he is called upon to testify of some thing and punish the deceiver.

*Christ's saying* (Matt 5:37) *"let your speech be yea, yea, nay, nay: swear not at all"* *does not remove all use of oath*, but is: (i) opposed to *inconstancy* of *men-vessels*, who now affirm, now deny — of whom Augustine (Ep. 154) and Ambrose (*De sermon. Dom. in monte* lib. 1) say: incredulity is evil, declaring. (ii) Opposed to *levity of men*, who are too easy to swear, not only in common life, but even offer themselves to oaths in judgment, not weighing the peril they oppose themselves to: where more praiseworthy is *simple assertion* than too great facility in swearing — for as *Augustine* says (Ep. 28 *De verb. Apost.*): *false swearing is destructive, true swearing perilous, no swearing is safe*. (iii) Opposed to *rash oath*, such as of the Pharisees, against whom Christ there professes his sermon — who partly judged it licit even in familiar discourse, on any matter, in any case, to swear, though for the highest they did nothing for God's glory nor the utility of the neighbor. And partly what by simple promise had been agreed, they easily violated, thinking God to be at least the avenger of things committed among men. They swore not only by God, but also by heaven, by the temple, by the earth, and similar oaths. To these Christ opposes: *swear not at all* — reprehending in these examples all *rash* oaths without cause and necessity.

The universal particle *at all* (*omnino*) is therefore to be understood *with restriction* — namely of rash and illicit oaths, as elsewhere. So Sir 46:20: *there did not remain anything of him*, where *nothing* means only the omitted works. Thus Luke 7:28: *there hath not risen among them that are born of women a greater than John the Baptist* — the universal particle is to be restricted, as concerning those who by carnal generation were born. Which without doubt *Sirach* observed: therefore when he prohibited unnecessary oaths, he explicated it altogether in the words of Christ (Sir 23:9): *accustom not thy mouth to swearing, neither use thyself to the naming of the Holy One*.

### Case II. Since therefore it is established that oaths are not simply prohibited, what shall we say — is it licit to swear by God and all saints?

**Respondeo.** This oath, though frequent in the Papacy, we hold not to lack profanation of the divine name. For God approves only those oaths which are made in his own name (Isa 19:18; 45:23; Jer 4:2), and disapproves those which are made in the name of idols (Jer 5:7): *thy sons have forsaken me, and have sworn by those that are no gods*. Penalty also he threatens to those who in oaths add creatures to God (Zeph 1:4–5): *I will consume them who swear by the Lord and who swear by Melcom*. And Christ himself reprehends in general oaths which are made through creatures (Matt 5:34), whence *Jerome* infers, Christ simply disapproved formulas of swearing through creatures.

And the reason is manifest. For an *oath is part of the divine cult*, which agrees neither with saints nor with any creature. And as saints are not to be invoked, so neither is one to swear in their name: since an oath is a *species of invocation*, in which God is invoked as witness of all things which are said or done, and is invoked as avenger of those lying — which surely cannot be attributed to saints.

For which cause *Jerome*, on that place of Christ concerning the oath, cites: *Christ prohibited oath by creatures, lest the honor of the creator be transferred to a creature*. And it is established in the *Council of Toledo* c. 22, *he who swears by creatures is to be reprehended most acerbly and afflicted with penances, and if he persist, is to be excommunicated*, from which is decreed in the canon-law (c. 21 q. 1): *if anyone shall swear by creatures, let him be excommunicated, and let penance be assigned to him according to which the Synod judged*.

**We cannot approve, therefore, that Mahomet swore by the sun, moon, stars, fiery splendor**, animals, and things of this kind. And of the gentiles the swearings by various creatures were used: as *Aelius Gallus* by garlic and turnips as most holy numen; certain of the Greek Isles by their oyster shells; the Greeks by *Rhadamanthus*; the *Athenians* by *Aegimium* and *Anubis*, and among the *Cappadocians* by their *Mithras*; the *Tyrians* by *Melkart*, that is, by the sun; the *Persians* by excellent men; the *Parthians* by their paternal gods; the *Ionians* by cabbage; *Zeno* by the caper; the *Muslim* by the anchor; the *Egyptians* by the dog, the platanus, the oak, and by the goat (for by the gods he refused to swear); the *Socratics* by *Castor* and *Pollux*; the *Pythagoreans* by their *quaternion* — because that number pertains to the integrity of the soul, in which they said one must consider mind, science, opinion, and sense, &c. Of all which see *Alexander ab Alexandro* (*Genial. dier.* lib. 5 c. 10).

But no pious one has easily imitated the customs of the gentiles — for it is no wonder that they, in that blindness and ignorance of the true God, erred in this part of the cult and religion partly ridiculously and partly turpitly.

More is to be wondered at, that among Christians men of great name are found, who in this part of divine cult joined creatures to the true God. Among whom is *Justinian Emperor*, who orders new magistrates to swear thus: *I swear by God omnipotent, and his Son and only-begotten Jesus Christ our Lord, and by the Holy Spirit, and by the sacred and glorious mother of God and always-virgin Mary, and by the four Gospels which we hold in our hands, and by the holy Archangels Michael and Gabriel*. (Nov. Constit. de sanctionibus per *Iohannes Papam* it. per Iac. Just.)

*Impiety* also is not lacking in that *in the Papacy oaths are made by the Gospel*, and such oaths are sometimes imposed by ecclesiastical magistrates even upon the *Evangelici*, although *Sylvester* (*V. iuram.* de iure iur., prop. num. 6) rightly holds *this to be understood of the hypostatic Word, that is, of the Son of God, not of the letters of the Gospel*. Yet it is not right for us to use in oaths formulas of adversaries by which they intend other than we do — since to know is not ignorant. Better therefore altogether to abstain from such a formula of oath, than in favor of adversaries to seem to collide with them.

*The Papists acknowledge that only by God should one swear*, but since even they swear by saints, thus they defend it — they say: they swear by the saints not on account of them themselves (as though the saints held anything of numen and divinity) but on account of God, who is the author of all truth and sanctity which the saints have; just as *images are worshipped not on account of themselves but on account of God, the giver of all sanctity* (see Azorius, lib. 11 c. 8).

**But then**, since God nowhere commanded to invoke saints or to swear by them — nay rather prohibited this — the oath which is made by saints, howsoever palliated, is by God's precept contrary, by that very fact impious.

Then no consequence follows: *saints have their sanctity from God, therefore they are to be invoked, or one is to swear by them*. For the same I could also say about *Jerusalem*, which is called *the holy city* in Scripture (Matt 4:5), by which nevertheless Christ denies one should swear (Matt 5:35).

Others object *Joseph's oath by the salvation of Pharaoh* (Gen 42:15), *Moses' by the head of Deuteronomy 30:19*, *Elisha's swearing "by the Lord and by the soul of Elijah"* (2 Kgs 4:30) — whence they infer creatures can be joined to God in oaths. But we have taught above, those formulas are not so much oaths as serious obtestations and asseverations, of which many kinds are in common life — as when one asserts something by his faith, by his existence, by his life, by his soul, and this is done without injury to the creator, since no invocation acceded, no postulation of vengeance if we deceive; but it is simple assertion to make greater credibility.

### Case III. Whether an oath made by a Gentile through a false God, or by a Papist through saints, is a true oath, which binds the swearer in conscience

**Respondeo.** Gentiles swear by what by nature is not God — by Jove, by Hercules, &c. Turks by Mahomet. Papists by all saints. Such oath is indeed *illegitimate*, since one should swear only in the name of the true God; but in *value or effect* it is a true and binding oath.

For that by which one swears is not indeed the true God, but in the opinion of the one swearing it holds some numen. So *Abraham* admits *Abimelech's* oath, though he swore by false gods (Gen 21:23). *Laban* in his oath adjoined to the true God the gods of the gentiles: for he swears by the *God of Nahor*, who was a strange God, whom Nahor and his fathers served in Chaldaea (Gen 31:53) — which oath was in itself illicit, as it is written: *by the name of foreign gods do not swear* (Exod 23:13). Since however *Jacob* held Nahor's gods (which Laban acknowledged) as if for the true God, therefore *Jacob* holding Laban's oath as ratified in part, added his own: *he swore by the fear of his father Isaac*.

In the same manner today we can act in pacts with the *Papists*. Papists in their oaths join saints to the true God, and swear by both; which in itself is impious. Evangelical princes swear by the true God alone; Papists we join with our oath not as if we were confirming an oath sworn by anyone who swore by creatures — but the fact that he sworn is enough to keep faith with him. So the *Roman Emperor*, confirming a treaty with the *Carthaginians* by oath, admits the *Carthaginians* swearing by Jupiter Herculeus. And though on both sides something of vice acceded — the *Carthaginians* swearing by their *Hercules*, the *Emperor* by his *Gods and holy Gospels* — yet each is held to preserve what he swore. For not the *form* of the oath, but the *soul and intention* of the one swearing is to be attended.

To the same effect *Augustine* on this question proposed by *Publicola* responds (Ep. 154): he indeed *who swears by false gods, and does not keep the promised faith, sins twice — first because he invoked a false God, then because he did not keep faith* — from which is inferred, *even one who has sworn by false gods, is nonetheless bound* to observe what he pledged.

### Case IV. To what extent is it licit or not licit to swear when the oath is deferred to us?

**Respondeo.** It is commonly said: *not everything that is licit is honest*. But regard should always be had more to honesty than to liberty. So to swear indeed is licit, but not always is it useful or honest.

*Levity in swearing is vicious*, and against the Word of God — swearing ought not to be a *bond of iniquity* (*l. 15 Instit. tit. 17*), and *what is against good morals ought not to bind* (*l. 27 ff. de act. et obligation.*).

Since therefore in the world among men we live, many things must be tolerated which cannot be changed. Anyone therefore, if it can be, should abstain altogether from every oath, and so accustom himself to truth, that his simple speech has the force of an oath. For not the very nature of promising, but the *weakness of men* makes oaths necessary. If in the morals of men there were no one who was not just and truthful, as they ought, fraud and lie would be hated by all — nor oaths nor laws would be needed. But as *Herodotus* remarks, *oaths were introduced by our laws*, that as *Theognis* feigns *strife or contention was of nature*.

Therefore let no one accustom himself to swear, lest he make himself an argument of perfidy — of which most grave admonition of *Sirach* (Sir 23:9): *let not thy mouth be accustomed to swearing*. And *Augustine* writes (Serm. 28 *De verbis Apost.*): *I swear, but as far as concerns me, from great necessity compelled, when I see I am not otherwise trusted unless I do, and when I see it is not expedient for the hearer not to trust*.

**The matter of the oath therefore** ought to be:

**1.** *True* — for of doubtful things we cannot even affirm, much less swear (*where truth has no place, oath will not have place* — *l. In fin. C. de non numer. pecun.*).

**2.** *Of great moment* — either undertaken for public commodity or for utility of the neighbor: for light things, or those in which private lucre only is looked at, are rashly confirmed by oaths and not without abuse of the divine name. Therefore *Chrysostom* admonishes: *do not by oath commit any small thing*.

**3.** *Honest and agreeable to God's Word* — for what is base is not even to be affirmed, much less confirmed by oath, since an oath ought not to be a *bond of iniquity*, and *what is against good morals ought not to bind* (Ulpian *l. 1 Instit. tit. 17*).

**4.** *Possible* — for what among the ancients walked *pari passu* with the honest, whatever was contrary to good morals was called dishonest (*l. hac lege sub condit. instit.*); to impossibles no one is obligated (*l. impossibilium ff. de act. et obligation.*).

**5.** *Deliberate* — from a firm proposition of soul, not by mere impulse of anger, impatience, or fear.

The pious man therefore sees how many things must be considered, how diligently he must circumspect himself before he swears, lest he fall either into temerity or into peril of perjury, and by profaning the name of God he incur the penalties spoken in the Law (Exod 20:7).

### Case V. Concerning the persons to whom the oath is deferred

**Respondeo.** Even here caution is needed. For as with vows, so also with oaths, not just anyone should be promiscuously admitted, but only those who *are of their own right* and can weigh what they swear.

Cannot swear therefore:

**1.** *Children* who neither understand the force of the oath and the penalties of perjury nor rightly weigh them. Yet today, alas, no one more frequently swears than the immature — even boys and girls scarcely ten years old — from collapse of domestic discipline.

**2.** *Women* — the power of vowing was taken from them (Num 30:4, 6, 8, 11). Therefore also of swearing, if father or husband contradicted, to whose power they are subject, on account of the weakness of a sex which does not accurately weigh what may follow.

**3.** *Ministers and others* who depend on the power of superiors, who without consent of their superiors cannot render an oath — especially a solemn one — unless in certain cases which jurisconsults are wont to teach.

**4.** *Ecclesiastical persons* in causes of religion can indeed swear, but in the *forum* the oath is not to be deferred to them — of which *St. Thomas* on 22 q. 5 alleges four causes: (i) since an oath is a *torment*, and priests ought to be free from all torture of body and soul; (ii) since it is not verisimilar that he would deceive in the least things, who has not been detected deceiving even in the greatest and divine things; (iii) since every oath ends in *execration* — a truly sad thing — and it is absurd that he who preaches blessing and salvation should be compelled to execrations and dire things; (iv) since the peril of perjury exists in oaths, occasion of which we ought not to offer to a priest.

**5.** *Drunks* cannot swear in judgment, because they lack judgment and easily abuse the divine name. Therefore of old solemn oaths were made with the fasting, of which we have example in the history of Isaac, Abimelech, Ahuzzath, and Phicol (Gen 26:31).

**6.** *Light and suspect men*, and those suspected of perjury, are not to be admitted to an oath. *He therefore who forces such a man to swear, whom he knows will perjure himself, is worse than a homicide: for the homicide takes only the body, but this one destroys the soul.*

**7.** *The insane* cannot swear, since they cannot understand what they swear nor weigh the penalties of perjury.

**8.** *Coerced and unwilling* oaths also should be spared, but if extorted, what is to be established, I will explain below in a peculiar case.

From all these the *requisites of a licit oath* can be gathered: it should be made *by a person who is of his own right, in the name of God alone, of a licit thing, from deliberate proposition, either to give faith to a hearer about the truth, or to impose upon others the necessity of not deceiving*. About which are the ancient little verses:

> *Stulta, dolosa, placens, mendax, temeraria, frustra*
> *detestans, iterata, procax, superstitiosa, temembra*
> *Not without sin is every oath.*

### Case VI. What ceremonies are to be used in oaths?

**Respondeo.** Various were the *rites of the gentiles in oaths*, of which some are recounted by *Alexander ab Alexandro* (*Genial. dier.* lib. 5 c. 10). Sometimes with a boar seized and a stripped sword to the throat, they were wont to invoke heaven, earth, sun, and avenging Furies; then the boar being sacrificed and cast into the sea, they gave their oath, in which manner *Regulus swore among the Poeni*. Sometimes those swearing touched the *altars of the gods*, and this they called the most holy oath — of which is the example of *Ptolemy Ceraunus* in *Justin* (lib. 24). Some, touching altars or lambs, held their right hand a flint, and attested gods and men, that if they should knowingly deceive, so should Jupiter strike them as they themselves struck the lamb (see Livy lib. 1 *Decad.* 1; Valerius Max. lib. 9 c. 1).

The Roman custom was that those about to swear by Jove would either at the altars of the gods (the sacrifice having been performed) touch fire, altar, and entrails, or else swear over cast victims (Livy lib. 3 c. 20); sometimes holding a flint stone they were wont to say the following words: *if I knowingly deceive, so may Diespiter cast me out from the good, as I cast out this stone* — which enunciated, they held the stone in hand and spoke: *to swear by the Jupiter Stone*, which was the most solemn and holy oath (see Sextus Pompeius lib. 10; Cicero lib. 7 *Epistol. famil.* 13; Gellius lib. 1 c. 21) — which rite especially in *public confederacies* was solemnly observed, as in *Polybius* lib. 3 *De foedere Romanorum et Carthaginensium*.

**Among Christians** certain rites are also used, especially in those oaths which are imposed by the magistrate — not indeed from cause of necessity, &c., but on account of some useful *admonition*. God himself, though he has no bodily members, is nevertheless said to have sworn *with hand raised to heaven* (Isa 62), that he might admonish us, that our minds during swearing should be raised to heaven, where is the searcher of hearts, the witness of truth, and the avenger of perjury. Whence *to raise the hand* in Scripture — when it is said of God — is the same as *to swear* (Deut 32:40; Ezek 20:7). Angels also with lifted hands to heaven swear (Rev 10:5). And *Abraham*, with hand lifted to the Lord God most high, possessor of heaven and earth, swore to the *king of Sodom* (Gen 14:22). To this example of ancient Christians also swore *with hand raised to heaven*, as *Cyril* in his *Apology* (De virtutibus) writes of a certain old man, that he swore with hands raised to heaven *by the sacrosanct Baptism and the venerable mysteries of Christ*.

When inferiors swore to superiors, they did not raise the hand, but placed it *on the thigh* of him to whom the oath was to be given — by which rite *Eliezer*, Abraham's servant, swore to his master (Gen 24:2), and *Joseph* to his dying father Jacob (Gen 47:29) — by which rite they remembered the covenant with God entered into *in circumcision*, just as today by touching the Book of the Gospels those swearing are admonished of the *evangelical faith of their Redeemer Christ*, proposed in the Gospel, or remembered the seed of the blessed Virgin, which by the ancestors was foretold as to come forth in their time — by which faith they were wont to swear by this rite.

Christians in the primitive Church swore either by touching the *tomb of some holy martyr*, as *Gregory Magnus* refers (lib. 3 ep. 33), by ancient custom, as *Gregory of Tours* refers (lib. 5 *Histor.* c. 3); or with hand imposed on the sacred book of the Bible, as *Chrysostom* refers (Hom. 15 *ad populum Antiochenum*), or on the book of the Gospels, according to *Sozomen* (lib. 5 *hist. eccles.* c. 10).

The common people, joining the *index-fingers* of each hand into the form of a cross, and thus swore by *the sign of the cross of Christ*, though this custom is scarcely observed today except in execrations and lesser oaths, and rather from a vicious custom than from any evangelical consideration.

Today in judicial proceedings *lights* are sometimes kindled, before which men swearing on their knees hold up *the index and middle fingers of the right hand* to the image of the cross or to the sacred Bible or raise them heavenward, the rest of the fingers being contracted below the hand. Women swear with hand placed against the right breast, from ancient German custom (see Peter Gregorius Tholosanus *Syntagm.* lib. 10 c. 9).

Interpretations may be given for these ceremonies. *The lights are kindled*, because in the sight of God (to whom no creature is invisible, but *all things are open and naked to his eyes* — Heb 4:13), man is placed swearing. *He kneels*, on account of the reverence of the present Numen. *The index-finger is stretched out*, since the one swearing shows as if by index-finger whom he calls witness of his speech, and whom he wills to be avenger if he deceive. *The middle finger is raised*, the rest being contracted, that the integrity of mind and affect be shown — that nothing is done or spoken from hatred, envy, or any other morbid affect toward the adversary. *The two fingers are joined*, to note the consent of the one swearing and of him by whom he swears.

Though this rite of raising at least *two* fingers seems maximally common and used, whence commonly of those swearing it is said: *give the fingers, take the oath* — while some — opening not three but only two fingers — reckon it enough, from the constitution of *Charles V*. But there are many who think *three fingers* — thumb, index, and middle — should be raised, in honor and reverence of the Blessed Trinity.

Which custom is still observed in our consistories, and a certain interpretation is added, which is customarily pre-read to the one about to swear before he is admitted to render the oath. This interpretation I add, since it is elegant and grave, which has deterred many from perjury. Thus it goes:

> *Three fingers of thy right hand thou raisest: the thumb signifies the Father; the index, the Son; the middle, the Holy Spirit. But the two other fingers of the hand are contracted, of which the fourth (the ring finger) notes the precious body of our Lord Jesus Christ crucified, buried, and again resurrected; the smallest finger notes the very body which in relation to the soul minor is seen to be. The whole hand notes that both God and every creature is in the head of heaven and earth. Whoever therefore is so extremely fraudulent and mendacious as to commit perjury, when the oath is undertaken, on the divine sacrosanct Trinity, in the passion and death and precious body of our Lord Jesus Christ he swears, no less than the Devil to whom he pledges his soul. Anyone therefore who commits perjury swears against the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, sacrosanct Trinity — that he may be cut off from communion of God and the true light; against himself and against his soul, being infamous; against the ancient body of our Lord Jesus Christ that neither aid nor solace be in the agony of death, and that when the body is about to be dissolved, if perjury is committed, then I entreat thee, God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, that this most precious body of our Lord Jesus Christ, with acerbest pain and death, and all innocentissimic torments infer to me miserable sinner an irrite reddition; if I commit perjury, my soul, when I take these fingers back, on the newest day, may be denied, where to me perjured shall be to stand before the tribunal of just Judge, and I myself with my mouth confess, that I am to be cut off from communion with God and his elect and all saints. Wherefore may our Lord Jesus Christ preserve me from perjury: I do entreat the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, sacrosanct Trinity, that I may be excluded from communion of God, if I commit perjury.*

From these appears, that ceremonies are not necessarily required for oaths, but may be adhibited on account of salutary admonitions.

### Case VII. When in oaths the words are ambiguous, how are they to be accepted — according to the mind of the one to whom the oath is deferred, or of the one swearing?

**Respondeo.** Much is disputed of this by scholastics, more subtle than useful (see *Sylvester Aetius Instit. moral.* cap. 4). But the case arises from the words of the one swearing, which are sometimes sufficiently clear — the intention of the one swearing can be easily recognized — but sometimes are ambiguous, whence about the intention it is doubted.

**When the words are ambiguous**, no doubt is that they are to be accepted *according to the mind of the one swearing*, since anyone is the best interpreter of his own words. And God, by whom one swears, is not deceived by words, but looks into the heart. Therefore *Gregory* writes (16 *moral.* c. 5): *human ears judge our words such as they sound outside; but divine judgments hear such as they are brought forth from within*. And again: *he who according to the same intention and mind of another swears variously, evidently perjures, since it is not right to consider words simply, but should serve not verbis but intentioni*. Which words are cited in canon law (c. 22 q. 5 c. 12), where the *Gloss* clearly notes: *God does not accept an oath as does he, namely, in whose mind he thinks, that is, in which is sworn, but rather, as he who swears understands, when to the receiver he offers not from within, but from what is brought forth freely*.

**When on the contrary** the words of the oath are not ambiguous, neither in signification agreed on for themselves nor in common use of men, nor have any but a single sense — then in the sense so brought forth we ought to use them, nor be permitted to twist them to a hidden thought of soul: since to lie is not licit for us; but if we speak otherwise with words than we conceive with mind, we lie. Everyone therefore who swears, to this attends: that he speak what is true; and as in an oath *no perfidy is fitting*, so also in words *no simulation should be*.

**Against this doctrine bifariously** the *scholastics* trip. For some among them think that though the words of the oath be not ambiguous in signification, yet the oath can without lie hold a hidden mental cogitation, in the true sense of speech, if only *hidden* to him to whom the oath is made, otherwise it may be understood. Thus they think it licit for anyone under oath, to redeem his life, to promise money to robbers, though in soul he holds none to give — because tacitly he says with himself: *I will give, if I owe*. To an adulteress they permit under oath to affirm to her husband, that she has not committed adultery — with the tacit cogitation, namely, *what should be shown to man*.

But this doctrine is impious, which gives to men license to lie. For nothing could be so heinous which by a lie cannot be freed, if it were licit to insert some falseness at our arbitrement. Who could not swear, that he had not seen or heard something, so as to deceive another? Speech is the character of the mind; with which if we do not respond, we are lying. If then the oath supervenes, it becomes perjury.

Then some think, *the words of the oath can be ambiguous* if the true sentence is held in the mind, without peril of perjury — namely if a priest is asked about what in sacred confession he has heard. Now to this question we respond as follows: to a priest who has heard something in sacred confession, he is not held to respond, nor yet ought he to deny that he heard something, but he should say he did not hear — as a private person, but as a minister of Christ, to whom to reveal secrets of his Lord is not licit. Likewise about one's own crime, though outside judgment inquired, one should not swear he committed nothing evil, but he may decline the oath and refer the cognition of the cause to its own judge. An adulteress convicted in her own conscience of the crime should not deny it through such oath, though not asked in place and time — but rather refuse the oath. For though verbally sometimes it is licit to simulate and deceive the curious inquirers, oaths admit no simulation, since they are made with invocation of God, whose name is not to be profaned.

### Case VIII. Whether oaths which impede offices of piety, charity, and the public good are to be observed?

**Respondeo.** To this no one is bound. For levity it is to swear what one cannot and ought not to perform. Whatever we ought not promise, we cannot even swear: therefore oaths must be made by those who are free from affections. For many out of anger, impatience, fear, swear things which repent them afterwards to be told.

If then someone under whatever affect surprised, has sworn things which are against piety and offices of charity, and which impede the public good in any way — to render such things he is not held, as if one swore he would not give alms, would not go to the temple, would not lend, nor be a surety, nor share his art with anyone. If one swore he would not undertake some public office — all these pertain to rash oaths, in which is great abuse of the divine name, and just as they should not have been made, so if made, they do not bind the one swearing to keep them: for a promise per se illicit cannot be confirmed by oath. As the jurisconsults speak (*l. 15 ff. de conditio. instit.*): *acts which wound piety, our reputation, and generally against good morals, are not to be believed we can do*; and *De pactis, pacts which are against laws, constitutions, or good morals, are held for nothing*. But oaths ought not to be a bond of iniquity, nor should justice, love of neighbor, and public commodity be neglected.

### Case IX. If one swore something *per se* indifferent, whether such an oath is null?

**Respondeo.** A thing merely indifferent is that which is neither good nor evil in itself, and which is not necessary but can be otherwise than it turns out. Just as we said above of vows (*Casus VI* of the preceding chapter): so here it is to be held, a thing which is merely indifferent falls not under oath. For rashly one would swear he will contract no friendship with someone, will not enter a certain house, without just cause.

But if that thing has some *ratio of good* under itself, an oath about it made obliges in conscience: as if one swore he would avoid the conversation of some man, lest he be seduced by him.

But when the thing is *merely indifferent*, under which no good can lie — as when one swears he will touch something with the right rather than the left — it is *levity* to promise such things, much more to confirm the promise by oath.

### Case X. What law, if one swore he would do something for a bad end?

**Respondeo.** Distinguish between what is *per se* evil, and between the *good* which arises from evil. A thing *per se* evil is not to be promised, nor confirmed by oath. Example: if one swears he will commit theft, adultery, or homicide; that he will take part in a war which he knows to be unjust — the oath is rash and illicit, therefore he is not bound to hold what he swore.

But another reasoning is if one swears he will *do something useful and pleasing to God*, if he shall have returned safely from war (even iniquitous), if he shall have taken up offspring from adultery, if in theft, homicide, and similar delict he shall have remained safe. Such oath he is held to perform. For not that in unjustly warring, in adultering, in stealing, &c. he sins — but *liberation* from war, *reception* of offspring, *preservation* in perils during time of delict, is not an evil thing, but a benefit received from God, for which in that name something of gratitude — even with oath, if need be — we can promise.

### Case XI. Whether an oath about a small and light thing binds the conscience to observance?

**Respondeo.** Scholastics disagree on this. Some *distinguish* an insignificant thing, insofar as it is *part of the whole and not part of another*, but *per se* it is integral. In the first respect they say: if it is not performed, though it was under sworn promise, one is not bound in mortal sin but only in venial — since not from the whole but from part is the oath violated. As if one swore he would recite daily the seven *penitential Psalms*, and in reciting omitted only one verse. In the second respect they say: if what is even the smallest thing sworn is not performed, mortal sin is committed, since the subject of the oath is indeed the smallest per se, but integral and total matter of the oath — as if one swore he would give a *pear-apple*, nor gave it. In this sentence is *Cajetan*.

*Others hold* that mortal sin is never committed, though the oath were adhibited in a promise of the smallest thing not observed — but the one swearing is indeed bound, but by a light bond and obligation. In which sentence is *Sotus* (lib. 8 *De just.* q. 1 art. 5), *Navarrus in manuali* c. 12 n. 20 and 40, *Azorius* lib. 11 *instit. moral.* c. 4.

But this disputation arises from the false distinction of *mortal* and *venial* sin. For they think certain sins, which they call small and least, are by their nature worthy of venial pardon — which is false.

**No sin can be so small** that it does not merit the wrath of God and eternal malediction, since every sin is *transgression of the law*, to which God threatens malediction (Deut 27:26). *Venial* sins are said to be those which are done by the regenerate, unwillingly and with resistance, and which therefore obtain pardon and are not imputed, since the person is in grace with God. If therefore an oath is licit — even if the thing sworn should seem the smallest, provided it is honest and can fall under oath — the violation of it wounds conscience and merits malediction.

Whence let no one easily swear in any small matter, as that he will give a pear-apple to a boy, a nut, or something similar — but if he has sworn, since the thing is honest in itself and possible, to observe it he is bound not by some light obligation, but equally as in graver things — since every oath is made with invocation of the divine name, which must be profaned in no thing.

### Case XII. Whether oaths extorted by force or fear bind in conscience, so that one is held to observe them?

**Respondeo.** Intricate is this question, on which jurists dispute differently from theologians, and not all theologians agree in decision. We, cutting off disputations, will see how conscience in this part may be consulted.

All oaths *about a licit and possible thing, made with election by those who know and are not plainly unwilling*, are to be performed, unless he to whom the sworn promise was made spontaneously remits the thing promised. For such oath is made with invocation of the divine name, which is not to be profaned.

**No Papal or ecclesiastical dispensation avails here.** For the Pope cannot make the Word of God irritating.

But an oath extorted by fear or force about a licit thing, when it is made with some election by those not plainly unwilling — since no one can be *compelled* to swear itself, and one has still liberty either of suffering some damage, or of freeing himself from damage by a sworn promise of the illicit thing — therefore to render what he swore he is bound, lest through him the name of the Lord be profaned.

*Example*: someone falls among robbers, promises them by oath a certain sum of money, that he may not be killed. Here if it had been only a simple promise of money, it could become irritating and he would not be bound to pay, since it was made to a man who inflicted fear and extorted the promise against good morals. But since the oath acceded, he is bound to pay — (1) because the oath was made to God, whose name is not to be profaned; (2) it was not made simply by the unwilling but is a *mixed action*, in which something is voluntary, since between paying money and redeeming life he chooses that which is better, and to redeem his life he promises money by oath; (3) the thing promised is possible and private, to which religion and truth should always be preferred; (4) by this performance of the oath something good is promoted for the commonwealth, insofar as some member of the commonwealth is preserved — which though it be with some detriment of a man, that detriment is at least private, to which the life of a man should always be preferred. Thus reason both political and theological persuades the performance of the oath.

Which the more prudent among gentiles also well understood — those who in similar oaths, even extorted, remained constant. Therefore *Cicero* laudably commemorates *Regulus* (lib. 3 *officior.*), who constantly kept what he had sworn even to enemies compelling him under fear.

*If thou sayest*: by this reasoning piracies and rapines are stabilized, if thou pay to robbers what they by force extorted. Not so at all: neither by the sworn promise did *Regulus* approve robbers, nor did he approve of them by his fact, but he redeemed his own life by paying what he promised by oath, that if he could resist the robbers and prevent public damage, if he could bring the deed to the magistrate to punish. Therefore of certain right it is, that oaths which are against God and love of neighbor, and offer occasion to evil and illicit things, are to be rescinded — since oaths have all their force from the Word of God, and where this is adverse, they have no force or power of compelling.

### Case XIII. To what extent therefore may oaths be revoked with safe conscience? What if I have sworn a rash thing, or if my fact should not be revealed to the magistrate?

**Respondeo.** Difficult it is in this genus to establish something certain. Safer nevertheless it seems, if a rash thing not be observed, and no small ones be revealed to the magistrate, unless it be a public work — for none, that is against God, obliges. Therefore who so retracts an oath, let him not think himself made perjured, since that promise has no place of a true oath — whence commonly it is said, *break faith to the ill-promised*.

And this retraction of the oath *has place the more*, when one has sworn something illicit either from love toward others, or from an affect of anger — as *Herod* out of love for the dancing girl by an oath promised her the *head of John the Baptist* (Matt 14:9), which he should have rescinded. So *David*, out of anger and desire of vengeance, swore the destruction of the house of *Nabal* — but admonished by *Abigail*, he did not perform it, giving thanks to God that through this woman he was withdrawn from an evil purpose (1 Sam 25). Whence *Augustine* (Serm. 1 *De decoll. Ioann.*) writes: *David swore rashly, but did not fulfill it, with greater piety*. So *David* punished *Shimei*, who had cursed him — that he would not die (2 Sam 19:23) — and yet later he retracted this oath, commanding *Solomon* not to absolve the guilty (1 Kgs 2:9), since that oath was made from precipitation, in a matter less honest. For the Lord in the Law forbade: *Thou shalt not revile the gods, nor curse the ruler of thy people.* (Exod 22:28). To a man therefore federately transgressing this law, life ought not to have been promised — therefore what David *inconsiderately* swore, *justly and prudently* he retracted.

Then in respect of *matter*, one also swears evilly if the oath fights with the salutary laws and institutes of some commonwealth. Such oath is to be rescinded, since we are bound to the observation of laws made by the magistrate (Rom 13:1, 5), where *he is said to resist the ordinance of God, who resists the magistrate*.

Third, when the thing sworn is impossible and illicit, though at first licit and possible it seemed — as when someone binds himself by vow to perpetual celibacy, but afterwards feels he does not have the gift of continence — the promise, though made with oath, does not bind.

**2.** One swears *evilly* in respect of *persons* who cannot swear — as boys, madmen, fools, phrenetics, or those who otherwise cannot use judgment of reason either on account of age or some defect. Such are also those who live under others' power — children, slaves, women, &c. — who if with oath, unwilling to those subject, to something bind themselves, they are not bound but ought to rescind, by the precept of the Lord (Num 30:4), even if this be done under pretext of cult and religion. Therefore in the *Council of Gangra* c. 15, anathema is pronounced on children who *forsake their parents under pretext of divine cult, and do not render due reverence to them*.

### Case XIV. Whether oaths made from an *error* of the fact-of-oath about the promised matter bind

**Respondeo.** If about a licit and possible thing, they oblige, in whatever they are ignorant. For not the mind of the one deceiving, but the intention of the one swearing is to be attended. Example of this occurs in Josh 9, where the *Gibeonites* by imposture put on Joshua and the princes of the people, giving out that they were of a very distant country, and requesting peace with him: *whom Joshua and the princes of the people admitted to a treaty, and swore to them*. Afterwards, when their imposture was known, since the Gibeonites had been commanded by God to be exterminated, some of the Israelites wanted the oath rescinded — but they held that it should be observed, even to their loss, only with this condition: that they should be as *quasi-slaves* of the Israelites, so long as they should be preserved. Therefore Joshua and the princes withstood the people, who thought the Gibeonites could be killed by right of oath, but they responded: *we have sworn to them in the name of the Lord God of Israel; and now we cannot touch them* (Josh 9:19). Moreover, by miracle God confirmed this thing to please him: for Joshua fighting for the Gibeonites, *the sun stood at the middle of the sky until the end of the battle* (Josh 10:12). *E contrario*, when *Saul* after about a hundred years had killed some of the Gibeonites, for that perjury Israel was afflicted with famine grievously, and seven sons of Saul were suspended in gallows and removed from the middle (2 Sam 21:1).

### Case XV. What is perjury, and how many kinds are there of it?

**Respondeo.** *Perjury*, in the definition of *Isidore* (which stands in canon law c. 22 q. 5), is *a lie confirmed by oath*. Where some doubt, whether perjury is a lie, since a lie is only in *words* — perjuries however are done also in *facts*, as when one does not do what he swore he would do.

But in every perjury there is a lie, if not in words, at least in facts. If one swears something to be true, which nevertheless holds otherwise, *perjury* is joined with a lie in *words*. If one swears he will do something, which he does not do, *perjury* is joined with a lie in *facts*.

Every oath demands *truth* and *justice*, of which if one is desired, *perjury* is committed. Truth is in *words* or in *cogitations*, when the one swearing thinks his words are true. Justice is in *facts*, which either should have been performed and are omitted, or should have been omitted and are performed.

**Whence a threefold way of perjury**: **(1)** when one swears things to be true which he probably knew were false; **(2)** when one by oath promises something, but never thought of performing it, but rather constituted himself to deceive; **(3)** when one swears things which are honest and licit, and even when swearing thinks of performing, yet does not perform.

Hither some refer, when one swears he will do an *illicit thing*, and does it also — but he is not indeed perjured, since he does what he swore. He is *similar to a perjurer*, since he abuses the divine name and violates justice, if he does not perform what he swore, he commits perjury.

**Note**, however, that for *perjury properly said* a malicious proposition of deceiving is required, and not from a proposition, but from ignorance, incogitance, or seduced by another, or transgressing the laws, may be seen. Others refer to perjury also when one does not perform what he swore *by creatures*, in which sentence is *Azorius* (lib. 11 *instit. moral.* c. 6). But *perjury is opposed to oath* — as therefore oath by creatures does not bind, since it is illicit, as we proved above, so no perjury can be given, if such oath is not performed. If however one has sworn by false gods, whom he thinks are true, if he does not perform what he swore, he commits perjury.

*Also to perjury refer some* when one swears without judgment — that is, rashly and lightly. But properly speaking it is not perjury, since there is no lie in words or in facts; but on account of the abuse of the divine name it can be reduced to perjury. Thus, who swore he would obey the laws, and from a fixed proposition and given work he does not obey — by that very fact he is perjured. But if he submits himself to the penalties which have been established for transgressors of laws, he is free from perjury, since oaths bind to the law, and law obliges either to obedience or to penalty. But by that very fact, when he sustains penalties, he is judged not to perjure from proposition, but either from ignorance or incogitance, or seduced by another.

### Case XVI. How atrocious is perjury, and how carefully should it be fled?

**Respondeo.** Great is the improbity of many, to whom nor is faith, nor is anything sacred kept in his faithful pact: who neglect all right and honesty, so they may obtain power. Trite is that of *Euripides* in mouth and hand:

> *For the sake of ruling faith may be broken, but preserve justice in the rest.*

No less is the *temerity of many*, who make it a light matter to perjure themselves: therefore they easily perjure themselves and gladly deceive, either because they do not care about perjury, or because they impose some *species of right* on the fraud.

The *causes therefore are to be held* which make *perjury detestable*, so that all who fear God, and wish to have a tranquil conscience, may flee it.

**(1)** *We have the express prohibition of God* (Zech 5:3): *every one that swears falsely shall be cut off, and every thief in like manner*. And (Wis 8:17): *And let none of you imagine evil in your hearts against his neighbour; and love no false oath: for all these are things that I hate, saith the LORD.* (Zech 8:17). *And ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God: I am the LORD.* (Lev 19:12). He therefore who loves God's mandates, rightly hates perjury.

**(2)** *Perjurers are excluded from the kingdom of heaven*, since *he shall stand in the holy place who swears not deceitfully to his neighbor* (Ps 15, 4). *Malediction* shall come *into the house of the swearing in my name deceitfully* (Zech 5:4). *A swift witness against perjurers, saith the Lord* (Mal 3:5).

**(3)** *Examples of punished perjury are most many.* Israelites, not keeping what they swore to the *Gibeonites*, are punished by famine, and *seven sons of Saul are hanged* (2 Sam 21). *Zedekiah*, perjured, is taken by the King of Babylon and blinded (2 Chr 36) — which the *Lord* had predicted through the prophet: *because he despised the oath, that he might dissolve the treaty, he shall not escape* (Ezek 17:15–16). *Alcimus* the pontiff dies of apoplexy for perjury (1 Macc 9:54). *Menelaus* the perjured in the very place where he had killed *Onias* the priest, was killed (2 Macc 4:38). Similar examples of punished perjury are read in histories: *Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.* (Exod 20:7).

**(4)** *Perjury is a heavier sin than homicide*, since the perjurer sins against the first table of the Decalogue, violates piety and religion, abuses the divine name, opts God as his own most just and most powerful judge as avenger — and thus twice sins, at least since, while he deceives, he becomes worthy of the penalty. But it is undoubted, how great a sin is *homicide*, which by the sentence of God renders man subject to temporal and eternal penalties (Gen 9:5–6; Gal 5:20; 1 John 3:15).

**(5)** *How much perjury displeases God, he has attested by certain prodigies even in the gentile world*. In marvelous ways sometimes perjured men, when otherwise unable to be detected, have been divinely made known and punished — of which see *Alexander ab Alexandro* (lib. 6 *Genial. dier.* c. 10). Of *Palici* — twin gods from the *Aetnaean Zeus of Sicily* — *Macrobius* (lib. 5 *Saturnal.* c. 19) records: there was a place there religious, brief but profound, always shining, at which the *Sicilians* were wont to give their oaths; and those who chaste and without wounded crime swore, drank unhurt and unblemished — but those who against the religion of the oath figured had broken faith, were guilty of the crime, were plunged into the lake. Whence *Vergil* (Aen. 9): *Sympetha around a fulmen, where is a fat and placable altar of Palici*.

*Aristotle* (in *De mirabilibus auscultationibus*) recalls of the fountain *Acadinus*, which flows next to *Palnos* in *Sicily*, that oath-tablets inscribed with the swearing — if truly sworn — floated on top and were not affected by livor; if perjured, they were immediately snatched into the deep, and appeared no more. In *Sardinia* certain water-springs there were, in which if the perjured were immersed, they were deprived of their eyes; those who had rightly sworn, dipped in these waters, saw more clearly (see Solinus 10).

Near a *Tyanaean* fountain *Philostratus* (*Life of Apollonius* lib. 1 c. 4) records was calm and sweet to taste, but caused *livid and vomiting pustules* on the perjured. *Herodotus* (lib. 6) and *Pliny* (lib. 21 c. 10) mention *Stygian waters*, and many others, which to the perjured were always noxious. Whence *Ovid* (in *Ibin*) calls Stygian water *perjuratam*. Of a *specus of Palemon at Corinth*, that perjurers could not enter unpunished, *Pausanias* is author (in *Corinth.* lib. 2). Thus even nature seems to avert the perjured.

**(6)** *Gentiles taught by the law of nature*, how great a sin it was to perjure oneself, afflicted the perjured with the gravest penalties. *Cicero* (lib. 2 *De legibus*, art.): *let the penalty of perjury be divine — destruction; human — the disgrace of violated oath*. Among the *Indi*, whoever is caught false and convicted of perjury has the last joints of hands and feet cut off. Among the *Scythians* the penalty of perjury is amputation of the head (Strabo lib. 15). Of the *Egyptians* Diodorus Siculus writes (lib. 2 c. 1): *the perjured are punished with capital penalty, as those who are held by a double crime — those who violate piety toward God, and destroy faith among men, the greatest bond of human society*.

**(7)** *Christians punish perjury with infamy.* For by canon law all who confirm a lie by oath, or do not keep sworn faith, are pronounced infamous by the judge's sentence (see *c. finibus*). The canons impose a further penalty on the perjured (in c. *quicunque* in 6 q. 1): they are penalized with a *40-day* fast on bread and water, and *seven following years' penance*. And *from giving testimony they are excluded* (in c. *praedicandum* c. 2 q. 1). To perjury is imposed such penalty as is owed to adultery and homicide, and the rest of capital crimes. *A cleric detected in perjury*, according to the canons, is *deposed* (as is in *c. cum sinces.* et *c. ab homine*).

According to civil laws the *perjurer* is not infamous in the *assertoric* oath, but in the *promissory* one — as *Baldus* teaches (*l. Lucius ff. de fide*) — they are marked *infamous*, especially if it be publicly and solemnly performed. Also they are extra-judicially *infamous*, who commit perjury to another's injury (*l. si major*). Established by all these is the atrocity of this delict, since always by divine and human laws it has been judged worthy of the gravest penalty. Whence by all to whom the favor of God and of men is dear, chastely first and last it must be shunned.

### Case XVII. In what cases can it happen that a sworn promise does not bind?

**Respondeo.** We are not treating here of the *assertoric* oath, which properly is not said to bind — for obligation is of promise, not of assertion. But in the *promissory* oath work must always be given, that what we swore we may render — for it leans on double virtue: *truth* and *faith*; and thus twice sins the one who does not perform: (1) he is a liar; (2) he is perfidious and infidel. Yet some cases can arise in which a sworn promise, though otherwise valid, does not oblige (of which disputes *Aquinas* IIa IIae q. 89 art. 8; *Cajetan* on the same q. 89 art. 1; *Navarrus in manuali* c. 11 n. 7).

**(1)** *If the thing promised is illicit, useless, or impossible* — for it falls not under the oath, nor is it presumed anyone had earlier sworn it. What therefore is against divine right sworn, the one swearing is not held to perform. So *Herod* swore to give the dancing-girl whatever she asked (Matt 14:7); but when she sought *the head of John the Baptist*, he was not bound to give it, since the thing was illicit — even if he had not promised her; for he was contradicted, when he *saddened at the petition* (v. 9).

**(2)** *If the status of things or persons changes*, so the one swearing according to the judgment of the prudent would not have willed that event to comprehend — which can be judged from circumstances. For as *Seneca* says (lib. 4 *De beneficiis* c. 34): *always he does, who what he promises is required to do, requires that all things immutable remain: else the one making the promise is not a liar in what he promised, since he promised what he had in mind, from the intellectual conditions understood. Nor is he unfaithful, not fulfilling what he promised, since the same conditions did not remain.* Thus *Paul* the Apostle is not mendacious, that he did not come to *Corinth* as he promised — for impediments came which moved his purpose (2 Cor 1).

**(3)** *When oaths are mutual, and from one part what was promised is not performed*, then the other part is not held to stand by the promise, but can use compensation — for the oath seems made with this condition, *provided the other also has stood by his promise*. Here holds that saying: *frangenti fidem, fides frangatur eidem*. For that oath mutual is always presumed made with this condition, if by turn the other also stands by the promised.

**(4)** *When something was promised for a cause* which was supposed to be, but is not — as if thou hast sworn thou wilt do something because thou hopest to obtain some benefit, but nevertheless thou dost not obtain it — then to fulfill the promise thou art not bound, since that condition was tacitly included in the oath, if the benefit was obtained. But if the condition is not implemented, the promise, though sworn, ceases to oblige.

### Case XVIII. Whether men have the power of relaxing oaths?

**Respondeo.** Here also is not the question of the *assertoric* oath, in which relaxation has no place — but of the promissory, as *Aquinas* admonishes (IIa IIae q. 89 art. 9), and *he who has a conscience* dares not easily perform this: for the *vinculum of oath is of natural right*, which can be relaxed by the authority of no man.

But to the *Roman Pontiff* whatever he wishes is licit: for he dispenses in oaths, absolves from them, commutes them, relaxes them at will. Hence it happens that he absolves subjects from oaths of their magistrate, rescinds treaties of kings and princes, when he sees it useful for the *Roman See*.

Which *Martinus Becanus* indeed denies in the *Appendix disputationis obedientiae Christianae mag. exam. propos. 2*, and yet forced by the truth, at once admits it, when he denies that *the Pontiff can dispense in contracts of princes and kings of Christians*; but adds, *unless necessity of spiritual good presses*. It is conceded therefore that the Pope can dispense, if urgent necessity of *spiritual good* is present — that is, when it is seen to be for the increment or utility of the *Roman Church*. For this is that urgent necessity in spiritual things.

This power of dispensing in oaths some attribute to the Pontiff in those things in which the relaxation of *vows* is reserved to him. Others contend that bishops have the ordinary power of relaxing every oath, and nothing is reserved to the Roman Pontiff — which contention thou seest in *Azorius* lib. 11 *instit.* c. 9. Whence from that *feigned power and dominion*, which they attribute to the Pope over the consciences of men, flows this his dispensing in oaths at will. For much has been exquisitely devised by our ancestors, than the *religion of the oath* — with no other bond stricter to bind fidelity our ancestors willed us to be, which even *Cicero* recognized (in his books *De officiis*), where he sets forth the example of the Roman consul *Regulus*, whom neither *fatherland*, nor *parents*, nor his own *love* could retain, but that he should return to the enemy at the given faith, even to the most cruel *Punic tortures*.

If therefore *without just cause*, or at least the pretext of some necessity, oaths are absolved by the Pope or someone else, that absolution is false, and *sins* he who seeks it and grants it. But if a just cause is present, there is no need of dispensation of the Pope or bishops, but anyone is held to retract what he unjustly promised, according to the vulgar saying: *break faith to the ill-promised*.

Just cause is when *turpitude or impossibility* is in the sworn oath, so that the oath cannot be preserved without peril of salvation or honesty.

If it is doubted whether an oath has place or not, there is no need of the arbitrament of the Pope, but of a judge — ecclesiastical or political, according as the matter of the oath is ecclesiastical or political — the judgment can be recognized and recognized either imposed on the one who swore that he might observe, or on the one to whom he swore, so as to render the oath judged.

If the one swearing is not of his own right, he to whom he swore can rescind the oath, since it is tacitly understood to have been made with this condition, *if it please the superior* — again the Roman Pontiff has no business here.

If someone swore to injure another and pledged something illicit, before the one to whom he swore holds it ratified, no other man can relax it — just as no one can take from another a right acquired. If however he to whom he swore does not wish it kept, then he remits, and frees the swearer from obligation — for anyone can concede from his own, and pardon the debt owed to himself.

These about *the relaxation of oaths* suffice: more the scholastics dispute, but nothing bears on our institute, which was to consult consciences, not indulge in litigations.

### Case XX. What things by way of conclusion are to be observed in oaths?

**Respondeo.** Of these by way of conclusion a few things I will subjoin:

**1.** *Puberes* are not admitted to such oath, as is prescribed in *c. pueri* 12 q. 5. *Recantants*, *convicted perjurers* also — priests also are not held to swear before the civil magistrate, as is contained in *c. non liceat* 22 q. 5 — not even when they are produced as witnesses.

*When however a priest's testimony is needed*, before a bishop or consistory this is done — and this happens especially in these cases: if by defect of other proofs someone loses his fortune and things, if the common good of faith and religion cannot otherwise be arrived at, if the common salvation of the commonwealth so demands, if one is compelled to purge himself from note of infamy, &c.

**2.** Oaths must be given before a *competent judge*.

**3.** The competent judge sometimes can compel to an oath, if a witness by hatred or fear withdraws himself from giving testimony, nor otherwise can truth be sought.

**4.** Oaths in trials should be *on the fast*, as is in *c. honestum* 22 q. 5 — which yet is more required *ex aequo et bono* than from right and law.

**5.** To swearing he ought not to be compelled, whom the judge knows will swear falsely, or not observe the oath, though the one swearing be ready to swear, since no one ought to compel another to lie. This holds also when there is only a suspicion of perjury, though vehement. Therefore *Abbas Panormitanus* on *c. clericos* de habitat. clericorum judges, clerics should not be compelled to swear that they will dismiss their concubines. If however a *sufficient admonition* precedes from the judge, and disputes cannot be otherwise ended, and the one about to swear is prompt, and severely with sacred things attests his truth-speaking — then on account of at least suspicion of perjury he is not to be excluded from the oath.

**6.** He who is *marked with infamy*, or with disgrace of some crimes, cannot swear that he is free from these crimes, on the ground that in *confession* he was absolved from them. For we are absolved through *penitence* in the judgment of God, but the authority of the judge is preserved, who can still damn and punish these delicts.

**7.** *Licit is the oath of calumny*, if from the judge, at the instance of the other litigating party, it is deferred.

Now *the oath of calumny* is when one swears that *he not from cause of quarrel or maliciously intends litigation against others*, and five things are required for this: (i) that the litigator estimate he intends a just suit; (ii) that when asked by the judge he not dissimulate the truth; (iii) that knowingly he not adduce false proofs; (iv) that in fraud he not prolong the suit or cause; (v) that he swear he has promised nothing to anyone, nor will he promise anything thereafter for cause of his suit, unless what laws and rights permit, &c.

*So much of oaths.*

— ❦ —

## Chapter X. On Cases of Conscience Concerning the Hearing of the Divine Word

*De casibus conscientiae circa auditum verbi divini.*

The exercises of divine cult are to be considered according to the virtues of the *second* and *third* precepts of the Decalogue, because chief among them is placed the *sanctification of God's name and Word*. Of the second precept hitherto we have treated, so far as sufficed. Now we come to *the third*, which is to *sanctify the sabbath* — that is, to be occupied in sacred things, which have their ordination from the mouth of God himself. In the first place occurs the *hearing of the Divine Word*, by which the Sabbath of all is most sanctified. Concerning it fall not a few cases of conscience — as much from the side of the ministers as from the side of the auditors.

Of the ministers of the Word we treated in the proper place; here it pleases now, the Lord willing, seriously to consider what things chiefly are necessary for pacifying the conscience of the *auditors*.

### Case I. Whether hearing of the divine Word, or public sermons, may be intermitted

**Respondeo.** *Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils;* (1 Tim 4:1). Among these are those *fanatics* who lead men away from the Word to *colloquy with God* — as the Anabaptists and today certain others are, at their own great peril and that of others whom their author *Weigelius* has drawn along. These *contemn the public ministry of the Word*, and to their private speculations, dreams, and visions ascribe more, thinking that they have here the foundation of their business. They wrest what is said in Scripture, that *all shall be taught of God* (Isa 54:13) — but there is noted the *efficient cause of the profit* which comes from Scripture: when all are said to be taught of God, but yet there is not excluded the *divine ministry* by which he treats with us, to which he attributes great efficacy (Isa 55:11; John 6:44). And they wrest the words of John: *ye have no need that any teach you, for the anointing teacheth you all things* (1 John 2:27) — but here the *public ministry* is not impugned, but rather the institution of the Holy Spirit (which is ordinarily done through the ministry) is opposed to *false doctors*, who were seducing the flock. That the Apostle wished the *pious auditors* to keep themselves *free* from these, is what the Apostle wished.

**Against these** the mind is to be munited by certain arguments, that the *public hearing of the divine Word* cannot with good conscience be intermitted by any of the pious.

**(1)** *Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.* (Exod 20:8) — which chiefly consists in the hearing of the Word and the use of the sacraments. We are recalled from dreams and visions to the *law and the testimony*. Here pertains the Apostolic precept: *let the word of God dwell in you plenteously in all wisdom* (Col 3:16); and Wisd 6:1 *hear, O kings, and understand*; and Sir 6:34 *if thou incline thine ear, thou shalt receive doctrine, and if thou love to hear, thou shalt be wise*. And lest this be taken of *private instruction*, the places are to be observed by which we are excited *to public gatherings in temples* — where we are bidden *to enter into the gates of the Lord* (Ps 100:2), *to come up to the house of the God of Jacob* (Isa 2:3); where *God himself addresses us*: *Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, and I will testify against thee: I am God, even thy God.* (Ps 50:7). *Let us not forsake our assembling together, as some do* (Heb 10:25). These voices are as it were *bells*, by which we are invited to the auscultation of the Word in the temple. Let us therefore excite ourselves with David: *I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD.* (Ps 122:1).

**(2)** *The hearing of the divine Word is required of us by highest necessity.* For upon this hearing depends *our salvation* in the ordinary mode: *faith is from hearing, and hearing by the Word of God* (Rom 10:14–17). In the name of Christians we cannot rejoice, without the hearing of the Word. For *my sheep hear my voice*, says the good Shepherd, John (10:27); and *he who is of God, heareth the Word of God* (John 8:47 with 1 John 4:6).

**(3)** *There also accedes the incredible utility* which we have from the hearing of the Word: *blessed are they who hear the Word of God and keep it*, says the Savior (Luke 11:28). And that beatitude extends itself widely. For the hearing of the Word *conjoins man with God*: for when he reads (and thus also when thou hearest), *God speaks to thee; when thou prayest, thou speakest to God* — says *Augustine* on Psalm 85. *The law of the Lord illumines the eyes* (Ps 19:9); *it consoles the afflicted* (Ps 119:50); *it kindles the love of God in hearts* (John 14:21). It makes sons and friends of God: for *he who hears the Word and keeps it, comes to the Father* (John 6:45). It is the food of the soul, which preserves us unto life eternal, and frees from eternal death — as Christ says (John 8:51): *if any keep my Word, he shall not see death for ever*. Of all these benefits he is deprived, who neglects the hearing of the divine Word.

**(4)** To this utility pertains also the *sanctity of the labor*, which in the auscultation of the divine Word is spent. For what can be more holy than to hear God speaking with us? — so that Christ himself called this labor *the best, and the only necessary* (Luke 10:42); on which words *Ambrose* writes (in Luc. lib. 7): *the study of divine reading is that which we should take up, which cannot be taken from us — not perfunctory but diligent hearing.
