And *Bernard* (Serm. 1 *In ramis palmarum*): *he who was a little one born, and first fought the array of the little ones, today no less excludes the little ones from grace, since neither is it uncongruous to piety nor difficult to his majesty, if by the supplement of grace he brings whatever nature does not yet permit as possible*.

[*Augustine* has also that memorable saying (Serm. 5 *De nativitate*): *to all of us this joyful message pertains, since Christ came for all; nor should any be excluded, especially in the place where the fountains of joys are opened. Let the saint rejoice, since he receives remuneration; let the sinner rejoice, since he is invited to pardon; let the gentile rejoice, since he is sent to life. Exult, holy children, since a boy is born; exult, virgins, since a virgin has borne; exult, sanctified ones, since he is your justifier; exult, weak and sick, since a savior is born; exult, captives, since a redeemer is born; exult, servants, since a Lord is born; exult, freemen, since a Liberator is born; exult, all Christians, since it is the birth of CHRIST.*]

Thus he is said to *bear the sins of the whole world*, and is called *Savior of the whole world*: from the world however infants are not excluded. And although through the ordinary means of consequent faith (through which the Savior of the world is apprehended) they are destitute, yet God does not lack faith, whom he knows extraordinarily to work in them — as we have shown above by given examples.

**Here fourthly pertains the examples**, of which the Scripture testifies, that *in the womb of the mother they were donated by the grace of God*. *David* certainly testifies (Ps 51:5) *he was conceived in sins*, yet confesses (Ps 22:10) *from the womb of the mother thou art my God*, and (Ps 139:13): *thou hast possessed my reins, thou hast received me from the womb of my mother*, &c. To *Jeremiah* says the Lord: *Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.* (Jer 1:5). Such projection into God, and sanctification, cannot be without faith. These examples do not show what ordinarily God does in all, yet teach *what he can and is wont to do*, even without ordinary means, since he is a most free agent, and does not so bind himself to certain means, that in the case of necessity, in defect of those means, he cannot otherwise operate.

**Fifthly**, examples are not lacking in *terms terminating*, as they say — namely of those who, before they had obtained the sacrament of initiation, yet had a good hope of their salvation. Among these were all those infants and adults in the primitive Church who, before they received baptism, were made *martyrs*, and to damn all these were of extreme temerity. Let pious parents cogitate therefore, that their infant also is *seed of Abraham* to whom the promise is made — therefore God will have care of him, that he perish not, deprived at most of the ordinary medium of salvation. For God has attached to himself in no place the grace of God to his glory: and where two or three are gathered in the name of Christ, there is the Church, and in its midst is CHRIST (Matt 18:20).

*All those infants and adults deprived* — the *Israelites among the murmurers*, who by God's command have not received his temple, and the flesh of no one damns them; those *Hebrew males*, who by Pharaoh's command as soon as born were exposed to death (Exod 1); *the infant Israelites*, who in the time of *Antiochus* the killer perished on the sabbath (1 Macc 1); *the infants of Bethlehem*, that first flower of NT martyrs, who by Herod's command were extinguished (Matt 2:16) — all these to make heirs of damnation, or at least excluded from the sight and glory of God, would be of great tyranny and impiety. Hither refers to certain, the infant that David begot from adultery, who on the seventh day (which we understand of the seventh from birth), died — before he could according to the law be circumcised (2 Sam 12). Yet the parent does not doubt that he is saved, when he says (v. 23): *I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me* — that is, he hopes to see him in that other blessed world. Some also consider that if he could have been suddenly cured, before he was baptized by his father's care, when Job says: *he sleeps and rests in slumber* — as of the blessed is described (Job 3:13). Since therefore in place of circumcision baptism succeeded, the same can be the consolation of pious parents whose infants by celerity of time are defrauded of baptism, not by the will of the parents.

**Finally**, that God not only *has been able*, but also *has willed* in infants in the case of necessity to work faith and regeneration, from the following arguments it is established:

**(1)** That to those indeed who have been baptized and believe, salvation is attributed, and when of the damned it must be said, no mention is made of the non-baptized, but of the unbelievers, as in Mark 16:16: *he who has not believed shall be damned*.

**(2)** God does not will that anyone perish, but wills that all be saved (2 Pet 3:9). *God wills all men to be saved* (1 Tim 2:4); and *of infants his will is that we not have contempt* (Matt 18:14). Since however those who do not believe must necessarily perish, it must not be doubted, that to them extraordinarily he bestows faith.

**(3)** For certain are the promises of God concerning the hearing of prayers, especially those which by two or three conjoined in Christ's name are made (Matt 18:19,20,22).

Since therefore an infant is still borne in the womb, let the parents acknowledge the *gift of God*, by which they have blessed him with their marriage, giving thanks that he has dignified them with the illustrious honor of *fathers* and *mothers*, let them avoid all external things by which some detriment can be inflicted on the infants in the womb: above all, however, with ardent prayers let them invoke God, that he himself may have care of the work of his own hands, guarding the infant in the womb, and on account of his most beloved Son the *Infant*, cleanse him from sins in which he was conceived, and receive him into the *covenant of grace*, and effectuate the *end of life eternal*, for which he was created.

**These prayers God will not permit to be idle**: for he himself mandated them, and he promised the hearing (Ps 50:15; Ps 65:3; Matt 18:19; John 16:23). Whence we have already heard, that *the Sacrament of Baptism is chief of those things by which infants are offered to the Lord*. Wherefore, when a father *dies* by *celerity of the time was prevented*, that he does not lose salvation by his faith — from which two-fold testimony of the fathers *Bernard* speaks (Ep. 77): *he plainly and evidently shows* (Saint Augustine) *that the faithful and one converted to the Lord, if he cannot but has contemned baptism, and cannot be deprived of baptism — hitherto he leans on two columns* (I speak of Augustine and Ambrose): *believe me, difficult it is that thou lookest back. With these, I say, either to err or to know I confess, believing myself, faith alone can save a man, when the desire to receive the sacrament: if however anticipating pious desire, or any other invincible thing obviated, see also, lest by chance on this account it be saved. For when he said, "he who has believed and been baptized, shall be saved," so cautiously and vigilantly he did not repeat: "he who has not been baptized" — but only "he who has not believed," he says, "shall be damned" — namely, indicating faith alone sometimes to suffice for salvation, but without it to suffice nothing*. In the same epistle *Bernard* writes: *the profitable will is imputed, where the fact is excluded by necessity*.

All these things, for tranquilizing the conscience of pious parents who by this case of their children are consternated, can suffice.

### Case IV. Concerning those who in the Papacy were baptized with other rites than those used among the orthodox, and though baptized in the Papist faith, are yet in adult age not addicted to that religion — if they later are anguished on this name, whether concerning their baptism they should doubt or not

**Respondeo.** When we treat of the truth of baptism, we should always distinguish its *substance* from its *ceremonies*. The substance is recognized from the words of institution — namely, that he be baptized in water in the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Ceremonies are either taken from the Apostles themselves, or added post-Apostolically in time. Those [Apostolic] the *Damascene* calls *Apostolic ecclesiastical ceremonies*. Apostolic are the prayers, thanksgivings, actions, and exhortations to the people: that of this kind ceremonies were used by the Apostles, is established from Acts 2:38 seqq. Ecclesiastical ones are either in themselves right (which commend the dignity and necessity of baptism, and render it more illustrious — pertaining to the doctrine of piety, and to the ornament and decor of the Church, serving edification — as is the triple sprinkling of water, the imposition of the name, the induction of the white garment, the confession of the infant made through the sponsors, exorcism, &c.); or *superstitious and inept*, joined moreover with impiety, having no solemn commonstrations, but similar to Egyptian rites, and *hieroglyphic-like* transform that action into a certain theatrical spectacle, and include some peculiar force and efficacy from the superstition of men — such are in the *baptism of the Papists* the *exorcisations of water*, chrism, adjuration of the demon (to which adjuration a certain force of expelling the demon is assigned), the taste of salt, the salivas by which the nose and ears of the one to be baptized are touched, unction on the breast or on the shoulders.

Concerning ceremonies in general, we should hold that *for the integrity and essence of baptism they are not necessary*, but should be held as *adiaphora*. For as *Lombard* speaks (lib. 4 sent. dist. 3): *the Word and element are of the substance of this sacrament, but others pertain to solemnity and are called sacramentals*.

Since however the administration of baptism is not to be a mute action, but the chief part of divine cult, it cannot lack all ceremonies whatsoever; where the best of all are those which either proceed from the Apostles, or from Apostolic men, and lack impiety and superstition.

If it should come about that anyone in the *Papacy* has been baptized with impious and superstitious ceremonies, one must yet distinguish the substance of baptism from its rites. The substance is *the Word of God*, the *element of water*, from which comes the *washing away of sins*, the *blessing of God*, the *entrance into the Church of God* — which *the doctrine of the Papacy* does not affect. Therefore its administration with impious and superstitious rites can *derogate nothing*.

**And although the infant is baptized from the intention of the priest into the Papist faith**, yet since the efficacy of the sacrament does not depend on the intention of the one baptizing, therefore there is no cause why the one who was baptized as an infant should doubt about the truth of his baptism, though in adult age he becomes alien from Papist doctrine. For he was baptized into the *faith of the Church* — not this or that particular Church, which can err, but the *Catholic* one, which professes the Apostolic faith — just as those who in the time of the Pharisees received the sacrament of *circumcision*, indeed from the intention of the Pharisees were admitted to circumcision *into the faith of the Pharisaic Church*, yet in truth were received into the *faith of the Israelite Church*, that is, into the *doctrine of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob their fathers*. They were circumcised into that people who were the peculium of God, from the ordination of God — of whom many in adult age *contradicted the Pharisaic doctrine*, among whom were *Zechariah*, *John*, *Simeon*, and *others*, as from the Evangelical history is established.

### Case V. Whether pious parents who live in a false Church can commit their children to those ministers, from whom in faith they dissent, to be baptized?

**Respondeo.** Better indeed would it be that the pious *should altogether abstain from cohabitation with the malignant*, following the counsel of the Lord: *depart from her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins* (Rev 18:4). But since civil conversation with them cannot altogether be avoided, nor in Scripture is it prohibited, otherwise we would have to depart from the world, as *Paul* speaks (1 Cor 5:10) — it sometimes happens that pious ones rightly informed in doctrine dwell among those who are penitently imbued either with *Antichristian* or with the leaven of some other heresy.

Among these therefore one must live so, that we not be polluted by their sacred rites, but the use of the Word and sacraments should be sought elsewhere in the assembly of the orthodox. Therefore if it can be done, even the baptism of infants should not be sought from heretics among whom we live, but in the vicinity we should seek *homodoxous* to our faith, to whom the infant may be committed.

**If however this cannot be had**, it must be considered whether the *particular church* in which we live is *in the substance of baptism* or not. In the substance of baptism err those who baptize either *not with water, but with some other liquor*, or *deny the article of the Trinity*: for these cannot baptize *in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit*. If any error is *in the substantials* of baptism, it should be considered whether it be *of the whole Church, or only of the minister baptizing*. If it is of the whole Church, as in the assemblies of the *Arians*, then from it baptism is not to be sought, and he who was there baptized should be held as *not baptized*, because he did not receive baptism according to the institution of Christ. But if the error is only of the minister, while the Church remains orthodox, and it must be occult (for if it were notorious, the orthodox Church without doubt would not tolerate such a minister) — then baptism administered by such a minister is *true and legitimate*, notwithstanding the error of the minister: **because the sacraments are of the whole Church, not of one or another person, and their efficacy does not depend on the faith of the minister, but on the institution of CHRIST, which he still uses**. And while that error of the minister is still occult, nothing obstructs, but the infants may be offered to him to be baptized. And if some particular Church has erred *in other than in principals* of things, but retains the substance of baptism integrally, though in certain rites she departs from the orthodox Church — from her ministers the baptism of our infants can be committed. Hence it happens that *baptized by Papists* and *Calvinists* we do not rebaptize, because these, though they differ from us in many things, retain the *article of the SS. Trinity*, and the substance of baptism which is administered in its name.

Since therefore no plenty of orthodox ministers can be had in other places, and the parent offers his infant to a heretical minister of his own to be baptized, he sins gravely and in some manner denies the confession of the truth, for the reasons indicated above (Cap. 6). **Only from defect of a pure ministry** (as is the case in a *pressed church*, where neither in the vicinity can a sincere minister of the Church be had) — as in the *extreme case of necessity* — is the ministry of a heretic to be used, but with *a certain confession of truth and protestation*, that he will educate his infant in *the orthodox faith*. Thus at least a *epieikeia* (equity), which can trouble the conscience in this kind.

**For as far as the disparity of rites is concerned**, I have said before, that they neither change nor take away the substance of the sacrament: but whatever there is of superstition or impiety, this is not on the part of the one being baptized, but of the one baptizing, whom the parents of the infant sufficiently contradict by their confession of truth — whence there is no peril that they render themselves participants of that impiety. So *the Pharisees* had a corrupt ministry, and in it *circumcision* polluted with many traditions, yet many pious parents offered their infants to them to be circumcised, when they could not have other better doctors: nay, it is credible that *Christ himself and the Apostles were circumcised by the Pharisees*. For although *the Pharisees were thieves and robbers* (John 10), yet *circumcision was in itself established from the ordination of God*, who through the hand of those most impure doctors administered this sacrament. In the same manner *God it is who baptizes*, though through the impure hand of a *sacrificer* — from whom, if we cannot have better doctors anywhere, we can both seek and receive baptism without sin.

If any sin were in this kind, it would follow that our elders, who in the Papacy were carried to the baptism of some Papist and were baptized by his hand, acted impiously; and it would annihilate also the preaching of the Word made by monks, and the consolation of a monk drawn from Scripture; and all who even in the *Papacy* are baptized, and afterward transfer themselves to our churches, should be rebaptized — if the *Papist baptism* is in itself impure and illicit.

These reasons all with the docile easily satisfy: for what if the *Papacy is full of heresies*? What if baptism is filled with *Papist superstitions*? What if the one baptizing is a heretic? — that can nothing derogate from baptism, integral in substantials, since it must be judged not from those accidents but *from the substance of baptism*, which is not from men but from God, from whose efficacy alone it must be judged.

### Case VI. What if however heretics — as today happens in the Papacy — refuse to baptize infants even offered to them, until the parents by public confession transfer themselves to that malignant church?

**Respondeo.** To this has today progressed *the tyranny of the Romanists in Bohemia* and other places — without doubt not without God permitting, and punishing ingratitude for his Word.

Although here is truly a *most acute sword* which pierces the hearts of pious parents, yet in no way should they be moved, that consenting to those impious postulates they should betake themselves to the *Papist churches*, which they know to be *synagogues of Satan* and *schools of Antichrist*. Therefore any extreme things whatsoever must be borne rather than to consent to that turpid and most sad apostasy.

**Yet that they may consult** not only for their own consciences but also for the salvation of their infants: first of all, an orthodox minister of the Church should be sought, even for some miles distance — notwithstanding the expense either of the journey or of costs. If he cannot be had, one must supplicate the *Papist Magistrate*, under whose jurisdiction we live, use also the intercessions of others, that our consciences he not permit this yoke to be imposed — since no man is of such majesty or power as to have power over the consciences of others.

**If yet nothing be prevailed**, then as *in the extreme case of necessity* the parents themselves privately can baptize their infants, in the manner in which in the time of the *Antiochian persecution* even women circumcised their infants (1 Macc; 2 Macc 6:10).

For although *in the ordinary way circumcision and baptism should be administered by certain persons constituted in ministry*, yet in that case of necessity that order can cease, which should not *dominate* over the sacraments but *serve* them: nor does baptism depend on the *dignity of the person administering*, but on *the words of the one instituting*.

**In vain also** does *Beza* inject a scruple in loc. cit. (lib. *Sanct. epist.* to *T. Beza* c. 6), where in *plenary assembly of the Church* he wants baptism to be administered: which indeed *outside the case of necessity* even we consider consulted; but when every access to public assemblies is precluded from us, no scruple ought to be, that in private houses it stand, since *God does not attach his grace to any place*, and *For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.* (Matt 18:20).

Therefore the *Apostles* did not always baptize in public assemblies, but sometimes in private houses (Acts 16), sometimes even *on the road* (Acts 8), or in other places, as the matter demanded, and where they had a supply of water. In these circumstances therefore no one ought to be too solicitous.

### Case VII. What if the mother alone, with witnesses or arbiters removed, in the case of necessity had baptized the infant of her own accord — could the infant when he comes to adult age be sufficiently certain of his baptism?

**Respondeo.** *Blessed Luther* proposes this case (Tom. 8 *Jenensis Germ.* fol. 39) and responds: *if the mother in the time of birth were so preoccupied that she could not summon anyone, but she is alone, and the infant before it is fully brought forth periling of life, in this case the mother can baptize her infant sprinkling water, in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.*

*If the infant immediately upon receiving baptism should die, she ought not doubt that he has truly received baptism, and has died happily. But if the infant should remain living, let her indicate to no one that she has baptized the infant, but let him as an unbaptized be led into the assembly of the Church, and offered to the minister to be baptized — not as though the baptism administered by her were not true and salutary, but that the infant when he grows older may have his witnesses against the fiery darts of the devil, that he has been baptized: which testimony he can request from the Church, the matter requiring it, especially from those who are for this purpose adhibited — from the witnesses, whom they call godparents.*

*It would be too much for a mother alone as a witness in a matter of such moment, which the salvation of the soul concerns, that faith should scarcely be adhibited to her. And this baptism is not to be held for iterated — for as *Ambrose* says: *what is not known to be done, cannot be said to be iterated*.

### Case VIII. What is the use of the godparents (patrini) or susceptores, who are adhibited in Baptism?

**Respondeo.** We refer therefore to the ancient rites of this sacrament, and indeed among the most ancient: for *Tertullian* mentions it (lib. *De baptismo*), and *Dionysius* (in *Hierarch. Eccles.* c. ult. ad finem), where he calls the *divine parents of the boy* *the παραδώκοι of the initiate*.

The origin of this rite some refer to *Hyginus* Bishop of Rome, who around the year of Christ 140 instituted it: occasion for it was given by the baptism *of the catechumens*, concerning whom *Eusebius* refers (lib. 7 c. 20 and lib. 8 c. 21), that *susceptores as witnesses were destined, who could testify the faith and baptism of the catechumens*.

Others attribute the *occasion* of this rite to *parents who from Gentilism were newly converted to Christian religion*, and who either by ignorance could not, or by incuria did not wish to educate their infants in the true faith of Christians — therefore others of better judgment were elected, who not only about the *baptism of the infant* would testify, but also would undertake the *care of education in piety and true faith*.

Hence it can be collected what is the use of the godparents. **(1)** They are *fideijussors of the infants*, in whose name they renounce Satan and profess the *Christian faith*, which ceremony *Augustine* vehemently approves (in the *place cited*) — not as some *disposition* to baptism, as *Lombard* speaks (lib. 4 *De sacram.* c. 11), nor as if the faith of the godparents suffices for the little ones unto justification, as *Gregorius de Valentia* thinks (tom. 4 in *Thom. Aquin.* q. 3, punct. 2, ad 3) — but because it shows *the infant is baptized into that faith which about the SS. Trinity the Church holds*, and it recalls to our memory the *sponsio* of the *supreme Advocate of little ones*, saying (Mark 10): *suffer little ones to come unto me*.

**(2)** They are *co-fathers* (*compatres*), that is, coadjutors of the parents, or also, after their death, *pro-fathers* and vicars in the education of the infants in that faith, in place of which they responded for the infants. Diligent care therefore they should give, that they render the infant most alien from all works of the devil, which in baptism he renounced, and always addicted to God — by exhortations, commonstrations, and instructions, no otherwise than as if he had been generated by themselves. Hence *Augustine's* admonition to the godparents (*Sermon 116 De tempore*): *let those who wish to receive sons or daughters with religious fear, understand that both before they are baptized and after they are baptized, they should not cease to admonish or teach them of chastity, humility, sobriety, and peace: and let them acknowledge that they are their fideijussors — for they respond for these, that they renounce the devil, his pomp and his works. And so those who receive as those who are received, both fathers and sons, that they may pact with them, that they might inscribe them together with CHRIST in the sacrament of baptism, and endeavor to keep them, nor ever concupisce anything of the pomps of the devil or of the luxurious oblations of this world*.

**(3)** They are also *witnesses*, who should testify that baptism was legitimately conferred on the infant, and the same has been inserted into the act of the Church, and made a member of the *city of God*.

Since *in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall be established* (Deut 19:15), hence it is done that most often *two or three* susceptores are adhibited, whither some refer the example of *Isaiah*, who, about to have a son named, adhibited two witnesses (Isa 8:2).

But this matter is of free observation according to the custom of each Church, which no one temerariously ought to convict; much less for the sake of gain in a multitude of witnesses is one to consent, since the abuse of this in itself pious and useful institution is deservedly prohibited by the magistrate.

From all which is collected, that this rite is not indeed simply necessary, so that it cannot be omitted without sin, yet also is not to be neglected rashly, since it has so illustrious a use.

**Which is to be observed against *Musculus Bucanus*, who in the *loc. commun. De baptismo* condemns contra tradition, which is not consulted (as I judge, more convenient), so that *if the father of the baptized infant is present at the baptistery, and asks for baptism for his little one, and by the minister before those standing present is interrogated concerning faith, not what the infant has, but what he himself has in Christ the Lord and Savior — into which faith he wishes his infant baptized and instituted — that thus interrogated he express with clear voice the *symbol* of Christian faith, and then he should ask religiously that Christ seal in his infant this faith and grace* — thus he. But this novelty arises from an error of the *Calvinists*, who think that infants of Christians believe by the faith of parents — which error is refuted elsewhere.

We oppose to this in general *Musculus Buchanus* (loc. cit. 1.47), who does not simply reject the use of godparents: **(1)** because it originated *from the imitation of the baptism of the catechumens*, who could themselves respond concerning the faith to be baptized when interrogated, and gave *their own faith as if by witnesses and sponsors*; **(2)** it does not fight with Scripture; **(3)** it is a most ancient custom in the Church; **(4)** it happens not without utility; **(5)** it looks toward the salvation of the infant; **(6)** it has nothing of iniquity or dishonesty; **(7)** it proceeds from charity; **(8)** the whole thing pertains to the edification of the Church; **(9)** *just as at facile birth in carnal generation the midwife is adhibited, so at spiritual regeneration in baptism someone is adhibited, who functions in place of the midwife, and *pedagogue* in those things which pertain to the Christian faith and life* — thus he.

Since therefore preclarous is the use of godparents, this rite is not only rightly observed but is even necessary, that men of mature judgment (not boys), and instituted in the faith rightly, fearing God, and from every graver crime immune, be elected for this office of piety. For not can those rite perfunctorily discharge this office who either do not understand it, or who themselves have a great defect of true faith and piety.

### Case IX. Who are to be rejected, or requested and admitted as godparents — whether such may be admitted who live dissolutely, or with infamy noted with some, or from *our religion* are diverse?

**Respondeo.** We are not here treating of the efficacy of baptism, as though it were taken away or enervated if such men were admitted to baptism. For since it depends not on the dignity of the minister baptizing, nor on the faith of the witnesses, provided that otherwise according to the institution of Christ it be rightly administered, no one about the efficacy of his baptism should doubt, though he had *impious susceptores*. But there are other causes on account of which caution is needed in this kind.

**Pious parents, who are themselves pious**, and have known the true use of godparents, and wish well for their infants, and desire that when they themselves are defunct they may be rightly educated, elect none as godparents except those of whose *piety, probity, and integrity — especially orthodoxy in religion* — is established. And that all should do this, they should be admonished by their pastors, chiefly for three causes:

**(1) *Reason 1.*** Many are the exhortations of Scripture which dehortate us from *conversation, friendship, and familiarity with such men*: *be ye not unequally yoked with the unfaithful*, says *Paul* (2 Cor 6:14). *But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat.* (1 Cor 5:11). *Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us.* (2 Thess 3:6). *If any comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither greet him* (2 John v. 10). Hither pertains the *example of David*, who in many places testifies how greatly he abhorred *familiarity with the impious*, who dissented from him either in morals or in doctrine (Ps 26:5,4; Ps 119:113,63,158, &c.).

**(2) *Reason 2.*** The office of godparents requires pious men and integral of life, and *sincere in religion*. For they are *fideijussors of infants*, in whose name they profess the *Christian faith*, for whom they also pray, that God receive them into grace, and in true faith preserve them. This indeed cannot be done by those who are not themselves in grace, nor have true faith, nor can pray — because *God does not hear sinners* (John 9:31). Infants ought to be educated in *true faith and piety* in place of the parents: how then can this be discharged by those who are wholly alien from true faith and piety? They should also testify concerning the *baptism of the infant*. But those noted with infamy and polluted with manifest scelera are repelled in civil judgments from giving testimony (c. *testimonium* 4.4 extra *De testibus*; c. *super* 15 eodem). How therefore can their testimony in a matter so holy be admitted? *Christ* did not admit the testimony *of the devil* even when speaking truth: and shall you admit the testimony of him who is *the devil's slave*?

**(3) *Reason 3.*** The Apostolic admonition is: *abstain from every appearance of evil* (1 Thess 5:22). But that most narrow necessity with the impious has the *appearance of collusion*, and if the godparents are addicted to a false religion, also of *security* — as if the parents cared for no religion, and were indifferent by whom their children should be educated. It has also the *appearance of avarice*, if from distant places especially they summon men marked with ill fame, and elect them as *susceptores* of their infants, when they could have pious and religious ones near at hand.

For these and similar causes must the parents be admonished to be *circumspect in the election of godparents*. To be admonished also are auditors *improbi* and contumaciously evil-living, that unless they abstain from their enormous crimes, they will be *warned off from the use of the sacraments*, nay, they will be *cut off wholly from the body of the Church as morbid members*.

**But if the parents, whether from ignorance, or even from having those admonitions postposited**, and *ex proposito* have elected such impious and erring-in-faith men as godparents and susceptores of their infant — then in the very act of baptism the *minister of the Church* should exclude no one from the office of godparent: for this would not be done without ignominy, and by this reason many would be offended, of whose conversion there could otherwise be hope.

**But here caution and distinction is needed.** If he is *notoriously impious*, blasphemer, adulterer, usurer, or polluted with a similar scelus — let the matter be referred by the minister before baptism (if there is time) to the *ordinary Inspector*, who should act with the man himself, and solicitously seek his conversion. If he profits nothing, let him refer the matter to the *Consistory*, in which is the jurisdiction of the ecclesiastical magistracy. If he does not admit the admonitions of even this, then publicly by his authority and communion of sacred things let him be deservedly warned off. These are the grades of admonition, according to Christ's precept (Matt 18), to be observed among all who are apprehended in some delict.

**But if such a one, though often admonished and yet impenitent still, intrudes himself into that act of baptism**, then the minister is indeed bound to tolerate him, but *let him finish the action*, and afterward may deservedly reprehend the parents that they chose such — and with the impenitent one himself deal by right; but *in the action itself let him avoid the scandal of the weak*.

**If the godparent is not *openly a blasphemer, nor a contemner of our religion, but by some error fascinated on account of defect of better instruction, yet still docile*** — he should be admitted to this act of baptism, because by his presence he approves our baptism, and by this reason acknowledges some Church among us, whose key is baptism: *he who is not against us is with us* — and hope appears in such, that if right information accedes, they may at length recognize their errors and lay them aside.

For which cause let him be admonished by the pastor either before or after the completed baptism about his error, and let him be commonstrated not to bring on himself peril by pertinacity in it.

**The same is the ratio of those whom fame at least has noted**, though they are not yet convicted of some more insignal scelus: these cannot be warned off from baptism, because they are not yet cut off from the Church as morbid members, but they should be admonished to wash off the stain sprinkled on them, lest anything harsher be established against them.

**This is the practice of our Churches, according to the *Elector Ecclesiastical Constitution*, art. 10**, which both for the removal of scandal, and for converting the *improbi*, seems most accommodated of all, and consents with the judgment of the *Wittenberg Theologians*, which may be seen (*Consil. Wittenberg. dec. 1 conf.*).

### Case X. If someone is asked by another parent of diverse religion to receive his infant from the laver of baptism, whether with good conscience he can grant or ought?

**Respondeo.** No one should offer himself in this kind to those who are not of our religion, lest among the ignorant he fall into suspicion of collusion. But if we are requested by them, we should look: **(1)** what the *confession* of that Church is, in which our work is requested. If there the three persons of the Trinity are denied, or otherwise the substantials of baptism are violated (as among *Arians*, *Photinians*, and *Anabaptists*), this office is to be refused, lest we be made partakers of others' sins.

**(2)** It should be considered *with what mind* this office is asked of us. If it is for the sake of tempting, this end in view — that by our presence we give a *tacit confession* of the doctrine which in that Church, in which the baptism is administered, sounds — it should be refused, *since when adversaries wish to explore our liberty which we have in Christ, that us into servitude they may reduce, by the example of the false brethren, they should not yield*. Neither should we grant, if by this our fact the weak would be offended, and would conceive of us some opinion of collusion with the adversaries. For on account of scandal even from *middle things* one must abstain, as *Paul* writes: *I speak as to wise men; judge ye what I say.* (1 Cor 10:15). For these causes the *Electoral Ecclesiastical Constitution* art. 10 dissuades, that we not attend the *baptism of Papists*, nor otherwise *co-participate*.

[More concerning this may be read in the *integral German tract* which *D. Meltzer* Episcopal Superintendent Evangelicorum Coburgensium wrote, entitled: *Grundt und Bericht, warum an vieler Christen den Papst und Confession von Gewissen halben zu Papst gestehen sampt kurtzer Erklärung der fürnembsten Ehrwürden und Streckten, gedruckt zu Coburg 1594*.]

**But if there be no peril of temptation or scandal**, and the baptism is administered also *in the substantials integrally*, I do not see what obstructs that we can consent to a petition of this kind: yet let there accede a *solemn protestation before the adversaries*, that we with their doctrine have nothing to do, and by this our fact wish nothing else than to testify concerning *the baptism of the infant*.

The reasons of this sentiment are:

**(1)** Because those whose baptism in substantials we believe to be true, of them also we can testify by our presence. Such is the *baptism of the Calvinists and Papists*, as we have taught above. Ergo.

**(2)** Since the chief use of the susceptores is that the infants have witnesses of their baptism, our testimony too cannot be denied about a baptism in substantials legitimately administered, though by those who in other capital things of doctrine differ from us: just as in the forum, even before an unjust magistrate, we can perhibit testimony of innocence to someone.

**(3)** By this reason the *infant is delivered into our power*, and to us some part of *education* is committed — of which right we can use, either by admonitions while the parents are yet living, or by *plena institutione in vera religione* after the death of the parents.

**(4)** Through this office is *spiritual friendship* contracted with the parents of the infant, whom by our conversation we can more easily win — as *Peter* writes concerning faithful wives and honestly living ones, that *Likewise, ye wives, be in subjection to your own husbands; that, if any obey not the word, they also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives;* (1 Pet 3:1) — the fruit of which by intempestive *tergiversation and morositas* would be impeded. For it is not likely that *pertinacious adversaries* and *openly blasphemous* toward our religion would implore the work of any of us in this kind: therefore if the *weak* do this, they should be helped rather by our *facility* than repelled by *morositas*. Let him know therefore, whoever is adhibited to this sacred office, that he has by this very thing as it were received a *vocation*, that he may both recall parents and infant from error, and, as much as in him is, instruct them in true religion — which even before the act of baptism he should predicit to the parents seeking his work, that hereafter he will do so.

### Case XI. If someone is asked to receive an infant from baptism, can he honestly refuse?

**Respondeo.** There are found who think they can do this honestly either when the infant is not legitimately born, or when they are asked by an enemy with whom perchance they litigate in court, or even to save money, since they are too frequently adhibited to this office.

But since it is an office of *piety and charity*, I do not see how it can honestly be refused. For **(1)** since the office of susceptors is to testify the *baptism of the infant*, and to educate him in the true faith rightly, any sound-minded *φιλόχριστος* ought to be prepared for the matter: according to that of *Chrysostom*: *let each of us see how he may snatch the neighbor from the jaws of the devil*.

**(2)** *Reason 2.* This requires the *bond of charity* by which as members of that mystical body under Christ its head we are collected. *Charity is officious and beneficent* (1 Cor 13:4), which to the neighbor also with some incommodum of its own (which yet in this kind cannot be) serves.

**(3)** *Reason 3.* There postulates further honesty itself, which is violated when for a very light cause, and above all through *tenacity of ours*, we fail so pious an office: which how sordid a thing it is, and how noxious to our fame, anyone can estimate.

**(4)** *Reason 4.* One must spare the reputation of the neighbor, who bearing a rebuff is diffused with shame, is affected with ignominy, and into *suspicion* not without cause is drawn. *God however is no respecter of persons* (1 Cor 12:4).

**(5)** *Reason 5.* Finally, whatever any wishes not to be done to himself, let him not do to another: therefore let him be prompt and ready for this pious office, that he may in similar case find others such for himself.

Those reasons which can withdraw someone from this obligation are of no moment. For if the infant is not legitimate, he himself neither can prestate the fault of the parents, nor cast on himself the reato.

If someone by respect of his dignity or office does not wish himself to be present at the action of baptism, let him gladly through another prestate what he was asked, provided at least the miserable infant does not seem to have been completely deserted.

If from an enemy he has been sought for this office, let him congratulate himself that he has found the occasion of *reconciliation*, which each of the pious ought to seek with highest study. Nor ought forensic actions to impede him, which nonetheless can stand safely with the offices of piety, and by the reconciled persons litigating can be more easily and happily terminated.

If any for the sake of money neglects the addition of the infant to Christ, he is not worthy that a place among Christians be conceded to him. For the *salus and education of the infant* ought deservedly to be preposited to all riches of the world. Add, that the *essential part* of this office is not the *oblation of gifts*: nor do pious parents attend to this, but can be content either altogether to lack, or with a slight one; nor does the occasion for God be wanting, that this *beneficentia* — especially, when the parents are poorer — compensated more largely.

He therefore who is a lover, I shall not say of *honesty* but even of *piety*, will easily deny this office to no one.

### Case XII. What, if baptism is administered without exorcism — is it legitimate?

**Respondeo.** *Exorcism* is called that action in baptism by which the *unclean spirit* is adjured that it come out from this small servant of Christ, in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

This action was in use in the time of *Tertullian*, *Chrysostom*, *Ambrose*, *Augustine* &c. — all of whom commended exorcism as an *ecclesiastical tradition* useful, both to Greek and to Latin Churches.

**But we do not understand by exorcism the gift of casting out demons from the possessed** — which in the primitive Church was numbered among the *χαρίσματα*, as is established from *Justin* (*Dialogue with Trypho*) and *Tertullian* (*Apologeticum* c. 32) — but in baptism it has no place: for we do not believe our infants to be corporally possessed. Nor do we understand some *magical force and efficacy of expelling the devil*, such as the *Papists* feign, as is to be seen in *Bellarmine* (lib. 1 *De baptismo* c. 25) and *Gregorius de Valentia* (disp. 4 quaest. 6 *De ritu baptismi* punct. 2). Nor do we attribute to it *Apostolic authority*, such as *Leo I* (Ep. 4 c. 5, and from him Bellarmine loc. cit.) attributes to it. For nowhere do we read that Christ commanded, or Apostles used exorcism in baptism — but we use it as an *ecclesiastical rite humanly introduced*, whose use is merely *σημαντικός* (significative). For it signifies and shadows *the spiritual captivity of man in the kingdom of Satan*, in which he is born, and *the liberation from thence made through Christ in baptism*, where they are translated from the kingdom of Satan into the kingdom of Christ — who has no more of right in those who have been baptized. Therefore *adjuratur*, that is, by *grave obtestation* he is warned off from the infant, who through *original sin* has spiritually occupied him, that he give place and yield the place to Christ the Redeemer. For *ἐξορκίζειν* here does not mean to bind by oath, as in Matt 26:63 it is used, but by *obtestation* to drive out, as Christ Satan drove out (Matt 4:10; 1 Cor 8:5). And of this use of exorcism speaks *Chrysostom* (in c. 11 Marci): *the unclean spirit comes out from the man, when through Baptism he begins to be in the name of Christ, and *he shall no longer be of the devil, but of God*.

Since however the words of the exorcism seem harder, rightly *D. Chemnitz* admonishes (part. 3 *Loc. Theol. Tit. De baptismo*): *the Church has liberty, that it should propose and explicate that doctrine about original sin, about the power and reign of Satan, and about the efficacy of baptism, in other words of Scripture more consentaneous*.

*Nor is exorcism a substantial or integral part of baptism, but an ecclesiastical rite ἀδιάφορον, which can not only be omitted during baptism, but plenary abrogated, if it is done by the consent of the whole Church rightly and in order.* Therefore, if anyone has been baptized without exorcism, he should make no *scruple* about his baptism, since *external rites can neither derogate anything from the substance of the sacrament, nor add anything*.

[*Exorcism is an adiaphorous rite, which can either be omitted or retained.*]

**When it is abrogated**, it ought to be done: (1) by *the authority of the magistrate and of the ministry* (Sir 33:30); (2) *with the Church consenting, or non-contradicting*; (3) *with the true and pure sense preserved*; (4) *without any doctrine unclean or damnable condemnation*; (5) *without any preposterous superstition or religion adulterated*; (6) *without the scandal of the weak* (Matt 18:6). *When in one or more of these conditions there is delinquency, an incursion is made on Christian liberty.*

**No one however by private judgment should dare to abrogate this rite**, especially since in its usurpation there is no peril of scandal, since the whole Church has been instituted about baptism. For *adiaphora become necessary, if rashly and without cause, with the scandal of the weak, a mutation of them is undertaken*. More concerning exorcism see elsewhere; and let it not suffice for the ratio of the institute.

### Case XIII. How can a man in adult age use his baptism?

**Respondeo.** *Baptism is not a transitory act* which has its use only in the infancy of man, through regeneration; but *it endures also in adults even to the end of their life for its efficacy*. For the *covenant of God*, into which we are received through baptism, is perpetual, according to *not by faith and covenant everlasting he departs from thee, thy covenant of peace shall not be moved*, as the Lord said.

**Now the use of baptism in adults is three-fold:**

**(1) *Preservative* (*praeservativus*), against the suggestions of Satan, by which he instigates us to sin. There let baptism come into our mind, in which we said farewell to the kingdom of the devil and all its works, and were received into the covenant of God, that we might serve God in *sanctity and righteousness* all the days of our life. Let us therefore resist the tempter: the baptized are no more under sin, nor more under wrath, but *under grace, and sons of God*. Since then a new life and new morals ought to follow from baptism, our life ought to be consonant to baptism (as *Augustine* speaks *De fide et operibus* c. 24): *for if fugientes returning to the pollutions of this world after the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ, they are entangled again therein and overcome, their last state is worse than the first: for it were better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than after they had known it, to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them* (as *Peter* speaks, 2 Pet 2:20,21).

This use of baptism *Paul* notes (Rom 6:3): *we are buried with Christ through baptism into death; that as Christ was raised from the dead, so we also should walk in newness of life*. So our baptism is as it were a *shield*, by which we can prostrate that *infernal Goliath* with his tenebrous suggestions, and *avert the wounds of conscience*.

**(2) *Consolatory* (*consolatorius*), and indeed doubly: first, if after baptism we have relapsed into sins, and on that account Satan wishes to render our salvation doubtful. There *recordatio of our baptism pellit dubitationem*, and *suggests most efficacious solace*, because God in baptism has remitted, blotted out, not only the sins in which we are born, but *all* which we can commit throughout the time of our whole life, received us as his sons, and dignified us with the *covenant of grace*: from which although through sin against conscience we fall out, yet the return to it lies open through *penitence* — *for the converted the return is always open*.

[*Voice of Christ to his beloved sons: 'I open,' says Christ, 'the gates of penitence like the eye of a needle: and I open to you the gates of mercy, through which horses can pass.'*]

**This consolation and efficacy of baptism the Papists enervate**, when they establish that the grace of baptism is valid only for the remission of past sins, or of those which the time of baptism finds in the man — so that although the sinner after baptism return to penitence, nothing yet of profit is the grace received in baptism, but it is by his lapse wholly to be destroyed, broken, and annihilated. In penitence therefore, as it were on another plank from shipwreck, grace and reconciliation must be sought — which error *Luther* refutes (*De captivitate Babylonica* Art. *De sacramento baptismi*), where he writes: *my most powerful counsel is, the solid and invincible ship, nor is it ever dissolved into any planks, in which all are carried who to the harbor of salvation are borne — which is the truth of God promising in the sacraments &c. So then once for us the divine promise of baptism is laid: he who believes and is baptized shall be saved, and unto death the truth of it perseveres; so faith in it should never be intermitted, but even unto death should be nourished and confirmed by the perpetual memory of the promise itself in baptism made to us.*

*Therefore Scripture says in the present: baptism saves us (1 Pet); in the past: he saved us (Titus 3); in the future: he who believes and is baptized, shall be saved (Mark 16).*

Wherefore, when from sins we rise, or when we do penitence, we do nothing else than what to the *virtue of baptism* and to the *faith* from which we had fallen, we return, and to the promise then made we return, which through sin we had deserted. This our sentence is stabilized by the *perpetuity of the covenant* entered with us, which on the part of God remains ratified always, because *the incredulity of men shall not evacuate the faith of God* (Rom 3); *If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself.* (2 Tim 2:13). We indeed through lapses against conscience have fallen from the covenant: through penitence we can return to it — therefore God also *has bidden us remember our baptism, that we are washed by his blood, and are members of one body baptized* (1 Cor 12:12,13).

**Peter** in his sin the Lord bade to remember his baptism (Matt 26:75). *Others* also without doubt recorded baptism of theirs; therefore after conversion he writes: *baptism saves us* (1 Pet 3:21). For the same cause he calls *baptism the stipulation of good conscience with God* (v. 21) — because through stipulation our conscience is founded upon God propitious, who the promise of grace made in baptism will not retract.

*Illa item vox est* consolatory in *afflictions of tempted Christians*, of Christians tempted on account of sins referring themselves to their baptism: *if any tempter or persecutor after baptism assail thee* — as *Chrysostom* says (Hom. 6 *ad populum Antiochenum*): *thou hast whereby thou surpassest him*: *for if trained to look on him thou remainest, remember Christ, and that with faithful faith thou art baptized; with which all the darts of that little one are extinguished. Spirit indeed is he, yet loosening mountains: from which indeed the fire of the terrible Deity has its force. Where the flame flees not, the members of the wax delinquesce, there Ambrose (In cap. 3 Isai.): *In baptism is bestowed the emendation from sins.*]

The second consolation baptism ministers *contra difficulties and dangers, in which for the office of our vocation we fall into sudden cases*. Just as the faithful in the OT with enemies impious mindful of their circumcision as of their standard, aggressed the enemies uncircumcised (since they had the sign of the covenant in the flesh, by which they confirmed themselves from the fear and help of God) — as is established from David and Jonathan (1 Sam 14:6) — so Christians in perils placed should ex their baptism draw efficacious consolation of the presence and protection of God. For God knows how to snatch the pious from temptation (2 Pet 2). Hither pertains that hardest promise (Isa 43:1,2): *fear not, for I have redeemed thee, and I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine. When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee, and rivers will not overflow thee, when thou walkest in fire thou shalt not be burned, nor shall the flame kindle upon thee, because I am the Lord thy God*, &c. *God has therefore called us out of his sons in this laver of baptism, in which we are made his peculium: our baptism therefore can most firmly promise us the presence and protection of God in dangers.*

**(3) *Third use of baptism in adults is nomen atticum* — that of *admonition*, and this indeed manifold. The first admonition is for the *neophytes* who through baptism have recently acceded to the Church. *Cyprian* calls *baptism the first battle of salvation*. That baptism admonishes to act circumspectly. For Satan *lays snares for the baptized more* than for those who are outside the Church. And as Christ soon after receiving baptism was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil, so the baptized is straightway from baptism called to *militancy*, where one must always watch and pray, lest the *palm of salvation* be turned aside from us by the tempter. Hence is the admonition of *Sirach* (2:1): *son, when thou approachest the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare thy soul against temptation*. That we may escape the hand of the tempter, it is consulted to avoid the *occasion of temptations* — that is, the enticements of the flesh, the places and times of the world in which our corrupted nature is enticed to sin: and as *Seneca* writes (Ep. 117): *what we cannot escape, from a slippery place let us recede, in a dry place with somewhat firm footing let us stand*.

*So says Paul* (1 Cor 12:13): *we all through one Spirit are baptized into one body*. Therefore let us mutually be members, joined by the bond of charity, kind, dear, gentle, one to another, lest among themselves *schisms* — through which the mystical body would easily be dissolved — arise: let them know that they in baptism have been consecrated wholly to Christ, whom there they put on — therefore *let them offer their bodies a living sacrifice, holy, well-pleasing to God* (Rom 12:1), with certain purpose that what through the sponsors they promised in baptism, in every time of their life they will renounce to the devil.

**Finally, for those who have relapsed**, that without delay they rise, since through no other means than through serious penitence there is return to grace. To the impenitent then the grace of baptism will be lacking, and when they ought to hold it in a fund of grace, they change it into a testimony of just punishment, so that from their baptism they will have more grief than joy, more cruciate than solace. *Baptism* like the *equipment of soldiers*, *convicts the deserter and confounds the fugitive*, as *Augustine* wrote (Tract. 24 in Ioh. Serm. 44 *De verbo Domini*): *for the works of the flesh mortify the spirit, when the flesh concupisces against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh*.

Then for those *standing*, that they *see that they fall not*: therefore let them walk cautiously, live peaceably with the neighbor with whom under one head Christ through baptism they are conjoined.

[*If a thousand times a man has fallen, and a thousand times has been rejected, in no way will GOD reject him.* — *Athanasius* to *Antiochus*.]

— ❦ —

## Chapter XII. On Cases of Conscience Concerning the Lord's Supper

*De casibus conscientiae circa Coenam Dominicam.*

The *Lord's Supper* is a *Sacrament of the New Testament* instituted by CHRIST in that night in which he was betrayed, to this end — that by the most precious pledge of his body and blood together with the bread and wine exhibited to us, we individually believing might be more surely confirmed concerning the obtained remission of sins and the grace of God.

Its rightful use is *one of the chief parts of divine cult*, not only on account of the mandate of Christ, but also on account of the *spiritual aliment* by which, receiving from this Supper, we are rendered more prompt to serving GOD. For truly *the taste of good things comes*, as *Chrysostom* speaks (Hom. 83 *in Matth.*): *when we are called to CHRIST, we are stirred to prestate freely, that whereto we are more tardy*.

But since this part of divine cult is subjected to many *scruples* on the part of those using it, that these not be left in suspense, we shall propose in order those scruples, and, as far as it can be done through us, examine them.

### Case I. Since the Holy Supper is not salutary, unless it be worthily used, the first care of the pious is what is to be done, that we may worthily accede to this sacred table

**Respondeo.** Deservedly this *first care* of the pious is in this part of divine cult: for *For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body.* (1 Cor 11:29). Now none of us is worthy of this sacred banquet either by nature or by any habit, but for all of us it must be confessed, that this benefit by which GOD dignifies us is *above our merit*, since there is no comparison between us sinners and the most sanctified flesh of the Son of God, from which *we not only have not any suppositum, but we use it as a natural participation of nature*, as *Cyril* speaks (in *John* 10; and 1 John c. 3). And this very *acknowledgment of our own unworthiness* is the *first grade* of the *usurpation of the Supper*.

[*Therefore we are members of Christ, and from his body we participate; and from these being taken and drawn we do them, that they may be in CHRIST and Christ in us*. — *Hilary*.]

*Dignity therefore of those rightly using this sacrament* is to be considered both *on the part of God* and *on the part of men*. On the part of *God*, who alone dignifies us with this convivium, in which — divinely arranged — he offers us the *aliment of the soul*, and gives at the same time grace by his own, that we may be participants of this benefit. On our part, all that dignity consists in *worthy preparation*. For to nuptials, to convivia, to the colloquy of most excellent men we prepare ourselves, lest with unwashed hands (as they say) we come into their sight. How much greater preparation shall be needed, when to the table of the Lord — where the Son of God himself is host and food — in the sight of the most holy Trinity and holy angels we appear? Therefore the ancients acclaimed to the communicants: *sursum corda* — lift up your hearts! Because *then there is no place for earthly cares or carnal desires*.

**That preparation involves the following members**:

**(1)** *Dijudication of the body of the Lord* — for this cause the unworthy judgment eats and drinks: *not discerning the body of the Lord* (1 Cor 11:29). Diligently therefore should be expended what that food of the Lord's Supper is, and how much it differs from other vulgar meals.

This dijudication involves the following: **(a)** here *not bread alone and wine* are set forth, but *the very body of the Lord*, which is given to us for death; *the blood of the Lord*, which is poured out for us — as the words of institution teach.

[*Not yet enough was it to the love of the Son of God, that he became man for us; he wished that also he should become food for us.* — *Tauler*, Serm. 2 *de cor. Dom.*

Hence *Leo* (*Serm. de jejunio*): *So we ought to communicate the sacred mystery, that thou hast no dubiety of the truth of the body and blood of the Lord: for this is received by the mouth, which is believed by the heart.*]

**(b)** Other foods sate natural hunger, and nourish the body to this natural life; but this food so sates spiritual hunger, that it also excites and augments it. For the more often anyone uses the Lord's Supper salutarily, the greater is his desire for this most salutary board. For as *Cyprian* speaks (Serm. *de Coena Domini*): *the use of this flesh is a certain of the vine, and desire increasing itself extends it: through which sweetness of charity is imprinted in us, that it may cleave to our palate, and, infused into our viscera, penetrating and imbibing all the intimates and recesses of the body*.

**(c)** Other foods are transmuted into the substance of the recipient; but this food transmutes the man himself into itself. These things taken and drunk make it that *Christ dwells in us, and we in Christ*. *For that Christ is in us not otherwise than truly, when he himself is in us; nor otherwise than corporally we in him, and if he takes* — as *Hilary* speaks (lib. 8 *De Trinit.*). Which consideration kindles in us reverence for this heavenly banquet, renders us devout and circumspect, and impedes all those things which could render this food, in itself most salutary, noxious and perhaps *pernicious* to others.

**(2)** *Probation of self.* Preparation requires *probation of self*: *But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.* (1 Cor 11:28). This probation consists most in the *serious examination of our whole life*, according to the precepts of the Decalogue — which is why usually the *penitence of sinners* is proposed, and afterward *absolution*, and the *amendment of life* is promised.

Let each therefore who desires this Supper thoroughly *dijudicate his own conscience*, and without hypocrisy with fear and trembling accede to the holy table, bringing a mind truly humble, meek, abhorrent from sins, and desirous of perfect sanctimony — such as in this weakness of our flesh can be done. For, *however anyone is bitten with sin, provided he has not the will of sinning in the future, and communicates satisfaction with tears and prayers, and accedes to the divine ministration, which usually is wont to grant remission by pious confession, let him accede to the eucharist tranquil and secure* — as *Vasquez* speaks (in *Concilium Toletanum* de consecration cap. 43).

**(3)** *Divine consideration.* Preparation requires the *divine consideration of the most sacred Supper*, which is conjoined with the highest joy — arising from the *consideration of the benefits of Christ*, above all of that most narrow *conjunction of ourselves with him*, whereby he wished us not only to adhere to him mind and soul through faith, but also to procure the *fellowship of our bodies with his body and blood through the communion in the sacred Supper*. By which reason he *luculently proved his intimate affection toward us* — which *Chrysostom* (Hom. 60 *ad populum Antiochenum* c. 32) expresses in these words: *If the men of my tabernacle said not, Oh that we had of his flesh! we cannot be satisfied.* (Job 31:31).

[*On account of this both body and cup are mixed together, that we may be conjoined with him.* — *Chrysostom*, Hom. 22 in 1 Cor.]

**(4)** *Grateful memory of Christ's benefits.* Preparation requires *the grateful memory of Christ's benefits*, above all of his most holy passion and death — which each should apply to himself by true faith, and not doubt that these benefits pertain also to himself; for which he should be grateful to Christ his Redeemer.

This too is *to commemorate the death of the Lord*, which *Paul* postulates in the usurpation of the Supper: and this *meditation abstracts the heart of man from the desire of earthly things, elevates it aloft, mitigates all the tempests of this age, and gives a taste of the age to come*. And this meditation alone prepares the soul of man for this table, so that it makes him almost fit alone to worthily perceive it. For as *Chrysostom* elsewhere speaks (*Ad Diligenter discipulos*): *what art thou, who art called; and whither from what he set thee; how much thou lovest thyself; when it were, unless we knew we were separated*.

[*This is the price of our redemption, the monument of the redeemer, food of the redeemed.* — *Augustine*, *De virginit.* c. 8.]

**(5)** *True reconciliation with the neighbor.* Preparation requires *true reconciliation with the neighbor*. For as by faith toward God, so by charity toward the neighbor our heart ought to burn, if we wish worthily to use this sacred sacrament. This Christ demands of us, when about to offer our gifts at the altar, he wills us first to be reconciled with our brother (Matt 5:23,24).

*[The Holy Supper is a sacrament of union — a sign of unity, a bond of charity.]*

**(6)** *External discipline of the body in food and dress.* For preparation the *external discipline of the body in food and dress* pertains. For we must live temperately, that we may have leisure for prayers, and be able to expend this mystery. In dress also let there be no levity, but all be honest and decent: for those external things are often *characters of the mind*, which is ill disposed in those who accede to this sacred table as to feasts and dances.

Let us accede therefore *with pure conscience, humble heart, true faith, holy purpose of amending life, with pious desire, and sincere love toward the neighbor*. *Let us see*, says *Chrysostom* (Hom. 83 *in Matth.*): *with what care nurses receive infants with which they arrive to the milk-station and grasp them; and let us with much greater desire come to this table and to this cup of spiritual milk we suck as suckling infants of grace of the Spirit — nay rather, let us have grief, and one at heart, if we be deprived of this spiritual aliment*. More on this preparation for the sacred Supper, see in *lib. 1 passion. Christi typ.* 2 comm. 5.

### Case II. Who are those who accede to the sacred Supper unworthily?

**Respondeo.** Unworthy are:

**(1)** *Impenitent* — all who with sins against conscience are polluted, and have not yet conceived serious grief about them, much less have they the purpose of amending life.

**(2)** *Infidels*, who deny the *presence of Christ's flesh and blood in the Supper*, or otherwise about the person and merit of Christ do not rightly feel.

**(3)** *Blasphemers*, who with impure mouth *dishonor the sacraments and the wounds of Christ*, and yet receive his most holy body with impure hands, and admove it to the execrable and nefarious mouth.

*All these eat judgment to themselves*, and *become guilty of the body and blood of the Lord*, and therefore incur most grave penalties. For, as *Chrysostom* (Hom. 82 *in John*) speaks: *if any coin the royal purple, no otherwise than as if they should smell it, they punish. Would that any of us should confess to Christ's body accepted, than that they should suffer supplice, who nailed him to the cross?*

When anyone therefore understands himself culpable of this unworthiness, let him abstain from the sacrifice, and count himself among the dogs and swine, before whom this pearl is not to be cast. For although he can deceive the eyes of men by his simulated piety, yet let him not think that he can deceive God, whose eyes behold the heart. But if in this manifest unworthiness he should accede, and by that name should be convicted by his own conscience, let him not have that matter for jest, but among the most abject to be set, unworthy that he come into sight of God or of pious men — like one who has deceived the ministry of the Church, and *addicted himself to judgment, that is, to eternal damnation*.

Yet let him not utterly despair of the grace of God, but even this itself let him consider among the maximum sins, for which Christ died. Let him therefore rise up, spare himself not, but accuse himself, seek remission on account of Christ, and hope with faithful heart, and confirm this his confidence by more worthy usurpation of the Supper — with *serious purpose of perfect amendment*.

And that it may stand to all, that this purpose is not simulated, in the matter itself let him testify that he has abstained from blasphemies, rapines, impure libidines, and similar sins, with which he was hitherto polluted; let him do good to the neighbor whom he had held in hatred, and by the fact itself let him testify that he is *wholly changed*. For he who does not perform *real penitence*, in vain glories in words about amendment.

*Unworthy indeed to admit to the usurpation of the Supper is not permitted* — not indeed, as *Chrysostom* (Hom. 83 *in Matth.*) speaks: *not small punishment threatens us, if anyone whom we know to be evil, and to bear away nothing profitable from this participation: knowest thou, than to admonish another, that we sooner die, than to give the Lord's body to the unworthy? So too the blood of one of us should suffer, than to admit the unworthy — except that we might concede*.

Yet when *serious signs of penitence are present*, and hope of amendment appears — so far is it, that such a one should be warned off, that he should rather be reckoned among the most worthy convivia of this banquet, who from the cup of the Lord draws *refreshment for his soul*. Hence *Paul* did not therefore repel the *Corinthians* from the Supper, although he had indicted penalties on them for their unworthy use — but that they *repent, dijudicate themselves, and otherwise than hitherto they had been accustomed, come together to eat the Eucharistic bread*, he bids (1 Cor 11:34).

### Case III. If someone of malefactors — a homicide, adulterer, or one who has enormously committed himself in some crime — has obtained the remission of the ordinary penalty from the Magistrate, and has also returned into grace with those whom by his private delict he offended, can he securely accede to the sacred Supper, before he by public deprecation is reconciled with the Church?

**Respondeo.** We incline to the negative part, for the following causes:

**(1) *Reason 1.* Ecclesiastical.** Because a malefactor of this kind has offended by his crime not merely certain private persons, but also the *whole Church*, has cast scandal: therefore he was *excommunicated*, and by true members of the Church is to be held as a *morbid member*, until he does *public penitence*, according to the Apostolic saying: *But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat.* (1 Cor 5:11). Therefore that anyone should free himself from these bonds of excommunication, it suffices not that he has satisfied the magistrate or certain private persons, but he must return into grace *with the Church whom he offended*: which is done by *public deprecation*.

**(2) *Reason 2.* Scandal.** *The scandal cast on the whole Church is not to be lightly esteemed*, because *But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea.* (Matt 18:6). Now that scandal by no other medium than public deprecation can be taken away.

**(3) *Reason 3.* Conversion.** Since the magistrate may indeed remit the temporal punishment to the malefactor, yet does not convert his mind, this pertains to the ministry, which is the *ministry of reconciliation*, which operates true penitence through the Word — of which the sign is *public deprecation*.

**(4) *Reason 4.* Distinct fora.** *The penalty or its remission from the magistrate pertains to the forum of the same alone, and justifies no one in the forum of God*. Even if therefore the magistrate has either remitted to the malefactor, or exacted penalties from him himself, yet has God not remitted — unless by public deprecation it stand of the serious grief of the sinner.

**(5) *Reason 5.* Levitical parallel.** Hither pertains what the Lord in the Law says (Lev 19:20): *if any lay with a slave concubine, he indeed with flagello is to be beaten by command of the magistrate; but afterward for his delict he was bound to offer at the door of the tabernacle of testimony a sacrifice for sin, and let the priest pray for him, that he might be propitious to him in the sight of the Lord* — that public deprecation, common with the Church (Lev 15:20 seqq.).

**(6) *Reason 6.* Practice.** Hence it was done without doubt, that the *Electoral Constitution*, Art. 10, on the notorious *malefactors from whom the magistrate has exacted no ordinary penalty*, enjoins that, for averting scandal, on certain Lord's Days, before the doors of the temple they stand, holding white staves in their hands — which is a sign of penitence, and until they be received again into the Church. This rigor was formerly observed, so that *Ambrose* the Emperor *Theodosius* forbade to enter the temple on account of the same slaughter of Thessalonians, until publicly he did public penitence. But the severity of this discipline, along with many other most useful constitutions, has now almost collapsed: therefore it is no wonder if atrocious crimes grow.

Yet whoever has still a wounded conscience, in this kind will be his own accuser, and with those whom by his delict he publicly offended, will not refuse to return into grace publicly, since otherwise concerning true penitence — without which the reception of the Supper cannot be salutary — he must always doubt about himself.

**How public deprecation is to be made:** Public deprecation can be done thus — that the malefactor (with his name suppressed indeed) through the minister of the Church indicate that he has serious grief of soul because of the perpetrated public and scandalous crime, ask pardon, and intercession with God, and promise amendment of life. Thus with tranquilized conscience he can accede to the sacred Supper.

### Case IV. Whether those who litigate in the forum are worthy of the sacrament of the Supper?

**Respondeo.** This is one of the *chief causes* why we ought not to be so ready for forensic lawsuits — that is, so that we may be prepared for the use of the sacred Supper: for it is difficult to lay aside all acrimony toward one with whom we litigate, so that our heart may no longer accuse us on that name. Whence *Paul* writes to the Corinthians: *there is altogether a delict in you, that you have judgments among yourselves; wherefore not rather do you suffer injury?* (1 Cor 6:7).

This is the cause why some litigants in court, while the suit lasts, plainly are not admitted to the sacred Supper.

But we cannot simply approve this. For from the sacred Supper *nothing repels save sin against conscience*. But to litigate in the forum *per se* is not sin: for Christ himself in judgment stood, and being struck on the cheek, defended his cause against the unbelieving judge (John 18:23).

Yet is it not right that Christians altogether should proceed to legal suits, but rather to remit their own right, than to contend in court. If however on account of the gravity of the cause and the importunity of the adversary it cannot otherwise be done, it is indeed licit that he commit the whole business to the judge — provided that he himself from the sentiment of his mind has remitted to the adversary, and has conceived no hatred against him.

This is the *fraternal reconciliation* which suffices for worthy usurpation of the Supper: but *cognition of the cause in court is not thereby removed*. Where, if to the accused a penalty be imposed, it is not to be held as *private revenge*, but for the exercise of public judgment — which we cannot impede, although privately with the adversary we are reconciled. Which reconciliation, if it be without hypocrisy, does not deny to the other party the offices of piety and charity, but does in this kind what Christian charity requires — negotium controversum committit judici. He who has such a mind toward his adversary — even with the suit pending — can use the sacred Supper.

*But we least of all can approve* that the patrons of causes dissuade their clients from colloquy and conversation with the adversary, on the ground that the laws prohibit, and that the goodness of the cause is impeded by such conversation. Whence it happens that litigants frequently accede at the same time to the sacred Supper, and yet neither dignifies the other with even a look or a greeting. Which certainly nothing can be more alien from the office of a Christian man. For such gestures are not obscure *indications* of an angry mind and of one ill-disposed toward the neighbor — and Christ judges that anyone even by gestures of this kind can render himself liable to most grave penalties. Therefore he dissuades, that whoever wishes to offer his gift, first be reconciled with his brother (Matt 5:23,24).

*The usurpation of the sacred Supper is a sign and pledge of mutual love*, that just as from many grains one bread is made, and from many berries wine flows into the cup — so also communicants should be *My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.* (1 John 3:18). With what mind therefore do they betake themselves to this sacred table, whose hearts still burn with hatred toward the neighbor? These indeed before the face of God are *homicides*, as *John* testifies (1 John 3:15).
