**Respondeo.** The *quadragesimal or forty-day fast* is that which in the last 40 days before Passover, commonly is inchoated from the *Wednesday of ashes*, which is vulgarly called *Wednesday at the head of the fast*. But *before Gregory the Great* it was always inchoated on the *Lord's Day*, which is called the *first of the quadragesima*, as *Ambrose* openly teaches (Serm. 34, which is *De quadragesima*); *Cassian* (*Collat.* 21 c. 24, 27, 28); *Gregory* (Hom. 16 in Evangel.); with which agrees from the *Jesuits John Azorius* (lib. 7 *instit. moral.* c. 12): *this, he says, is the common opinion of writers, that in cap. quadragesima, de consecrat. dist. 5 it is openly said, four days before the first Sunday in Quadragesima are added, that all plainly should observe the *quadragesimal fast* of forty days*.

Of *Pope Telesphorus* is read in c. *statuimus* dist. 34 § 4 *ad clerum*, that *he ordered clerics to fast for seven weeks: prescribed only, that others should inchoate the fast from the fourth day of the week*.

The *end* of this fast is commonly referred to *the fourth day of the great week*, which is called *the fifth day at the supper of the Lord*: others end it at the *Sabbath which immediately precedes Passover*; whence the authority of the *Council of Laodicea* (c. 50 which is cited in the *canon law* Gratian c. *non oportet* de consecrat. dist. 3): *it is not lawful in the fifth of the last hebdomad of Quadragesima to dissolve the fast, and the whole quadragesima to dishonor, but through all days of quadragesima to fast*. The same is decreed in c. *non liceat* de consecrat. dist. 3: *it is not lawful on the sixth feria, and on the Sabbath of any hebdomad, to preserve the fast, unless the fast be for the whole quadragesima* — whence *Ambrose* wrote: *the quadragesimal fast up to Passover has forty days*.

In this fast either from all food they abstain up to supper, and this they call *perfect and full fast*; or from meats and those which draw origin from meats, though more often than once they eat, and this they call *imperfect fast*.

*This fast Bellarmine calls Apostolic tradition*: for those things which are from the Apostles have divine authority.

They adduce also *certain sayings of the fathers* — as *Ambrose* (Serm. 25) writes *this fast to be indicted by Christ the Lord*; and (Serm. 34) *this quadragesima the Lord commended to us as the greatest and greatest of all*. *Chrysostom* (lib. 1 *de bono operib. in partic.* c. 14) — but concerning its authority they do not agree.

Some think *it is of divine right, which by his example Christ commended*, in which opinion is *Stapleton* (in *Promptuar.* dist. 3).

But those who hold the earlier opinion think that indeed the *whole quadragenary* is completed by the *fifth feria of the great hebdomad*; and to it the two ferias following (sixth and Sabbath) are added from the *common fast of the whole year*: because *through the whole year the Latin Church has consecrated by its fast*. So *Maximus* (Hom. de quadrag.) writes: *the quadragenary fast has not so much been instituted by men, as consecrated by God, and precepted by celestial majesty*. *Augustine* (In Psalm 100) writes: *the quadragenary fast is precepted to us both by law and by the prophets, and by the very Gospel, which has testimony from the law and from the prophets*.

But *Azorius* (lib. 7 *instit. moral.* c. 12 q. 4) contradicts this opinion, and says *this is not of some sanctimony, since the fathers did not rightly understand it*: *the common opinion of Scholastic Theologians*, however, is that the quadragenary fast is *not of divine right, but of Apostolic tradition or mandate, and of canon law, and of general ecclesiastical custom to be cultivated and celebrated*. And the fathers, he says, said only this — that this kind of fast in the *Old or New Scripture has examples, in Christ, Moses, and Elijah*: which yet he thinks are not to the proposal of imitation, since *not whatever Christ himself did, we too are also to do*.

**We willingly acknowledge the antiquity of the *quadragesimal fast*, but under law of necessity, and under opinion of merit and satisfaction, we are not willing to be bound to it**: nor indeed at antiquity was it on that name indicted. But since from *Eusebius* it stands (lib. 5 *hist. eccles.* c. 24) that in the time of *Irenaeus* a *public fast a little before the feast of Passover was instituted*, because about that time the public penitents were received, and *adults were baptized*; and to the *meditation of the Lord's passion* they prepared themselves — afterward they instituted the *solemn fast for mortification of the flesh and exercises of penitence about Passover, that with Christ they too might suffer something*. For, as *Augustine* asks (Ep. 119 c. 15): *in what part of the year the observance of quadragesima could be more congruously constituted, than as close and contiguous to the Dominical passion?*

They chose however the *quadragenary — that is, forty-day — fast* chiefly *in imitation of Christ*, who fasted 40 days; to which they added also the *examples of Moses and Elijah* — which examples still today are urged by the Romanists, especially by *Stapleton* and *Bellarmine* in the loci first quoted.

But many of the Papists notice this ratio to be *cold*, because the fastings of *Christ, Moses, and Elijah* were miraculous; and in *miracles* Christ is proposed to us *not for imitation but for admiration* — which reason *Alexander of Hales* and *Azorius* have (loc. cit.).

They have also *other reasons of this number*, but *ridiculous* rather than solid: as that *the tenth part of the year is to be paid to the Lord*, which reason they draw from *Gregory* (Hom. 16) and *Cassian* (Collat. 21 c. 27). But since the tenth part of the year consists of only 36 days, they number the beginning of the fast from the *first Sunday of Quadragesima*: from that day up to Passover they say are 42 days; with the six Sundays subtracted, on which they do not fast, there remain about 36 days.

But this calculation will not stand with those who begin quadragesima on the *day of Ashes*, namely four before the *first Sunday of Quadragesima*, and end at the *fifth feria of the great hebdomad*. And how can the fast be called *quadragesimal*, when it is only of 36 days? Which doubt gave occasion for the distinction between *full and semi-full fast*, on which see *Azorius* (lib. 7 c. 22 q. 3).

Others have other causes of the quadragenary number: because we are obliged to *satisfy God for the transgression of the Decalogue*, according to the inordination of the *four affections* against single precepts: but *four times fourteen makes* — wait rather — the *virtue of the Decalogue* is fulfilled through the *four Gospels*, since *ten times four makes 40* (*Augustine* Ep. 118 lib. 1 *De consens. Evangel.* c. 4): because God for 40 days and nights *rained the waters of the deluge*; because *forty days were given to the Ninevites* for penitence; because *for forty stations Israel came from Egypt to the promised land*, and things of this kind.

**All these reasons are of not so much moment, that they should oblige the conscience to observation of the quadragenary fast.**

Nor was this fast *uniformly received in all churches of antiquity*, which the *Romanists* cannot deny. For some inaugurated quadragesima *from the seventieth*, others *from the sixtieth*, others *from the fiftieth*, others *from the fortieth*, others *from the day of Ashes*, others fasted *only one day in Quadragesima*, others *two, not few more, many forty*, writes *Irenaeus* (lib. 5 c. 25). *Socrates* (lib. 7 *hist. eccles.* c. 38) and *Nicephorus* (lib. 12 c. 34) refer that the *Romans* used to fast only three weeks before Passover. Nay the *Synod gathered in Trullo* (can. 55) reprehends the *Roman Church* because, contrary to the custom of the Church, on the *Sabbaths in Quadragesima* she fasts — which ill *Azorius* takes (lib. 7 *instit. moral.* c. 12 q. 5 p. 570). Therefore he writes that this canon is *not received*, since the *Roman Church, mother of all churches, was reprehended*.

It appears from this how much variety there was always in the *quadragesimal fast*; yet today it is obtruded on all under the *thunderbolt of anathema*, according to the rite of the Roman Church.

**As however the ancients retained liberty in time or number of days, so also they did not suffer laws to be prescribed to them in a fixed kind of foods.**

Concerning *Spiridion*, who lived around the times of the *Council of Nicaea*, *Sozomen* writes (lib. 1 c. 11) and *Nicephorus* (lib. 8 c. 42), that at the time of quadragesima a guest weary from the road turned aside to him; at what time others were content to live on bread and *polenta*, but those foods failing, on the feast day he had *swine's meats* — which at home he had salted — set before the guest, of which he himself also ate, and exhorted the guest to do the same. Who when he refused to do this, saying he was a Christian: *for this cause, said Spiridion, thou shouldst refuse less, the Word of God pronounces all things to be clean*.

*Irenaeus* objected the variety of fasting to *Pope Victor* (in *Eusebius* lib. 5 c. 26).

Some think one day is to be fasted, others two, others more, others counting the *forty diurnal and nocturnal hours*, establish their day.

And this variety of fasting is not of our time only, but much earlier began by those who before us, ruled by accurate diligence (as it is likely), had held the reins of things, and *simple and common custom* they laid aside and changed — nothing however less kept *peace among themselves*, and even today we retain, and the *dissonance of fasting the concord of faith commends*.

**From all these therefore we can collect reasons not to be contemned, why the *quadragesimal fast*, in the manner it is today observed in the *Papacy*, cannot bind our consciences**: (1) because such a custom of fasting is not from a mandate of the Lord or of the Apostles, but *only from an idiotism* (as *Irenaeus* speaks), that is, from *private sentiment or devotion introduced*.

**(2)** Because the *quadragenary number*, which the *Romanists* so precisely exact, has no *solid foundation*, but *partly on the μυστήριον of Christ, partly on other frivolous ratiuncula it leans*.

**(3)** Because always *uniform* was not in the whole Church such an observation of fasting: because that *dissonance* did not obstruct, but rather profited the *consonance of faith*.

**(4)** Because the Papists themselves do not yet agree, when it should be *inchoated* or *ended*; but about an uncertain matter, laws obliging the conscience cannot be made.

**(5)** Because of old, in the very quadragesima also on the *reborn nature*, they ate meats.

**(6)** Because to the quadragesimal fast is ascribed the *expiation of sins*.

**(7)** Because the quadragesimal fast, in the manner it is used in the Roman Church, in a solemn council was *contradicted*.

**Which reasons all can munite the conscience, that we do not err, when we do not care about the quadragesimal fast of the *Romanists*.**

The *Papists* object to us **(1)** the heretic *Aerius*, of whom *Epiphanius* writes (haer. 75), that *he rejected fixed days of fastings*, saying: *if I wish to fast, I choose a day for me freely, and I fast for the sake of liberty*.

But this matter could not make *Aerius* a heretic, since *Paul* does not want anyone to judge us in food and drink (Col 2), nor to observe days (Gal 4). This did *Eustathius* and others of the *Montanist school*, who prescribed a rigid discipline about the days of fasting, with whom *Epiphanius* holds — so it is no wonder if he held *Aerius* who contradicted for a heretic. But *Aerius* contradicted from a solid foundation, because the *times of fastings are not fixed and ordered by the Apostles*: which even *Augustine* says in Ep. 86 to Casulanus.

**As to what *Aerius* said, that he would fast from liberty on any day he wished, in this he did not sin — for where there is neither precept nor statute of Christ or of the Apostles, there in things otherwise licit *Christian liberty* finds place. Therefore *Tertullian* (lib. *De jejunio* c. 2) writes: *in the NT indiscriminately fasted from choice, not from imperium of new discipline, in the times and causes of each one*.**

They object **(2)** *the decrees of councils* which are wont to be taken up for *resurrection of the Lord*, and by sacred communion in Passover we are deprived. *Erasmus* alone (can. 9) it is mandated to *priests*, that they should preach to the peoples the quadragesimal fast, and *accurately observe*. They add the saying of *Augustine* (Serm. 62): *not to fast in Quadragesima is a sin*.

But these things perhaps are to be understood *of those who in the time of quadragesima not only do not abstain from certain foods, but live most intemperately*, and when the *passion of the Lord* is to be meditated, they themselves *from the highest morning to the evening ingorge themselves with the most delicate foods and wine*: these certainly *most gravely sin*, and are unworthy that they enjoy the *resurrection of the Lord*.

But to fixed days of fastings not to suffer oneself to be bound, when otherwise one lives *temperately enough*, is not a sin, because that observation of days is not divinely precepted: *Because the law worketh wrath: for where no law is, there is no transgression.* (Rom 4:15).

**And if it be so great a sin, why are the *Papal and bishops* so easy in dispensing, who indeed by no cause the most grave, much less by money, ought to be moved to dispense with sinning? For *God himself neither commands anyone to sin, nor gives space for sinning* (Sir 15:21).**

Nothing therefore is the *Papist Quadragesimal fast* to us. Meanwhile we do not deny that we should give operation with highest study, that the time immediately preceding Passover should be spent in *sanctimonious meditation*, and from all *enticements of the flesh* — whether in victual or in other external pleasures — one should diligently abstain, because that time is the *time of penitence*, which requires *chaste morals, temperate and sanctified life*.

**Nor would they err who at that time on certain days abstain from food and drink, to be more apt to exercises of piety and penitence. But to a fixed number of days, and from certain foods, to abstain under opinion of necessity and merit — this is what especially in the quadragesimal fast we improve.**

### Case IX. Can anyone impose fasting upon himself?

**Respondeo.** The *vow of Jerome* is (Ep. 28 to *Lucinius*, which is cited in the *Canon Law* dist. 76 c. 4 *utinam*): *would to God we could always fast, since in the *Acts of the Apostles* (c. 13:2, and 27) *on the Sabbath and on the Lord's Day, we read that Apostle Paul, and with him those sitting, fasted*.

But since we understand this of *continuation of fasting*, it would be superstitious, and less convenient to our nature.

**Therefore by reason of times fastings are variously distinguished in the *Papacy*.** They have: (1) *fasts assumed* — when someone, without precept of the Church, freely for a certain cause indicts a fast for himself. (2) *Votive*, when someone from a vow fasts, whether it be a vow of some *monastic order*, or peculiarly emitted. (3) *Injunct*, which the priest in confession enjoins in place of satisfaction. (4) *Instituted or indicted*, which by the Church solemnly are indicted. (5) *Fasts of counsel*, which are not precepted to all, but only counseled to those who through *works of supererogation* contend to the *state of perfection*. (6) *Customary*, which in some region from institution of the ancients are customary. (7) *Extraordinary*, which according to the ratio of incident causes extraordinarily are indicted.

All these species of fastings can be reduced to two: they are either *public fastings*, as are the *injunct, indicted, customary, extraordinary, and of counsel*, or they are *private*, as *assumed and votive*.

**Concerning these *private fastings* we say that they are not only *licit*, but also have great *utility*.** One can therefore assume, or even vow, privately a fast for certain incident causes — and this pious people should do:

**(1)** When they are to be for the *hearing of the Word and divine cult* on the *following feast* or *Lord's Day* to be instituted, that on the preceding *reborn nature* they may prepare themselves.

**(2)** When they are to accede to the *sacred Supper* — as some on the preceding day for a whole day abstain from all food, some from lunch, some from supper only, some indeed do lunch and sup, but *more sparingly* than they are wont at other times.

**(3)** When they mourn on account of the recent death of one of their own.

**(4)** In *public calamities*, which for their part with ardent prayers they seek to avert — the *foment of prayers* however is *fasting*.

**(5)** When they feel *depraved suggestions of the flesh*, which kind of demon is not cast out except by *prayer and fasting*.

**(6)** When after a committed sin, in which the flesh conquered the spirit, the man animadverts to the lapse by *subtraction of food*, whereby the *lascivious flesh is subdued and subjected to the spirit*. For this is to *mortify the members and crucify the flesh* (Col 3; Gal 6).

**In such fasting they have examples of the saints, who, no one commanding but spontaneously fasted, as incident cases postulated** — such were the *fastings of David* (Ps 35:13; 69:11; 109:24), of *Esther* (c. 4), of *Judith* (c. 8), of *Daniel* (10:3), and of others.

**But that this *private fast* be legitimately instituted, the following *cautions* are to be observed**:

**(1)** *Let not the fast be superstitious*, that is, restricted to a certain kind of food, as if it made much difference if one abstained from meats, and indeed on certain days, meanwhile filling himself with other foods. For above we have heard that in fastings consciences are to be bound neither by observation of foods nor by days. *He who cannot fast*, says *Chrysostom*, *can live temperately, and by sobriety subject the flesh*. And *Jerome* to *Nepotianus*: *let thy fast be daily; better it is daily and sparingly to eat, than rarely to fasting excess. Let thy foods be sober, simple, and chaste, humid moderation, and not superstitious. It should be so, that we not subject ourselves to the necessity of fasting and abstinence.* — See *Petrarch* *De vita contempl.*]

**(2)** *Let not the fast be *inhuman*, by which the body is so weakened that it becomes inept for prayers and exercises of piety* — for this is to *overturn the legitimate fast*. The Apostle *Paul* wills that we *exhibit our bodies a living sacrifice, our rational service* (Rom 12:1). If therefore *the service of our body ought to be rational*, we should certainly avoid *immoderation in fastings, vigils, labors, and other exercises of the body*, which even *Thomas* prohibits (in quodlib. art. 28 quaest. 3): *rules of the same abstinence cannot be prescribed to all, since the constitution of nature is not the same in all*. General is however the observation, that fasting is so instituted, that the *end of fastings — devotion, sobriety, and humility in prayers — is not impeded*. Honor therefore is to be had for the body, lest it obstruct the soul. Therefore *Jerome* is cited in the same book of the *Canon Law* dist. 76: *the fast which is not moderated, either without judgment do we perform, or those things which are necessary we withdraw from the body — that which through the Prophet the Lord speaks: I am the Lord hating rapine in the holocaust. Now the rapine of the holocaust is either an excessive abstinence, or a superfluous eating*.

[*Thus Bernard* to *sisters* (col. 1545): *fasting*, he says, *not from too great a plenitude, and thence disturbs us — but daily according to our measure*. Cf. *De inter. dom.* c. 14: *from the body flee I cannot, nor to leave anything of me, to carry around it is necessary, because it is bound to me by law of nature.*

If a man *afflicts his flesh above measure, he kills his citizen*. — *Anton.* in *Vita patr.*: *fasting is not the end of penitence, nor an operation contrary to trembling ways solvit*.

*Jerome* to *Rusticus*: *let fastings be moderated, lest they excessively debilitate the body, and force a greater refection of eating after crudity*.

*Fulgentius* to *Prob.*: *let fasting be a temperance, that our body neither security should excite, nor immoderate food debilitate*.]

*Peter the Cistercian* (*Confat. i. materium*) bids Papist fastings to be assumed *for expiation*. But this fights with the *satisfaction of Christ*, as we have taught above. Therefore he sins more lightly, who intemperately lives, than he who fasts to this end.

**(4)** *Let it not be *scandalous*, which happens when others who do not fast are contemned, as if those fasting were of better condition in the eyes of God, who is a *spirit* and *whose fasts do not need indigence*. Which matter offends others, so that they think they have gravely sinned, since they too have not observed a similar fast — whence *opus operatum* and *ostentation* are worked from fasting.

[*Ridicule not thy brother fasting, nor him who does not fast, that thou mayst be able to eat*: — *Ecclesiast.* 8:15.]

**(5)** *Let it not be *inept*, when someone from an inept end (as they do who to avert the pain of teeth abstain from the eating of meats in the highest festivities, and who for similar milder diseases, or others fast on certain feasts of the saints, as those who on the day of *Saint Barbara* live on bread and water only, that they may not die without participation of the sacraments — partly out of gullibility, partly out of self-love, so that this their work they may object to God; that they may not die evilly).*  Which follies among the Romanists are not infrequent, and are gathered by *Lorich* in *Thesauro theol.* voce *ieiunium* n. 10.

*With these cautions rightly observed, private fasting can be undertaken rightly and without sin.*

### Case X. What are the general virtues which are required in fasting, that it may be pleasing to God?

**Respondeo.** Although we have already treated some things about *private fastings*, yet *general* things still remain to be applied to all species of fastings. Three chiefly there are, which make every fast *unpleasing in the sight of God*: (1) *impiety*; (2) *hypocrisy*; (3) *inhumanity*.

*Impiety* is when from fasting men place *merit and expiation of sins*. For nothing that is ours can *to expiation through Christ* be added or opposed, since Christ alone claims for himself all parts of our salvation. Therefore those who fasted in this way are said to have *fasted to themselves, not to the Lord*, that they might set forth this work of theirs to God — as of these the Prophet complains (Isa 58:3): *why have we fasted, and thou hast not seen? — why have we afflicted our souls, and thou hast not observed?*

Therefore *to that impiety* the *true ends of fastings*, of which we spoke above, should be opposed. *For at fasting will be lightly, taking with him*, says *Augustine* (lib. de moribus *Manichaeorum* c. 13), *if we not — with the mockeries of the Papists — fast so, that we might satisfy God*.

*Hypocrisy* is, when men fast, and *glory of men they seek*, so that they may condemn others not fasting — like the *Pharisee*, of whom *Christ* speaks (Matt 6:16): *when ye fast, be not sad, as the hypocrites: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast*.

True fasting is not from sadness of mind, but from *joy of spirit* to proceed, nor from *contempt* of others, but from *examination of one's own*. Because so is fasting. *If thou fastest*, says *Basil*, *as ancient nightingales serenely and alacrious excipe, nec vertere neque lacrimare, but with mind well composed, spirit well fastened, subterrestrial to the animate soul penetrating some illuminates, delighted, entertains; softens the tongue, praesumit strenuous* (Serm. 1 *de jejun.*). That is: *fastings, which alacrious and merry, bear things away*.

Many err, when *plenty of pleasure of fasting they seek* — an *absurdity* which *Augustine* (*Sermone quotam*) observes: *at the time when the flesh was to be chastised, so much sweetness they promised to the flesh, so provided for it in food, sic captabantur voluptates, quadragesimal quasi ipsi essent tempori et anno, ut in inanibus mundi rebus vivere, and utilibus laboribus vestibus, vix possent sentire jejunia sua*.

If therefore in all divine cult, so in fastings also, *hypocrisy* is to be avoided: for men can be deceived and deluded — *God however who sees the heart, is not deceived*.

*Inhumanity* consists in this, that in fasting one gives the *field a foot*, moderation in food and drink adhibits, since he *neglects other parts of penitence*.

[*They who from foods abstain but do evil, imitate demons, whose food always is not, and to whom this fault is.* — *Anton. in Amoi.*]

For just as *phlebotomy* is not profitable unless the body be first evacuated, so *fasting* is not useful unless the *soul be first purged from vices*. *Great and general is fasting*, writes *Augustine* (Tract. 17 in John): *to abstain from iniquities and illicit pleasures rigidly — which is the perfect fast — that abstaining from the impiety of the world, we may live soberly, justly, and piously in this age*. And *Leo* (Serm. 4 *de Quadrag.*): *not in our abstinence alone stands the sum of fastings, or the fruit of foods withdrawn, unless it be joined with mercy*.

[*Fast from sins, take not the least food of malice, drink not the pleasures of glutton pleasure, kindle not the wine of luxury; fast from evil arts, abstain from evil sermons, do not touch the stolen bread of perverse dogma*, &c. — *Origen*, *Hom. 6 in Lev.*]

These agree with the words of the Lord, by which he reproves the *fasting of the Jews* (Isa 58:9): *in your days of fasting is found your own will, and all your debtors ye repeat; behold, to strifes and contentions ye fast, and ye strike with an impious fist: fast not as ye have done up to this day, that ye may make your clamor to be heard on high. Is this the fasting that I have chosen, that a man should afflict his soul? — is it to bend his head as a circle, and to make sackcloth and ashes his bed? — will you call this a fast, and a day accepted to the Lord? Is not this rather the fast which I have chosen: dissolve the bonds of impiety, lose the bands of the yoke, and let the oppressed go free, and break every yoke*.

Since therefore with true fasting is conjoined *innocence of life, hatred of sin, love of virtue, and alms* (whence that saying: *fasting without alms is like a lamp without oil* — *Caesar. ad monachos*), *chastity, humility, patience, ignoring or compassion* (which *Augustine* called *a species of alms*): with these *virtues as with jewels* the *true fast is adorned*, in whose expression, of *all the members* he had capacity of sanctity — as *D. Bernard* elegantly (Serm. 3 *de quadrag.*): *if only gluttony sinned, only fasting; if however the other members have sinned, why do they too not fast? Let the eye fast from illicit sights; let the tongue fast from detraction and rumors; let the tongue fast from detraction; let the hands fast from illicit works; let the soul fast from vices. This is the perfect fasting, since if by external abstinence from foods we contend, and — with respect to the Lord — from the heart the vices we retain, we shall have no utility from the fast*.

[*Right life more than the rest of things all profits. Right life however I call, not the labor of fastings, nor cilice, nor recumbency in ashes; but if thou art merciful, if with thy money thou dost bind the wounds of thy neighbor, if the hungry with thy bread thou dost nourish, if thou art superior to wrath, if empty glory thou dost not concupisce, if by envy thou art not deceived.* — *Chrysostom*, Hom. 47 *ad populum*.

*Voluntarily also a fast to me pleases*, says the Lord, *if it is meet — be it granted to me to speak from the primitive primitive fathers elegantly to add — that the just fast will subdue the flesh to the spirit, drives back concupiscences, extinguishes the ardors of the eye, kindles the light of chastity*. So *Chrysostom* (lib. 5 *in Matt*): *fasting is the aid of prayer* (Hom. 1 *de poenit.*): *fasting to the body is nutriment to the soul*. So *Athanasius* (*de jejun.*): *fasting heals sicknesses; dries up defluxions; drives away demons; expels evil cogitations; renders the mind more brilliant; purifies the heart; the body sanctifies*, — *Cyprianus* (*De jejun. et tentat.*): *the fasting of Christ, if with discretion is exacted, tames all rebellion of flesh, tyranny of the throat spoils and disarms. Fasting closes and controls extraordinary motions in a wooden block, and constrains and binds vagrant appetites. Fasting is adorned with humility, makes servants of God, contemners of the world. Fasting cleanses the flesh, azyma, hardens, decomposes, consumes and dries out putrefactions which from fat proceed. Fasting is fed by the delicacies of Scripture, refreshed by contemplation, stabilized by grace, nourished by celestial bread. To Daniel the interpretation of dreams is revealed through fasting; three boys in Babylonia are guarded uninjured from the fire. Moses in the mountain for forty days perseveres in fasting, and the familiarity of colloquy with God he attained; Elijah abstains from foods, and in the wilderness is fed miraculously. So Origen (in c. 17 Matt): those persevering in prayers and fastings expel the malignant spirits*.

*Therefore, it is well, when to the Lord one spares, of what is superfluous in his hand.* — Horace, *l. 4 Od. 6*.

*Therefore, if it be well to the stomach, if to the feet, to the sides — nothing can royal riches add to this.* — *Horace* lib. 1 Ep. 12.

*Therefore, live not to eat, but eat, that you may be able to live.* — Juvenal.

*It is agreeable to fasting*, says *Hippocrates* in *Stobaeus* (Serm.).

*Therefore, such temperance is to be adhibited, that our body neither should saturity excite, nor immoderate hunger too much debilitate.* — *Fulgentius* to *Prob.*

*Therefore, in sober victual let one behold the frugality of life.* — *Pluto* (*Instit.*): *just as of the Germans of old is praised frugality*, because *their food was simple, wild fruits and thick milk their dainties*. — *Cornel. Tac. de moribus Germ.*

*Therefore, fasting of the body is nutriment of the soul* — *Chrysostom* Hom. 1 *de poenit.* *Mother of health is abstinence.* — *Jerome*. *By quiet abstinence many diseases are cured.* — *Celsus.*

*Wine is given to us, that we may delight in it, not that we should be dishonored by it; that we may laugh, not that we should be laughed at; that we may be healthy, not that we should be sick; for correcting the body's health, not that with our soul's virtue we should be prostrated.* — *Chrysostom* Hom. 71 *ad pop. Antioch.*]

**So much of the chief difficulties which concerning cult and religion can disturb consciences: and thus we finish the second book of our tractate.**

— ❦ —

# Liber III. Toward Celestial Spirits

*De actionibus hominis circa spiritus coelestes — On the actions of man toward celestial spirits (angels, demons, astrology, magic, divinations).*

## Continuation

Above we said that the actions of man are either *toward God and religion*, or *toward celestial spirits*, or *toward the neighbor*: in all which the end of our treatise is to fortify the mind of man, that he sin not.

Concerning God and religion we have thus far treated, so far as for the reason of our institute suffices. Now there follow *celestial spirits created by God*; by which voice not only good and evil angels do we understand, but also the influences of the stars: for these too the Philosophers call *spirits*, when they dispute whether spirits superior to us influence our spirits. And although man is visible: yet with those invisible spirits we breathe out that there is great communion for him; nor is the operation of spirits about any creature of God more conspicuous than in the body or soul of man. Actions likewise of man are scarcely anywhere more prone to erring, than when about those invisible spirits they are occupied. Therefore must the mind of man be fortified, that he be cautious in this genus, lest he wound conscience.

Various things however here come into consideration. For *spirits* are either *rational*, or *irrational*. Rational are either *good* or *evil*. The good are *the holy angels*; the evil, the *cacodemons* or *devils*.

We must therefore treat here of the *cult and honor of the good angels*, and of the *works of the evil*, which are either *external*, where of magic and sorceries, of superstitious actions, of divinations, of possessed persons, of specters and the like: or *internal*, as evil suggestions and temptations, either to sinning, or to despairing, after a sin has been perpetrated.

*Irrational* spirits are the *influences of the stars*, where of Astrology and its annexes, how far they befit a pious man or not, must be said.

Concerning all which in this book I will treat, so much as the Lord shall have given: which shall seem sufficient for our institute.

*May the Lord our God by his Holy Spirit teach us in the way of true religion, direct our steps to good, and bid evils to be as far as possible removed from us. Amen.*

## Chapter I. On Cases of Conscience Concerning Association with Good Angels

Those whom Scripture on account of *nature* calls *spirits*, these on account of *office* it calls *angels*, since they are the *messengers* and *legates of God*, of whom Ps 104:4: *who maketh his angels spirits; and his ministers a flaming fire*. Of which place *Augustine* writes: *whose name is nature? spirit is. whose office? angel is. Just as in man the name of nature, man; of office, soldier: name of nature, husband; of office, magistrate*.

This name is *common* to all rational spirits, which *all God created* good, holy, just, and blessed; but the *lapse* made a distinction, so that those who stood in their integrity, remained *good*; those who fell out, *evil angels*.

**The good angels** are called *angels of God* (2 Sam 14:20); *holy angels* (Rev 14:10); *angels of light* (2 Cor 11:14); *elect angels* (1 Tim 5:21); *angels of the virtue of God* (2 Thess 1:7).

**Great is the power** of good angels, though distributed by their gradations, so that one is more powerful than another, in respect of which they are called *thrones, dominations, principalities, powers* (Col 1:16). They can do all things in corporeal matters, whatever by their nature can happen. *One angel slew all the firstborn in Egypt* (Exod 12:29); *one angel cut down the whole army of Sennacherib* (2 Kgs 19); *an angel moved the pool* to cure those who descended into it (John 5:4); *an angel opened the iron gate of the prison, well fortified with bolts, and led out the Apostle Peter* (Acts 12); *an angel wards off the flames of fire from the bodies of the three youths in the Babylonian furnace* (Dan 3); *an angel stopped up the mouths of the lions* (Dan 6:22).

[*One angel is more powerful than the whole world.* — *Luther*, sermon 1 on the *Table of Discourses*.]

Angels *move mobile bodies from place to place*, as an angel moved *Philip* (Acts 8:39), and *Habakkuk* (Dan 14:35), and *Ezekiel* (Ezek 8:3), for every creature obeys angelic power in local motion.

They have power *over the internal and external senses of men*. That which is said of the internal senses, is manifest from this, that an *angel appeared to Joseph in a dream* (Matt 2:19), where the external senses were bound: in sleep they admonish and exhort men to whom God sends them; the phantasms of things sometime seen or heard within they excite; many things which by oblivion were thought abolished, they recall to memory. As to external senses, there are two illustrious examples in Scripture, how first *they closed the eyes of the Sodomites*, lest they should enter the house of Lot (Gen 19:11); and *the Syrian army*, lest they should see *Elisha*, who was in the midst of them (2 Kgs 6:18); then, how they *deceived also the ears of the enemies*, as was done (2 Kgs 7:6) in the army of the Syrians, where the Lord by the work of angels *excited a sound as of many horses and armed soldiers* in the camp of the Syrians, so that they seemed to themselves to hear the tumult of chariots, horses, and a most numerous army: hearing which, they betook themselves to flight, abandoning the city which they had long besieged.

And although the power also of the evil angels is great, yet greater is that of the good, which even over the very *cacodemons* have power; therefore whenever a battle between good and evil angels is described, always the good are read to conquer, as in Dan 10, Rev 12, and in the history of *Tobit*, where *Raphael bound the demon Asmodeus* with chains (Tob 8:3). Whence it follows that the good angels, through whom we are guarded, are always more powerful than those by whom we are assailed. For, as *Gregory* says: *the powers of the angels are subject to the adverse virtues. All however of their power is subject to divine authority, so that neither more nor less can they work, than God shall have willed, whose will in heaven the holy angels always do*. So in Ps 103 the *power of angels is joined with the will of God: bless the Lord, all ye his angels, that excel in strength, that do his commandments, hearkening unto the voice of his word: bless ye the Lord, all ye his hosts; ye ministers of his, that do his pleasure*.

This their power the angels exert in *offices divinely destined to them*. These offices are threefold: one *in respect of God the Creator*; another *in respect of the whole universe*; a third *in respect of men, especially the pious*.

**In respect of God** they are created, that they may minister to him, execute his commands, and praise his name without end. Of their ministry it is read (Dan 7:10): *thousands of thousands ministered unto him*. Of their execution of the divine will it is read (Ps 103:20): *bless the Lord all ye his angels, that excel in strength, that do his commandments*. Of the praise which they sing to God it is read (Isa 6; Rev 4:8). They are also *ministers of Christ*, to whom they were present at his nativity (Luke 2), at the beginning of his ministry (Matt 4:11), at the passion (Luke 22:43), at the resurrection (Matt 28:2), at the ascension (Acts 1:10). They themselves sing the hymn (Rev 5:11). And of their works some he will use on the last day, in gathering the elect and separating the evil ones (Matt 13).

**In respect of the whole universe**, of the angels' office is not only to move the celestial bodies, but also to preserve this whole aspect of things; which indeed is proper to God, who alone bears all things by the word of his power (Heb 1:3), yet it pleased him to execute this his conservation through his holy angels, by whom the celestial orbs are moved, the Philosophers laid down, and from Scripture it is known that one is destined to one, another to another *province*. *Daniel* enumerates the *angels* of the *Persians* and the *angels of the Grecians*, with whom the angel spoke with him fought over each one's province (Dan 10:13). Hence *Clement of Alexandria* (Stromat. lib. 6): *singular in a most sacred manner are distributed also the presidencies of the angels through the individual nations and cities*. Which sentence is also of *Hieronymus* on Daniel.

The *Hebrews* extend these offices of the angels further to the parts of the world. For (as they say in the books of the *Cabala*) they attribute to individual planets, to each sign of the Zodiac, to each part of the world, to each wind, its presiding angels. Those who preside over the planets they name by these names: over *Saturn* presides *Zephiel*; over *Jupiter Zadkiel*; over *Mars Camael*; over the *Sun Raphael*; over *Venus Haniel*; over *Mercury Michael*; over the *Moon Gabriel*. This did *Trismegistus* also, who calls the *seven governors of the world* by his own names.

Over the *signs of the Zodiac* they preside: *Aries Malchidiel*, *Taurus Asmodel*, *Gemini Ambriel*, *Cancer Muriel*, *Leo Verchiel*, *Virgo Hamaliel*, *Libra Zuriel*, *Scorpio Barchiel*, *Sagittarius Adnachiel*, *Capricorn Haniel*, *Aquarius Gambiel*, *Pisces Barchiel*.

Angels are set over the *four winds and the four parts of the world*: to the *east* wind is set *Michael*; to the *west Raphael*; to the *north Gabriel*; to the *south Nariel*. To the *elements* also they place angels: to *fire Seraph*, to *air Cherub*, to *water Tharsis*, to *earth Ariel*.

[*The Chaldeans call angels of the sun, and of the dominion of the moon, angels manifest of God at things which by the influx of the celestial angels are engendered in these inferior parts.*]

Which although we recite from foreign origins, since the curiosity of men in things not-most-necessary is thus greedy, yet does not appear expressed in Scripture.

**The chief office of the angels** is that which *respects men*, and which is committed to them; where indeed it is not to be securitated, what many hold, that to each man a certain angel is his own guardian and ruler assigned. Whence is that of *Jerome* on Matt 18: *great is the dignity of souls, so that each has an angel deputed to its guardianship*. But although God, for his immense goodness, allows also the reprobate sometimes to enjoy the protection of good angels, of a certain angel however destined to each man scarcely so much is written in Scripture, for Scripture (Heb 1:14) restricts the guardianship and ministry of the angels *to the faithful*, when the angels are called *ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation*; and (Matt 18:10) *their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven*; and (Ps 91:11) *he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee*; and (Luke 16:22) *the angels are read to have carried Lazarus into the bosom of Abraham* etc.

Of the pious therefore are the ministers, the holy angels: to whom, as soon as through the laver of regeneration they are made sons of God, God has added holy Angels, as *paedagogues*: as *Bernard* names them (Serm. 12 on Ps 91:1 *He who dwelleth*, etc.).

Of the *paedagogues* however is a threefold office. **1.** *To guard the boys of faith* committed to their care, lest they suffer any harm. So the holy angels, since first we were born, keep holy watches for us against the force of the devil, as far as expedient for us they know. Therefore *guardians* of ours (*custodes nostri*) they are called (Ps 91:11). They guard our bodies, lest they be torn by the devils, lest they fall, lest they suffer any detriment of any members; they guard our going out and coming in (Judith 13:15, 20); they accompany us in journeys, which happened to *Jacob* (Gen 32:1), *Eleazar of Abraham* (Gen 24), *Moses* (Exod 3), *Israel* in the midst of the enemies of Egypt (Exod 14), etc.; they guard our substance and our little wealth, lest without the permission of God anything hurt them, which the devil would have done in the *history of Job*, that God had built a hedge round him and his house, and his whole substance.

This happens to the faithful on account of *Christ*, through whom they are made sons of God, who came into the world to destroy the works of the devil.

**2.** *To direct us to salutary counsels, to raise, to erect the fallen, to remove obstacles*. Even now the angels present themselves in this way, which of old they did most illustriously with visions in sleep by internal inspiration. So the angel manifested the mystery of the incarnation to the *most Blessed Virgin* (Luke 1); angels were the first who preached the nativity of our Saviour (Luke 2); an angel taught the *shepherds* what they should do (Luke 2); the angel warned *Joseph* to flee into Egypt (Matt 2:13, 20); *the angel* instructed the *magi*, as from the historical fact appears (Matt 2); the angel of the Lord *snoring* awakened the *shepherds* to go into the way of the commandments; the angel forth-drew *Peter* from the prison, that longer he might serve in the divinely offered office (Acts 12:7). *The angel* is *Uriel* who first (as *Peucer* interprets) opened to *Ezra* the *scripture* which he read (Acts 8:29). The *angel of Cornelius* announces to him that his prayers were heard, and Peter was to be summoned (Acts 10:22, 31). The angel *in the form of a man* exhorts *Paul* to hasten to succor the *Macedonians* with the preaching of the Gospel (Acts 16:9). And even today too the holy angels, in various ways as it shall have seemed to them, are *directors* of the pious.

**3.** *They render likewise operations of hostility to enemies*, when not only those whose guardians they are they snatch from present peril, but also strike enemies with terror. Thus one angel struck down 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians in one night (2 Kgs 19:35). Not only did they refute Ahaziah's counsel through the good angel to Elijah (2 Kgs 1:3); they scattered the army of the king of Assyria into peril (2 Kgs 19:35). In the extreme agony of death also they console the pious, and lead their souls into the *bosom of Abraham* (Luke 16:22).

Since therefore so many are the benefits of the holy angels toward us, pleasant it is for us to converse with them, but cautious ought to be the conversation, that we neither too greatly by honoring them dishonor God, the giver of angels; nor much less against those very angels sin.

We shall therefore propose *Cases* on how our association with them should be arranged.

**Casus I. Whether first of all it must be solicited that we retain those faithful paedagogues, the holy angels, with us?**

*Reply.* Great is the mercy of God, that not only he himself is our protector, but has also sent forth armies of holy angels into our ministry, who *encompass* us and *keep us in our ways*. *Give the countenance of thy Spirit, O God: and lest anything be vacant in the celestial from the work of thy solicitude, thou dost send those blessed Spirits into ministry for us*, exclaimed *Bernard* on Ps 91.

In place of this singular benefit, God promised to his people (Exod 23:20): *Behold, I send an Angel before thee, to keep thee in the way, and to bring thee into the place which I have prepared thee*.

Which words although properly of the Son of God, that great and uncreated Angel, are to be understood: yet he himself is not without the accompaniment of the created angels, nor is he his bride and matron faithful without such company: *the accompaniment of the maids befits the bride ascending, as of the angels the Lord*, says *Bernard*, serm. 41 on the Canticles.

*Sic ergo omnis Spes et Salvatio nostra dependet a solo Christo; sed candidatum hunc exercitum sanctorum angelorum* — *So then all our hope and salvation depends on Christ alone; but this select army of holy angels God has ordained for our use*, and to them has given in commands, that they hold us in their care.

Then let us pray, lest on account of our sins the angels take this protection so quickly from us; but that *always he send his good angel before us in fear and trembling of the greatness of his arm, that they fear who are against us* (Judith 6:15).

*Yea let us rejoice that always they rejoice over us, and that we always may rise up through them in us: that we may confess all together to thy holy name, O creator of men and of angels*. — Augustine, Soliloq. c. 27.

Afterwards let us so institute our life, that always we have God propitious and the angels our friends: which cannot happen to us more happily, than if the presence and inspection of God and of the holy angels over all our works we set before our eyes. God is he, who *My beloved is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice.* (Cant 2:9). What is it, to stand behind the wall, and through the lattices to see, than so to see, that another whom thou seest not, thou mayest not notice? God however sees all things which are done in secret: *The LORD is in his holy temple, the LORD's throne is in heaven: his eyes behold, his eyelids try, the children of men.* (Ps 11:4). But *he who from far off my thoughts is judge and witness* (Jer 17:9-10). Nevertheless sometimes he is as if *sleeping* and not seeing (Ps 78:11), therefore so much more the more feared. Angels also are in our circuit, our observers, indices, and witnesses. If therefore before an honest man to commit anything base we are afraid, much more is the presence of the holy angels to be feared, lest anything base be done or said, which by them may be observed to us, so that either they be repelled from us, and become our accusers before God.

So *Seneca* exhorts his *Lucilius* to hold always someone good in view, as if before that one's eyes we live, and act everything as if in his sight: *Some good man to us is to be chosen, and always to be set before eyes, so that so as if before that one seeing we may live, and everything as if by him being seen we may do*.

This did *Epictetus* also teach, that we set up such *guardians* and *paedagogues* to us, and not without merit. *Great part of sins is taken away, if to those sinning a witness stand near. Let the mind have someone whom it may reverence, by whose authority even its secret it may hold sanctified. O happy him! not only when he is present, but also when he is thought of, who amends! O happy who thus of one can be reverent, that to the memory also of him he composes and orders himself. If someone thus can be reverent, quickly indeed he himself will be reverent. Elect therefore Cato; if this seems too rigid to thee, elect Laelius, a man of gentler mien: elect him whose life pleases thee, and prayer, and even those things of his mind before thee bringing forth, so that thou always show him to thyself either as guardian or as example. It is needful, I say, for us to look up to someone, to whose morals ours may erect themselves: unless by rule, thou wilt not correct depravities.* Thus that most wise master of morals.

We more rightly hold those whom God himself has given us as guardians and paedagogues: let us make them also witnesses and judges of our whole life, whose sight if we shall fear, we shall omit many evils. This counsel *Bernard* also suggests to us (Serm. 12 on Ps 91): *Walk cautiously*, says he, *as one to whom holy angels are present, as it has been commanded them in all thy ways. In every diversory, in every corner, to thy angel have reverence. Do not dare, in his presence, that which if I were seeing thou wouldst not dare: or dost thou doubt him to be present, whom thou seest not?* — Yea, God himself has suggested this to us. For when he had said (Exod 23:20): *Behold, I send my angel, who shall go before thee, and keep thee*, immediately he added: *Beware of him, and hear his voice: neither think him to be contemned, for he will not pardon, when thou hast sinned*. And *Sirach* says (5:5): *Say not before the angel, "there is no providence," lest God be angry*.

*Let us be devout, let us be grateful for so great guardians; let us love them as much as we can, as much as we ought.* — Bernard, serm. 21 on the Canticles.

As however are to be *avoided* those *snares* whereby the angels can be driven from us: so must we *imitate* the virtues in the angels conspicuous, whereby also we may be made *similar to them*, and they our friends.

**The first virtue is *obedience*.** For as they know perfectly the will of God, so they never depart from it in all things; therefore *Christ* bids us to pray that the will of the Lord be done in earth as it is done in heaven. There is no office so servile, to which those *ministering* spirits are not prepared. At the command of the Lord they go to the three youths in the fiery furnace; to Daniel in the pit of lions; to Peter in prison; they journey with Tobias, accompany *Hagar* and *Elijah* into the desert; in nothing are they averse to God their creator, but as he himself hates and punishes the sins of men, and departs from sinners, so also they. Such an office does God require also from us: which although it cannot be perfect and everywhere absolute, as is the angelic, yet also to him is pleasing when begun, provided it be voluntary and prompt to serve God perfectly in all things, if it were in our powers.

[*Virtue obedient: the ears the moved-one bears; the tongue to the voice, the feet to be gone, the hands to be worked, and the sight within collects, so that it may execute the command of the one working.* — Bernard, *De praecepto et dispens.*]

Such zeal and obedience the angels advance: but those who resist the will of God by their sins from proposition, from these they depart, and the malignant spirit works in the sons of disobedience (Eph 2:2).

**The second virtue is *humility*.** For although on account of the spiritual nature and constancy in good they are much more excellent than we, yet they lower themselves to our ministries, nor is there a man so vile who does not have his angel, provided he be pious. For truly he despises none of his condition, but *impious* only from the guardianship and patronage he excludes.

And although there are grades of angelic dignity — some indeed are thrones, some principalities, some dominations, some powers, some archangels, some angels — yet all are *Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?* (Heb 1:14). For false is what *Thomas* teaches (I q.111 art.1) that the *Cherubim* and *Seraphim* are *not sent forth for our ministry, but only the inferiors are* — the *Cherubim* namely and *Seraphim* from intimate ministry retire. But this is against the general pronouncement common to all angels, whom Scripture calls *ministering spirits, sent forth* on account of those who *obtain salvation*. And *Cyril* said on Isa 6: *as if it were natural for all superior spirits to serve inferior ones, thinking that they are not less to serve, thinking it an honor. Far from these is pride, whereby to no one willingly do they serve; but from the ministry of even lesser ones they abstain.*

[*The good angels are called on this account attendant, since to a work of this magnitude of salvation they are deputed, that from the guardians of the humble they administer and rule all which are of the highest good; from the highest, evils of misery.* — Bernard, serm. of the Nativity.]

The more they are of a more excellent nature, so much the more they submit themselves: since they acknowledge themselves to be born to the offices of others, and to be enriched with divinely given gifts, which in the Son of God himself and the holy angels is most conspicuous. The lower however and more abject anyone is in the eyes of God, so much the more he swells up: as appears in the *foolish*, in the demons and in *the devil himself*, who *the prince of all the proud* is called (Job 41:25).

Who therefore desires familiarity and ministry of the holy angels, let him not swell up, let him deny his offices to none, but to the humble let him accommodate himself, as he himself will be great in the eyes of God and of the angels.

[*If thou wouldst please the Angels of God, be an elect virtue* (Rev 3:7). *If thou throwest thee down, God elevates thee; if thou extollest thee, God throws thee down.* — Augustine, serm. 21 *de verbo Domini*. *A high thing shall be to Christ; if to thee is life vile. If thou breakest great things, God breaks thee. All that is unstable, is compressed to be more; those pressed together, remain* (Ps 30).]

**The third virtue is *chastity*.** The holy angels abhor from man's uncleanness; they love chaste conversations, chaste morals and gestures; but the devil is the *unclean spirit* (Luke 11:24). Whoever therefore rejoices in the friendship of the holy angels, let him study chastity in every part of his life. That which those who have written the *Lives of the Fathers* wished to teach, whether by history or by an *apologue* about a certain holy man, who having first seen the angels standing among the monks conversing, and them retreating a little way, saw a great herd of swine wallowing among them. Wondering vehemently about this thing, and diligently inquiring the cause, he detected that they had at first begun to mix spiritual and divine matters in mutual conversation, but then by lapse of tongue they had come to various colloquies of talk. Which that holy man hearing, by revelation made known, vehemently deterred them from such colloquies, and to honest and salutary things exhorted, in which the angels willingly are wont to intermix.

[*The chastity is uncorrupt kept in check by* — *1. sobriety; 2. labor; 3. austerity of cultivation; 4. inhibition of the senses; 5. rarity of speech with honesty.* — Cassiodorus on Matt.]

**The fourth virtue is *concord***, which is among the holy angels of the highest degree, distinguishing them from the fallen. Let there be therefore among us mutual love, one honoring another, *Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.* (Phil 2:3); brotherly one in heart and one in soul. For such is the conjunction of the holy spirits, who by broils and strifes are put to flight, like bees by smoke. *Angels of peace* they are, who promote peace to the peaceful; but by broils and dissensions of men they are saddened.

[*Of what tenor is the harmony in the singing, of the same is the concord in the church. Cannot have concord with Christ, who has willed to be discordant with a Christian.* — Augustine, *de verbis Domini*; from *Elect. Dei* c.12; see John 17:22; 1 Cor 11:16; Matt 5:9.]

**The fifth virtue is *devotion* and *assiduity in prayers***. For they too incessantly adore God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all things which in them are, and the fountains of the waters. They are present at the prayers of the pious, which they bear up to God, and add their own to them (Tob 12:11; Zech 1:12). *Let us believe the holy angels to stand near those who pray*, says *Bernard*, *offering to God the vows and prayers of men, if without deceit be lifted up pure hands*. Let us therefore pray also with them, if our prayers are far from our defects, and the guardianship of the angels our solace.

[*In the morning ought to be prayed, that the future may be governed by strengths; in the evening ought to be prayed, that past things be remitted, and things done well be conserved.*]

These are the chief virtues of the holy angels, in which we can be made imitators of them. He pleases them, as *Bernard* says (Serm. 12 on Ps 91), *those which in us to be found delight, as sobriety, chastity, alms; and in songs of gemitus over all things, they demand truth and peace*.

[*Let us usurp the office, whose fortitude we share.* — Bernard, serm. 7 on the Canticles.]

To this is added, what *Bernard* says (Serm. 12 on Ps 91 *He who dwelleth*): *Invoke thy guardian, thy leader, thy helper, in opportunities and in tribulation: cry to him; say, "Lord, save us; we perish."* And in the sermon *On the triple guardianship*: *from the holy angels help must be sought in occult passages, in frequency of tears, that those under most eminent majesty they offer our prayers, and bear back to us grace, since they are ministering spirits, sent forth on account of us, that we may obtain the inheritance of salvation*.

*Bellarmine* on the strength of these arguments propugns *invocation of the holy angels* (lib. 1 *de Sanctis beatis*, cap. 19); of which afterwards.

**Casus II. Since therefore so many are the benefits of the holy angels toward us, is it right they be honored by us through adoration, or invoked, that from them we may implore help?**

*Reply.* To many it seems that this is done without sin, both on account of the pre-eminence of the angelic nature, and on account of their beneficence toward us. For as an *pious man*, to interpose his prayers before God for me, I ask, so also from piety it does not seem foreign, if the angel of the Lord, whom I know to be present to me, I compel, that from his help and intercession with God me he may aid; especially since of angels it is read that they pray for us (Zech 1:12), and that they offer our prayers to God (Tob 12:11), and their prayers with ours join (Rev 8:3-4). To which is added what *Bernard* says (Serm. 12 on Ps 91 *He who dwelleth*): *invoke thy guardian, thy leader, thy helper, in opportunities and in tribulation: cry to him, say, "Lord, save us; we perish."*

*Bellarmine* by certain arguments propugns invocation of the holy angels (lib. 1 *de Sanctis beatis*, c. 19); of which afterwards.

We however by sacred learning taught, honor the offices of the holy angels indeed, but that we may either *adore* them, or *invoke* them, that they with their help may aid us with their prayers, we consider *impious*. For **first** we have express *command*, that God alone is to be adored, so *Christ* says (Matt 4): *the Lord thy God shalt thou adore, and him alone shalt thou serve*: which precept is much clearer than that by any glosses of human genius it can be obscured; and the reason is manifest, since the cult of *invocation* is so proper to God alone, that *invocation* is sometimes put for every cult of God, as in that saying which *Paul* took from the prophet Joel: *whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved* (Rom 10:13; Joel 2:32).

**2.** No example is extant in Scripture, that the *holy angels* have been so adored by any of the pious: since however many with the holy angels have been conversed, and by great benefits affected. *Jacob* strengthened his sons in the camps (Gen 32); *Peter* in prison (Acts 12); they did not invoke them.

**3.** We have *express prohibition*, lest we adore the angels; and that too from the angel himself. For when *John* on account of some preposterous devotion before the angel would fall down on his knees, about to adore him, the *angel* prohibited him, and said (Rev 22:9): *see thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren the prophets, having the testimony of Jesus*. Something similar (Rev 19:10). Adore God alone.

**4.** *Adoration* and *fiducia* are most closely conjoined, according to that Apostolic saying (Rom 10). Therefore *Augustine* writes (De vera religione c. 55): *when we invoke saints as friends of God, in no way in them ourselves we ought to fix or to hope*: so also in no angel of them do we place hope or fiducia; for this belongs to God alone (Ps 118:6; Rom 15:12); *I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images.* (Isa 42:8).

**5.** *Cult of angels* is that ancient error, which *Paul* reprehended in the pseudo-apostles among the Colossians, foreign to Christians (Col 2:18): *let no man beguile you in humility and religion of angels*; which the orthodox fathers concerning the cult and veneration of angels understood, so *Augustine* (De haeres. cap. 39) refers heretics who cult holy angels, and them call *angelic*. *Epiphanius*, De haer., c. 60. Same in cap. 39.

**6.** *Council of Laodicea* prohibited (can. 35): *A Christian ought not to leave the Church of God, and to depart to angels of names* (which is *nomenclatura*, i.e., *to invoke angels*); *and if anyone occultly to this idolatry be found devoted, let him be anathematized, since he abandoned the Lord our Jesus Christ, and to idolatry approached*. And so this canon *Theodoret* on the invocation of angels chiefly interprets (cap. 2 on Colossians): *long did this vice remain in Phrygia and Pisidia, whence circular synods gathered at Laodicea, by law prohibited that angels not be invoked*.

**7.** *The holy Fathers* laid down that it belongs to the *evil* angels, who *seek* to be adored; good angels indeed refused for themselves *sacrifice to be offered*, or *divine cult* to be shown: so *Augustine* (De vera religione c. 55; and De civ. Dei lib. 10, c. 16; and lib. 10, cont. Manich. c. 21; and *In enarrat.* Ps. 96). *Augustine* also reprehends those who *look up to angels, worship, invoke*, when they are our fellow servants, *ministering spirits*.

These all from Scripture and testimony of the church are firmest, by which are solidly convinced in that thing, all those who angels — by whatever name they be called — beyond piety compel.

*Bellarmine* however holds certain testimonies of Scripture, by which he dares even to palliate this idolatry. **1.** He produces the place from Gen 48:16, where *Jacob* blessing the sons of *Joseph* thus speaks: *let the angel, who has redeemed me from all evils, bless these boys*. Here says (Bellarmine): *Jacob invoked an angel*.

*Reply.* But it is not treated here of a created angel, but of the very Son of God, whom in Scripture also *angel* is called, it is known.

For not of created angels, but of the very God is it to bless men: not a created angel, but God himself snatched *Jacob* from all evils. It refers however to the history of the angel-wrestler in Gen 32, who himself there calls himself God, saying to the Patriarch: *not with men, but with God hast thou struggled, and prevailed* (v. 28), whence also *Hosea*, when he mentioned this history, calls that *angel Jehovah* (Hos 12:5). *God snatched Jacob from the hand of his brother Esau* (Gen 32:24; 33:2); and *that angel*, from whom he beseeches a blessing for the boys, he expressly calls *God, in whose sight walked the fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob* (Gen 48:15); *God, who fed him from his youth up to the present day* (Gen 48:15) — which surely can befit no created angel.

*Athanasius* (Serm. 4 contra Arianos): *Never has anyone been read to receive of God and of an angel, or of any of the created things*. *Nor has anyone conceived this form of prayer: God and Angel* etc. *That therefore Jacob in blessing the grandsons Ephraim and Manasseh spoke in this manner: God who fed me from my boyhood up to this day, the Angel who freed me from all evils, bless these boys — he did not join anyone of the created angels, and asked the sons of Angels through them; nor did he associate God with a foreign God, but from an angel his blessing petitioned for his grandsons: but since expressly he spoke of the Angel, who had freed him from all evils, he sufficiently declared, not of the created Angels he intended, but of the Son of the Father, whom he associated with the Father in prayers, through whom God frees whom he wills. Him alone did he know as the Angel of the great counsel of the Father: nor another, but the Son himself, whom he blesses, who frees from evils, in his words he expressed*.

*Cyril* (Thesauri lib. 5, c. 1): *No one will suffer patiently those who say: True God, Father of the Angel, of the word, of grace, someone who directs thy way, etc. But wherefore Patriarch Jacob blessing the grandsons of Joseph's sons says: God who fed me from infancy up to this day, and the Angel, who frees me from all evils, bless these boys? Behold, God is named and the Angel with him, and indeed in the singular number to bless is said. If they confess the prophetic Spirit was adorned, they do not deny holy Jacob was a man, on whom of the same grace how did they concede, that the Angel by the will of God he thought could bless with God? Do not therefore, they say, blame the holy man: but rather the sense of his true words inquire, whose he was, they think. But if he was not sane, why by his authority to confirm dogmas do they use?* But we not out of contempt of heretics, we expound the words of the Patriarch briefly. *The Spirit therefore that pious one led to the truth of doctrines, first prayed to God that the sons might be blessed; likewise also the Angel who freed him from all evils, so that by God the Father he might signify, by the Angel however the Word of the Father. For he did not ignore that his name is Angel of great counsel.*

**2.** He brings forth the place (Job 5:1): *call now, if there be any who will answer thee, and to which of the saints wilt thou turn?*. And adds *Bellarmine*: *where by the name of saints he understands angels, as Chrysostom expounds*.

*Reply.* The words are of *Eliphaz the Themanite*, who overcome by the vehemence of Job's crushing, and cursing the day of his birth, calls to memory the examples of the holy men, *Abraham, Isaac, Jacob*, and similar, of whom no one outside the darts of calamities was so constituted. The Hebrew therefore voice *kara*, does not signify *to invoke*, but *to name, to recount*. Nothing therefore here about angels, nothing about *invocation of angels* is held.

*Augustine*, in an annotation on Job, though he retained from a vicious version the vocable *invoca*, yet holds nothing about invocation of angels, but this at least on those words notes: *unless those who by the world are of pure heart shall answer*: which annotation not the holy men nor the angels, but only God looks to, who them alone, who are pure in heart in the world, hears.

**3.** Job 33:23 says: *if there is an Angel speaking for him, one of a thousand, he will announce to a man righteousness, and will pity him*. And by this proof *Bellarmine* wants that at that time was the custom to invoke angels.

But arises an error from a vicious version: for in the fountains it is not held, that an angel with God speaks for a man, much less that on that account he is to be invoked, that he may speak or intercede for us. But so the words hold: *if there be over him an angel eloquent, or interpreters one of a thousand, to indicate to the man his rectitude, and to have mercy on him, and to have said, "redeem him,"* etc. The sense of the passage is: *if there be by him a Prophet of the word, or a minister of the word* (which as angels in Scripture to be named it is known) *one out of a thousand, who a man ill of gravity admonishes, that he repent, and by the name and will of God interprets to him, and expounds, what from him God requires, teaches also what is honest, and what iniquitous also, and finally what a flagitious deed, then will have mercy on him God*, etc., *and will free him from his disease*. Of the office therefore of ministers of the word, not of the patronage of the holy angels, is there treated.

Which if greatly it were held in the text, that any angel prays for a man, which however nowhere appears, yet not therefore it must be received, that they on that count, are to be invoked by us. For neither do we deny, that God even through angels sometimes admonishes men, and dissuades from sins, but neither in that text is this said, nor is invocation of holy angels, whom themselves refused, drawn out. Thus by a very frail foundation the papistic dogma about invocation of angels rests.

Therefore let no one this honor, which to God alone is due, and which the holy angels themselves refused to receive, attribute to the angels; meanwhile whatever the angels of their own accord, even unasked, may offer as patronage of ours accept, on which score not the angels are to be solicited, but let thanks be given to the Creator of the angels.

**Casus III. Whether pious men should affect visions and colloquies of the holy angels?**

*Reply.* There have always been, and today too there are, those who to colloquies and visions of angels have attributed much. Of *Natalis*, who many things in the Samosatene heresy fell into, writes *Eusebius* (Hist. eccl. lib. 5, c. 28), that he by holy angels was admonished about his error in sleep, but when he neglectfully received the visions, he was by holy angels through the whole night scourged, and by grievous pains was tortured.

*Jerome* about himself writes to *Eustochium* the virgin, how he was recalled by angels from too much study of profane books, that voice sounding among the scourges: *have mercy on me, O Lord, have mercy on me*, until prostrate before the knees of Christ presiding, those *holy angels who stood by* were praying, that he might grant pardon to the youth.

*Fanatics* today boast of *angelic information*, and a peculiar mode of *evoking angels* they claim, that from them we may learn, as *Sozipatius* first in part of the *Postill*, on the feast of *the Circumcision*, cap. 85, writes about *musicianship*, which the ancients used sober when going to bed, if they discussed and through their angel future things they might know.

We however do not deny, that of old, when God still spoke in many parts and in many manners with his people, of old he himself even used the ministry of the angels, by whose apparitions he made the Patriarchs certain of his grace and will, as was done to *Abraham* (Gen 18:17), *Lot* (Gen 19:1), *Gideon* (Judg 6:11), *Manoah* (Judg 13:3), *Joseph* (Matt 1:20), *Zachariah* (Luke 1:11), *the Blessed Virgin* (Luke 1:26).

With these he spoke either *in sleep*, or *in vision*, or indeed *in body*, though not without some *species and figure of body*, or in rapt-alike-manner, or finally in some *manifest assumption of body*.

When in bodies they appear, they do this either in bodies of nothing created, or from *some preexistent solid matter fashioned*, so that they can be handled or eaten. So the angels ate for Abraham (Gen 18); Peter was awakened by the touch of an angel (Acts 12); with an angel *Jacob* wrestled (Gen 32); or finally in *foreign bodies* naturally their own, which the angel entered.

[continues p. 490 anomaly-note omitted — describing bird-form Zachariah 1:9 with Augustine's *Enchir. ad Laur.* c.59, Zanchius on angels indwelling our bodies (2 Cor 12:7); *others estimate that angels do not mingle blessed with our souls, but as Cyprian says (In prol. super serm. in Deut. of morals: to us and by us they manifest by visible and audible signs, by some reason to help us, not by commingling of their substance with ours*, in which sentence *Danaeus* on Note c. 59 of Augustine's *Enchiridion* is.]

Today it *can* happen that angels appear to us, admonish us in dreams, but that we hold them for our *doctors*, and to the doctrine and suggestions which by holy angels seem to have proceeded, in all things we have faith, is *not safe*, for many causes.

**1.** Since the Apostle *Paul* names *the sign of preaching* (2 Thess 2:9), rejecting the *ministry of the word*, to seek *institution of spirits*. And he says: *Ecce, quia a fide deficient, in the last times will attend to spirits* (1 Tim 4:1). From which place we merit to name *Apostates*, all who today expect visions and colloquies of angels.

**2.** *Ready to deception* is this genus of matters. For since even the *And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.* (2 Cor 11:14), no one from all things can be certain, whether the good or an evil angel has appeared to him or spoken. In the form of a good angel appeared *to a certain young man named Anatolius*, as is in *Severus Sulpicius* (In vita Martini c. 15), that under monastic humility for some time lying hid, he was said to say that angels spoke to him, and to induce belief in this by certain signs he most often exhorted. Among other signs was a garment, which he said was put on him by God, and *by Clarus Sabbatius, and other brothers, with a candle applied diligently, was inspected and touched*, of highest softness, extraordinary whiteness, mingled purple, yet what was its stuff or of what sort of fleece, they could not recognize: nothing however did all see other than a garment. They wanted to refer the matter to *Martin*: the youth refused, indicating to them that it was forbidden to him; but when they compelled the unwilling to go, in the hands of those dragging the garment vanished, and it appeared to have been an illusion of Satan. In the same chapter it is read that the devil appeared to *Martin* praying in his cell, covered with light purple, clothed in kingly garment, girt with a diadem, gems, and gold, wearing golden shoes, with serene countenance, with joyful forehead, saying: *acknowledge me, Martin, whom thou discernest; I am Christ, about to descend to the earth, first I willed to manifest myself to thee*: and to these things again respond *Martin*: *the Lord Jesus did not predict himself to come clothed in purple and with tender face; I will not believe Christ has come, except in that habit and form in which he suffered, and unless he bring the stigmata of the cross*. And in that religious act the demon vanished. Of another monk it is related in the *Life of Martin* and in the *Life of Clement to Sulpicius*, that he had a father not far off dwelling, who visiting his son bore an axe, that in returning he might cut wood for the home to be brought; therefore the demon in the species of an angel appeared to this monk, that the devil was coming in the form of the father with an axe, to slaughter him, announcing and affirming himself for this cause to hasten to warn the hermit, that he might forestall Satan's attempts, by killing him first, before he was killed by him. Therefore in wrath the father coming and greeting he took for the devil, immediately slew, and in turn the demon put the monk down straightaway. More of this genus see in *Iohan. Wierus* (De praestigiis daemonum lib. 2, cap. 16). And who now in these illusions of demons could discern whether a good or an evil angel he sees?

*Petrus Thyraeus* (lib. 4 De apparitionibus cap. 16, num. 17) gives some sign, whereby diabolic address may be discerned from angelic. *Angelic* — says he — *in the beginning terrifies, then leaves the mind quiet: contrary, diabolic in the beginning solemnly insinuates itself, but in the end leaves troubled and unquiet mind*. The same mark he holds (in cap. 4 of Job v. 16). But this sign can deceive. For in the history of *Samson* the angel of the Lord appearing to his mother, in no wise terrified her, but rather animated her, so that she ran to her husband, announcing the angel not being able to bear the angel to address: *thou art he, who hast spoken to the woman*; but after the departure at length of the angel, tremor and horror seized him (Judg 13:6). And so Saul (1 Sam 28:21) and Samuel (1 Sam 28:20), the devil from the beginning of those whom he attacks, in fear so exhausts them, that then some joy in the name to bear he refreshes, but often not by strokes he drives back to the very last.

Others from the beauty of the form which the appearing spirits make themselves *lovable*, gather that they have seen a holy angel; but even the devil in most elegant form appeared to Martin, feigning himself to be *Christ*, as above we heard.

Nor are they always good angels who counsel good things, or from us expect them. For evil ones too can give good counsels, and expect good, but for an evil end. As *Bodinus* notes (lib. 3 *Demonomania* cap. 6): *Satan fastings, prayers, and orations imperates and vows sacrifices, that the imprudent he may deceive*.

Much less from the place where they appear can good angels be discerned. For even the devil sometimes stood among the sons of God (Job), in paradise also of all evils he made the beginning, and *Christ* he led up on the pinnacle of the Temple.

Most truly therefore is it, which from the beginning I said, that prone to be deceived is the way, in colloquy with angels, which on that ground we ought not to seek.

**3.** Nor are examples lacking of those, whose curiosity in this genus and rashness of examples was exposed to derision.
