Of the *Cataphrygians* records *Eusebius* (Hist. eccl. lib. 5, cap. 14), that wonderful visions they boasted, from which they said themselves to have perceived that the world was soon about to fall; but the event taught how basely they were deceived: the same happened in our fathers' memory to *Mohammed* the Antibaptist. *Mohammed* is said in a certain persuasive way to have been carried into heaven, and to have received through the archangel Gabriel that doctrine of his *Alcoran*. Many fanatics today, who from visions and colloquies of angels (as they claim) have predicted futures — about the mutations of kingdoms, about the ruin of the Pope, about the destruction of the saints — whom events already are refuting, and without doubt soon, at the approach of the very seculum of the Holy Spirit of which they so much glory, will confound them entirely. In *Papism* much is done by apparitions of spirits, from which they have wanted to know the seat of theirs in purgatory, but how miserably they have been deceived, experience — which is called the mistress of fools — has taught. But this was done by the just judgment of God, punishing the curiosity of men, to whom, *And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie: That they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness.* (2 Thess 2:11-12).

**4.** Seriously admonished us the Apostle *Paul* to beware of the astuteness of Satan, who is wont to *And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.* (2 Cor 11:14); so *let no man seduce you in humility and religion of the angels* (Col 2:18); which the ancients understood about those, who venerated angels, and used their information, as above from *Theodoret* and the *Council of Laodicea* we heard. The Apostle wants us also so much to abhor from all information of angels, that even from an angel who should announce another Gospel from heaven, we should not believe, since there is not another, than that which has been preached by the Apostles (Gal 1:8), insinuating that it suffices us to believe those things which God has proposed to us to be believed by the labor of the Apostles: *curiosity* therefore it is, when Scripture being neglected, to expect *revelations* from angels.

**5.** *Angels* have no calling to the office of teaching, *no mandate we have* to hear them: as therefore they themselves do not obtrude themselves upon that office of teaching, so we too, without a mandate of theirs, should not expect their instruction. No certainty in this instruction can be, since it is not evident to me, that it is from God: and general is the sentence of the Apostle (Rom 10:14-15): *how then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? and how shall they preach except they be sent?* — where faith and mission of doctors are joined by the tightest bond. Certain therefore about those things which I am taught, I cannot be, unless of the vocation or mission of the teacher, whether man or angel, is evident to me.

**6.** No place have the angels in the *number of those through whom God has willed to teach us*. For *Paul* when here he described the hierarchy of the Church (1 Cor 12:28; Eph 4:11), makes no mention of angels, but only of *men* through whom God has willed to gather his Church.

**7.** Nor is it now the *time of the apparitions* of angels, when God with our fathers spoke, but this was proper to the *time of the promises* through his ministering angels. When *Christ* ascended into heaven, he committed the office of teaching in the Church to the ministers of the Church (Eph 4:11). About the ministry therefore, and mission of the angels, there is silence. For these are the *legates of Christ*, through whom God exhorts us (2 Cor 5:20).

**8.** Two causes are there why God today does not thus act through angels with us, as of old it was done. First, *because as boys* the ancients needed *ceremonies*, so also *apparitions of angels* for solace and confirmation: now Christ having been made flesh, and the Holy Spirit largely given to us, he does not send angels any more, but wills that our conversation be in heaven, not that of the angels on earth. In the beginning of the New Testament apparitions of angels were still customary, because then work was needed of celestial confirmations, now however sufficiently confirmed is the word of God, so that angelic confirmation is not needed. Nor are there lacking reasons why God should not use angels, but *mortal men*, to instruct us. **1.** For as toward us *goodness* he declared, how greatly he loves the human genus, when he deemed men worthy of this honor, that through them with us on things especially divine he speaks, admonishes us, and on this account also ministers of the Church the *word* not of men, but of God the *voice* they are called (1 Thess 2:13). **(2.)** He wanted to *prove our obedience*: which when we make good to the ministers of the Church, to God himself we have exhibited the debt, for it is said (Luke 10:16): *he that heareth you, heareth me*. **(3.)** His divine power he wanted to show, since through the ministry of men in the Church God abolishes the kingdoms unworthy of him. **(4.)** To our *infirmity* he consulted, since for colloquies with angels by nature we are less apt as long as in this earth of our pilgrimage we are, therefore through men of the same lot and condition he willed to act, who more gently us can handle, and to our imbecility can grieve, since angels *shall not lift up our humanity from the sublime dignity of angelic conversation to bodily conversation*, as *Chrysostom* speaks.

From all these it is easy to gather how perilous, and how far from good, it is to seek *visions and colloquies of angels* from God himself. Which custom on that account by whatever little rings, fables, or booklets it is embellished, in all manners we disapprove, and exhort the pious to abstain from it.

If however God himself either through *internal suggestions*, or through the appearing *visions of the holy angels*, warns us, and preserves us from perils (which sometimes to be done we do not deny), let us with grateful minds *paternal that care of God* over us recognize, and to the ministry of his word we shall be more obedient. For those who *fear God*, and love his word, these have blessed monitors and guardians divinely added, from the sacred letters is certain.

**Casus IV. Whence can I be certain, that not only the thoughts of the heart, but also the external operations, are from a good or evil angel, if any of these things are by us either done or suffered?**

*Reply.* Without doubt many and *good* things are suggested by the angels, and evil. Those which are good and conformable to the law of God, are from the good angel, who not only himself does the will of God, but also so that by others it be done, labors: therefore *impure thoughts* he resists, to prayers he kindles the mind, and *keeps him more strongly in duty in the mission of the divine word* (2 Cor 4:4). And that which in this genus he does with the impious, he tempts with the pious, and, with the Lord withdrawing his hand, he sometimes brings it forth into an effect. For the pious *feel the suggestions of Satan*, at least *stimulus of that carnifex*, of which *Paul* complains (2 Cor 12:7), whom by the grace of God powerfully operating in their infirmity they conquer: sometimes however by their vehement force are they oppressed, so that for a time they succumb; as of *David* is written, that *Satan incited him, so that he numbered Israel* (1 Chr 21).

When therefore such things are suggested to the heart, which without doubt to the law of God, and to honesty itself are adverse, that *smoothly may glide into thy soul, occult, promise usefulness, as if for good and family will they be received more benevolently, are loved for the sake of the arts, are said to be counsels. They put on also the habit of venerable persons, so that greater and prompter reverence may be paid to them* (John 8). For their servants they can suggest, that they be present at the sacred assemblies, hear the word, use the holy Eucharist, expect prayers and suffrages of others, but only through *hypocrisy*, lest they appear such as they are, sometimes even the holy Eucharist they lead into their own for detestable things they abuse — *falls in persuading good on account of evil, in dissuading good with fear of doing evil, in persuading good, that it may lead worse. Thus God is so good, that he permits no evil to be done, out of which he does not know to elicit a greater good. Thus the Devil is so evil, that when he persuades good, so that from good ill he elicits evil out of it.*

From the *end* therefore judgment must be made about suggestions of this sort, whether they be from a good or evil angel. Very often indeed as to species they are good, which from an evil end are worst, and worthy of detestation.

**Casus V. Whether pious men can predict from angelic revelation?**

*Reply.* And this is not the last of the fruits of *colloquies of angels*, which is boasted by fanatics, that in this way many secrets are known, many futures also in the mutations of the church and of kingdoms, which they later can predict.

But in vain is this persuasion, from the curiosity of human genius exiled, which in many modes can be refuted. **First**, Scripture recites many and various offices of angels, which God uses for other things, and for procuring the salvation of his elect, partly for illustrating his glory, partly for our greater consolation, partly also of narrower friendship between us and the holy angels to conserve and confirm grace: but that they reveal secrets to us, and confer on us the *prophetic gift*, nowhere is either mandated to them, or by them done, it is read. Concerning the mandate however of God and some examples of the holy, nothing to us either from angels to expect or to await is licit.

Then *future contingents*, which depend on *free will*, are not known even to angels, unless by *God they be revealed*. God alone it is, before whom both futures, and those which now exist, are present, by which *idiom* he is distinguished from the gods of the nations in *Isaiah*: *tell us what is to come, and we shall know that ye are gods* (Isa 41:22-23). God alone also knows all futures in their causes: to angels this is not given without *revelation of God*: therefore neither *of that last day are they said to know* (Matt 13:33); and in the *fourth book of Ezra* (4:41), to Ezra asking the angel *whether he himself was about to see those days* about which he had spoken to him, *and what things would be in those days*, the angel responded: *of the signs*, and about which *thou askest me, in part I can indicate to thee, however of your life to declare I am not sent to say to thee: but I do not know*. Hear from that book, to which the fanatics much attribute, that angels concerning the life or death of a man can predict nothing, but such things only in part can know, so much namely as God to them has revealed.

Although in *eternal wisdom*, which the angels from the beginning have seen and see, as in a mirror all things shine forth: yet more in that they see than *God* himself has willed to be seen. For also the last day in that mirror shines, and yet *Christ* affirms it to be unknown to the angels; the mysteries of salvation in that mirror shine forth, and yet the *vocation of the Gentiles* was hidden for eternal ages in God: *To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God,* (Eph 3:10); the decrees of God about the salvation of men shine in that mirror, and yet they are not known to the angels, unless by *revelation*, in which manner the holy men know them through the Holy Spirit. For *what things of men* the Spirit *For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him? even so the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God.* (1 Cor 2:11).

The angels indeed say to *Daniel*: *Now I am come to make thee understand what shall befall thy people in the latter days: for yet the vision is for many days.* (Dan 10:14); but this cannot be otherwise accepted than that the angel from God revealed to the Prophet those things which he himself from God had in his mandates.

Wherefore since fanatics of ours boast much from the vaunted colloquy of angels about the future state of the Church and republic, they must show — **1.** that what they predict, they have certainly received from a good angel; **2.** that to that angel it has been revealed by God; but such revelations outside Scripture we cannot seek, in Scripture however they do not find, whence follows, all their persuasion by a *slack foundation* to be founded.

Thirdly, full is the matter of peril to boast of divine revelations, and *angelic predictions*. For in that way the mind of man of what is *new* eager is drawn away from the word once tempered: *arises presumption of proper worth*, *from which conceit of heresies arises*, as *Basil* said (in the book on the true integrity of virgins, cap. 2): *which happens to heretics, that they are transformed as into angels of light in pride, when they are those who have spoken with God or been instructed by an angel; by that way if it grows insolent, more licit than becomes them from colloquies audaciously to predict — they announce, then the ordinary and in Scripture demonstrated way of wisdom despise, sermons of penitence, as if in the ordinary ministry they were not sufficiently frequent, by a peculiar scheme they mock, the immundane suggestions of Spirit for divine revelations they seize, in this manner finally by a plain and thick fashion way is laid open*. Which by the example of *Marcus* and his associates (as in *Irenaeus* lib. hoc. cap. 3, and of *Maximilla* and *Priscilla* wives of some *Theodotus*, who first of that prophecy defended, an *Apostolic Hierapolite* of old taught, referring *Nicephorus* lib. 4 hist. eccl. cap. 43. In which if we should refer the fanatics of our Prophets to the claws of heretics, nothing far from the truth we would say).

Moreover the gift of *prophecy* long ago ceased in the Church. For although to the Church of the N. T. were promised *Prophets*, who visions might have, without distinction of sex (Joel 2:28), *Peter* however that promise's fulfilment expressly refers to that time in which the *Apostles* visibly received the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:16). And although in subsequent times there were not lacking those who with the prophetic gift were adorned, as from Acts 11:27-28; 21:9-10, and from other places, and also from the history of our times, is evident: yet of *rashness* it is easily to arrogate to oneself this gift, whereby many themselves and others basely have deceived.

Finally the *vanity* of *those prophecies* is manifest, so that of the *certitude* of them partly from *the genus of things predicted*, partly from *the event alone* judgment can be made.

For as to what pertains to the *former*, those things which concern the *Church*: — if predictions ought not to be contrary to Scripture, then not even an angel is to be heard (Gal 1:8). If therefore *prophecies* must be examined from Scripture: why then are we not content with Scripture? If it is the *Commonwealth*, then must be seen, lest it disturb the state of the commonwealth or of any man's order — which disturbance often with those new prophecies is conjoined, and on that name *the celestial prophets* were rejected by *Luther*, who in insane frenzy armed rustics against the magistrate, as it is in *Luther* (Book against the celestial Prophets).

As to what pertains to the *latter*, the event of all supplies the best probation of prophecies, as *Irenaeus* teaches (Lib. 4 cap. 44). About each of these *kriteria* of proving prophecies the Lord speaks (Deut 13:1-5; 18:15, 19). If therefore the event alone probates prophecies, better it is that these things be committed to *others*, and we be content with the *Word*, in which is no deception.

Let each therefore beware of himself, lest by *zeal of novelty*, or *curiosity*, from the opinion of *angelic colloquy*, both to himself and to others he weave snares, and finally with his own *vaticinia* offer himself to be derided by others: which today, alas! I have known to have happened even to great men, as experience — which is the mistress of fools — is wont to confirm.

**Casus VI. Whether we can be in doubt if in sleep from a revelation of angels an interpretation of Scripture be furnished to us?**

*Reply.* It is the same, whether *from revelation of angels*, or from *sleeps*, thou seekest interpretation of Scripture: for those who dream such things, from a good angel to have been informed they think.

Did this *Zwingli*, as from *Substance* of the Eucharist (Vol. 2, fol. 383) is manifest: *the true certainly of the words of institution of the Lord's Supper I saw in a dream from a monitor of some, of whom whether he was white or black, I do not remember*. Did this *John Fox*, as, referring *Georgius Abbates* (in the Demonstration of Antichrist c. 8, p. 138), and himself writing (lib. 1 in the Apologetical Preface), that on a certain Lord's day in the highest morning-sleep it fell to him, how the words of Rev 11:2 — *months 42 days* — the times — times and half-times — he should understand: *however, in itself with majesty he holds the diadem, the Lord's response often to have opened: because* it explains those *months* in *hebdomads*, through *hebdomas hebdomadum* explaining, from *Sabbatha Sabbathorum* Ex 24:2 of the Old Testament, *Sabbath of the Sabbatical years*, i.e. *of seven* to be interpreted.

*Excogitate and paint* these adversary things, however they may wish, this genus of interpretation of Scripture no *certitude* it produces.

**(1.)** For God has not constituted angels as interpreters of Scripture, but the *Spirit*, whose it is intelligent to those who understand. That gift however of interpreting Scripture *diarraibut Spiritus Sanctus prout vult* (1 Cor 12) distributes: not however through angels, but through the ministry of men, who from the very phrase of Scripture and from context derive the true sense, not from visions and dreams do they extract them.

**(2.)** God has not willed us to attend to visions and dreams, but *ad legem et testimonium se convertere* (Isa 8:20), i.e., to Scripture, which to understanding is sufficiently sufficient in itself.

**(3.)** Scripture is not of *private interpretation* (2 Pet 1:20); therefore to a *private speculation* of this sort — although from an angel it be said to proceed — no one should trust, since it does not rest on any solid foundation.

**(4.)** An angel who should bring *another gospel*, is called *anathema* (Gal 1:8); therefore also, when he brings a sense of Scripture foreign, of what sort was that interpretation of *Zwingli*, that it signifies which is against the letter and nature of the New Testament, in which significations and figures have vanished.

**(5.)** It is dubious whether an angel in sleep is dealing with us, whether black or white, as of himself with monitors *Zwingli* doubted: an angel can even suggest some sense of Scripture, in order to deceive men, as our first parents experienced, whom by the depravation of the words of the Lord he led away, and made disobedient, and cast into the most present peril.

**(6.)** *Paul* wills that the *spirits of the prophets* be *And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.* (1 Cor 14:32). If however to angelic interpretations must be trusted, no one, who should boast of them, would concede to another (as also it is thus) that with better reasons furnished: because he was boasting of having his interpretation from an angel.

Which discomforts all, since from that persuasion of angelic interpretation they would flow, no one confidently in this part should act, from an angel should he not seek the sense of Scripture, and if even in the greatest degree something of this sort in sleep to himself he thinks to have been revealed, that very thing however to the *Lydian stone* of Scripture, and to the analogy of faith, he should examine, outside which he readily falls into error.

[*Wherefore in every sleep let we be cautious of futures, that we be not deceived, especially of dreams of this sort, most watchful.*]

## Chapter II. On Cases of Conscience Concerning the Nature, Qualities, and Operations of Evil Angels

Just as conversation with the holy angels is pleasant and full of consolation, so with these evil ones the consideration is exceedingly ungrateful, on those things which sometimes happen to man in communion with evil angels. Nor however can they be entirely omitted, since the evil angels obtrude themselves even upon us unwilling, and it is better that the astuteness and forces of Satan be expedited than that they be feared and dreaded.

Therefore also God in many places of Scripture treats of the evil angels and their operations, adducing examples in daily use, and demonstrating the power of the demons — that when notice is taken of the astuteness, virulence, and unrelenting zeal of harming of the enemies of our host, we too may be more alert for resisting, according to the Apostolic admonition: *For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places. Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.* (Eph 6:12–13). And again: *Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour: Whom resist stedfast in the faith, knowing that the same afflictions are accomplished in your brethren that are in the world.* (1 Pet 5:8–9).

Various are the names of evil angels in Scripture, whereby either their *nature*, or their *appearance*, or their *offices and works* are in some way expressed. **From nature** they are called *hairy ones* or *shaggy ones — se'irim* (Lev 17:7; Isa 13:21); *mammon — Deut 32:17*; because they appear in the form of a beast, of a fawn, of a goat; and the great *dragon, that ancient serpent* (Rev 12). **From qualities of spirits**, unclean spirits (Matt 12:43); lying spirits (1 Kgs 22:22); *spirit of infirmity* (Luke 13:11); *spirit of the world* (1 Cor 2:12); *power of darkness* (Col 1:13); *principalities and powers* of the darkness (Eph 6:12); *God of this world* (2 Cor 4:4); from wrath, *strong* (1 Pet 5:8); from astuteness, *spiritual wickedness* (Eph 6:12); *spirits of iniquity* (Isa 25:14); from zeal of harming or adversary-standing, *the tempter* (Matt 4:3; Luke 4:2); from malice, *the devil*, because he is our *slanderer* and *accuser of our brethren* (Rev 12:10); *enemy* (Matt 13:39); *evil one* from evil works (Matt 6:13); *homicide* (John 8:44); *the Pythonic spirit* (Acts 16:16), who is the author of all sorceries and incantations.

[*The devil is a serpent on account of astuteness, a lion on account of ferocity, a dragon on account of cruelty. We name the devil accuser, since he draws to God his accusations against his own. — Augustine, in Ps 8*.]

Which name-catalogs first admonish us in how great peril we are. In no world-corner can there be doubt how full the world is of evil angels, among whom we must live and struggle so long as we live. Where snares meet everywhere, in which of them can they not be informed the mind of man, lest we be caught in the nets of Satan? Of these we shall in order proceed to treat, making beginning from the very *devils*, before descending to their handmaids, magi and sorcerers, wizards and diviners; then to *possessed persons* in whom the devil most powerfully exerts his power and malice.

**Casus I. Whereas many by their words indeed profess to believe there is nothing from the devil, or at least not so much of danger from him should men beware — how are these to be refuted, since Scripture and daily experience refract them?**

*Reply.* Not for a little error but a great one was theirs, who denied that there is an angel or a spirit (Acts 23:8). And today are found many who call the concupiscences of the flesh, or wicked cogitations, at least by the name of *devils*, and to intercept the works of others deny the existence of any Satan. But the *Manichaeans and Priscillianists*' error is impious, that the devils were of God created as they now are, evil indeed and unclean. For *no angel of God derelinquished his own principate* (Jude 6), writes *Jude*; and nothing evil or unclean can be from God, who *And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.* (Gen 1:31).

**Proof of the devil's existence** (that there are devils) is shown from Scripture in many places, as **1.** from their *fall from the beginning* — in *John* (8:44): *he stood not in the truth*; in *2 Peter* (2:4): *[the angels who] kept not their principality, but left their proper habitation, are reserved unto the judgment of the great day, held in chains of eternal darkness*. God therefore first created angels, and out of these some fell to become devils.

**2.** From *many operations of malignant angels* — Scripture presents plentifully the impurities and wickednesses which the devils operate in men, tempting to lust, blasphemy, homicide, avarice, and every sort of vice, of which more below.

**3.** From *apparitions of demons* — in the form of a serpent to Eve (Gen 3); *Christ* also, whom the devil accosted, tempting him (Matt 4); to Satan appearing in the form of Samuel to *Saul* (1 Sam 28:14); appearing among the sons of God to *Job* (Job 1:6); as *hairy ones or shaggy ones* (Lev 17:7); in the battle at Michael, most bloody in the Apocalypse (Rev 12), where the dragon is full of the blood of those whom he slew or caused to be slain; and appearing to *Christ* also in visible form aggressing the Lord (Matt 4).

**4.** From operations *of malignant angels* — which can be attributed neither to God nor to good angels nor to men, since the devils are the beginning-perpetrators of them: *ecce fecistis me odiosum vobis*, as *Jacob* speaks to his sons, saying to them: *ye have made me hateful to the people of the land* — that is, God has permitted through such operations that men-of-good become adversaries and *the man is made hateful*, that he falls into calamitous miseries, that he perpetrates hateful crimes, and, made vile with troubles, is dispersed with them; which sort of iniquity is by Scripture ascribed to the devils.

**5.** From *battle of good angels with them*, of which Scripture in many places testifies. In *paradise* also they made their beginning (Gen 3:1). By their own folly *Eve* seduced *Adam* (2 Cor 11:3); first *fratricide* he made (Gen 4:8); of prophets he thrust himself in among the *number*, and their tongues he filled with lies (1 Kgs 22:22); to *disciples* of Christ he brought no less enemies, whom in the manner of wheat he purposed to sift (Luke 22:31); the Lord himself in the desert he did not spare (Matt 4:11); of *the sowers* Christ instructed us in the parable of the fourfold seed (Matt 13:19); Christ himself confesses that he is *the beast that walketh about* (John 10:12; Job 1:7); and *David* writes that he *walks about us in the manner of a roaring lion, that he lies in wait to strike* (Ps 91), where — much more resist should the *chorus of the pious* — those who guarded us angels-among-us-guardians in the guard of the *higher principate of your face — Tertull. c. 3 Apologetic.*

**6.** From *the pains of hell*, which are prepared for the devil (Matt 25:41; 2 Pet 2:4).

To all these testimonies of Scripture is added *experience*. For that the world is filled with so many and horrid crimes; that so many homicides, adulteries, perjuries occur; that so many wars in the world, so many religions, so many persecutions of the Church — without doubt is at the instigation of the devil, whom to be efficacious *Paul* declares as *the spirit which now worketh in the sons of disobedience* (Eph 2:2).

Nay, our very children are witnesses. For no boy, no adolescent, sitting alone in darkness or on solitary paths, is not frightened, dreading specters and incursions of demons, — which indication is too manifest, that they are aware of them, who lie in wait everywhere for men.

**7.** Then, though the devil is called *the prince of the air* (Eph 2:2), he is nevertheless in the world among men, so that as *Luther* says: *there is nothing which he does not by mode or by mode of guile assault. That very mind is by devils occupied and possessed*.

Let us learn therefore from all these that impious it is to deny that there are devils, whose operations are known: our part rather is at every single moment to beware of the astuteness and power of that impure spirit. *For he walks about us in the manner of a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour: whom resist steadfast in the faith*, admonishing *Peter* (1 Pet 5:8–9). Let us flee the doctrines of the Epicureans, who write that the devil is dead: for that he lives, and indeed not far from us, is testified by his horrid works. *Luther* elegantly depicted the devil in the form of a certain man, according to the precepts of the *Decalogue*, and against every single precept its *antithesis* he shows. *As God in the Decalogue is the thesis*, says he, *so Satan is the antithesis: for what God prescribes, this Satan prohibits, and vice versa. The head of the Devil is against the first table, in the first precept diffidence, blasphemy, profanation of the name of God, contempt of the word. His mouth is Satan the preceptor, filled with disobedience, sedition, and rebellion. In the fifth is the heart of Satan filled with hatred, envy, imprecation, and homicides. In the sixth is the belly of Satan, filled with gluttony, drunkenness, lasciviousness, libido. In the seventh are the hands of Satan, plundering, rapine, harming, cruelty. In the eighth is the tongue of Satan, with lies, calumnies, wounding of neighbor's reputation. In the ninth and tenth are the feet of Satan, wherewith he hastens to harm others: for concupiscence, evil-having stimulated to evil*. This mystical Satan-body has *B. Luther* depicted, that we always hold it in our sight, lest we be secure, but the astuteness and power of the malignant spirit we shun. For who casts the devil far from himself, and cares nothing, he neither esteems the holy angels much, whose guardianship is so much greater as the malice of the evil angels is more evident.

Therefore does *Divus Paulus* exhort, that we always prepare for the battle with the devil. *Be strengthened in the Lord*, says he, *Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might. Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places. Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.* (Eph 6:10–13).

**Casus II. In how many modes can futures be known, and how does the devil know them?**

*Reply.* It is worth observation-of-note that futures are diversely known and predicted. **1.** They are known by God alone in themselves, since he is the author and lord of them, and one of Isaiah's own words (Isa 45:5) *besides me there is none*, — with which knowledge he distinguishes himself from all idols. **2.** They are known to the Trinity, in so far as they are certainly future, by reason of revelation and afflatus of the divine Spirit: in which mode the Prophets predicted futures. **3.** They are known and predicted from natural signs, such was the *nightowl* and the *oracle of Delos*; who from natural signs futures often can predict. **4.** They are known and predicted also *in creatures* — as by the flight of birds, examinations of entrails, and other lots, of which experience abounds, both in *the history of Saul* (1 Sam 28:15) and elsewhere.

But this notice of futures is not of one mode. For either the causes are *necessary*, which produce a necessary effect (which from its own causes can certainly be predicted; by which mode from seed projected into the earth the harvest can be predicted, and from many years' observation of the weather); such things are also predicted by men, without revelation: such knowledge and prediction competes to God alone, who has all things which are, were, and shall be in one — as it were, in one point *in himself* has present, since he is himself outside all time. And by this mode both good and evil angels know futures — such as they are natural for either possibility, so that they can equally happen or not happen; and hence arise also predictions less certain.

Whereby therefore men from their causes can predict, or by more mediated events, so much more certainly can the *devil* predict; because he holds their causes and hindrances more known, on account of the subtlety and agility of his nature, on account of his more acute senses and long experience.

Which all bring it about that, as *Augustine* speaks (De divinat. daemon., cap. 5): *some things from natural signs future are known, and some things by these signs, before they should be foreseen, they can before predict. Every soul is aerial*, says *Tertullian* (Apolog. adv. gentes, cap. 22) — that is, angels and demons — *this is the spirit, of extreme mobility. Whence they easily know all things: yet they know not except when they know from him*.

Three are the reasons for these diabolical predictions: *(1)* the subtlety of their substance; *(2)* the agility of their motion; *(3)* the acumen of the senses, and their long experience. Therefore *Augustine* says in the book *On the divination of demons* (c. 3): *demons by natural quality of body, by senses of aerial bodies, easily prevail; by celerity too on account of the same body of aerial nobility, not only through the terrestrial spaces of whatever seat of the animals to precede, or from us to precede, so that they surpass birds beyond bodily nature. With which two things, so far as the body pertains — subtlety, that is, and the same senses, and celerity of motion — many things they foreseeing predict or announce, which men, by tardiness of the senses, wonder at. Access there is also for demons through the long time in which their life protends, longer experience than can be to men, on account of the shortness of the life of these. From these efficacies, which are of aerial bodily nature, not only many futures do demons predict, but even many marvels do they work*. The same repeats in the book *On the spirit and soul*, c. 28.

[*It is enjoined that experience is not of all youths, as *Aristotle* admonishes* (Ethic. 6, cap. 4, and *Rhetoric* cap. 2, since requires a long time — *ibid.* cap. 6; *Nichom. Ethic.* i cap. 9); which *Ovid* also sang: *— to me many years have rightly given to know* (*Metamorph.* 14).]

Yet there are other causes of *diabolical predictions*, sometimes those which are revealed to the *Prophets* through the Holy Spirit of God, and by the divine reading of Sacred Letters (of which the devils are not entirely ignorant), and these they seize; and especially in the time of imminent fulfilment, as though from themselves they predict, lest anything they seem to ignore.

*Concerning Alexander the Great* had *Daniel* (cap. 8), by divine afflation, predicted the *transferring of the Empire from the Babylonians to the Grecians*: therefore to *Alexander* consulting the *Delphic oracle*, the same responded: *invincible art thou, Alexander*.

Had *Antiochus* predicted the sacking of *Tyre*, as from Josephus (Antiq. Jud., cap. 6) is manifest, and by *Alexander* Macedonicus that same *Alexander* was announced. *Homer* holds this Satan, when he wrote *Diomedes* fugitive as Diomedes fleeing before *Aeneas*; then said to the *Apostle* as future to be the city, as if from that idol this prediction were, which however God had revealed to his Prophet (whom often Satan consulted).

*The overthrow of gentile simulacra* predicted the Lord through the prophet *Zephaniah* (1:1): *horrendous shall be the Lord against them, when he shall attenuate the gods of the earth, and every man from his own place shall adore him, all the isles of the nations*. When therefore the time of fulfilment was approaching, *Serapis*, the demon of another of their cults, made known, so that his own divinity even fleeing he might commend: see *Augustine* De divinat. daemon., c. 6.

Sometimes demons, from natural causes probably, more quickly than others recognize (with singular *sagacity*, and most rapidly, in one moment being able to traverse many spaces of places, and to note what is done there), — these, when the events are already in progress, or now are, as futures they predict, and by that reason to their people the authority of some divinity conciliate.

Sometimes what he himself was about to do, he predicts as future from God. God permits sometimes to the devil that he may disturb the air, may excite storms, rain, thunder, and other tempests, so that he may hurt the fruits and the animals; likewise that he may agitate the minds of men, that he may move discords and wars, — which before he brings them into effect, through his ministers he predicts: for *the demons predict their own disturbances-in-the-making, which they intend* (Augustine, lib. 9 De civ. Dei, c. 22).

Sometimes God himself to the devil reveals something certain and future, even about things of great moment, since he sees the impious more willingly listening to the devil than to God himself. From just judgment God permits Satan, that predicting to them what things are too certainly future — either for their own pernicious end, that they be blinded, or in testimony against them, that they could have had the truth, which however they were unwilling to hear. Whereto pertain the *predictions of the Sibyls* and of the *Chryseae Sertes* which by divine afflation to the ethnics were dictated, so also the spirit through *Balaam Chaldean* vaticinated: for God willed also the ethnics, who to *Christ* were unwilling to believe, through their own men to render inexcusable.

Sometimes demons *by conjecture from adjuncts* predict as future, when they *see the mother in signs and pregnant with son to come forth in ambages* — obscurely they respond.

By these five modes the devil can predict futures.

[Verses: *Matrem in signis ambages*, etc.]

**Casus III. Wherefore then, if not all his predictions we can consider dubious, why then do we not cure nor entirely attend to them, much less affect them.**

*Reply.* Since therefore not all his vaticinations we can call in doubt, yet we ought not much to cure them, much less to attend, and much less to affect them. *The demons predict*, says *Damascene* (lib. 2 De orthodox. fide, c. 4), *sometimes those things which distant futures are prospiciant, sometimes present things prowl about, whence often they are refuted: nor should they be believed, though sometimes true things they profess*.

**Firstly**, God expressly *has prohibited* that we seek truth from the dead, but be content with the *law and testimony* (Isa 8:20).

**Secondly**, he seeks the ruin of men, whom by this method from the word he abducts, so that by his vaticinations and lyings-in-wait they hold nothing more sincere.

**Thirdly**, when his presages incline to false religion or otherwise openly to evils, we have a clear mandate, that we hear him not, though what he says come to pass, for this permits *God, that he may tempt us* (Deut 13:1–5).

**Fourthly**, we do not read in Scriptures anywhere that the faithful attributed anything to devil-predictions of this sort; for they are content with the infallible word of God: the *ethnics* however willingly consulted their *oracles*, their *pythonic wives*, *pseudo-prophets* (Rev 22); *Saul* the *Pythonic wife* (1 Sam 28); and they were miserable men, and had *deceived*.

**Fifthly**, the devil, even when he predicts truth, mixes in much falsity, sometimes indeed by ambiguities, sometimes by falsities, which the ignorant either impious, in whom the devil has some just right, are inclined to believe.

By these *impostures* uses Satan, either when he sees some impediments intervening (by which, if the predicted thing does not succeed, it may be imputed to them), or when to curious ones eager he confides — to whom to deceive he is always ready. And since he himself is dubious of the outcome, he uses *ambiguous or obscure words*, so that into whatever part it fall, he in no way seems to have predicted falsely.

[*Hence that of Cicero: Ostensibly Apollo. — de divinat.* On the *oracles*, *Chrysippus* filled a whole volume, partly with falsities, as I say, partly with chance ways, so that from every oration wisdom, partly with equivocal-obscures, of which is an interpreter and interpreters and lot must be referred to lots, partly with ambiguities which to the *dialecticians* are borne. Thus *Delphic* Apollo *Croesus* responded: *Croesus, crossing the river Halys, will overturn a great empire's force*; which *Croesus* interpreted as if he himself were to overthrow the kingdoms of others, — while contrary he experienced. The same demon *Pyrrhus* responded: *thou, aeacid, canst overcome the Romans*. Which oracle either favors the *Romans* or promises to *Pyrrhus* victory: *Pyrrhus* interpreting for himself was received.]

Add examples of Diabolical Sophistical predictions, which are so plurime by *ambiguity* and *amphibology* — *(1)* *Suidas* refers, that *Daphnidas the Sophist* consulted the Delphic oracle: could he find his lost horse? (though truly he had none, only in mockery had he asked this) — the demon answered him: *thou shalt find thy horse*. Coming back, the way took him past a rex whom he had often provoked with insults, — who since he asked *if thou wast a horse, headlong-cast, thou shalt discover — Valerius Maxim.* lib. 1 cap. 8. *(2)* From the same oracle *Philip*, king of the Macedonians, was admonished, that he beware *four wheels*: therefore he imperated throughout the kingdom that chariots be disjoined; but Pausanius in the hilt of the sword, whereby he was pierced, had inscribed a *four-wheeler*. *(3)* The demon responded to *Albertus Placentinus*: *Prince Placentinus, if thou wishest to inhabit safe, if under gilded citizens' bricks — thou shalt begin to make lifted-up light*, — that is, if thou dost not have sense, be secure, — but shortly they would set fire. *(4)* The devil to *Anonymous Meliadensis* the *legatus* responded: *thou wilt not be a captive in the ale-cellar* — which ought to be understood *that thou also wilt not be a captive*. *(5)* Thus *Philippus Macedo* the *Pythia*: *"Philippi son I hear," Philippi son I hear at Pheras is set; Philippi son eugoue, thence the ephebe, from that place, at his hand made sacrifice, being victim* — so it fell on *Philip son of Amyntas* being killed by *Pausanias* in one deed. *(6)* The devil deceived *Manfred*, son of the emperor *Frederick*, when he waged war against *Charles Andegavum* by the sound of Neptune, responding: *rejoice, no palm will overcome thee*: which double reason to incautious prince *ambiguity* was, whom *Manfred* did not observe.

The astuteness of the devil in the *knowledge and dispositions of men's thoughts* — has he power?

**Casus IV. Whether the devil knows the cogitations of men?**

*Reply.* Concerning the impious, since they are in the power of Satan, we clearly hold from Scripture, that the devil, when he wants, inflicts on them evil cogitations, — which he also knows, since not from elsewhere than from *his own cogitations* they proceed, does he attend. It is read of *Judas* that *And supper being ended, the devil having now put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon's son, to betray him;* (John 13:2). And *Paul* also of the *Devil* speaks (2 Cor 4:4): *In whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them.* (2 Cor 4:4).

Concerning the pious we have said above, that the *evil angels* have no right over them (for they are emancipated from the power of them through Christ), yet by God permitting they exercise great power over them, as the history of *Job* testifies. Nor even to the cogitations of the pious do they spare, but *doubly* harm — first *by their own suggestions*, then *by outward apprehension*.

For firstly, the *devil is troublesome to the pious with wicked suggestions*: shows an object, and an occasion of sinning, adds persuasions, — knowing whether the mind of man delights in his suggestion, and if he sees him delighted, every stone he moves, so that from the will assent may follow, and effect succeed — which he knows to be conjoined with the peril of first-man, which he seeks.

Thus *Eve* was besieged by the tempted apple, forbidden; the word of God he called into doubt, saying: *why hath God commanded, lest ye eat of the fruit of every tree?* If she opposed the authority of the divine precept, to the word of God he expressly contradicted: *ye shall in no wise die*, and mox he commended to her the beauty and softness of the fruit, directed *Eve*'s eyes to it, and enticed the miserable one to eating of the apple.

*Satan* showed to *David* a beautiful woman, removed from his eyes all shame, reverence of the divine law, and fear of divine wrath, showed him a solitary place, suggested a counsel by which he could enjoy her without infamy, — and when he saw *David* inflamed in mind, exhorted that what he had conceived in mind, he should complete in work.

Here occurs the doubt of the devil: *My defence is of God, which saveth the upright in heart.* (Ps 7:10)? *He alone looks upon the heart* (1 Sam 16:7); *for the heart of man is inscrutable* (Jer 17:9); *For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him? even so the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God.* (1 Cor 2:11). Whence *Augustine* writes (De ecclesiast. dogm., cap. 71): *the interior of the soul's cogitations the devil sees not certainly*.

But it must be known that *the cogitations of man* are perceived either *in themselves*, as they still hidden lie in the mind, and by no external indications have gone forth: and by this mode *God alone* knows them, who to that eminent-most and abditest society of his knowledge admits no angel: or they are known *by certain external signs*, from *dispositions, words, or studies* — as by the reason of the face are known shame, from the mind, from the fervor of the eyes wrath, from paleness love, from the pulse also the hidden affect of the soul may be judged. By this reason the devil also from the dispositions, words, or studies of a man in some way can collect the affect of soul, what and how much man responds to his suggestions, and to what he is propense: — and then the *evil will* of a man, to that toward which he inclines, he can push more strongly to *the effect*.

In this sentence held much *Augustine* (in lib. De divinat. daemonum, epist. 115 ad Neandrium); consents *Cassian* (Collat. 7, cap. 15): *no one can doubt the impure spirit to be capable of the quality of our cogitations, but from those signs which they take externally, either from our dispositions, or words, or studies, in which more propense they perceive us to incline: but those which are not yet drawn forth from the sentences of the soul, they cannot at all pertain*. In *Bede* (lib. 2 in Marcum, cap. 7): *the devil, as an intruder, can be creator of evil cogitations of ours, but not is he powerful*.

[*Demons cannot understand cogitations, unless by signs shall have proceeded — Aquinas, Matt.*]

Not therefore, when they see us slack, or by hostile darts of Satan already inflamed, ought we to think that our hearts too are exposed to him: but from the bodily habit and gestures let us estimate what we bear within — verbi gratia: if we should have seen a beautiful woman and are aware of drawing her in, we understand we are among the mouth and eye stricken, etc.

Great weight has this doctrine to true piety. For if the devil is not the accurate scrutator of our secret cogitations, our part is to compose all motions of the soul so that we indulge not evil cogitations, — also to avoid all occasions of sinning; to compose sudden motions of wrath, of libido, of avarice, of envy, and similar: for those who willingly listen to wicked suggestions and delight in them, easily to full consent, and finally to the effect of the evil work itself, are led — as the examples of *Eve* and *David* clearly testify.

Always therefore must the *Devil* be resisted by prayers, by word, by labors, by exercises of piety, of chief-obstacles, and with all other things too in temptations especially of *Satan*, who whom he sees resisting he easily quits.

**Casus V. Whether the devil can produce miracles, and how much is to be attributed to them, lest we be injurious to God who is the true author of miracles?**

*Reply.* Truest is the authority of the divine oracle in the Psalm (Ps 72:18): *the Lord God of Israel doeth marvellous things alone*. Whence many incline to the sentence that neither to devil nor to any creature can true miracles and full be attributed, but to God alone.

Yet it cannot be denied that Scripture, both sacred and profane, often mentions *miracles and prodigies of the devils*, which either he himself or through his other ministers he emits. Such are the *prodigies of the Egyptian magi* (Exod 7 & 8), whom *Paul* recalls *Jannes* and *Jambres* to have resisted *Moses* (2 Tim 3:8). The Lord himself of *pseudo-prophets* prodigies and portents to be about to emit testifies (Deut 13:1); and of the *pseudo-prophets* Christ says, that they *shall be about to emit great signs and prodigies before the last day*, so that, if it were possible, even the elect might be seduced (Matt 24:24); and of the *son of perdition* it is written, that his coming will be according to the working of Satan *Even him, whose coming is after the working of Satan with all power and signs and lying wonders,* (2 Thess 2:9). *Simon Magus* also by his portents deceived many in *Samaria* that they said him to be *the great power of God* (Acts 8:10). What things prodigy-like *Simon* emitted, is recounted by *Egesippus* (lib. 2, cap. 2) and *Nicephorus* (lib. 2, cap. 15 & 27): for, as *he says*, statues moved themselves, and in dwellings vessels and household instruments at his nod ran hither and thither on their own; he himself, encircled by flames, was not burned; he was even borne flying in the air; from stones, with the deception of men, he made bread; the form of a dragon he put on, and into various species of animals he was changed; with double face he was seen; and stones into gold he transformed; doors well fortified with bars and clasps and closed opened at his word; iron chains he broke; at banquets he exhibited images of every sort of forms; etc.

Of heretics too, especially *Donatists*, writes *Augustine* in many places, that they emit miracles, God permitting: see lib. 83 questionum, quest. 79; lib. 10 De civ. Dei, cap. 16; tract. 15 in Johan.; De unitate ecclesiae, cap. 16; and Theophylactum on Matt 24. Similar has profane history: *Maximum Val.* of *Tuccia*, a *Vestal Virgin*, tells that in demonstrating her virginity, she drew water in a sieve; and that *Claudia Quintia* drew a ship weighed down with a great weight to the shore of the *Tiber* (Livy 1 decad., lib. 1). Of *Actus Navius* the augur, that he cut a whetstone with a knife. *Philostratus* in the life of *Apollonius Thyanaeus* refers that he *evoked Achilles from the tomb*, predicted plague and drove it away, revived a girl. Of *Vespasian* the emperor tells *Tacitus* (lib. 10 annal.) that at *Alexandria* he cured the blind; similar things of the *priests of the gentiles* refers *Valerius Maximus* (lib. 1, cap. 8). All these works are of Satan no pious doubts.

Then Scripture also *marvel-works of Satan* calls by names, that we are wont to give to divine miracles. Called are these *signs and prodigies* (Mark 16:17; Acts 6:8); the same name is attributed to the works of pseudo-prophets (Matt 24) and of *Antichrist* himself (2 Thess 2:9).

It must be known therefore that *miracle properly said*, if in all its causes it be considered, *fits God alone*. For miracle is not only *beyond the order of nature*, but even *by proper virtue of God* — whose cause is hidden to all, and to the best ends, especially to God's glory, confirmation of his word, and neighbor's salvation, is directed.

[*True miracle is: 1. an external and visible fact — excluded are transmutations rational; 2. a true fact — excluded are the illusions of the devil; 3. simply marvelous, i.e., before all others, whose causes are all hidden; 4. to the best ends*.]

If however God shall have permitted to Satan to work marvel-works, whose either causes in nature are none, or are not conspicuous to all, or apparent but false, or finally feigned: whence great distinction arises between *miracles of God* and *marvel-works of Satan* — of which afterwards.

Therefore *three* on this matter must be explained: **1.** the genera of diabolical miracles; **2.** the distinctions between miracles of God and marvel-works of Satan; **3.** why God permits Satan to make many marvel-works.

**On the first**, there are four genera of marvel-works of Satan.

**(1) First genus:** Some are *truly and altogether such* as they externally appear — which God for certain causes permits him to do. For when Christ said of *pseudo-prophets* that they *shall emit great signs* (Matt 24:24), this indeed cannot be understood of certain phantasmatic delusions: and God of *pseudo-prophets* affirms that *true prodigies they shall do* (Deut 13:1). And there are also today many things in *paganism*, which that they truly are done, cannot be denied, that in the temples of Aesculapius the sick are cured, the leprous cleansed, the lame restored, sight given to the blind, hearing restored to the deaf. Of this genus are also those wondrous works of the gentiles, — as of the water drawn in a sieve, drawing the ship out with the girdle, cutting the whetstone, and similar, in which the devil shows great power, so that the greater with himself among his cultors he may conciliate authority.

These sorts of miracles are truly done by ministers of Satan, sometimes with God operating, — as Christ himself confesses that many at the last day are about to glory, that in his name they have *cast out demons*, whom yet he will not know as his own (Matt 7:22): in which things the effect is not so much to be ascribed to the organs of the devil as to God himself, whose name they abuse, — who either the sacred doctrine through these miracles, even done by the impious, confirms, or by his own just judgment reprobate men, who did not want to hear truth, into errors precipitates, so that they abscond into lies; sometimes also *Satan* himself, God permitting, that the devil in his organs be efficacious, — provided however invocation of the gods of the gentiles intercedes with the ministers of Satan, whom he thus so fascinates that they think themselves true cultors of the true God and true God to know. Thus can Satan suddenly, and as it were in one moment, transport bodies from one place to another, — so that they seem to have been newly produced, when in truth the thing is present, though insensibly from elsewhere into our sight brought. As is related of some magi *dispensators*, who by their incantations produced true serpents, true frogs, — but produced from occult seeds of serpents and frogs, whence transported.

If however such miracles are true, by the Apostle *Paul* they are yet called *prodigies of lies* (2 Thess 2:9), partly because their author the devil is fallacious, partly because they are compared for deceiving and beguiling.

**(2) Second genus:** Some marvel-works of Satan have causes in nature, but *occult* and not obvious to everyone. Great is the force and efficacy in stones, herbs, seeds, and other natural things, however occult, through which many things can happen and are wont, which are held for miracles by the ignorant, when yet naturally they occur, though not according to the customary order of nature. Thus sometimes diseases are cured suddenly by sorceresses, applying certain herbs which have in themselves a natural antidote against that disease, — which however neither the sorceresses nor the sick understand, so they hold as a miraculous cure. But the devil is an *exercised physicist*, who knows well those occult qualities of things, and applies them to some suitable matter, whence an effect comes forth which seems to us marvelous, but which in itself is not, but has its causes in nature. In such cases therefore the devil is not the *efficient cause* of the thing produced, but only *the minister of nature*.

Here *Augustine* refers the *serpents and frogs of the Egyptian magi*, whom he thinks to have been true serpents and frogs, but produced from occult seeds. So he writes (De Trin. lib. 3, cap. 8): *of all these things which corporally and visibly grow, hidden certain seeds lie hid in those corporeal elements of this world. But we ought not therefore to think either good or evil angels the creators, but from probability their subtle senses know the seeds of these things unknown to us, and they by congruent temperations of the elements latently they hide, and thus of things to be generated and of increments to be accelerated they present occasions... For it is one thing indeed from the intimate highest order of causes to found and administer the creature, which he alone who is Creator does: another thing from the granted powers and faculties to bring to bear some external operation, so that at this moment or that, thus or thus, may come forth what is created. Also this is to see, how many men know from which herbs and flesh, or from whatever things by juices, or humors, or thus placed, or thus buried, or thus rubbed, or thus mixed, what animals are wont to be born, — of whom who is so demented as to dare to say a creator? What wonder therefore, if just as any most wretched man can know whence flies and gnats are born, so evil angels for the subtlety of their sense in the more occult seeds of the elements know whence frogs and serpents are born? — but here by certain and natural temperations opportune, by occult motions to be adhibited, they cause to be created, they do not create, etc.* Thus Augustine.

To this genus of marvel-works of Satan pertains what *Alexander* writes (lib. 8 De variar. histor.) — the *Vestal* judgment of a certain woman, who in the form of a dove appeared to him, from the crow accepting the mask, so as to render human form to his daughter, and that they perceived themselves *illuded by demon*. Illusions diabolical of this sort are read in the *life of Martin* by *Severus Sulpicius*.

**(3) Third genus:** Some [of Satan's marvels] are through his celerity of transport. Since Satan can transport bodies swiftly from place to place, sometimes the miracle seems, when in fact he has secretly moved the object elsewhere.

**(4) Fourth genus:** Some are *fantastic delusions* — false apparitions in the eyes of men, wherein nothing real is done, only illusion, as often happens with obsessed persons.

**On the second point** — distinctions between divine miracles and Satan's marvels:
- **Divine miracles** proceed from proper virtue of God, are unfalsifiable, have God's glory + confirmation of doctrine + neighbor's salvation as ends.
- **Satan's marvels** proceed from creaturely power (either God-permitting, or from occult natural causes, or from bodily celerity, or from fantasm), aim at seduction and ruin of souls, and mix truth with falsehood.

**On the third point** — why God permits Satan to make marvels: **(1)** to *test* the pious, whether they cling firmly to God (Deut 13:3 *Dominus Deus vester tentat vos*); **(2)** to *punish* the impious with efficacious errors (2 Thess 2:11); **(3)** to *manifest* the difference between his true miracles and Satan's marvels, teaching us not to trust every wonder but to examine by the Word; **(4)** to *provoke* the pious to greater vigilance and prayer.

**Casus VI. What therefore is to be done, lest we be seduced by devilish miracles?**

*Reply.* The end of devilish miracles is *seduction* and *ruin* of souls. Lest therefore we be seduced, let us first of all be certain that the devil can produce marvel-works: that we lay down thence *five cautions*:

**(1)** *Watching that we place no faith in miracles at odds with sound doctrine.* Since God tests us by permitting them, we must cling to the Word alone. *Even if we or an angel from heaven preach another Gospel* (Gal 1:8).

**(2)** *Judging every miracle by its end.* If it tends to God's glory, confirmation of Scripture, and neighbor's salvation — it may be divine. If it tends to seduction, superstition, or false religion — it is diabolical.

**(3)** *Judging every miracle by its cause and author.* If it comes through orthodox ministers of the Word, with prayers and Scripture, and confirms received doctrine — it may be divine. If it comes through those who preach another gospel, or through incantations and superstitious rites — it is diabolical.

**(4)** *In caution of those who look at such things, lest they adore those who emit miracles*, since such things can also be perpetrated by ministers of the devil, as we hear. That men are prone to this superstition is manifest from the history of Paul, when the *Lycaonians* wanted to adore *Paul* and *Barnabas* on account of a miracle they had done on a lame man (Acts 14:11).

**(5)** *In caution of those who probate religions*, lest they judge religion from miracles alone, or reject any as *false* which is destitute of miracles, since indeed both demons and reprobate men emit miracles and prodigies.

Therefore from external works, however prodigious they be, let us not depend.

[*The end of devilish miracles is deception. For the devil lies, that he may deceive; he flatters, that he may harm; he promises good, that he may attribute evil; he promises life, that he may destroy; he offers peace, lest to peace one attain; he offers salvation, lest anyone come to salvation. — Cyprian*.]

Then, let us not *what* wondrous work is given, or *why* he does it, — but *how* it is done, let us attend. For if a work is done in confirmation of some false doctrine, we have a clear mandate that we should not believe the miracle, since *God tempts us, whether from our whole heart he is loved by us* (Deut 13:3).

Since therefore even miracles are not to be estimated above what we have said above, since even pseudo-prophets do miracles, so much so that even demons themselves produce miracles: — when therefore the *Pontifices* do nothing else *nisi fulcra falsae doctrinae*, no one ought to be moved by them. Only when doctrine first is proved from the word by which it is proved, do we leave miracles in their place. *If God shall have done through Papists some prodigy, God himself is to be praised, and his omnipotence to be preached; but if nothing they have of doctrine to be truth-approved, on that account not is he to be attended.*

Thus what those *Romanists* have — of sick giving themselves in vow to some saint, from whom sanity is feigned to have been given — do not believe: since from the sane, of whom Scripture says (Isa 5:6) *the Lord hath taken away the physicians and physical remedies*, they think — even *gods* certain, in whom to confide, to whom to fly and seek aid they ought to. But this is idolatric, — nor to be attributed *miracles even those which are said to occur at statues of saints* is something to be given, — however great a species they bear.

Are to be weighed from their *ends*. Of this see elegantly disserting *B. Lutherum* in *homily on the domestic gospel* (pag. 210, ed. Jena) *contra Missam vernaculam contra Missam episcopum non tam* — 2 *Iena* serm. german. fol. 434; and elsewhere many places, where he treats *miracles of pseudo-prophets*.

**Casus VII. Since we have learned above that not from miracles are we to estimate, so we have learned that pseudo-prophets can produce miracles, so even demons themselves do miracles. Since therefore Ecclesiastic can be moved by no false-teaching sign, — how are we to explain the diseases which sometimes God permits Satan to inflict on the pious?**

*Reply.* Firmly must it be held, that *evils and pains all — punishments, diseases* — God inflicts, that he may punish the sins of men (Isa 45:7): *creans lucem, creans tenebras* — I make peace, and create evil (Isa 45:7). Nor is any man who *offering to sin, incident into the hands of the physician* (Sir 38:15). And whom *Their soul abhorreth all manner of meat; and they draw near unto the gates of death.* (Ps 107:18). God himself to *transgressors of the law threatens diseases, wounds and blows* (Deut 28:21–22). Yet also in this genus he uses the executor the devil: for as *Augustine* speaks: *God has a thousand ways of chastening us*, but chiefly are *these — sometimes by himself, sometimes by his angels, sometimes by other bad angels, by men, by beasts, by fires, — beyond nature and by any other force, — to give a just injury to the offense done to God is compared*.

Therefore *David* testifies that God sent afflictions and wrath and indignation, and troubles through evil angels, nor spared to spare death (Ps 78:49); and in the *Evangelic* history it is read of a certain woman who could not walk erect, because Satan had bound her eighteen years (Luke 13:11). And of *Herod* it is read, that *And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost.* (Acts 12:23). In general also of those whom Christ healed, *Peter* says that they had been *oppressed by the devil* (Acts 10:38).

Great therefore is the power of Satan in the bodies of men, but restricted to God's will: *he cannot do more than God permits*, therefore he cannot afflict the body alone, nor invade the swine, unless he obtains power from God (Matt 8:31). And it is general, that *Christ* says, that *But the very hairs of your head are all numbered.* (Matt 10:30). Therefore also the devil, when permitted anything, is restrained by the Lord (2 Cor 5:23).

Various are the *modes* of Satan's harm. **1.** *Through natural media* — he induces intemperance and gluttony, from which diseases arise, — as *Bacchus* also *is a fine wine-mixer* (Luke 12:19); he suddenly disturbs the humors of the body; infects the air; breathes poison into the bodies of men with wondrous celerity, — so that through *sorceresses* things done may appear, which yet have their natural causes, and God cooperating with Satan.

**2.** *Life he disturbs*, sleep he restlesses, limbs he tears, the body with occult wounds he inflicts (*evil spirits, hunters of vanity, and warriors*).

**3.** Sometimes *prodigiously*, contrary to the nature and origin of the nerves in the brain he disturbs, and *marvellous species of convulsions* he makes, wherewith he also mocks the most perturbed doctors, — who referring such things to natural causes, apply useless medicines. Body he defiles, private parts with ulcer he stains, so he may induce the persuasion of estrangement.

**4.** Sometimes he pushes the incorrect ears, — which afterwards either come forth, or perturb; of which see *Wier* in *Praestig. daemonum* (lib. 4, cap. 12).

**5.** Sometimes also with a *horrible species* he terrifies men, so that from terror they fall into dangerous diseases; of which have examples *Alexander ab Alexandro* in *Geniali dierum* (cap. 5).

Difficult it is to *discern* however whether a disease is *specially sent by the Devil*; therefore let us not easily fall into such cogitations. Let us remember *that no evil be in the city, which the Lord doeth not*: let us know, that *the devil cannot vex us* unless the Lord permits. Not easily however does the Lord permit Satan this power over the pious, whose he is *most-loving*: if ever indeed he permits, he does not permit that Satan crush them, but only that he exercise them, — *There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.* (1 Cor 10:13).

[*Over the omnipotent God's rod power holds a certain man of the malignant Spirit, who was not permitted even to pass into swine except by his permission — Gregory in Job. Since however clemently in this proponent God, he can be sad if not evil. The devil does not tempt whom he wants without a mission or permission: he is sent as a good permission — Augustine, Tract. 3 in John. Very often he is powerful to harm, but he cannot, when the will is under his power, but the ability is not, when either it does not lie in wait to persecute for the pleasure of the just does not remain. — Bede in Ps. Therefore he said to Christ (Matt 8): "I send," but "send me down," since he can exhort, he cannot compel — Chrysostom hom. 5 imp.*]

The sick therefore first of all should recognize that on account of their sins they have fallen into the hands of the *physician*; let them acknowledge themselves stricken by God, — whose hand wounded and sanest, — from him let them seek help, and let them not despise the legitimate means; if however they conjecture that Satan has been permitted something against them, by prayers let them avert it, with earnest repentance: — from organs however of the word let them not seek remedies.

Yet if any through herbs, whose qualities Satan knows best, and other means think diseases can be cured, from him we ought not to seek medicine, since it is a species of servitude which we offer to the devil: but let us commit the thing to God, by whose permission Satan has hurt us, and let us instant with prayers, that at length from the bonds of Satan he may free us, patient meanwhile awaiting an opportune time, which although unknown to us, God has reserved to his power.

**Casus VIII. Whether the devil is wont to converse with men in assumed visible form?**

*Reply.* That devils *from their own proper bodies destitute* out of air, or *from denser matter*, take bodies for themselves — *Fleus* also *Rhodius*, who was formerly an Angelus, is known.

That matter he disposes in various ways, whence *in various figures of animate beings and of men*, in the manner of *Proteus*, he appears: yea, also in the form of a cat, weasel, mouse, goat, dog, and similar forms he is seen.

For as *Nicolaus Remigius* writes (lib. 1 Daemonolatr., cap. 7): many are the species of animals, which the demons for the sake of occasion do not usurp, when they weave their deceits and construct their tricks. None however do they exercise more willingly than the form of *dogs*, — since these to human intercourse and colloquy are most convenient, and seem officious.

Nor lack they *external forms*: but so disposed by the most merciful God, that they usually bear a *conspicuous mark of their body*. Sometimes on one foot they proceed, — whence by the *Greeks* they were called *emphelocolonices*, since they were believed sent-into from *Meridian regions*, when in the underworld they made libations. Sometimes they have hands claw-like, and villous, and hairy; sometimes the whole body is bristling; feet horned and cloven-hooved, — and are called *Rors*. Sometimes they have exceedingly vast bodies; sometimes exceedingly thin and short.

In these *assumed forms* they appear not only to their ministers, *witches and sorceresses*, with whom they hold *choruses* and beget *children — whom they call Concubites, Lares* — and similar things they perform: but they also *converse* with others, in *private houses*, whence also they are called *household Lares* (*Kobolds* by the Germans).

Some are gentle and quiet, whom the *Greeks* call *domesticos*, the *Germans Kobold* (as it were *edifiers*), since they imitate the manners of men, laugh, jest, blandish to men, apply themselves in kitchens, stables, cells laboriously by night, take up the *conviva-ministrations* of ministers, descend ladders, open doors, kindle fire, draw water, prepare food, and pretend to do many things when yet they do nothing. The Germans have given them the name from their *goodness — Gutchen — quia se benigne faciunt, & hominibus assident* — for they render themselves kindly, and to men seat themselves.

*Luther* recites the history of a certain nobleman, to whom the devil was in place of a *stable-groom*, and of a certain maidservant, who always had the devil in the kitchen sitting near, whom she called *Heinzchen* — he kept his seat clean. Similarly of a devil served by a monk.

Something similar tells *Wier* (lib. 3 *De praestigiis daemonum*, cap. 3) about a certain *domestic demon* in a parents' house, — where in the barn a great quantity of walnuts was stored, — if buyers were about to come, the preceding night the sacks would fall by stages, — which the parents took as a good omen, and judged the buyers not far off. It is credible that Satan knows what buyers say to each other about their affairs, and shows such omens before they come, that he seem to predict what has already been arranged. These are the *genera of domestic demons*, who — because they transform themselves into angels of light — are called *mild and benign*.

Some *domestic Lares* are *dreadful* and *formidable*, who bring detriment either to men or to things in the household, breaking domestic vessels, striking servants and maids, sometimes even the impious master with lashes, or otherwise something dangerous machinates, — of which sort was that demon which *Melanchthon* refers happened *at Wittenberg* in the year 1521 *at his paterfamilias with much business and pace*. Among other things he seized a bag full of hazelnuts from a chest, and began to crack the nuts, and a little later excited a great tumult, as if empty vessels were being thrown down.

Especially frequent are demons in *metal-places*: for Satan thinks all the riches of the world he has in his power, and gives them out afterwards as he wills.

These also are of two genera. Some *benign* and *modest*, appearing in stature small, mostly like elders, in the form and habit of *metallurgists*, whence they are called *mountain-men, Bergmännlein*. They appear especially where metals are now dug or are about to be dug, — hope is there. They are said to harm no one, unless they are met with laughter or curses. To others they simulate themselves very busy, running hither and thither in the manner of miners at work, and yet accomplish nothing.

Some however are *harmful*, dreadful and terrible, mingled with the metals, whom either by breath or by touch of the body they infect, or throw from ladders, or corrupt with terrestrial *air*, — so that on account of their savagery many mines, though sufficiently opulent, have been abandoned. With these *harmful devils* no one willingly converses, but they horrify and flee them, all who are of sane mind.

[*In Turkey in a certain cave the devil appeared in the form of a cassowary crested (with) an armed head. Elsewhere he made a certain summer-shaded seat in a specular corona of rose-red said. At Silberg* (*Silberberg*) *such a demon in a place of construction of a work-shed lifted-out (a) from the upper place of great voice of new-fashioning* — as reference *Georgius Agricola* (in *De animantibus subterraneis*, tit. 1, ad Coelestes Fidem, p. 138).]

The *barbarians* in *India*, by devilish specters miserably tormented, an image of the devil with dreadful sight, in a great throne placed, with certain ceremonies and sacrifices they cult, — lest he harm.

But that among *Christians* even are found who by these demons of *benign and familiar* they call, delight in their sight and conversation, address them blandly, invite them to meals, entrust to them domestic labors and similar things, — this indeed we cannot praise, — since *what agreement has Christ with Belial?* (2 Cor 6:14–15). The devil is a *sworn enemy of the human race*, whom always we must fear, — who, when he simulates himself the best, is the worst, — which *Luther* proves by example of *that Heinzchen*, whom a maid (of whom above) had sitting near the kitchen hearth, — whom when she asked to give himself in specimen form, he for a long time refused, but at length when the maid, understanding that a slaughtered infant had been in waters seen, — Satan, as author of the murder, resistant, — for that maid had once slaughtered an infant, whose memory the devil was now taking her hand.

[*Demons infringing power we can infringe, when, by observation of the divine precepts, we prevent their assault in us: we cut off. Greatest in these things is the guard for the guardianship of men from the flames of demons is piety — Hermes Trism. Piety helps man, nor demons multiplying, gods much less, — Rev. summum ad iram — 13, cap. 14, and orig. cap. 22. All the approaches of the senses let us close, so that neither through the eye's illection, nor by the ears' pruring, nor pulse-figment amid our hearing may enter — Olympiodorus cap. 30, in eccl. hist. As much in this evil the power of the demons the fear-name he wants was hostile-turnedhold in the trees, by whom of the depths to the sums thou dost climb — Origen 11 in Nnm. lib. 15, cap. 3. In his name he is conquered, who assumed man alike sine peccato. So an unarmed Christ soldier hastens; sudden, artful, sneaky solicits obstacles; he suits imperious; he entices imperfect. If however anyone the Lord's precepts keeping and constantly to Christ inhering resists thee, so that thou canst be conquered — thou art necessary, since whoever confesses is invincible — Cypr. ad Fortun. de exhortat. martyr.*]

Finally, let a man always remain in his ways, that is, in the office of his vocation: never let a man invite the devil to himself, none use his ministry, none rejoice at his sight: for a *natural* it is, so also it ought to be, *enmity* between man — with Christ's blood redeemed from the power of Satan — and that *ancient serpent*.

We are deceived also, who estimate that man through Christ has received power over the devil to call him, order him, and use his works at whim. Conquered indeed is the devil through Christ, for our good, but not is his ministry subject to Christ's, — therefore he traverses the earth, cohabits with men, not to be beneficial, but that he may harm, in whatever way God shall have permitted.

Always therefore we must pray, lest God hand us over to the power of the devil, lest our house be a *habitation of demons*, lest Satan come at any time into our sight. If however in such places, where the devil finds hospitality, we must dwell, before all things to true piety let us insist, and what things Satan delights in, these let us not do: for over them the demon has power, *who exclude God from himself and his mind — angel to Tob. 6, 7*. Then also let us not court the devil, nor blandish him in any way, but with prayers and exercises of the divine word let us resist: this is the *sword of the Spirit*, which the devil cannot bear.
