**Casus IX. What then are the chief studies and works of the devil, from which we can recognize his presence when he does not appear in visible form?**

*Reply.* The devil is called *Satan, ekthros* and *adversarius*, thus he is opposed to all things which are of good nature — to God chiefly, to the holy angels, and to pious men. And on account of these especially he is opposed to God and to angels whom he cannot harm in others: therefore he is called *adversary of men chiefly* (1 Pet 5:8).

**God he hates extremely**, and lest by any man he be loved or cultivated, he wishes. Therefore false opinions of God he instills into men; the purity of the divine word, by which we are instructed in the true cult of God, in every way he impedes, and the minds of men with lies he fills.

And since he is not ignorant that man naturally knows there is a God, and that he wants himself to be cultivated by us, — either God himself he makes, or by some other pact the cult of the true God he depraves, — arrogates to himself certain *divinity*, and, to find cultors, works miracles, cures diseases, predicts futures, — but so that he may involve truth in lies, as also above we heard. For impudent is the demon, who when asked, even of things he does not know, constantly affirms; and what he does know, if once true, ten times he refers falsely.

Here pertain all *species of idolatry*, by which — the author being the devil — men are led away from God: therefore the *gods of the gentiles are called demons* (Ps 96:5); and *tables in the temples of idolatry* are called *tables of demons* (1 Cor 10:21); and whatever things are offered to strange gods are called *demons*.

To this study of Satan are also referred *apparitions of specters* in cemeteries, at monuments and tombs, — even words at statues, — by all of which men are induced to new, illicit, and unknown cults.

Then the devil is opposed to *Christ* the Mediator, whom he knows to have come *to destroy the works of the devil* (1 John 3:8). This the devil in the possessed man confesses: *And, behold, they cried out, saying, What have we to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of God? art thou come hither to torment us before the time?* (Matt 8:29). Therefore in whatever ways he can, to Christ he opposes; from himself he makes Christ: — *Theudam Iudaeorum*, *Papam Franciscum* the *cultor* of St Francis, and *another Jesus* he calls; in place of Christ he wants to be held, — makes the Pope *Vicar of Christ*, out of all Saints he makes *mediators of ours*, — the doctrine of Christ he despises, — the miracles of Christ to his own virtue he ascribes, persecutions against the Gospel of Christ he excites, — those believing in Christ with their sins he wounds, from tempted he removes Christ from view, — into cruel tyrant he transmutes, — all which things to the ignominy of Christ and to the ruin of men tend.

Third, he is opposed to the *holy angels*, whom he knows on account of us — since we shall be *heirs of salvation* — to be sent forth, that we may be surrounded by them, kept in all our ways, and borne by their hands. Since with them therefore he ever wars, our works he impedes, — us with impure cogitations of body he vexes, whereby holy spirits are put to flight, — daily is molest, and to divulge us from the guardianship of holy angels sedulously labors.

Finally, and chiefly, he is opposed to *men*, whom in every part he harms: to depraved things against God he instigates; the office and order of the good he overturns; all places he fills with crimes; with tragic falls, misfortunes, dangers, and *discrimina* he renders minds anxious, so that against God from impatience they murmur; children against parents, husbands against wives, brother against brother, and the closest to each other, he arms with hatreds, suspicions, quarrels, and brawls, — so that by mutual wounds fallen they may pass their life with weariness. And that with one word I may say: all things whatever are of the world which are sad, unfavorable, whereby God's grace, conscience's goodness, and life's tranquility we lose, — all these have the devil as their author, of whom the voice from heaven sounds: *Therefore rejoice, ye heavens, and ye that dwell in them. Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea! for the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath, because he knoweth that he hath but a short time.* (Rev 12:12).

Of these works of Satan, whereby he lies in wait to man, an elegant *picture* is shown us by *Cyprian* (Serm. 2, which is *De zelo et livore*): *he goes about us singly, and as if enemies with barriers besieged of walls he explores, tempts, whether any part of the members is less stable and inconstant, — of whom the access to the interior may pierce. He offers to the eyes forming allurements, — offers easy voluptuous pleasures, so that by sight he may destroy chastity; strikes the ears with sweeter sounds, so that by heard sound may loosen the vigor of the Christian. The tongue he provokes to reviling, the hand to injury; the maker of persuasion, the enticer of dogs, of provisions increase, in delicacies scandal-taking; suggests noxious compendia, promises earthly honors, so that adamant may take celestial; shows false, so that he may snatch away true, — and when he cannot corrupt clearly, insidious lurking he does not cease: as when the world is on fire, in truth, the intervening persecution takes over; adds to habitual praise imposts, and *hoveringly* in peace pursues, in war unlooked-for*.

He is even *latent* still: from these and similar studies of the devil we can gather to us present, though in visible form he does not appear: nay, as often as we see the *sons of light* by the darkness of vices, obscured — sold under sin, who neither God nor men care, — we see them among the *devils enumerated in a state of vices, gone from among them*.

**Casus X. What therefore is to be done by a pious man, lest by these studies of the devil he be prostrated?**

*Reply.* This is the consolation and admonition of piety, which most-strongly the devil resists in the battle for the pious, that we may not fail.

The **fountains of consolation** are these: **(1)** The devil has no right over the pious: therefore neither can he harm them at his own arbitrium, but only as much and how much God permits. But God's *permission* has certain *fixed limits* fixed to him, which he cannot transgress: *and God is faithful, who suffereth us not to be tempted above what we are able* (1 Cor 10:13). Truly it is a great consolation, that he will not hand us over into that oppressive one, into the enemy.

[*Whatever happens to the just is imputed to the will of God, in whose power we are set; whatever therefore we suffer, God wills, — even if it seem to us evil. If God does not want, it cannot happen — Aug. in Ps. 26. See Job 1, v. 10. The devil is like a chained dog: — he barks at whom he can, but at whom he can bite, he cannot.*]

**(2)** Sure to the pious is *victory* prepared, who already have conquered in Christ their patron, whose victory is ours. Not to us are temptations to ruin, but to *probation*. For as *Athanasius* (in *Vita Antonii*) speaks: *since to us in this life, God has willed to be beyond this life, that our contest with them may be, — as ready champions our victory brings his glory of Christ, to make the devil pale — from the same, so that our victory may not be in vain that the coming, — the woman's seed be worn to press it — the head of Christ, Gen 3:15*.

Hence *discrimen* is recognized between *studies of the demon*, whereby the pious he assails, and the *impious*. For to the pious *he says*: *not to himself*, as by the impious he can, to whom he flatters, — but wills to compel — since to *corporals* and *fortunes* of them he harms, so that they either despair or blaspheme God (Job 2); or *by his ministers* he seeks to *lead them captive in his snares*, blind their senses, to push them to resist the truth, — in respect of whom also *Deus huius saeculi* he is called (2 Cor 4:4).

He who considers these things with himself will bear patiently the insults of Satan, since with an enemy already conquered he wrestles, — and that even at the nod of God on the destined day of certain victory.

Admonitions also are given to us, that to the battle with the devil we may not slacken, but in *counter-part* we may be alert. **1.** General is the exhortation of the Apostle (Jas 4:7): *resist the devil, and he will flee from you*; likewise *Peter* (1 Pet 5:8). *Divus Paulus* the whole armor of the Christian soldier for the battle wherein he must engage Satan describes to us: *the loins girded with the belt of truth, and the breastplate of righteousness, and the shield of faith, whereby the fiery darts of the devil are extinguished*, — of the *fasts and vigils* he does not cease to bespeak.

[*Our fast we call the moderation of soul — Ambrose serm. 16. Not the health of the body but of the calcaneus by whom is adhibited. By fasting the passions of the body, and the reason of health it makes for its own custom, our labor.*]

**2.** By *prayers*. *For prayer*, says *Augustine*, *is a subjugation of him praying, to God, and a sacrifice against demons, a whip: nothing more resists the devil-assault: he by prayers is prevented, — battles now stuck to our mind are broken*. Therefore *Christ* also his disciples bids to pray, lest they enter into temptation (Matt 26:41).

[*Faith makes strong the pious victor — 1 Ambrose, Faith, hope, love, prayer of the humble — Ambrose hom. 3 in Matt.*]

**3.** By *sobriety* and *fasting*. For *intemperance is the mother of many crimes*, and what the devil cannot impetrate from the sober, he easily effects through the drunk. Therefore *Christ*: *watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation. Bonum fenum est oratio, quando duo illa ignita spicula adversarii solvantur — Ambros. In the well are the arms and defences by prayers, whereby all the diabolical machinations we can repel — Chrysost. hom. 1 de orat. cum sacerdotalibus peccatorum eranticorum acuti sit: — the sound of pilgrimage prayer must-be subserved a strict-sound-be*.

**4.** By the *Word*, which is the *sword* of the Holy Spirit, wherewith the fiery darts of Satan we can quench. By the word departed the temptation of *Christ*, who to the tempter *Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.* (Matt 4:7); *avaunt, Satan* (Matt 4:10); on necessity from the word to arm ourselves against the devil and his studies, we too by word conquer, and without the word if we should be, we should perish in temptations. Thus *Luther*, much vexed by the devil, by the word overcame him, that is, by sayings of Scripture, which about *Christ* the works of Satan overturn; as of that *demon* who in monastic habit met him and provoked him to dispute, whom he recognized from the bloodless of his hands, and by the saying *ecce homo mediator inter Deum et homines*, he put to flight.

[*To the word of God even the diabolical powers tremble* (Matt 8:29). *For if the word of God is more powerful and higher than any sword — heaven and earth shall pass away, but the word of the Lord not — Luke 21:33*.]

**5.** By *fervor of fasting*, — *fervent fastings drive out demons* (Matt 17:21).

Also by the *Gospel*, which is the *saving and salubrious* Christ: *by the word of God the impure spirit of demonic infestation we can interpose — poisonous beasts of unclean spirits we drive away — Bede on Mark hom. 3, 6*. *What is this arrow of the tabular sword? What is the sword of the mouth of the Word of God, ejecting evil-crying, the entrance-holy-cross-Christ, whom we architect the tabular-holds firm faith of Scripture — Bede.*

**6.** By *patient longanimity*, that we not collide with the devil, nor at his monstrous attempts laugh or contemn, but *bear patiently his vexations meanwhile*, knowing that (*A great evil is not to be able to bear an evil, but a patient soul like a bulwark, is very firm — Prudent. in Psychomach.*). For as *Luther* writes on John 3: *the devil is a proud spirit, and nothing less can bear than contempt, whom when he cannot decline, he grows sick and departs. Grave and heavy is he indeed, so that anyone from mourning would die, but when he sees that we resolve to bear everything, whatever things burden us can be, and if we entirely nothing care and prefer, primum turba is placed. Far greater is his pride, than that our contempt he can bear*.

**7.** Before all, *resistance to the Devil* by exercise of piety must be perpetuated. For *when God is contemned, the devil has power* (Tob 3). It was a simple and upright man, therefore *the devil brought to him about his house, and* although the devil impetrated some power, yet from true piety to move him neither could he harm him more, than God permitted. Fear God therefore, keep his commandments, flee sins against conscience, — from the *impetus of the devil* be immune, as it is written (Ps 91:1): *he that dwelleth in the help of the Most High, shall abide under the protection of the God of heaven*.

*From the truth of God's Lord if we lack, we perish — Greg.*

*One and only the guard of the human race is prayer — Hermes Trismegistus.*

*Beyond soul human intercession* (God piety respects) *humility subjects patience, cleanses obedience, guides perseverance, gives faith, introduces charity — Aug. in soliloquiis, cap. 24.*

**8.** To these all be added, *assiduous labors in the offices of vocation*: for idle him easily supplants the *ideness has taught many evils* (Sir 33:29), which the example of *David* testifies. Who however his own affairs takes care of, is safe: *For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.* (Ps 91:11).

[*Whereby by attentive milk he is tamed, so also by continuous prey. The nature of humanity is more and more indomitable to become — Bern. Nothing of good if is not, this alone is to be able. — Chrysost. serm. 26. Man idle a footstool of devil — Bern. serm. 1 epist. 5. Woe to us! — 1. Foolish man extends himself unto the fatuous who leans on the brute: — a man well-occupied is truly a man, God — the mind rules the vices*.]

With these arms let us always be prepared against the devil, whether he attacks us sensibly, or through internal temptations disturbs our minds: thus the more we shall be crowned with the palm of victory, in this manner and mode with what is due to Satan resisting, victory we bring in. For this victory *Christ* to us has acquired, of the very itself: *good cheer, I have conquered the world* (John 16:33). Therefore his elect from his hands *he does not permit to be snatched* (John 10:28); and the Apostle *Paul* writes that *God tempteth no one above his strength, but from the temptation causeth also outgoing* (1 Cor 10:13); and hope also gives to us — *And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.* (Rom 16:20). Hence our souls we can rest, and to this battle be animated, — therefore *Peter* bids us *resist steadfast in the faith* (1 Pet 5:9), since to these promises we ought to trust, if we would conquer the devil.

## Chapter III. On Cases of Conscience Concerning Actions with the Possessed

*That an action of men is often exercised for the power of Satan, is manifest from the preceding: but scarcely anywhere with greater evidence does he exercise this cause than in the bodies of the possessed, and in melancholic souls*; of whom in due course must be said, — beginning from those things which come into the consideration of the *possessed*.

**The possessed** are called those miserable men into whose bodies the devil has entered, occupies, agitates, and cruciates, whose limbs he uses horribly, — of whom examples enough are supplied in the Evangelic history (Matt 8:28; 17:14; 12:22, etc.).

*Daemoniaci* they are called from him by whom they are possessed, — the demon: *energumeni* from his operation, since from *ex-energein* is derived — which sometimes is used absolutely and simply. For those who by some inspiration prognosticate something, are called *aphrontismenoi* from *a-phron-esis* — those who are in the manner *aphron*, prophesy through the *Spirit*. *Anathematoi* are called those *excommunicated*, since it is said that they at that time are handed over to Satan to be agitated by evil spirits.

Presupposition however is here to be made, that the devil can enter into a man not indeed *as to substance* but as to *virtue and operation*, just as the sun by force of its rays penetrates bodies, but not with its own substance, — which is manifest from that the devil in the form of a *serpent* deceived Eve (Gen 3), and from *the swine* into which he most eagerly entered, and precipitated them into the sea (Matt 8), and that *Christ* ejected demons from the bodies of many. And this was the *common opinion* of the Jews, who called *Christ himself daemoniac and blasphemer* (John 8:48); nor did Christ ever deny, in the possessed offered to him, that a devil was there, but he was recognizing *a certain kind of demons* by that name of them; likewise *Paul* also, by the *Athenians* accused of superstitious cult (Acts 17:22), did not by-negating-that-demons-can-enter-into-bodies-of-men, but only that he was *not having a demon*.

These teach the *insaner operations* of Satan, who cruciates the possessed with wondrous evils, and impels them, so that some cast themselves into waters, others into fires, others by poison kill themselves. In these actions is not eluded some accession of a bodily man, but his powers act in the bodies which they occupy, and move and impel, whither they wish, and as much as by God it is permitted.

Those who therefore converse with the possessed of such kind — to them various things can occur, on which the mind must be informed and confirmed, lest anything be done with doubting conscience: of which now we shall treat with a few Cases.

**Casus I. Whence can it be known that one is truly vexed by devil?**

*Reply.* Knowledge of this thing pertains not so much to *Theologians* as to *Physicians*.

Yet since something about the ways and behaviors of the possessed sometimes underlies, — sometimes even in comitial disease (epilepsy), in *lethargic*, *maniac*, *phrenetic*, and similar cases, — therefore *exorcists* very often are deceived, laboring in vain to expel the devil, since not the devil but the disease was there. And these sick ones are more easily cured by *physicians* than by *exorcism* they could have been.

Therefore even if we see in the sick convulsions and disturbances of body of the stupefied, we should not easily incline to a judgment about *obsession*. For many things in this genus can happen from *the nature of the sick person*, and many things also by the devil externally afflicting, and by God permitting, — the miserable ones by these tortured, — though not in bodies of the invaded of God to them are conceded.

How therefore also *anatomical* judgment about the possessed may be made in place of *natural* disease-suffering, to cure them — of what the *Devil* is playing sport — see in *Wier* (lib. 3, *De praestigiis daemonum*, cap. 13). Confer also *De metallicis subterraneis* the very *Alexander ab Alexandro*, and the observations of *Wier*.

Sometimes also simulated obsession, on which some cause has been permitted by evil men, — of which examples see near *Wier* (lib. 3, cap. 26). *Whence a boy dance recognized* — since that at Piacenza in 1595, when a small boy after a fit of laughter was found in extreme distress-like signs, the parents to himself in mockery took it and pretended-obsession, — and afterward himself recognized it.

Whom yet corporally the demon does not besiege, as of *Judas Iscariot* it is read, that *Satan entered into him* (Luke 22:3).

Although therefore *God-alone* it is to know these things certainly, yet some signs of that thing can be given. Firstly, it is compact that the devil sometimes shows himself by certain signs, — his ingress into the body of a man, — which indeed is not-out-of-danger, nor is it always to be presumed. But he sometimes acts, though he wills; and in this, as in many other things, God permits: — for also his advent sometimes with certain preliminaries is announced, as among other things is manifest from the history of *Elissabeth verlacontis* (etc.).

The *signs* by which the devil signalizes his advent for the possessed are chiefly *four*:

**1.** *Horrible aspects of a demon*, wherewith the spirit of the one about to be possessed disturbs. For a little before he enters into their bodies, he appears to them either in the form of a cadaver of a dead man, or blackish and of a fawn; sometimes indeed the possessed assert they saw serpents in the species of a dog or black *Ethiopian*.

**2.** *Horrible howling* — an unusual noise, unaccustomed sound, tumult, — which is hardly to be heard elsewhere than in the very place where they are about to be possessed, — his arrival betrays.

**3.** *Potence*, which the one about to be possessed brings — whom with a blow he strikes to the ground, hostile-cast, and afflicts — from which afterwards weakness and torments as it were as a *foretaste* he permits.

**4.** *Symptomata*, whereby the one about to be possessed seems to himself as attacked by demonic agitation, vexed, driven, — which after the ingress of the demon happen too vehemently.

Then are certain signs, which after the *ingress of the demon* into a man are gathered:

**1.** The possessed, although idiots, — knowing letters, — sometimes speak *foreign languages*: which is a most certain sign of obsession, since it is compact that the freed neither can know those languages nor recollect what they had said. The devil however knows all languages, and takes them up in the mouth of the possessed, even with them ignorant. Whence *Philippus Melanchthon* mentions in tract *De legibus* — *of a certain girl who neither could read nor write, yet could speak in Greek and Latin*, — and *save that certain Saxonic Belisin was so predicted in these words: — Baumbeis rot per Poplock cap fein, — vermel dora et in terra, and multus in populo iam* (*Hieronymus* in *Vita Hilarionis* concurs), *coactae voces dilatoris confert. Numerary a delicate tongue-tied demon obsedit, when many arcanis Syraque locutus est* (which had never been learned) — *and Rufas eloquens*. And how from the Greek tongue and use he was recognized, when the medic once curing him — was noted *Wier* (lib. 3 *De praestigiis daemonum*, cap. 3).

[*Verses hither are: — He plays with the boy, of a young man playing home with only two family boys with dry ears of malignant and quiet convulsion of tempered intervals, — the arm somehow at times feasting first arm to now dexterously, — sometimes even the digit-lower one to the higher-under his own hand-fastened, but of such celerity should he shake, that scarcely from a minister his body himself could be turned. The head however unshaken always remained, tongue and speech free, sense unimpaired, — as in unconsciousness only ferocity. He took ten days to be exhorted, — at intervals it was still, but by their labor came in — a true epilepsy or so of mind and sense injured that on this-medicaments-and-physical-body-of-water — no useful reason of experience of the philters — with some poisoned dust or with the ivy fungus-impacts-supped — from which vapor to the temples came, that from the throat much of these were disseminated. This believed cause the woman-wife stood-guard, — with clysters frequent, purgations by soul-clay, cleaning-poultices, and to boot her being placed on the anointing-drinks — she is filled first, with all the toxic-materia-tests he shakes, which of the body he might disperse. With these having profited nothing sudden sweats provoked — bathings, effusions, and refrigerations. When these too nothing profited, since all far from the *knowledge of truth* were, — if not the third day gulped over. As often as the ill father visited, from a distance-was-carried-into-mind-a-column: — pounding-the-back-with-a-block, and-somehow-repelling-him, or twisting-the-hair-from-the-neck-plucking — from which happened, either that they with fixed knights bore the image-suspended. Asked here who he was, or how or by what power these things it was operating, — replied to a shining ass of nothing to be an image, in which he was recovered and in quiet to others migrating — himself this body drove in from a certain one, whose name would not be born, from the feet entering-with-Regia, and from the feet exit — when the appointed day approached. Meanwhile the demon himself so bore the image up to a truth-as-strong-as-a-tuft-a-victim, that all bystanders escaped as evidence, — as if truly the truthful sculpting of any body was, — nor was there indeed suspicion, — since the head of God's image seemed of him — with-the-imitation-being-any-usage. What Christ did was as brave: taunted-that-thou-didst-fall (1 Cor 2), — Job just afflicted (Job 1), — Eve in Eden of God's-substance out-of-life-tempted-vine (see Fernel. 2 *De abditis rerum causis* c.16). Nay, of that fanatical, — the voice as a bathing, gone-through-words and sentences, — as much of things done, as much of what things Saul-caught-hearing-caught-word — Pfeamin. Many-of-the-medics-in-charity-detects.*]

**2.** *Occult things* — those which by our own senses are hidden — from a beast is known-with-forbearance: — with such a sign of the possessed, — since that revelation of hidden things may cede to the contumely of God and to the neighbor's injury: — some of the *Prophets* foretold things future divinely.

**3.** *Apparent form of animal* — the malignant spirit sometimes in the obsessed appears in the form of a *fly, spider*, sitting on the mouth of him, sometimes even on other parts of the body: — but in this form they are not always seen, nor easily, unless when they are about to be expelled, — where at the mandate of God under the species of such sordid animals they are compelled to attest their presence, as noted by those who wrote *De exorcismis daemonum*. *Thyraeus* also confirmed this in obsessed persons, refers *[Wier lib.] 3 De obsessis c.10*.

**4.** True obsession sign is also *foolishness* — untimely and out-of-place laughter accompanied, which foolishness indeed even from a disease can be, but when no signs of disease appear, it is a sign that the man is possessed by the *malignant*. Such a man *Apollonius of Tyana*, the *prince of the magi*, apud *Philostratus*, showed by a malignant spirit possessed, and himself liberated him, refers *Bodinus* De demonomania (lib. 3).

**5.** *From wondrous and stupendous works of the possessed*, can be gathered that a man is possessed by the devil: — as sometimes they *cintillate* like little birds, imitating the voices of other animals exactly; that they ascend inaccessible and precipitous places and on those sleeping — and by unstepping foot return through themselves; that from occasion of no danger of the ostentation of the diabolical also in their eyes may appear, may make.

**6.** Also on account of *hidden operations of the devil*, — like signs of the ram — the whole nation from the assumed skin — of the ram-signs — is now known even to their own — even from apparent-observations. But this hidden-power is different from that occurring of Chaldeans-and-Egyptians.

Great is the power of the devil in *bodies* — of *air-fluctuant-imperative — of him — of the demoniacs which are done according to variety*. In some at times *bites* — a *hard fastening* — Berg-mangelein signs *Christenlichem-cottage-open* — is called the *Berg-mangel*.

**7.** *When men horrify at the name of Jesus, from prayers, and from divine exercises to which by force also they are directed, and with great crying they exceed them*, — the indication is that themselves by evil spirit are possessed, — who these cannot bear.

**8.** *From wondrous works of the devil*, whereby he afflicts the possessed, can be concluded that a man is corporally possessed by him, — such especially are the *miserable body-vexations* — which with stupendous torments he cruciates, — whence the miserable ones' horrible cries and howlings are heard. Members dislocated, head turned in a circle, the body itself in *serpentine curl* rotated around, — whose horrible examples are shown in the Evangelic history in the daughter of *Chananaea* who is read to have been badly vexed by the *demon* (Matt 15:22), and in a certain adolescent, whom now in waters, now in fires the *malignant spirit* threw, so all cries by which they exceed and are dumb, — says *Wier* (lib. 4 *De praestig. daemonum*, cap. 15) — *so all clamors of a very acerbic being seem*.

**Casus II. From what signs can it be recognized whether a man is truly obsessed by a devil, or otherwise labors under a natural disease?**

*Reply.* The signs listed above serve for this purpose. But since these can also arise from natural disease, physicians must first be consulted. Only when *no natural cause* is apparent, and the signs point to *demonic operation*, should judgment of obsession be made. Even so, discernment must be done with much prayer and consultation with *ministers of the Church*, since Satan can also feign obsession in the healthy to deceive.

**Casus III. When are the crimes committed by the possessed imputable to them?**

*Reply.* It is certain that not rarely the possessed do many things which can in no way be excused — as that they blaspheme God, curse men, execrate ministers of God, wound others, and sometimes even *kill themselves*. Yet all these cannot simply be attributed to the possessed, nor to the besieging devil.

For the *obsessi* are of *two genera*: some are *pessimi homines*, who either through art simulate obsession for their own gain, or through penalty of prior improbity are possessed by the devil. These indeed, since even when sane they were always prone to sinning, and when possessed they perpetrate such things at the demon's instigation, — certainly are not to be excluded from culpa. For they are *slaves of Satan*, whom he leads captive at his own will, — therefore even when freed from the demon they do not cease to perpetrate such things.

Sometimes however good and God-fearing men are besieged by the devil, God permitting. Their limbs indeed the devil abuses, *the tongue* to blaspheming and reviling, the *hand* to killing and wounding, — but they are wholly either *unwilling* or *ignorant*, — which is gathered from this, that when Satan withdraws a little from them (for by intervals he tortures them), they remember none of these things, and things done by themselves they seriously grieve, — pardon they beseech, and lest similar things ever happen to them, seriously wish.

Just as therefore is not attributed to the possessed themselves the use of foreign tongues, revelation of hidden things, concussion and trembling of the body, but the devil operates these in them, — so also *sins* of this sort are not so much to be ascribed to those miserable men as to the demon himself, since the devil through them acts, no otherwise than in a *phrenetic*, — for whose account are they to be guarded, and if any harm is done by them by another, they should be forced to make compensation. Nor are they subject to punishment, — since the devil through them acts as in phrenetics, — nay, they ought to be guarded, — and if damage is done by them to others, — it is not their part to render account, but of those to whose custody they had been committed.

**Casus IV. Whether the possessed are excluded from eternal salvation?**

*Reply.* Obsession of demons is a *penalty of the body*, in which God to the Devil sometimes permits great power; in the souls however of men to himself alone has he reserved absolute imperium. Concerning therefore *eternal salvation* the devil has no such power, that he can deprive the miserable ones of these good things. Therefore we do not exclude the possessed, on that account that they are possessed, from the *kingdom of heaven*, or from *life eternal*, which Christ by his blood has acquired for them equally as for others. Which even they themselves do not always deny that they hope for, — since sometimes, when from the insidiousness and violence of the devil they are somewhat freer, they themselves confess, when about *Christ, faith, penitence, and life eternal* they piously speak, and *sound-minded and salvation-hoping* they show themselves.

There are however some who indeed do not exclude the possessed from *salvation*, but nevertheless deprive them of *faith* — which about *Petrus Thyraeus* (part 3, *De daemoniacis*, cap. 28) is manifest. But these no wise attend, — since they deny life and salvation, when it is impossible for anyone to be saved who lacks faith: yea, so is *the salvation of souls* (1 Pet 1:9). *But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.* (Heb 11:6).

Even if therefore the *acts and exercises of faith* do not always exert themselves in the possessed, since however to their sober intervals — from speeches and acts of them it is known — still yet faith in them was not altogether *extinguished*.

Here however are again to be distinguished the possessed. Some by *their own fault*, and on account of enormous crimes, are handed over to the *devil* to be tortured: some however are pious and God-fearing, — and yet God permits this *torturer* of Satan in them.

*The former* as concerns them, — just as before they had abstained from *penitence*, faith and *conscience* they had lost by sins their own, — so also under the plagues of Satan they live without faith, blaspheme God, are hostile to men, and hasten toward their own destruction, — which is gathered from this, that being left for a time by the devil, in their worst deeds they glory more than for those from acts they may grieve. Sometimes however it happens that, being sooner in that torture *Satanic* softened, they impiety renounce for which they were snared by *Satan* — bid farewell, and true *penitence* do — these, if afterward the devil proceed to cruciate, in the time of that *paroxysm* of faith and hope of salvation they have — of which we do not doubt.

But since scarcely much of space for vexation they have with the impious besieged by the devil, so that to themselves they come and about admitted sins do penitence, in the present life they seldom convert.

*The pious however* have another reason, who indeed do not incur the guilt but sometimes *(3.)* to the spiritual battle with devils Christ their leader, however-acerbic-a-medium, prepares — for who the plagues of the body from demon inflicted knows to overcome, is to enemies to whom to soul is molest, more firmly resist can.

**Casus V. Whether obsessed persons may be admitted to the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of the Lord?**

*Reply.* In the primitive Church it was not denied to them. Thus indeed from the *Cassiodorus* writes *Thomas* (p. 3, q. 8, art. 9): to those who are vexed by *unclean spirits*, communion of the sacred and holy is more distant from our altar. And when they are free from them, from the use of the *Cena Dominica* they do not exclude: so neither this last plague of the devil in the obsessed, — since indeed from this sacred banquet nothing except *impenitence* excludes, which however in all the possessed is not to be found.

Yet from this caution work is needed: not are to be admitted the possessed **(1.)** who from earliest almost *infancy* without ceasing are vexed by the devil, so much so that beyond external form they have scarcely anything of a man.

**(2.)** Those who have not long experienced these demonic afflictions, — those to whom these demonic annoyances have come, into that diabolical rage they too are not to be admitted. For those who wish to eat of the Lord's sacred table, first ought to *probate themselves*, — an ardent-desire of this sacred food they ought to have, and to *announce the death of the Lord*, and *to apply the same to themselves* — which how in these miserable ones in the very time of obsession can happen, it does not appear.

But those who from the *malignant spirit* have some *quiet time*, — as if restored to themselves are, — those to the *Lord's sacred banquet* to be desirous, the *Lord's food* from other common foods to be able to discern, themselves to prove, and worthy of this Lord's banquet to be able to enjoy, — therefore not in this time indeed are they to be admitted: since as *melancholy, mania, epilepsy* and similar most acute diseases men at that time seized-with-a-paroxysm those diseases-suffer, so more excruciating in patience they bear, — faith and good conscience even in time of obsession they retain, — and although *blasphemies, contumelies, injuries*, and other sins are heard from them, — yet not from them-self proceed, but from the devil, who abuses their limbs, — with themselves unwilling; they therefore retain integral *conscience*, and so also *faith*, which only by sins-against-conscience is lost.

**Casus VI. Since one, by their own fault, subjects themselves to this diabolical plague — what chiefly are those sins by which God hands a man over to be corporally besieged by the devil?**

*Reply.* Just as sins have their *grades*, so also of *punishments* is inequality, especially the *temporal*: — among which since bodily obsession by the devil is *most grievous*, sins also which merit such a plague ought not to be small.

Even if Scripture in this genus determines nothing certain, — from examples of the possessed in some manner we make judgment. What if, in the order of the *precepts of the Decalogue* we should proceed, scarcely any part of the Decalogue could be found, which by its transgression obsession-in-devils in bodies not merits.

*Concerning those who impugn the known truth*, writes *Cyprian* (Serm. *De lapsis*, cap. 7), — many of them by demons were possessed.

*Blasphemy* also opens for the devil the mouth: for from whose mouth frequently speaks the demon, — of them also the body as an enemy to invade he can. Whereto can be referred the example of *Hymenaeus* and *Alexander*, whom *Paul* is read to have *Of whom is Hymenaeus and Alexander; whom I have delivered unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme.* (1 Tim 1:20).

*On account of the abuse of the sacred Eucharist* writes *Aquinas* (in loco dicto) whom the *Corinthians* had, that *For this cause many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep.* (1 Cor 11:30), — and in the *hard-place-treatise of a certain citizen of Cologne* is read, that he had a daughter obsessed by devil, — since when she was cursed by-imprecation the devil possessed her, — of the promptness of the example — Prochor. 4 fol. 84.

*Injustice, hatred, and envy* opens the *inhabitation of demons*, — as *Saul*'s example testifies, — into whom Satan entered when *David*, from mere envy, he persecuted (1 Sam 18:8). *Homicides* also, from this cause. Thus *Gislebertum*, Duke of *Franconia*, was possessed, when *St Kilian* he had killed, — as writes *Sebertum* in *Vita Kilianum*.

*On account of illicit amors, incests, feminine libidines*, that impure Spirit is fasted, — where can be referred the example of the *incestuous Corinthian* (1 Cor 5), whom indeed corporally possessed we do not say, but by the devil we hold vexed — as the *Apostle Paul* testifies. Concerning a certain *virgin* refers *Prosper Aquitanicus* (lib. 6, *De praedest. et gratia*), that when she in a bath a *virile image* — Solomon-with-jars intueretur, — of her likeness to himself she formed, — by devil continually was possessed, and so vexed, that the *malignant spirit* the throat's ostium-shrieked, — food and drink for seventy days occluded.

*Chaldeus, King of the Chaldeans*, was seized by a demon, when the *temple*, so that he should despoil it, entered; seized also *some certain* on account of theft, which he had committed in a *sacred* something, — refers *Gregory* (lib. 4 dialog.).

In the *Life of Perondulus* it is read of a certain one, who, when he was in prayer distracted, — from the devil obsessed was. Of *Abbate quodam Mose*, refers *Cassianus* (lib. 7 collat., cap. 17), that on account of *impatience* and *stubbornness* some word from the devil possessed he was.

Finally, this peril are exposed all *improbi hominis*, who neither God fear nor men care, whom so in snares his captives leads the devil his own will, until at last from God's permission bodies of them altogether he occupies. Thus *Alexander ab Alexandro* (lib. 4 *Genial. dier.*, cap. 19) about a certain young man writes, whom with *horrible aspect* in the eyes of the standers-by the devil to invade appeared, — since it was compact that in most-bad morals and incivilities he had lived, with contempt of God for a long time.

Let us flee therefore sins by which we tempt devils to our own heart, that of the body power he take. Let us live in fear of God, and let us follow the leading of his word, lest he hand us over to *infernal torment*. For as often *by-parts we are impacted*, so often are we plunged.

[*Sins*, as *Origen* testifies, *are the life of the Devil*. See Luke 22:5. *As long as sin in man reigns, so long is he captive and held as vitiated by the devil, and vexed. — Augustine, Confess. Confer 2 Cor 4; Eph 4:2; 1 Tim 5:15. The devil reigns over those whom he pollutes: over those he dominates whom he defiles. — Cyprian, De iuvent. Those who have Satan as their suggester, will also have their emperor.*]

**Casus VII. Why does God permit that even the pious sometimes come into the power of the devil, so that they too are corporally possessed?**

*Reply.* Writes indeed *Augustine* (lib. 4 De sim. Dei, cap. 12): *the power of the Devil hostilely conquers or overturns no soul, except by society of sin*. But this he writes of what commonly is wont to happen. Others are not lacking examples, that even those who most-holy have lived, — nay even innocent boys and infants — have been seized by the devil. In these, hidden are the *judgments of God*, though not unjust, — of whose *providence* governs all things, which are done in the world: — therefore it is not doubtful, when the devil to bodies of the pious he concedes power, that this is done from just causes.

To the *providence of God* simply referred *Chrysostom* (in *lib. de provid. Dei*, c. 1) a certain thing (*whom he had permitted to be handed over to Satan*), — a pious man, whom yet the demon possessed. Not otherwise *Hieronymus* refers, in the *Vita Hilarionis*: *what cause is it*, says he, *that often little-boys and tender-lipped ones, mothers-being-present, from demons are seized-with-a-paroxysm? Certainly these are hidden of God, — in whose inscrutable judgment they are to be left*.

Concerning some causes however from sacred letters we can make *conjecture*:

**1.** *For the manifestation of the glory of God*, — as of that *born blind* it is read (John 9:3): *neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents, but that the works of God should be made manifest in him*. Manifests however God in the *obsession* of the pious especially his own power, in *terror of the impious*, whom to the power of the demon with easy business he can subject: *for if this be done in the green wood, in the dry what shall be done?* — and *And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?* (1 Pet 4:18).

**2.** *To atone for foreign sins* — of parents in children, of magistrates in subjects, of husbands in wives, and contrariwise; whence it comes, that sometimes the devil from the imprecation of another *body some invades*, of which thing example we have above. — Just is God, *And he sent young men of the children of Israel, which offered burnt offerings, and sacrificed peace offerings of oxen unto the LORD.* (Exod 24:5).

**3.** *For the spiritual battle* with devils, — his own to *hoc*, however-acerbic-a-medium — to prepare wills God: — for who plagues of body inflicted from demon knows to overcome, is to those enemies which molest to *soul*, more firmly resist can.

[*Gravamen this corporeal with medicament spiritual.*]

**4.** *For preservation from sin*. Correptio ista diabolica sometimes is a *preservation from contrary sin*. Even if the demon through the possessed some crimes commits, if they were pious, — with them-unwilling, often even ignorant, this is done — as above we have heard. Meanwhile with-limbs-corporeally-vexed from the internal soul-temptations more are they free.

Hence we read in *Severus Sulpicius* (*Vita Martini*, dialog. 1) — of a certain brother from God to have asked and impetrated, that through *months* some the body of him from the inhabiting demon should be afflicted, on account of *peril of sin*, which he feared from pride. Hard indeed the remedy against pride, and not to be easily imitated by anyone, — but manifest however from this the hermit-judged, that God sends to some the devil, lest man into sin fall, and God offend.

**5.** *Temporal-plague, that of the eternal admonish us*, — of infernal cruciates which longer-and-severer will be, — which pre-tutelage some we see in the possessed, — the more diligently we should shun sin, wherewith devils' plagues in the infernal-impious deserve.

**6.** *Fatal hatred of the devil against miserable mortals* shows God, when in their bodies also, — who innocent are, — so much he rages: — most estranged therefore we should be from those malignant spirits, and all society of them we should shun.

**7.** *Finally, is general*, which with all the plagues of the pious is common — that God even by this reason wills to *probate* the pious' *patience*, and to *commend* it to others. For who in this contest so perilous does nothing against God and conscience, but with great patience and meekness of soul the *will of the Lord* he recognizes, and freedom from this ejection-of-devil, which happens with destruction of the diabolical kingdom, — with great soul awaits, — he to bearing any adverse things sufficient is prepared, and with the *Apostle* he can say: *For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ.* (2 Cor 1:5).

**Casus VIII. Whether the devil can be expelled from the possessed by the arts of magic?**

*Reply.* The doctrine of Christ is, that *the devil cannot cast out another devil* (Matt 12:26), — otherwise his kingdom would not endure long. Most true is this indeed of the *ejection of the devil* which is done with destruction of the diabolical kingdom. But examples testify that Satan sometimes cedes from the obsessed to *characters, rites, words of the magi*, — if by this reason he can *superstition and idolatry* in the souls of men reverence and confirm.

Concerning *sortileges of the Germans* writes *Praetorius*, that after some *circles and characters* on the forehead of the demoniac had been drawn, they interrogated the demon that a mandate be given to him that he go out, — and immediately he went out.

Refers *Bodinus* (lib. 3 *De demonom.*, cap. 6): if some demoniac suspects a certain *evil spirit* had been imported to him by a witch, judges in *Germany*, and the very *Imperial chamber*, before the man affected such words by the witch to be pronounced order: *depart with me and in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit — a good end, with blood and Christ — a moment of the men affected — by magic arts to health to be restored*.

Which, if it be so (in the faith be the author), nothing certain else from that can we gather, than that the devil with the magi best agrees.

Hereto pertains what *Josephus* writes (lib. 8 *antiq.*, cap. 2), — that in the presence of *Vespasian* the emperor and his sons *Titus* and *Domitian*, — a certain man of the *Hebrew* people, *Eleazar*, at the nostrils of a certain demon-possessed, — a *ring*, whose seal had beneath it a *root of Solomon* found — applied, and the demon from the nostrils of the smelling extracted, — who when to the earth suddenly he had fallen, — *Eleazar* by adjuration in *Solomon's* song the demon proscribed. But here *Josephus* the *Jew*, *Vespasian* the *Ethnic*, and *Eleazar* the *Jew* — were deceived by the *prestiges of the devil*, who from the root — some pretense of power drawing — was simulating.

Of these sorts of *media* for expelling the devil no one of the pious ought to certainly use. For the devil is not compelled to go out, but *of his own accord* he goes out, — and greater damage he inflicts, — for since previously the body only of a man he was vexing, — now also souls of many he dement, whom in *superstition and idolatry* adhibited he confirms.

Thus the *root* mentioned in *Josephus* for expelling *Satan* is *inept*, — but that it was used the demon pallor was, lest men to *God, that unique liberator and expugnator of Satan*, they should flee. But that those *prestiges* might have *greater authority*, — *the name of Solomon* is pretended, as if from that this art were, — that of expelling the demon through *roots* — of which however his history nothing holds.

Let no one therefore suffer himself to be deceived. *Spirits are of demon* (says *Wier* in lib. 4 *De praestigii daemonum*, cap. 10), *who as by no elements are allured, plants or terrestrial substance, — so are not driven-out either, — even if very often their own cultors — are pretended to be invited or fascinated by some things of the pretended, — force, coerce, or even abige — that with impious credulity they may bind them more to themselves fraudulently they simulate*.

**Casus IX. What is to be judged of Papist exorcisms — which either for liberating demoniacs or for healing the sick they adhibit — in what confidence should we use them?**

*Reply.* Some make a *fourfold power* of ejecting demons: one is of *Christ*, another of *God*, third *of demon*, fourth *of the devil*, — of which the earlier two differences see near *Petrus Thyraeus* (part 3 *De daemoniacis*, cap. 34).

The power which *Christ* had, communicated indeed they say with the Apostles, and through them left in the Church: where a peculiar order of *ecclesiastical office* they constitute, — namely of *Exorcists*, who by peculiar rites for this office by the bishop were ordained, — the bishop handing to them a *Roman book* in which the *exorcisms* were written; saying: *accept and commit to memory, and have the power to lay hand upon the possessed, either baptized or catechumens*, — as appears from *Council of Carthage IV*, cap. 7.

In *Papatism* this power to themselves have snatched *monks*, who what modes in this so-called art they use, prescribe the authors of the *Malleus Maleficarum* (*secunda parte*, quaest. 2, cap. 6).

Even though *exorcists* by *magic art* sometimes some certain-species have, — no one however of the faithful in their operations ought to trust.

**(1.)** Since it has the *species of collusion* with those in the *religion of the Papists* (which from all the pious ought to be alien): since *And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?* (2 Cor 6:15), — who also we are commanded *Abstain from all appearance of evil.* (1 Thess 5:22).

**(2.)** Since very often all the most-wicked *nebulones* use those arts: they teach indeed *Romanists*, it makes no difference whether *exorcists* have pure conscience, or whether in sins they are constituted, since *ecclesiastical exorcisms* are valid in-and-of-operation, as have *Institoris* (part 1 *De daemonum-culti*, cap. 5) and *Lorichius* (in *Thesauro theol.*, voce *daemones*, num. 52). How however impurity of conscience can stand with *invocation of the divine name*, which for adjuring the demon they establish, I do not see: certainly *scrutator cordium* our God is *God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.* (John 4:24). The Apostle *Paul* in praying to lift up *pure hands* bids us (1 Tim 2:8).

**(3.)** *Media utuntur impiis* — since through their-organs they use, — by that very fact approve, and thus of their impiety participate. For over the possessed the *saints* they invoke, — the *Mass* also sometimes they perform, — and in *multiloquio* far indeed of their nostril *singular force of the exorcism* they place: which all *impious* and against Scripture, no one of the pious doubts. For the *invocation of the saints* prohibits the angel (Rev 19:9), *multiloquy* Christ (Matt 6:8); but *institutio Sacramenti* commends, that nature of the *sacrament* is *improved-elsewhere-taught*.

**(4.)** *They use media of superstition*: *they adhibit relics of the saints*, — with holy water they sprinkle the possessed, — *host consecrated*, *candle blessed*, and other *things blessed* (as they call), — that is, *exorcised — with oil* — and *from the-hand of the possessed apply*, — to which thing they are persuaded to be *singular-force* for expelling the devil, — which all *superstitious* (and *magna ex parte impia*) with all right-thinking is in agreement. For what would Satan care of those chants, — who not even *the majesty of Christ* he dreaded, — whom with *divine voice-benediction and testimony-of-heaven* being accepted, — as if with a most-present *amulet* fortified, — nonetheless with his *temptations* he attacked in the desert.

**(5.)** They *abhor* also from *sacred Scriptures*. For in the *Malleus Maleficarum* it is prescribed that the *exorcist*, if he knows how to *read Scripture* (therefore not all *exorcists* can read the Psalms — and yet they are *ecclesiastical persons*), let him read the *Gospels* of the four first *Evangelists*, — item the Gospel *of the angel*, and *the Passion of the Lord*, — which all have great virtue for the expulsion of demons of the *devil*. Item the Gospel of *St John* in principio erat verbum, is transcribed, and to the neck suspended. — This truly is with the *words and letters* of *pigs*, though not-unlearned, to attribute great efficacy, — which in the thing absurd is, and against the end of *sacred Scriptures*, which diligently *read, and rightly understood, are*, — not for *exorcising*, but for *consoling, comforting, admonishing*: which beyond these ends of Scripture otherwise communicates, — he *impiously abuses divine words*, — to which impiety no one of the pious ought to consent.

For these causes the *Papistic exorcisms*, which either for liberating *demoniacs* or for healing the sick they adhibit, — not only must we *flee*, but even *execrate*.

For even if many examples are recounted of them, in which such *exorcisms* have had their *efficacy*, — yet this is not on account of the efficacy of such *media*: but the devil *sponte* cedes, so that *superstition and impiety of exorcists* he may confirm, — of which *elegantly Johannes Sulburgensis'* sentence cites *Wier* (lib. 3 *De praestigiis daemonum*, cap. 13). *This is* (says he, lib. 2 *Palicratici*, cap. 17), *the fraud of the malignant spirits, that whatever ultimately they do and dictate to men — that this is to be done operose in a divine work* — *so is to be adhibited-in-name to appear more devoted*. *Themselves they retort — as if by-exorcism of some-virtue they are-extracted-forth do the perfect: and — those which are ordered by them — by-exorcism — as-if — by-the-name of the Lord, — of divine Trinity, — of incarnation-and-passion — virtue conceived they are pressed — the same-men themselves they hand-over exorcising them — to obtempering-they — thereby with-crime of sacrilege and of the punishment of damnation involving*. *Transfigure they themselves sometimes into aspects of angels, — good things they prescribe, — illicit they prohibit, — human-life they consecrate, — utilities they provide, — as if good and prompt familiaries be admitted, be heard benignly, — with a certain argument be exalted, — habit also they put on of venerable persons, — that great and prompter *reverence* may be spent-on them*.

**Casus X. What is to be judged of exorcists who to the *Papacy* have bade farewell, but yet claim to have among themselves some *gift of ejecting demons of the obsessed*?**

*Reply.* Such *exorcists* are found in some places, not only among those who are commonly *rude*, — but even among *pastors of the Church*, who *by-name-of-exorcists rejoice*. They think they have a *singular gift of God*, not conceded to just anyone, *of imperating demons of the obsessed to expel*. From which they make a *peculiar art*, — where not indeed *holy water*, *blessed candles*, *image of the cross*, in the *more-of-Papist-exorcists* they adhibit; — yet meanwhile they themselves use certain other *rites*, — the *possessed* into the *temple* they carry, in the temple with them they lodge-overnight, prayers and canticles certain they mumble-forth, — texts *biblical* over the possessed they read, — *characters of the cross* they make, and with great voice the *devil-that-from-the-possessed-should-go-out* they command.

Which even to name-called, and to *church-plebecular*, has *great applause*: — with them however no commerce ought to be, much less their art for expelling *Satan* to be used.

**Firstly**, their *art* has no *foundation*. Nowhere in Scripture is *public profession of exorcising demons* handed down, which divinely be instituted, — nor for this *office* are they ordained, — when they are *initiated with sacred rites*. Whatever however without *vocation divine* is done, — especially against so *astute* and *strong* an enemy, — firmly stand we cannot.

For what they *object*, of *CHRIST and the Apostles*, — who *ejected demons*, — they urge also the promise of *Christ*: *in my name they shall cast out devils* (Mark 16:17), — this contributes nothing to these *exorcists*, since not all things of *CHRIST and the Apostles* were done for imitation to be proposed: nor did they use *ceremonies* of *superstition*, nor *conducted-by-payment* did they expel the devils, nor is the promise in *Mark*, which was made only to the *Apostles*, — to others is to be extended: — otherwise it would follow, that our *exorcists* also with *new tongues* should speak, and with *hands imposed* should heal the sick, — for those things also there are promised.

We do not deny to be this *peculiar gift of God*, which not otherwise than *miracles* and the *gift of tongues* sometimes in the primitive Church endured, — until the *plenitude of grace* to the *faith of Christ* it was introduced: but this gift of God is neither *perpetual* to *offices of the Church*, — nor does he make *profession of the singular*, — but to those *extraordinary* pertains, — therefore no one to himself it *rashly should arrogate*, — just as neither the gifts of *miracles* nor of *tongues*, — until he have a certain *vocation* thereto from *God*.

There were even in the time of the *Apostles* some *sons of the Sceva*, who wanted to imitate the *Apostles* in this genus, — adjuring the devils *by Jesus, whom Paul preached*, that they should depart, — from the possessed which they heard-in-Ephesus: — *we exhort you by Jesus, whom Paul preacheth* (Acts 19:13). But the demon of their *exorcisms* — vilifying the men — said: *Jesus I know, and Paul I know: but who are ye?* — and he *leapt in upon them, and prevailed against them*, so that naked and wounded they fled (Acts 19:15–16). — Such is the effect of those who, without *vocation*, *Christ and the Apostles* dare to imitate.

**2.** Such *exorcists* abuse Sacred Scriptures, — which have not been given to us that the devil *may serve us*, — but for our *For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.* (Rom 15:4), that the *nature and will of God* we may recognize, that our *life we may rightly institute*, and to *eternal glory we may be prepared*.

**3.** *Moreover, superstitious rites* they adhibit, — sometimes even such which have *species of evil*, — with many words the devil they *increpate*, and with great clamors him to go out they command, — now through a *snake*, now through *the eye*, now through the *little-glass-orb of the window*. Not did the *Apostles* do this, — but in *the name of Christ* they *ejected the demons with few words*, — of the whole of nature the *Lord*, and *imperator of all virtue in heaven and in earth*, — and of the *spirit of omnipotence with his mouth carrying-forth*, — bearing witness *Eusebius of Caesarea* in the *panegyric*.

**4.** *Finally, if not all, yet most exercise this art from motive of gain*, — from whom otherwise far from ministers of the Church he wishes to be *D. Peter* (1 Pet 5:2). *Apostles and their disciples did not do this*: — *demons freely we cast out — without price without reward we drive-off*, — is said.

For these causes the *arts of the exorcists* nothing should we care.

*But often, and it works, that they seem to eject the demon*: — either they do not *truly* eject it — but from those in whom they seem to depart, but by some *natural disease* oppressed, — or *the devil sponte cedes*, so that the *exorcists themselves and many others* who *trust in them*, in *superstition* he may *confirm*, — whence it happens, that even *some man's body abandons* the demon, so that of many souls *inner* meanwhile *worse* he *occupies*.

For *easy it is* for the devil (says *Luther* on Matt 3): *that he even through a most-wicked man himself is expelled, — but yet from the man he does not depart, — but more strongly to men through superstition he besieges: — which is because he is not always driven-out from him, but of both men on that account, — since through souls of others in superstition and impiety himself he confirms — but since God-the-right does not-concede, but as-a-greater-damage-in-cheating-of-perils-cripples, — a-hospice-for-him in-body-of-man of some-time still-permits*.

From all these things well-considered, no one easily either the *gift of exorcising* the devil in the possessed for himself will arrogate, nor to those who do this, will have faith.

**Casus XI. What is to be done for the possessed, — that of the miserable ones in the power of Satan of freeing them, and by-some-certain-reason of expelling-the-devil?**

*Reply.* Of the *possessed* there are two *genera*: some, — either for the sake of gain, or by way of some convenience, — *simulate obsession*: these are *voluntary obsessi*, whom the demon invades and exercises at the *will, arbitrium, and libido of the very possessed*. Some *unwillingly* by the devil are occupied and cruciated, — which to many even *pious* happens, — who besides *plagues of body* and *foul abuse of members* nothing thence *lucre* to hope can.

Of *voluntary obsessi* the devil by *plagues* to eject some think, — by that reason, by which others have handed *those, whom truly he had possessed*, — the words are these: *who by the demon are said to have been seized-with-a-paroxysm and by manners chiefly of them for-figure and-habit to-be-simulated*, — feign, — such visited-by-verse-blows, — with-taming-of-them-labors — those subject-ought, — whereby they, who by the demon-truly-seized-are, — from the demon's operation may be freed, truly-subjected. — Refers *Wier* examples of this-sort of obsessi, who either with *rod* or with *twigs* egregiously received, — and immediately from *the demon relict* — to themselves returned, — lib. 3 *De praestigii daemonum*, cap. 18.

Of those who besides their own will by the malignant spirit are possessed, the *chief question* is what with them is-to-be-done, or a bad *liberate*. *Safest in this genus of way* is:

**1.** *First* let *skilled physicians* be consulted, whether it be a *natural disease*, or truly from-of-their-art let them judge: — for, as above we have shown, — there are some diseases which with the *manners of the possessed* have much in common.

**2.** *When true obsession is known*, — let the miserable one be committed to the *spiritual care of the church minister*, — who *sound doctrine* holds, of *life uncorrupted*, and the *mystery of faith* holds in *pure conscience*, — who nothing for the sake of *base gain* does, but all-from-soul.

**3.** *Let him diligently inquire* what *sort of life the possessed one has led so far*: if he had been *impious*, through the law let him lead him to the *acknowledgment of sins*, and *how deadly is the merchandise wherewith the devil his slaves he conducts*, — let him teach, — and to *serious penitence* and the *proposition of amending life* let him exhort. If however he had been *pious*, and of *un-blamable life*, — let him console him, — that even his own sometimes God the *demon's power* he permits — for certain causes, — which the history of *Job* and *Paul* testifies. For *the cross* is not to all *the same* nor equal-imposed, — but by all *with patience must be borne*, — since not to *destruction* but to *probation* it is remitted, — and at length to those *loving the Lord* it turns to *good*.

**4.** *With this preemptive* either *admonition* or *consolation*, — let also the work of *natural physician* be adhibited, — who *malignant juices* with commodious *medicaments* may purge. It is compact that the *possessed* mostly by a *twin disease* are burdened: one is of the *body*, which from *melancholic juice or other vitiated* arises, — the other is *of soul*, — as is *dementia, mourning, weariness of life, despair*, — with which the devil much business exercises.

And *Wier* testifies that the *possessed*, with the *vitiated humor expelled*, cease *marvellous things doing* (lib. 3 *De praestigii daemonum*, cap. 20).

**5.** *This medical care done, — let the minister of the Church continue his own care of the possessed*: where it is not necessary to place him in the *temple in sight of the people*, as is the custom with some. Nor is there need of much either *ambages or ceremonies*: — where the possessed is found, — there let the *confession of Christian faith from him be exacted*, — of the *works of the devil destroyed by Christ* let him be educated, — to this destroyer of Satan *Jesus Christ* let him faithfully be reformed, — to faith in *Christ*, to prayers, to *patience* let exhortation be instituted, — by which *adminicula* at last it is effected — that the *insults of the demons* be contemned, — or certainly with greater *tolerance* be borne. Of which thing examples we have in *Antonius* apud *Athanasius* in *Vita Antonii*, of *Hilarion* apud *Hieronymus*, of *Luther*, — who indeed not possessed, — otherwise however was gravely vexed by the demon, — with great strength of soul the *malignant spirit* they *have overcome*.

**6.** *Let prayers to God be poured out ardent*, — not only from the ministers of the Church, but even from the whole *Church*, — that *God the father of mercies*, — the man have mercy on for the sake of *Christ*, and might loose *the fetters of the devil*. *Pray for one another, that ye may be healed, for much the prayer of the just availeth, — Pax being with you inside the Lord's — Paul James*, cap. 5.

Which if not immediately liberation follows, — let prayers be repeated: — for we ought to *insist in praying*, and not to cease, until answer follow, — as *Christ* admonishes (Luke 18). Since however the benefit here is temporal, — therefore always in the prayers must be included *the will of God*, — into whose hand let us resign in full the liberation of the possessed. For *always answers God, if not to our will, yet to our utility*.

Much of old was attributed to *public prayers* in *liberation of the possessed*. In the times of *Chrysostom* the possessed were-brought not out-of-necessity, but according-to-the-good-pleasure of the *bishop* — into the public, — that the people, with the whole church present, — *common* for them supplications be made, — that all with continuous concord the common *Lord* they might beseech for them, — and that he might have mercy, — with great clamor they contended, — as *himself Chrysostom* refers (hom. 3 *De incomprehensibili natura Dei*). More examples see near *Wier* (lib. 3 *De demonis*, cap. 6). *Augustinus* however and *Sozomenus* attest that of old with the *demoniacs* nothing else was done, save prayers were-shed-forth to God, — no *family colloquy*, — no *facetiae*, — no *interrogations of Satan* were exercised, — as with some *exorcists* is customary: see *Augustinus* (lib. 10 *De civ. Dei*, cap. 22) and *Sozomenus* (lib. 6).

**(7.)** *With prayers let fastings be joined*: — for these two things *Christ himself* conjoined, — when he said: *Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting.* (Matt 17:21). For neither can *prayers* be *accepted to God*, unless with *temperance* they are joined.

**(8.)** *Let finally alms be added by friends of the possessed one*, — *good is alms with prayer and fastings, more than to lay up treasures of gold: because alms delivereth from death, and it purgeth away sin, and finds mercy and life eternal* etc. (Tob 12). And if for other great things about to be undertaken, or from God to be obtained, — with *alms* we mercy-solicit-others, so that toward our proposal they favor, — so with our prayers to conjoin theirs: — why not the same we do in a matter so grave, since from the power of the demon *the miserable one is to be liberated*?

These are the works *pleasing to God*, *adverse to the devil*, which of old in *liberating the possessed* were happily adhibited by the *holy men of God*. Nor is there need of a certain order of men, whom *exorcists* they call, — nor of *adjuration, compulsion, interrogation of the demon*. Thus writes *Origen* (upon cap. 15 Matt., tract. 27): *if ever it ought to become for us in taking-care-of such-a-sick-one, — of the demoniacs, — we should-consider-not, — neither should we adjure, nor interrogate, nor question, as-if by-hearing the unclean spirit, — but abiding in prayers and fastings we should obtain — a-longer-time-going-forth-from God, and drive-out with-Jesus-and-with-our-name spirits malignant*.

Not other mode of expelling the devils from the possessed knew *Lutherus*: what he indeed *procession-instituted*, when to himself a demoniac was brought — a *little-girl* of *Meyza*, and it-was-referred, referring *Manlius* (in *Theatre of the Devil*, part 1, p. 116): — the sum indeed is this — the little-girl to himself was brought, — asked if she held the Apostolic *symbol*: — when she affirmed, — to recite ordered. When therefore she came to those words: *and Jesus Christ, his only son*, — the *impure spirit* began to seriously *vex her*. To whom *Luther*: *now indeed, Satan, — thou willest with great pomp to be ejected, — that which I shall not do. Order thou therefore, for the future day, the little-girl to have-been-brought to the-sacristy — and afterwards into her-body — to be led-again*. She obeyed, — and to the *sermon* willingly was present, — but to the sacristy she was to be led, hands-and-feet resisting fought, — so that by *studious some* into the sacristy she had to be borne, and to the feet of Luther deposited. In the sacristy besides *Lutherus* were the deacons and other studious some. Then *Luther* first *exhortation instituted, — that the devil was not now *miraculously to be expelled*, according to the *manner of the primitive Church*, where on account of the *novelty of doctrine* the work of *miracles* was necessary. **2.** Neither to be expelled by *adjurations*, that he might be *from exorcists dragged-out*, — but by *prayers and contempt*. **3.** In prayers must not be prescribed to *Christ* the mode or time, when he *should eject the demon*: but *patiently his hour to await*, and meanwhile in prayers to insist. Then, at the finish of the *exhortation*, — hand-*imposed* over the head of the *little-girl*, and recited the *Symbol of the Apostles*, and the *Lord's Prayer*, adding from *Johannes* cap. 14: *Verily, verily, I say unto you, he that believeth on me, the works that I do, shall he do also, and greater than these*, etc. Then with the most-ardent prayers he invoked *God*, that this little-girl from the *malignant spirit*, if by him she was possessed, he would liberate. In the end of the prayers he touched the foot of the little-girl, — saying superbly to the devil: *Yes, Satan, wouldst thou with much pomp with thee to-be-carried-away, — but to-that-place-with-the-angels I-shall-not-follow-thee: — how-much-therefore-thou-so-pretermayest voluntary-thou-cede*, — say-I to-thee — *of the Lord*, — *the-holier-one, sanctuary*. — And-from-the-little-girl-departed. Whose parents afterwards to him wrote: — that at that time *violent-demons* into her they had not again *experienced*.

Thou hast here the *mode of ejecting the malignant spirit* from the possessed, — from *Luther* himself usurped, — which is far more certain than that which the vulgar *exorcists* are wont to adhibit: *for to prayers and word all things yield*: — hence *when a demoniac gathered — if he should stay — a longer time — hoping-with-firm-confidence — which certainly at the-time will follow, — if not according-to-will, — yet to our utility. Another cause is *the incredulity of the possessed themselves*, — who do not with certain-confidence approach, — from God asking liberation: — therefore Christ to the parent of a certain one at last *if perhaps liberation of the pious happens with reduction*. Hence *Cyprian* says: *adjured demons either shall exit — or shall vanish gradually, — since faith of the strong-one aids*.

## Chapter IV. On Cases of Conscience Concerning Actions with Melancholics

**Proemium.** Although *the possessed* differ much from *melancholics*, — for the bodies of the former, the souls of the latter, the *malignant spirit* agitates, — yet very often the possessed have kinship with the melancholic. For, as also above we have said, *the melancholic humor* is *the workshop of the devil* most-convenient, and the *demoniacs* by the malignant spirit are usually in melancholy carried. Multum of this had already handled *Petrus Thyraeus* (part 1 *De daemoniacis*, cap. 47); but two things are chief: some things that pertain to the temporal benefits which he intends by God's-free-will, others to the *melancholic spirit*, on whose account the devil distributes his own gift, — to which every success he commits.

By a *right order* therefore, from the possessed we descend to the *melancholics*, in whom is equally great, sometimes even greater peril than in *the drunk*. For, as *Chrysostom* writes (lib. 3 *De providentia ad Sagmium*): *nothing indeed of even diabolical machinations is more portentous for harming than the greatness of grief, since the demon, who is more powerful, by grief also overcomes*.

There are however *melancholics of diverse genera*: some by external senses from melancholic humor corrupted labor, whence also their thoughts, voices, and deeds very often are marvelous. Some believe themselves to be brute animals, whose voices they imitate; some flee earthen vessels, therefore they yield in the street to any oncomer, lest they be broken by touch; others are *fearful*, dreading lest either their homes fall down, or even the sky itself; some in this class perceive a great joy in their melancholy, of which sort was the *unfortunate Athenian* known to Aristotle, who was persuaded that all ships coming into the *Piraeus* were his — and them he recounted, dismissed, and led out; and with such a joy he received them coming in, as if he were master of everything that came — and if anything perished, he inquired no more; if they returned safe, he rejoiced. So with great pleasure he lived among his own, and when by the physicians' work he recovered from the disease, he said he had never lived more pleasantly.

There are however others, who as regards the external senses are not much moved, — but whose souls rather than bodies Satan agitates. Such *Christ* calls *evil spirits* (Luke 11:26). Of such especially here we treat, whose souls from grief have failed, whose voices, life, and deeds are wonderful. Nay, in this class many things can happen even to those who nowhere serve God, — ministers of the Church, and to others, yea even to themselves, while they make life bitter to themselves and hasten its end, which with joy of soul and pleasing course they could have brought forward.

It is worth the effort therefore, to consult consciences, lest we be absorbed by the abyss of melancholic grief, and, that others also — as far as it can be done — we may extract thence.

**Casus I. What is to be done, lest we be possessed by the melancholic spirit?**

*Reply.* This peril in-general we can avoid by living the *middle way*, — between *presumption* on one side and *desperation* on the other, — with *true piety* joined with *firm confidence in God*, according to that Psalm (2:11): *Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling*.

For *melancholy* fights with the *first precept*, — removes from the eyes the *power of God* and *paternal soul toward us*, — takes away *fiducia and fear*, — leaves a man suspended between two precipices, with great peril of soul.

On the one side is *presumption* and *spiritual pride*, since one disposes his affairs at his own whim, and speculates about futures — how to consult himself and his own, what to accept, by what means, and to how great a degree his affairs he might wish to augment. If from his soul's opinion it succeeds, then he swells up, and to his wisdom, counsel, and strength he ascribes all. This is that *proud melancholy*, which extols men, and into admiration-of-self bears them off, so that they often affect stupid and ridiculous things, which seem to them most serious. Meanwhile the *providence of God is denied*, his help is not cared for, prayers are neglected, and a man is carried around in his own speculations, as if of no God any longer he had need.

*Who therefore wills not to be melancholic, let him not be presumptuous*: let him not be persuaded that his own efforts cannot be frustrated. Let him think that man proposes many things, which God disposes otherwise. *The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD. A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.* (Prov 16:1, 9). Often even the best-thought turns out worst, and as in the verses it is said: *no effort is happy and effect, if God does not give counsel, aid, and help*.

By prayers therefore must God be solicited, that he himself may suggest sound counsels, and to those consulted may grant good outcome. If we have attained these, let us not be inflated, but with true humility of soul submitting ourselves to him, for his help gratitude let us render, and in our own prudence not to confide let us learn.

On the other side, if our affairs turn out otherwise than we had hoped, *melancholy* makes us *desperate* — which calls into doubt God's *paternal soul*, accuses him of unrighteousness, and imagines that God has ordained our unhappiness through all eternity, and immutably. Hence continual complaints, no patience, no hope of better condition, murmurs against God, hatred and envy toward neighbor. Hence is also that *primitive melancholy*, which along with the *providence of God* calls into doubt his *wisdom*, as if he could not sufficiently provide for all; his *knowledge*, as if our lot were unknown to him; his *mercy*, as if he would not put an end to the calamities of men; his *power*, as if he could not bring aid; finally his *truth*, as if he did not stand by what he promised.
