*Who therefore does not wish to be melancholic, let him not be incredulous*, let him not despair of God's aid, let him resign all his affairs to God's hand — in all anguishes and finally in death itself let him hold an *unshaken hope*. *Cast thy burden upon the Lord, and he shall sustain thee* (Ps 55:23); *Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.* (1 Pet 5:7).

In the *middle* stands *true piety*, which keeps a man's mind in equilibrium, so that he serves God *with fear* and rejoices *with trembling*. *The fear of the Lord shall delight the heart, and shall give joy and gladness, and length of days. To him that feareth the Lord shall be good in the last things, and in the day of his defection he shall find blessing* (Sir 1:12–13).

**Casus II. What if melancholy has already occupied the mind of a man — what is the mode of expelling it?**

*Reply.* What is said of *diseases of body* in this affection of soul chiefly has place: *resist the beginning, too late is medicine prepared after evils have been long strengthened*. Melancholy however increases moment by moment; a serpent it is which a man the longer nourishes in his bosom, — (1) since it has not God but *Satan* as its author, who inspires sad thoughts; for he himself is *the melancholic spirit* — sad, projected from the face of God, without hope of restitution, — therefore us also with himself into eternal sadness he studies to precipitate. We however are not created for sadness, but to rejoice eternally with God; and although for sin some cause of grief is given to us, — yet since God in Christ has restored to us hope of restitution, we have no reason to enslave ourselves entirely to sadness. *God rejoices our heart* (Ps 4). Therefore *melancholic sadness* — of the sort which by Satan's suggestion is offered to us — we should not embrace.

**(2.)** Because such sadness has no use, — it cannot amend things which are adverse to us, and meanwhile it *afflicts both body and soul* of a man; concerning which *Sirach* (30:24–25): *many hath sadness slain, and there is no profit in it*.

**(3.)** Because it is adverse to the nature of God, who is the God of joy and of all consolation (2 Cor 1:3), who fills us with joy of countenance, and gives to us the Spirit of joy in the word, which with great confidence receives him afflicted, — while he strengthens *the soul*.

**(4.)** It *impedes prayers*. Even though sadness can be expelled by prayers, according to that of the Apostle *James* (5:13) *if any be sad, let him pray*, — yet those who are too much given up to sadness, so that they hardly admit any consolation, in these is extinguished *the spirit of prayers*. For in prayers *pure hands are to be raised to God*, without diffidence (1 Tim 2:8); those however who have lost confidence in God, therefore find no measure in their sadness. But with confidence is conjoined *joy of the heart*, which is the fruit of the Spirit, — which in griefs shows pleasures, in death life, in poverty riches, in persecutions manifest triumphs.

**(5.)** In the second class are *incommodities and dangers most-present*, into which melancholy at last flows, when it is too much indulged. Perils are partly of soul, partly of body. As to soul, the *melancholic spirit expels the Holy Spirit*, when *faith in God is lost*, prayers are neglected, the grace and goodness of God are called into doubt — yea, by despairing plainly denied. It suggests wicked thoughts, instigates to hatred and envy, and finally to *shortening of life*: it makes men unfit for offices of vocation, sluggish to everything, cowardly in dangers, and finally desperate — into eternal death precipitating. As to body, the heart makes it dry, brain is disturbed, heart is straitened, appetite for food and sleep fails. *A rejoicing soul makes a flourishing age; a sad spirit dries the bones*, as *Solomon* writes (Prov 17:22).

In the *third class* are examples of those whom melancholy — to which they did not immediately resist — has *killed*.

Therefore in the very *entrance* must melancholy be expelled: the foundation is *exercise of piety*, diligent meditation of the Word, and assiduous prayer, — which two produce solid recreation (Ps 119:165 *great peace have they that love thy law*); let *serious penitence* be added, which consists in *acknowledgment of sins*, in *true faith in Christ*, with proposition of amending life. For in such a heart there arises *peace and joy of the Holy Spirit* (Jer 6:16 *stand upon the ways and see, and ask for the old paths where the good way is, and walk therein: and you shall find refreshment for your souls*).

These are the chief *darts* by which the melancholic spirit is extinguished at the very first threshold, and by which we can render our souls quiet.

**Casus III. How is a sad melancholic thought to be resisted in defect of temporal things — honor, wealth, health, and similar things human?**

*Reply.* There is no doubt that many are worn out with this genus of temptations, when they see others shining in honors, while they themselves stick fast in the lowest recesses; deserted by promoters and patrons, others abound in wealth, they are pressed with poverty; others enjoy the best health, they are always struggling with diseases.

And the longer this calamity endures, the stronger they have impulses that they are the most miserable of all, whom God has utterly abandoned. Hence they think of means of emerging, often illicit, which the melancholic spirit suggests to them, — at the least they murmur against God, why he has not provided equally for them as for others; they envy others' better fortune, they wish death for themselves, and by this reason make their life sufficiently bitter.

To overcome these torments, safest is: **(1.)** *Resign all one's affairs*, however they flow, to God's hands, *in whose hands are our times* (Ps 31:16), who directs either fortune, and distributes his gifts by his free will. *Good and evil, life and death, poverty and honesty are from God* (Sir 11:14); he it is who *is the humbler and the exalter* (Ps 75:8); *That he may set him with princes, even with the princes of his people.* (Ps 113:8).

**(2.)** Let us be persuaded that the will, counsel, and government of God no one can change: for *In the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider: God also hath set the one over against the other, to the end that man should find nothing after him.* (Eccl 7:14).

**(3.)** Let us remember that to those loving God *all things cede unto good* (Rom 8:28). For to whom many honors, wealth are not conjoined, so many molestations and occasions of sinning; and at last strict account is required *in the day of judgment* from those to whom much has been entrusted; but they who have received few, more easily can render account.

**(4.)** Let us consider that *the goods of this age are not the best*: for they are transitory, subject to many perils, common to good and evil: better things however are prepared in the heavens, whereby defects of temporal and transitory things are most largely compensated in those who fear God. Let us look up therefore, and *lay up treasures in heaven*, *which neither moth nor rust corrupts* (Matt 6:19–20).

**(5.)** Finally let us recall that *Paul* joins *piety* and *contentment* as it were the crown-jewels of true Christian virtues (1 Tim 6:6), and both conjoined the great *gain* of Christians he names. *Piety with sufficiency* — if we have food and covering, we are content (1 Tim 6:8). *If Deus mihi sic voluerit*, as *David* admonishes (Ps 62:11): if we enjoy commodious health, let us acknowledge the divine benefaction, and with greater alacrity and assiduity let us do our own office; but if of all these goods we lack, we have nothing worse, for nothing except the *will of God* do we know befalls us; we know we are in the hands of the Lord, we are as clay in the potter's hand, — to his whole arbitrium we commit ourselves; if by *contented poverty* we suffer from disease, in *patience* we possess our soul, — knowing that *the right hand of the Lord can preserve us happily*.

Thus far the *ethnic-wisest* *Seneca* to his *Lucilius* wrote (epist. 107): *no one will lack anything, when all things are equal to all; that which any one may effuse, if it comes into all — is easily borne. Add these things to accepted things — from your soul, — that they are the tributes of mortality laid down; those, who have written it. Winter brings cold: it must be endured; summer brings heat: it must be endured; the intemperance of the sky troubles health: care must be taken; wild beast will meet you in some place — and man more pernicious than all beasts. Some water carries off, some fire; this condition of things we cannot change: this we can, take up a great spirit and worthy of good, whereby we bravely bear fortuitous things and consent with nature. Nature however tempers this kingdom which thou seest, with mutations. Serene things succeed cloudy ones, seas are disturbed, when they have been quiet; the winds stand by one another, night follows day, part of the sky rises, part sets. Contrary of things eternity consists. To this law is to be adapted our spirit; let it follow, let it obey, and whatever things happen — let it think that they had to happen, and let it not blame nature. Best it is to bear what thou canst not amend, and to accompany God, from whom author all things are done — without murmur. That is an evil soldier who follows the general groaning*. Which counsel indeed, when to those which from the *Word's medicine-chest* we brought forth, joined, has weight for repressing motions of the unquiet soul.

**Casus IV. How is that sadness to be expelled which arises from persecutions and exile for the sake of the confession of the faith?**

*Reply.* Not for all is it given to bear this sort of cross with brave soul. To lose fatherland, kindred, honors and wealth, sad is exile, and consequence of many calamities. *Multa mala secum trahit exilium*, said *Euripides*: chiefly *poverty*, and *contempt*. *A life of hospitality from house to house, whither shalt thou be a guest, thou wilt not stand faithfully, nor shalt thou open thy mouth* (Sir 29:30). Which thing so enervates many, that they pass all the residue of their life with groaning and sadness.

For expelling this sadness are to be observed these *fountains of consolation*:

**Firstly**, *the will of God* must be recognized, by whom to us has been given, *For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake;* (Phil 1:29). Therefore *Christ* predicted to his disciples: *And ye shall be hated of all men for my name's sake: but he that endureth to the end shall be saved. But when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another: for verily I say unto you, Ye shall not have gone over the cities of Israel, till the Son of man be come.* (Matt 10:22–23). To this *will of God* therefore let us not resist by impatience, but let us rejoice rather with the Apostles, since *God has counted us worthy to suffer something for his name*.

**Secondly**, *consider examples of the saints* who suffered for the truth exile and even death itself. This our Master predicted (Matt 10:17): *they shall deliver you up in councils, and in their synagogues shall they scourge you, and ye shall be brought before governors and kings for my sake*. Similar things experienced the *Prophets* and other confessors in the people of God: *Elijah* on account of the furies of *Jezebel* went into exile (1 Kgs 19); *Amaziah*, king of Israel, expelled *Amos* the prophet: *flee*, said he, *Also Amaziah said unto Amos, O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there: But prophesy not again any more at Bethel: for it is the king's chapel, and it is the king's court.* (Amos 7:12–13). At the time of the Maccabees exiles for the faith were especially frequent (2 Macc 4). *Claudius* the emperor commanded the Christians to depart from Rome (Acts 18:2). *Nos non sumus meliores patribus nostris*. Let us patiently bear therefore, what they could not avoid. Common indeed is this the *lot of the saints*, to bear the wounds and hatreds of the world: *if they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you*, said *Christ* (John 15:20). *Christ* himself went into exile — together with his parents (Matt 2:13); *if Christ was an exile, why should we not be too*, says *Ambrose* (in Matt).

**Thirdly**, *great is the consolation, that exiles do not suffer as thieves and adulterers, but as confessors of the truth*. Beautiful however is *to suffer for the truth*, to lose honors and wealth, fatherland and finally life itself, if only a good conscience be kept, — the *treasure of the Word* which alone infinitely exceeds all wealth. Better it is to live with a free conscience under a rustic cottage, than to enter into the palaces of princes and to be entangled in human traditions. Farewell, honors, riches, ambition, — provided we be *the servants of Christ*, not slaves of *Antichrist*. Beautiful is to suffer *for Christ* the persecutions of *Antichrist*, in the *knowledge of the truth being constituted*, — to whom alone eternal salvation is ascribed (Acts 4:12). Of the pious therefore in faith and virtue is it *to endure*, and through exile and martyrdom to press on toward the palm and the crown: *if we shall have remained in faith firm — thus Christ said, ye shall be indeed my disciples* (John 8:31; Luke 14:26). Those who, for the sake of their own commodities, defect from the truth, and deny it, — are not of the number of Christ's disciples, therefore also they themselves shall be denied by Christ before the celestial Father (Matt 10:32–33).

**Fourthly**, *although exiles from fatherland they be, yet they are not exiles from God*: for the Lord's is *the earth, and the whole world excluded from us can he not be. Their fatherland is however the Word — everywhere*, where to Christ with unperturbed conscience *we can serve, there is our fatherland*. *How narrow is the soul, who so applies himself to a corner of the earth, that whoever from him is at his right, considers as exile*, says *Franc. Petrarch* (dial. 67).

**Fifthly**, *nowhere fails the God gracious and blessing his own confessors of the word*: for his son with *Joseph* to *Egypt* went into exile — provided a shelter; the same with *Elijah* the exile — through crows food he supplied to the fugitive; *Athanasius* exile for six full years in a pit he preserved. *Turnings-away of ours numbers he* (Ps 56:9); *therefore he receives the heaven which the earth does not receive*.

**Sixthly**, *ample remains the reward*. Whatever is lost for Christ, is not lost, but changed for the better. *And every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name's sake, shall receive an hundredfold, and shall inherit everlasting life.* (Matt 19:29). Nothing therefore is lost through the exile of confessors, but a *step to greater dignities, wealth, and honors* is prepared. *In persecutions of earth the eyes are closed*, says *Cyprian* (in *Exhortation to martyrdom*), — *but heaven opens up: Antichrist threatens, but the Lord CHRIST defends: death is inflicted, but immortality follows: mortals worldly are snatched away, but restored paradise is renewed with eternal life*.

Which all things piously considered, we do not bear sadness, but rejoice on account of Christ in exiles and persecutions and other things suffered, according to that of the Apostle *Peter*: *But rejoice, inasmuch as ye are partakers of Christ's sufferings; that, when his glory shall be revealed, ye may be glad also with exceeding joy.* (1 Pet 4:13).

**Casus V. How is one to counter sadness from delay of divine aid?**

*Reply.* The pious know that all their affairs are from God, who alone can give an outcome, that we may bear it, — which is a great consolation.

But Satan strives entirely to overturn this, when divine aid is deferred, wishing to persuade the afflicted, that God has utterly denied aid, does not care for our affairs, nor are we worthy of his aid.

Hence are those complaints of *David*: *How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?* (Ps 13:1); *Mine eyes fail for thy word, saying, When wilt thou comfort me?* (Ps 119:82).

But lest we macerate ourselves here with vain cares, three things are to be set against this temptation:

**(1.)** God has ordained a certain term for all things: *To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven: A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;* (Eccl 3:1, 4). So we should not doubt but that to our afflictions he has set certain limits, beyond which they cannot extend, — and when aid comes, longer it is not deferred. Thus for the *Babylonian captivity* he pre-fixed 70 years (Jer 25:11); when these were complete, *In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain.* (Dan 5:30), which gave the first occasion to the liberation from captivity. To *Egyptian servitude* he pre-fixed 430 years (Gen 15:13); when these were complete, *Moses* was raised up as liberator (Exod 3). A *just time* is therefore to be awaited, and if it is deferred, we should pre-think that *the hour of Christ has not yet come*: but *it will come at that time*, and by pleasantness of aid will compensate delay. In this way *God himself* has said to his people: *if it seem to tarry, wait for it: because it shall surely come; it shall not tarry* (Hab 2:3).

**(2.)** God has *just causes* of his delay, and indeed all directed to our salvation. First he wills that we recognize our miseries, and gravely weigh them, — so that when from him we know our aid to depend, his glory be more manifest; *just as in Cana of Galilee* (John 2), when his mother from him sought aid, he said that his hour had not yet come, since the defect of the wine was not yet in all the nuptials well-known. Then he wills to render us by delay more diligent in prayers. For prayer is to God grateful sacrifice, — which, when it is more frequent, multiplies its fruit; and while aid is deferred, therefore he bids to pray more assiduously (Luke 18:1). Third he wills to *crucify* the world in us, and to excite the desire of *eternal life*: which through continual cross more easily he can bring about, than if he suddenly should satisfy our vows. Moreover he wills our patience and faith to render manifest to others, as *of Job under great affliction* it is written; *therefore he permitted evils to come, that in posterity might be given a clear example of his patience, as of holy Job* (Tob 2:14). Finally by delay of aid God turns aside greater calamities, into which from *security of the flesh* men could easily fall, — those who always experience God's aid at their nod. Therefore *patient* must the delay of divine aid be borne: for God does not suffer either time or manner to be prescribed for himself, which by the illustrious example in the history of *Abraham* is confirmed (Gen 12; Heb 11:8, 10); *For ye have need of patience, that, after ye have done the will of God, ye might receive the promise.* (Heb 10:36).

**(3.)** *Let examples of the ancients succor*, whom God did not with light and momentary cross afflicted, but with long-lasting molestations exercised. A hundred years *Abraham* awaited up to 90 years of age, until he had a son from *Sarah*, — and yet firmly he clung to God's promise: *I will multiply thy seed as the stars of the heavens* (Gen 22:17). *Jacob the Patriarch* from earliest boyhood to old age suffered various calamities. The *Israelites* 400 years in Egypt, and 70 in Babylon, as it were in an iron furnace were forged, — and yet at last liberation followed. That poor man at the *Pool of Bethesda* was sick full 38 years (John 5); a certain woman was in the *hemorrhoidal-flow* full 12 years (Mark 5:25); another full 18 years by the spirit of *infirmity* was afflicted (Luke 13). Yet to all Christ finally restored health.

And daily examples exist how God his saints marvelously leads, — the long-oppressed at last again lifts up; many in old age raises to honors and wealth, others after many years snatches from the hands of enemies, and with glory and honor crowns.

Into these examples as into a *mirror* let us look, nor esteem ourselves better than our fathers, knowing that *Whom resist stedfast in the faith, knowing that the same afflictions are accomplished in your brethren that are in the world.* (1 Pet 5:9).

**Casus VI. What if even unto the last breath of life no hope of liberation appears?**

*Reply.* On this account we ought not indulge in sadness until death; for by nothing better would our condition become. But here also must be borne what cannot be changed.

The sad soul we can raise up by these meditations: **(1.)** *the ordinary way to eternal life is the cross and affliction*: for *through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of heaven* (Acts 14:22). Thus has God disposed, that those he *foreknew*, he also *predestinated to be conformed to the image of his Son* (Rom 8:29). From the cross therefore we gather that we insist on *the right way which leads to life*, provided otherwise we are *That ye be not slothful, but followers of them who through faith and patience inherit the promises.* (Heb 6:12).

**(2.)** *Let us consider how brief is our life*: — therefore also brief is all affliction. For *seventy years, or at most eighty*, is *Moses'* count (Ps 90:10). If therefore with continual afflictions one is always molested, scarcely of 80 years is the molestation, which time in God's reckoning is hardly a moment. Whence also all *affliction of the pious* is called *light and momentary* (2 Cor 4:17).

**(3.)** *God tempers sadness with joys*: — with whatever recreation, God concatenated even afflictions as it were to *intercalate* is wont. For no one is in the tribulations of this age so deeply immersed, who has not felt some refreshment sometimes. But as travelers on continuous journeys are indeed fatigued, yet by sweet spring or pleasant sight or colloquy or by some other means on the way are recreated, — so those long tortured with the torments of this age, sometimes even respiration also perceive. For *He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever.* (Ps 103:9).

**(4.)** *Hope of eternal life* takes away all bitterness in adversities. This hope alone is certain, — otherwise *If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable.* (1 Cor 15:19). Life however truly future by sweetness overcomes all bitterness of this life; the eternity of that life relieves the length of temporal molestations. For *For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory;* (2 Cor 4:17); *For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.* (Rom 8:18). Then shall be fulfilled fully what *the Saviour* said (Matt 5:4): *blessed are those that mourn, since they shall receive consolation*: and (Luke 6:21) *blessed are ye that weep now, for ye shall laugh*, etc. From the hope of this blessedness the Apostle *Peter* commands us *Wherein ye greatly rejoice, though now for a season, if need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations:* (1 Pet 1:6).

**(5.)** Finally let us remember that *God is that patriarchal, who those he loves he chastises*, so lest they think themselves utterly deserted, if they will still show themselves *For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.* (Rom 8:38–39).

While therefore the spirit is in us, let us hope for our liberation: for nothing can sadden them, but hope of coming joys they have in the heavens, having a father most-clement in the heavens, — in whose bosom they are, even when in the world they are held as most-abject. *As sad, always however rejoicing; as chastised, yet not made manifest; as poor, but making many rich; as having nothing, and possessing all things* (2 Cor 6:9–10). Their *For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God. When Christ, who is our life, shall appear, then shall ye also appear with him in glory.* (Col 3:3–4).

**Casus VII. How is one to resist melancholic thoughts which arise from consideration of death?**

*Reply.* Many there are who cannot even hear of death, so they fear and shudder at the name of it, — especially when they observe *its harbingers*, — so that they cannot expel sadness from their soul.

That here well counsel be taken, three things must be studiously inculcated to them:

**(1.)** *Death is not too much to be feared*.
**(2.)** *They should prepare for death rightly*.
**(3.)** *With death itself they should learn to fight in due manner*.

*As to the first*: — natural indeed is it to fear death, which even *the Philosopher* named the *most horrible evil*: but of a Christian it is to *moderate* that fear, so that if the Lord shall have willed, we may with quiet soul receive death itself. In this way that fear of death is *salutary*, of the sort which is in the sons of God, — who even in death have a father propitious in the heavens, — and use fear of death for *bridling the concupiscences of the flesh*, and for avoiding *security*.

That however this fear of death we may rightly moderate, partly the *necessity of death*, partly its *utility* helps. *The necessity of death* depends on the *decree of God*, who, that he might contain man in office, before the fall added that *in whatever day thou shalt eat of it, thou shalt die the death* (Gen 2:17). After the fall the execution of this commination followed: for *Adam* died first, and all who from him were begotten, so that death is called *the way of all flesh* (2 Sam 14:14; Josh 23:14); and *And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:* (Heb 9:27), — which the wise *Sirach* also calls a *testament of God*: *this testament from the Lord to all flesh* (14:12).

The *utility of death* is chiefly threefold: **(1.)** *In death sin ceases*, — which tempts the pious before it is perpetrated, and afflicts when perpetrated, so long as in this mortality they live. *He that is dead is justified from sin* (Rom 6:7). **(2.)** *In death ceases all misery*, wherewith our life is on all sides encompassed. *But if a man live many years, and rejoice in them all; yet let him remember the days of darkness; for they shall be many. All that cometh is vanity.* (Eccl 11:8). Death moreover is *the end of all evils*, which those to whom this life is calamitous do not so much fear as *wish for* (Sir 41:3). **(3.)** *Death is the gate of life and the beginning of perfect joy* — which *Christ* promised to his own (John 16). Nothing we lose in death, when we lose life, — therefore *Paul* called death *gain* (Phil 1:21); *Christ himself* attests that believers *come not into judgment, but pass through death to life* (John 5:24). Which all things excite in the pious *desire of death* and expel fear of it.

*As to the second point: — preparation for death*. Since we must all die and yet rarely think of dying, therefore the *holy men* pray for this grace from God, as *David* asked: *LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is: that I may know how frail I am.* (Ps 39:4); and *Moses*: *So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.* (Ps 90:12). To this end holy monuments and *sepulchers* were placed, so that mortal men might remember. Even the *ethnics*, the wiser, took care to be admonished of their own mortality daily. So *Seneca* writes (epist. 24): *we die daily, — daily is taken off some part of our life, and even when we grow, our life diminishes. We have lost infancy, then boyhood, then adolescence up to yesterday. Whatever passes of time perishes; even this day itself, which we lead, with death we divide*.

Preparation for death is made **(1.)** by *frequent meditation on death*, while we still are strong. We know we must all die, but rarely we think of dying, — therefore holy men beseech this grace from God.

**(2.)** By *daily examination of our life*, so that we correct errors, continue well-done deeds, and abstain from evils, — so that if death suddenly overwhelms us, it may find us clean from crimes, and quiet in conscience. *Pythagoras* persuaded his disciples to examine daily each day of their life. Such examination befits disciples of Christ, that they always retain *faith and good conscience*, — which those who wish to overcome death need. Therefore *Christ* bids us *Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come.* (Matt 24:42), and *Paul* bids us *to war the good warfare, keeping faith and good conscience* (1 Tim 1:18).

**(3.)** By *continual recollection of our daily misery*: for *heavy is the yoke upon all the sons of Adam, from the day of coming forth from the mother's womb, to the day of burial* (Sir 40:1); whence rightly it is said, *to live long is nothing else than long to be tortured*. Whoever seriously considers these things, will not fear death, but wish for it as *the happy closure of all miseries*.

**(4.)** By *assiduous dying* to the example of *Paul* (1 Cor 15:31 *I die daily*): which happens when lighter evils — such as diseases, poverty, calamities, loss of wealth and honors — we contemn; for whoever does this, remembers that daily he must die. And when in all the actions of our life we place death as our perpetual companion before our eyes. Verily then with *David* in all our operations we must say: *between me and death is one step only* (1 Sam 20:3), and *as we know it is our unmarried death* (Job 7:1). *Media vita in morte sumus*, as the Church sings.

**(5.)** By *desire of celestial things*. As Christ after the resurrection from the dead, for 40 days himself alive with certain signs to his showed, and then ascended into heaven, — so the pious rise with him from their sins, — a living faith through good works to others they show, — themselves lift up higher and daily to celestial things ought to hang more. And this is our *spiritual ascension*, which is commended (Col 3:1): *if therefore ye be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above*.

By these things is a *spiritual preparation for death* made. Adding also *guessed of true joy, and taste of eternal beatitude*: for such in this life to be given us testifies *the author of Ecclesiasticus* (6:5), by which he happens to die willingly, so that to a *full possession of those joys* he may come.

Guessed we however already goods of the age to come, when the good of Christ we expect through him: for we have him already firm in his own house of God the Father, *since our life he has preceded me*, going forward to God (John 12:32); which benefit also for us with the celestial Father he impetrated (John 17:24 *Father, I wish that those whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am, that they may see my glory, which thou hast given me*). Hence *Paul* writes: *To the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the beloved.* (Eph 1:6).

*As to the third*: — *with death itself we must know how to fight*. Arms of this battle are not carnal, but spiritual, whereby either the perils of death we may bear, or from us drive off, or *ours ourselves fortify*. The first genus of arms are *promises against the torments of death and of diseases, against separation from dearest friends, of body and soul*, of parents and children, spouses and similar, who in life were dear to us. To these thoughts let us oppose as it were the *seal* — the *providence of God*, — which disposes all things in the world, and to our life set *terminus*, without which nothing which crucifies us can happen to us; *But the very hairs of your head are all numbered.* (Matt 10:30). In this way *David* his adverse things patiently bore: *Remove thy stroke away from me: I am consumed by the blow of thine hand.* (Ps 39:10).

**(2.)** The *aid of God*, without whom *no one can suffer these things*, — as *David* speaks (Ps 116:15) — he alone *mitigates contritions and heals*, so that they are not so bitter to us as they appear to others: which is testified by the examples of martyrs, who bore the sharpest cruciates with brave soul, — praying they suffered torments, since *the consolator Holy Spirit* mitigated their tortures, and *virtue-from-above* refreshed the hearts of the patient.

**(3.)** *Hope of restitution of all things*. Bodies will be restored to their souls, children to parents, in that day *Marvel not at this: for the hour is coming, in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice,* (John 5:28); for we have not lost our own, whom we hold before God, whom in the order which he wishes his Imperator by his time will follow. Just as therefore *Joseph* his brothers to *Jacob* their father he shall restore, so those dying ought to say to their friends: *And Joseph said unto his brethren, I die: and God will surely visit you, and bring you out of this land unto the land which he sware to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.* (Gen 50:24). And just as Christ restored to the *widow of Naim* her defunct son and prohibited her from weeping (Luke 7:13), so eternal life for these who defect on account of Christ commodity, — truth denying, are not by name of disciples of Christ, — so they too shall be denied by Christ before the celestial Father.

**(4.)** *The condition of our death is other now than it was before Christ*. *For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.* (Rom 6:23), — which formidable makes death in itself: but let us think, how the *death of the pious through the death of Christ is qualified, — nay is transformed into a sweet sleep*, — so that God the souls of the pious dying with paternal arms receives, bodies however in his dormitories, up to *the day of restitution of all things* he lays away, and preserves for a better age. *Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.* (Ps 116:15).

By this shield the fiery darts of Satan are received when we by pains and cruciates of diseases, by injury of dearest ones, by the wage of sin — the extreme judgment which follows death — and by other similar things he terrifies. But we oppose the *victory of Christ*, that in nothing he may harm us: *So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.* (1 Cor 15:54–57).

**(5.)** *A sacrificial offering of our body*. Our sacrifice however ought to be *voluntary*: therefore when the hour of death shall have come, not unwillingly with heavy minds, but with *promptness of Spirit* let us follow our Lord, — resigning our will into his hands, and saying with Christ: *not my will, but thine be done* (Luke 22:42). *For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's.* (Rom 14:8). By this promptness of soul to death we conquer death, — its pains we feel less, — with joy hence we depart.

And these are the three heads which pertain to *the art of dying well*, and which from death inflicted-melancholy easily expel, namely, to fear death not too much, to prepare rightly for death, and with death itself in due manner and mode to fight.

**Casus VIII. Whether it can happen that suggestions of the malignant spirit incite to sordidness and other sins — of which sort, although consent does not follow, yet one is saddened at being defiled: — how however can one meet this?**

*Reply.* Most true is what *D. Paul* writes (Gal 5:17): *the flesh lusteth against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh: for these are contrary the one to the other*. And the pious experience *suggestions of Satan to sins*, in which they by no means delight, but rather so much they grieve, that on them to sit-still and to serve God with sober heart they cannot, — crying out with the Apostle *Paul*: *O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?* (Rom 7:24). How much of anguish of soul is here, they do not understand, but neither do they believe those who see themselves led captive in the snares of the devil.

The *Pontifices* however concerning these pollutions of body and other disordered motions of the heart care little. They teach indeed *those concupiscences of the flesh* to have been *natural*, — as if from the defect of human nature, from the condition of the flesh flowing, — as writes *Bellarmine* (lib. *De gratia primi hominis*, cap. 7). Whence follows, that whether one burns with love of another's spouse, or of illicit libidines, or with foolish desire of wealth and honors flames, — since these motions they do not think damnable, but *from nature of matter*, from *condition* — so easily they comfort themselves, and their name they contradict.

But those who fear God, and the malice of *original sin* weigh more deeply, on that name also *bites of conscience* too seriously and frequently experience.

That this evil may be countered, — lest sadness absorb the soul, **(1.)** must be *recognized*, and thence indeed to God we must not be plainly deserted, but rather *studium* praised, whom he seeks not to abandon: which infernal Satan we see, in the manner of a lion looking around whom he may devour. This evil we deplore, and the peril in which we are placed we always place before our eyes, and let us think — *let us fortify our heart, as much as we can*, — lest that *impure spirit* pollute us with whatever kind of impregnations; for which purpose especially there is need of *assiduous prayers*, lest God lead us into temptation, of meditation of the Word, of continual labors of vocation, — lest Satan find the *hospitium of our heart empty*.

**(2.)** If nevertheless the *tempter* occupies us, let us think that *we are not alone*, who suffer such things: but even to the holiest these darts of Satan he thrusts, — which the complaint of *Paul* above adduced testifies. Whence also of the *remission of sins* daily we ask together with all the saints (Ps 32:6).

**(3.)** Let us recall that God *the pious* himself now and then has tempted, promising to Satan some power over us, so that he might probe our heart, whether we sincerely serve him. — This did *not those tempted* — nothing worth-doing, nor do they flee to *Christ* (John 12:38), — nor do they pour out ardent prayers, — nor do they serve God with their whole heart. So of *Hezekiah* the pious king, when he showed to the ambassadors of the king of Babylon his treasures, it is written: *the Lord left him, that he might be tempted, and that all which is in his heart might be known* (2 Chr 32:31).

**(4.)** *Let us not think we are utterly deserted*, but let us seek God's aid to resist the devil, — which we in the whole age we experience. *For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.* (Eph 6:12). And to conquer these we need not human strengths, but the *armor of God*, — which God does not deny to his saints, whereby the malignant one they may flee, and *free their heart from impure thoughts*.

**(5.)** *Those wicked suggestions*, — of themselves indeed *worthy of death*, — although assent does not accede: *The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the LORD: but the words of the pure are pleasant words.* (Prov 15:26). — Nevertheless are *venial sins*, of the sort as *sins of the saints*, who through Christ are reconciled with God, — with the Spirit's aid resist those suggestions, and them at last extinguish. Therefore they are not imputed to them in the judgment of God, — but are covered by the *innocence of Christ*: because that wrestling with the flesh is not without pain over admitted suggestions, — which pain conjoined with *faith in Christ*, — so there is nothing of *condemnation* in such a pious man.

Which all things if considered, the conscience of a man on that account is not to be too much lacerated, — writes *Gregory* (lib. 5 *Moral*): *and yet from the depth by no means can they be, always for the flesh superfluous produces, always the spirit with the sword of solicitude cuts back*.

And elsewhere (lib. 11): *the minds of the elect, if in themselves they find any carnal thoughts, they consume them with the fire of penitence: nor do they permit their thoughts to be dilated with carnal pleasure, but by that they judge themselves more subtly they strike themselves, so that they anticipate the strict Judge nearby*.

Always therefore let be before our eyes the exhortation of *D. Jerome* (in his letter *ad Demetriadem De virginitate servanda*): *Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him; lest at any time the adversary deliver thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and thou be cast into prison.* (Matt 5:25).

**Casus IX. What however is to be done, if one is not only for evil thoughts tempted, but even for some grave, perhaps even often repeated, deed his soul is anguished?**

*Reply.* The general *remedium* against this temptation is *true repentance*, which we always teach; therefore from such sins we dehort, — we bid *concupiscences resisted*, and warn, — even if by some sin we have already been preoccupied, — that we do not to the same stone, after prayer done, again strike ourselves: false however it is, that voluntarily sinning and often returning, they have no longer any *hostia for sin*, nor to grace to return can, — which *heresy* — just as of desperation full — from sacred letters diametrically fights.

For **(1.)** *Christ* has bidden us to seek *remission of sins*, — not only about sins of *weakness* secure he makes us, but without distinction promises the pardon of all sins whatever, — therefore he especially makes mention of those sins which are *knowledges to us* (Luke 11:4) — spontaneously our own contracted debts, — which if Christ had promised remission of light delicts only, — it would follow that those who sin against conscience, and that with repeated attempts the Lord's Prayer to pray they could not, — even if of the delict admitted they seriously grieved: — which no one who is of sound mind would say.

**(2.)** Here pertains that voice of the Lord: *God wills that all be saved, — I do not will the death of him who dies, but that he be converted and live* (Ezek 18:32; 33:11), — with which consents the Apostle *Peter*: *God wills no one to perish, but all to come to penitence* (2 Pet 3:9). — This his enitent will God has confirmed by examples in either Testament: *Manasseh, idolater and parricide* he received into grace; *David* adulterer and homicide; *Peter*; *the thief on the cross*; *the prostitute — of a woman* — old — and inveterate meretrix (whom some think to have been *Mary Magdalene*); *Paul* also, the acerbic persecutor of the Church of Christ, — he received into grace.

**(3.)** For this the *universal use of the keys* of the Church, — of which the promise stands (Matt 18:18; John 20:23): *whatsoever ye shall remit on earth, shall be loosed also in heaven*. — No distinction here of sins or of sinners: — but solid *from this flows for any sinning — but truly penitent* consolation.

Two things however have *Novatian* and *Photinus*, which here except, — with which they burden the consciences of the *infirm* without cause. First is, that examples of certain sinners, whom Scripture mentions to have obtained pardon, do not make a *rule*. Another is, that not for *habitual sins* — that is, voluntary and often committed — but only for *infirmities and ignorances* did Christ offer the *hostia*, — as it is written (Heb 9:7).

But these are not of such moment, as to disturb a truly penitent man's soul.

For as to the first: — rightly here we apply that of the Apostle: *For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.* (Rom 15:4). — By which reason of arguing uses the *author of the Epistle to the Hebrews* (9:13–14): *if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctifieth to the emendation of the flesh: how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge our conscience from dead works?*

Here pertains also that God very seriously to sinners promises pardon, — if only serious penitence shall have accessed. For (Ezek 18:14): *God has attested with an oath that he wills not the death of the impious, — who is a thief, who sheddeth blood, who eateth in the mountains, who defileth his neighbor's wife, who afflicteth the poor and needy, who taketh spoils by violence, who returneth not the pledge, who lifteth up his eyes to idols, committing abomination, receiving usury*, — if that impious one shall have done penitence, — says the Lord (Ezek 18:20): *from all his sins which he hath done, and shall keep my commandments, and shall do judgment and righteousness, — he shall live, — he shall not die: — of all his iniquities which he hath done, I will not remember*.

And lest anyone doubt that this promise pertains even to those who seriously penitent, and after penitence sin anew, — must be noted the words of the Lord (Ezek 33:12): *son of man, say to the sons of thy people: the impiety of the impious shall not hurt him, in whatever day he shall have been converted from his impiety*. And *John* the Apostle calls *Christ* the *And he is the propitiation for our sins: and not for our's only, but also for the sins of the whole world.* (1 John 2:2).

No sin therefore, at whatever time, and however often it is committed, is excluded. For as *Fulgentius* speaks piously (In *epistola de paenitentia*): *for the merchandise of Christ, — our — no plague is incurable, so neither for any wound and time — heavenly medicine — can it fail*.

These all are not said for confirmation of the impious in their sins: for we know that every sin merits eternal death; nor is penitence to be delayed, lest either we be indurated in sins, or by the hour of death overtaken, — but in consolation are said of those who by gravest sins and often repeated see themselves defiled, — lest of the *remission of sins*, if in serious groans they seek from God, they despair. For, as *Augustine* says (Hom. 41, book 50 hom.): *lest despairing we augment sins, God has proposed us the port of penitence, — lest despairing we augment, the day of death has been given uncertain*.

*What however is said in Heb 12:17 of Esau*, that he *found no place of penitence, though with tears he sought it*, — pertains in no wise to grave and frequent sinners, but concerns the *primogeniture of Esau*, which he had once sold, — afterwards could not recover, even if with many tears he lamented that loss (Gen 27:34).

From what has been said it is manifest, that all hope of *sinning ones* is *serious penitence*, which sins deletes, — even most numerous — from a contrite spirit, if of admitted things one repent, — says *Augustine* (De ecclesiasticis dogmatibus, cap. 48).

**Casus X. But what if to a certain penitent it may happen, that he cannot remember all sins, either that he cannot conceive worthy grief over them, — should he ever conceive that all-grace of God he had lost, and thus rather utterly despair?**

*Reply.* The beginning of true penitence is *recognition of sins* and *deploration*. For as *Solomon* writes: *He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.* (Prov 28:13). Which incommodities from denial of sins or palliation shall follow, *David* by his own example has largely taught (Ps 32).

**Two ways** however can it happen that one grieves for his sins, but not for the singulars, nor loses all hope of pardon:

**(1.)** *On account of infirmity of memory*. For those who examine their life and dispute of themselves — although they cannot remember all things which they perpetrated from earliest boyhood. To such a general confession of their sins suffices, with special enumeration of those which they can remember, — provided *hypocrisy* is not there, whereby they suppress those things which nevertheless best they recall. God requires an *ingenuous confessor*, — that all things be open before him. But if the grand delicts of God to him more securely he confesses, — and could not remember, in specie, of the delicts, — a general confession suffices (Ps 19:14): *from my hidden ones cleanse me, Lord*.

Then *David* also has admonished us (Ps 25:7): *sins of my youth and my ignorances remember not, Lord*. For no one can remember all his sins, much less seriously grieve for all, — and that this be done in the sudden of some case and peril of life. For then the sinner with *general repentance* over all his delicts, whatever and of whatsoever sort they are, — can implore pardon, — for whoever of some one sin seriously grieves, and being at the time excluded, cannot bring to memory and specifically grieve for the rest, — his part is to conceive a serious sorrow for all. For *faith in Christ* removes all sins, and *the penitent one of remission of them* renders secure. Thus the thief on the cross, — in the extreme moment of the hour of death, obtained grace, — even if by the time excluded from all his sins he could not commemorate, nor a general confession make (Luke 23).

**Casus XI. What however is to be judged, if one cannot conceive serious grief for his sins (although one greatly would wish), — should he despair of remission?**

*Reply. Authentic* is Christ's word: *And ye shall be hated of all men for my name's sake: but he that endureth to the end shall be saved.* (Matt 10:22). With whom consents the Apostle (Heb 3:14): *we are made partakers of Christ, if only we hold the beginning of his substance firm unto the end*.

*Various however are those things which can intercept that perseverance*: chiefly the *allurements of the world*, *persecutions*, *continuous calamities* — which many well-running from the path deflect, and precipitate them to destruction, — as the examples of *Judas* and *Saul* testify. Many are therefore too much anguished, and always fear lest they too at last suffer *shipwreck of faith*.

To these not only by *this exhortation* is comfort given: — first must be commended their *studium*, that they do not out of Epicurean *security* neglect their salvation, but its care they hold solicitously, taking care lest by *palm* of it they lose. For the Apostle wants: *with fear and trembling let us work out our salvation* (Phil 2:12); and *happy is he who always is anxious* (Prov 28:14). *For as Bernard says: he who fears, takes care*: whence also blessed *Job* always feared, lest by some work he offend his own God: *of all my works I feared*, said he, *I am afraid of all my sorrows, I know that thou wilt not hold me innocent.* (Job 9:28).

Then the *certainty of our salvation* must be persuaded to the infirm by *firm arguments*.

**(1.)** *The promise of salvation to all believers*: for *whoever believeth in the Son, hath everlasting life* (John 3:16); *whoever shall have believed, shall be saved* (Mark 16:16); *he that believeth on me, hath eternal life, and comes not into judgment* (John 5:24). *The promises of God are unchangeable* (2 Cor 1:20). *So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.* (Rom 10:17); *Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.* (Ps 119:105).

If thou doubtest whether thou hast faith, examine thy heart, whether the *So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.* (Rom 10:17).

Nor does it matter, that in *temptations* thou dost not always feel the motion of faith: — for not upon the sense of night depends faith, but on the *word of promise*, which thou lovest. Defect of sense is a sign of *infirmity*: — but infirm faith is still faith, — to which with serious prayers and assiduous exercises of piety succor must be brought.

**(2.)** *To the promises of God accedes the testimony of the Holy Spirit*, — of which *Paul* speaks (Rom 8:15–16): *we have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry: Abba, Father, — who bears witness with our spirit, that we are sons of God*. That testimony of the Spirit is made, when *by means of grace* the promises to us are applied, and eternal life which is promised in the Word, on our hearts he seals.

If thou doubtest whether thou hast that testimony of the Spirit, — even now those who believe themselves-to-have, who yet are far from truly-having, — learn true signs of not-presumptuous testimony, of which there are two: first, *love of the divine Word*, its reading, preaching, meditation, prayers, and use of the sacraments, — through which media the Holy Spirit is efficacious, kindles faith, and quiets our heart. Second sign is, that such a pious man from the impulse of the Holy Spirit *cries to God with serious groans of soul*, — since prayers to others are only perfunctory, — or even nothing at all. Prayers of the pious of this sort, — from the Spirit of prayers excited, — are made in *faith in the Son of God*, on whose account we dare to call God our *Father*, and what things from our own we can expect from him. Who therefore still can pray, of his own faith he should not doubt: — where however faith is, — there is the Holy Spirit, and there is hope of eternal salvation.

**(3.)** With this testimony of the Holy Spirit is conjoined the *testimony of one's own conscience*, which through the Spirit is *renewed and sanctified*. *Sanctification of heart* however is *the note of those who shall be heirs of eternal salvation*: — thus *Paul* describes the *candidates of eternal life*: *And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.* (1 Cor 6:11). Of this sanctification of ours we are compact from its motions, — which indeed are more certain in time of security, — yet not entirely hidden in time of temptation, but exert themselves. *Blessed are they that are of pure heart* (Matt 5:8).

**(4.)** *Confirms the certainty of our salvation the calling to eternal life*, — which as regards God's part is immutable: for *the gifts of God are without repentance* (Rom 11:29); *If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself.* (2 Tim 2:13). *If even greatly we fall away from the grace of calling*, return however lies open to it by true penitence, — during which continuing, — we have no cause to doubt of our salvation, even if we know ourselves not to be free from stains of sin. For *Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began,* (2 Tim 1:9).

**(5.)** *This makes God's universal, merciful will*, from which no man is excluded, — but *all he wills to be saved* (1 Tim 2:4); *not willing anyone to perish, but that all come to penitence* (2 Pet 3:9). — Every sinning man therefore, — who by penitence to God returns, — assured of his salvation ought to be.

**Casus XII. How is it to be countered, when the malignant spirit tempts men to *lêthargon* — that is, to loss of hope in God's providence, or to despair of God's aid?**

*Reply.* The *malignant spirit* by many modes can solicit us to *lêthargon*, — which by aid of God we can drive off by the *remedies hitherto shown*.

**Casus XIII. What if some, by prevented melancholy, should have inflicted violent hands upon themselves — should we utterly despair of their salvation?**

*Reply.* Most grave is the sentence of the Son of God: *He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned.* (Mark 16:16); *He that believeth on him is not condemned: but he that believeth not is condemned already, because he hath not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God.* (John 3:18). Which sentence *those who out of desperation lay hands upon themselves* condemns simply, — since to believe and to distrust or despair are opposites. Whence *Sirach* writes: *woe to those who are dissolute at heart, — who believe not God, — therefore they shall not be protected by him* (Sir 2:15).

The *Fathers* also hold no hope of the salvation of them, who kill themselves; writes *Origen* (lib. 1 in John): *never shall they have quiet, nor shall they find refreshment, — but their souls immediately when from the body they go out, into darkness shall be led*. And *Augustine* (lib. 1 De civ. Dei, cap. 16): *the guilty of their own death shall the better life after death not receive*.

For this reason it has been provided by civil laws, that those who from *desperation* lay hands upon themselves, shall be *deprived of honest burial*: for it is right that those who wickedly lived and perished in their sins, — even in the burial of their bodies from the members of the faithful of Christ shall be separated.

Not lacking however are those who this deed a *self-slaying*, — if not utterly excuse — try to soften. They pretend the example of *Samson* (Judg 16:30), whom no one condemns, though he brought death upon himself.

But the deed of *Samson* was *heroic*, which no one without a peculiar *calling of God* should imitate. *Samson* was *judge* and *savior of the people*, — and for this divinely raised up, — that he should liberate his people from the hand of the *Philistines* (Judg 15). When therefore he was already in the hands of the enemies, blind and captive, he preferred himself with the enemies to die, rather than to desert his calling, — which deed, so far is Scripture from reproving, that rather it commends, — because more he killed dying, than before living he had killed (Judg 16:30). Therefore in the *catalogue of the faithful* he is found: *Who through faith subdued kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions.* (Heb 11:33). And *Augustine* refers the deed of Samson to the *Holy Spirit*, since *the Spirit had latently ordered this, who through him did miracles* (Lib. 1 De civ. Dei, cap. 21). Moreover Samson is thought to have been in this genus a *type of Christ*, who *laid down his life for the sheep* (John 10:11); and that those which typically were done by the saints, *not for imitation to be proposed*, — all know.

Others think that a life ill-lived is corrected by violent death.

But to these we oppose the celebrated Greek proverb: *the end, not the battle, crowns*. Scripture teaches that God will not remember all *former righteousness*, if *from his own righteousness the just have turned aside and shall have done abomination* (Ezek 18:24). Perilous therefore is it to promise salvation to those who have themselves despaired of their salvation, — and either from *avarice, envy*, or *from impatience of cruciate*, or from another evil purpose, desperately laid violent hands upon themselves. *The timid and the incredulous shall have their part in the pool burning with fire and brimstone* (Rev 21:8).

Another however is the reason of those who from *too much sadness* have inflicted upon themselves a lethal wound, — but before they die, come to themselves, and *serious penitence signs* show: — of the salvation of these we should not despair. For God also *receives the last groans of the penitent*, — just as the *thief on the cross* a little before death was converted (Luke 23:40); and *Philip the jailer of Ephesus*, with the drawn sword having about to kill himself, was led to penitence (Acts 16:27). Rich is God in mercies, nor is his hand shortened, so that he cannot save, nor is his ear so weighted, that the cries of those who at the gates of death cry to him, he does not hear.

Thus, if one not from desperation nor from an evil purpose, but from *phrenesy* of melancholy laboring, upon himself shall have inflicted death, — before he dies has repented, — our part is not to precipitate judgment, — especially if before he had piously lived.

For great is the force of temptations, — which weighs down the most-firm soul of *Job*, and about the *day of his nativity* he wishes it be *cursed* (Job 3:1–4).

Interrupted is in such-ones the reason and human sense, — so that truly they know not what they do. If therefore before the *phrenetic and melancholic paroxysm* prevails in them, they detest their sins, — a confession of faith in Christ they utter, — commend their soul to God, — and lest longer God permit anything against them, they pray, — and yet afterwards, as it were mentally captive, upon their own body they become homicides, — they are not rashly to be condemned. For they did *another's work* beyond their will, from *weakness of brain*, — as the pious very often experience with themselves, — and complain that they are unable to do the good they will (Rom 7:19).

For which cause some are of that opinion, that such are *by the devil*, who in *phrenetics and melancholics* is most occupied, killed. As it is decreed in *Decretum* 15 q.1: *this we certainly affirm — that this ought to be believed — that a man of sound mind and mind — himself for-life should not be admitted*.

Just as therefore in political judgments the crimes of *phrenetics inflicted* are not imputed to them, and on that account they are not punished, since without will and purpose they did them: — so neither *culpa* here can be imputed to the miserable, who out of *impotence of mind* upon themselves violent hands laid, — which if they had been of sound mind, they had never done.

Just as also God himself, in his judgment, does not impute the *sins of weakness* to the pious, — but *remits them and covers them*: so we believe entirely, that he for his immense mercy will not impute — but out of grace remit for Christ's sake — the *self-slaying* which from *weakness*, — with themselves as-if-unknowing-authors, — is committed, — into whom the miserable have believed, — whose faith on their part perpetually did not perish, — as of those who indeed by natural death, but by hours before their end are through the *violence of disease deprived of reason and all senses*.

[On the *Christian virgins* of whom is well hoped, — refers *some* who, lest they lose *shame*, put themselves to death, — which *Ambrose* commends (in *De virginibus*, lib. 3); *Nicephorus* (in *other places*, lib. 7, cap. 11). But although *laudable* it is, that those chaste-ones were so-observant of the shame of their soul, — yet in this by no medium of their salvation could they consult: — *For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all.* (Jas 2:10). *He who said, do not commit adultery, said also, do not kill; if therefore thou hast not committed adultery, but hast killed, thou art made a transgressor of the law*. Then the *Apostolic rule* is: *evils are not to be done, that goods may come* (Rom 3:8). About which *Augustine* has written (lib. 1 De civitate Dei, cap. 25): *neither for the sake of obtaining goods, nor for avoiding evils, is it lawful to kill oneself*. Moreover *divine providence* is not to be despaired, whereby God even from the midst of perils can make evasion. — *Lot* certainly from the hands of the most-impure *Sodomites* he marvelously snatched (Gen 19); *Susanna* also chastity and innocence in marvelous ways he protected. Similar things attest in Ecclesiastical history of *Potamiaena Alexandrian virgin*, of *Agnes*, *Theodora*, and *others*, — of which see *Eusebius* (lib. 8, cap. 14), and *Ambrose* (Serm. 15). Finally we must remember, that although the body has been vitiated, chastity however is not taken away, — if the assent of the will has not come. *For the will assenting violates chastity, not the impetus of the violator: nor of the very body perishes chastity, since the sanctity there of the will using perseveres, as much as in itself, even the facultative-force. — Augustine*, lib. 1 *De civ. Dei*, cap. 16. — Which if greatly a sin had been committed, better it is however to have surviving life, — that one can repent, — than to lose it where the sinning is-taken-not-away. *Is it not better*, says *Augustine*, *to commit an offense which one can heal by penitence, than to do such things where the place of penitence is not left behind?* Finally they have no just cause of their deed: for either they wish to guard their chastity, — and that they lose it not by unwilling concubitus, — or they take pleasure from the deed, and thus in their sins they perish. Hence are those verses not inelegant on *Lucretia*, who wished to redeem her chastity with her life:

*If pleasing to thee, Lucretia, was the adulterer, — thou hast merited deservedly by thy death to be captured. But if by force chastity was taken from thee, — what fury is it to wish to die for another's crime? In vain therefore, Lucretia, thou hast caught praise, — for either wickedly-cast or maddened thou fallest.*

For these causes it is dissuaded, — chastity indeed intent, — which if it be perfect, — we do not see, what hope of salvation there can be, — since this deed fights with the *sixth precept* on account of the *inflicted death*, and with the *first* on account of the *denial of divine providence*.]

## Chapter V. On Cases of Conscience Concerning Actions with Magi and Sorceresses

**Preamble.** The name *magus* is from the number of those words which either simply, or in a middle-sense, are called, — for both good and evil sides can be usurped. This word is *Greek, Persian*, and *Chaldean*.

*Magia* is also a *Persian* voice, signifying the *knowledge of divine and human things*: — *magus* is the same as *wise*, — *sophist* and *priest of the Persians*. Whence in Scripture the Persian *sophi* are called *magi from the east* (Matt 2:1).

Afterwards this word was accepted in a bad part, — since most, under pretext of religion and of the arcane science, exercised *maleficent arts*, as *Pliny* complains at the beginning of his 30th book of *Natural History*.

Hence *Philo* (in his book *De legibus*), noting *Casaubon* (Exercit. 1 in the annals ecclesiast. Baronii, num. 3), makes a twofold *magia*, — which distinction also *Hieronymus* (ad Paulinum), and out of the fathers many others, recognize:

**(1) *Legitimate***, — one which revolves around the *knowledge of nature*, — cultivated among the greatest kings, especially of the *Persians*, — of which writes *Coelius Rhodiginus* (lib. 9, *lection. variar.*), that *magi sometimes are called Prophets*, when they *presage futures*, and *conjoined with religion medicine* they cultivate.

**(2) *Second* — *sorciary*** (*sortiaria*, *maleficii-artes*), — an adulteration of the former, — a *cheating-mother* of the demons, — a common instrument of the Etruscan-cheats for deceiving.

Of *magi of the second genus* here we treat, — therefore with *veneficis* we conjoin them, though from these they differ in that these by *venom* remove men, — those not always, but *deceive* only and *delude*, — or if they harm, this they do not by venom, but by *pharmakoi* — that is, by *herbs, ligatures, incantations, and other sortileges*: which distinction *Plato* notes (lib. 11 *De legibus*). Such magi have diverse names in diverse tongues.

Among the Hebrews they are called ***chartummim*** (Exod 7:11; 8:18) — which word is from the root *pethreh, ostentation-of-eyes*. The LXX Greek interpreters call them ***pharmakoi***, which word from them indeed marks *venefici*, who harm by venom; — but since the *magi* mostly harm men, by potions, bones, and venomous animals, — therefore they too are called *pharmakoi kai epōdoi kai pharmakis-magoi*, but women *pharmakis-tai*, which word also to Ethnic writers is familiar.

For with *Aristotle* (lib. 8, cap. 18, *De historia animalium*), magi are called *magiai pharmakis-gerai*; *Hippocrates* in the book *De morbo sacro* calls the magi *maganeousai, alethiakous, alazontes*, who boast to *bring down the moon from the sky, to obscure the sun, to raise storms, to subjugate the gods*.

The Greeks also call the magi *lamias*, whence in *Hesychius* are *lamiokakion gynaikeion*: the Levites' *maccapha* the *Hebrews* by *lamia* expound, — which some translators think comes from *lania — from the verb lanio*, to *lacerate and dilaniate*, as *Bruno* noted. Rather however it is to be held as *Greek*. For *lamia* is *from lamos* or from voice *lamos*, that is, *gullet*, — noting the *demon of the muliebre sex* elegantly appearing, — who *entices travelers on the way, and — as soon as first they approach — most-avidly devours*. This word was transferred to the *sagae*, since they *drink human blood*.

Afterwards this word was granted Latin currency, and *poets and prose-writers* call the *sagas lamias*, — and *Horace* (in his *Art of Poetry*): *Let not the lamia dine on a boy alive and dredged forth from the belly*. And when in *Isaiah* 14 (v. 23) *Babylonians* are reproved for their sortileges, — and among them *fauns* and *satyrs and demons* — there commorants are predicted, the Latin interpreter renders the Hebrew word as *lamia*.

There are also who think even the *word for magic* (*strix*) to be *Greek*, as *Isidorus* (De originibus lib. 8), — as those who derive that from the verb *strizo*, which is *to press and subact*, — and either because to *magical arts* devoted are they too by cooking sometimes occupied. But this word is *Latin*, as we have noted above.

To the *Latins* magi are called *sortilegi*, — those who cast lots either from paper, or membrane, or leaves read, — and exercised their art, — which indeed is a certain *species of magi*, but the *vulgar magi in general* have those names. They are called by many *Latin* names: *praestigiators*, since they *fascinate the senses of men*; *divinators*, since they *dare to predict futures and hidden things*; *cantatores*, since with *incantation*, — because with charms they invoke demons; *sagae, — from sagando* or *from sagiendo*, as with some, — better however from the *Hebrew* *sagan*, — which denotes *priest or seer*.

*Augurs*, who observed *both flights and voices of birds* for prognostics — of this name is *Hujus of Ovid* who wrote (lib. 6 *Fastorum*): *some bird which by its horrendous fear* — *whom Isaiah* (cap. 34, v. 15) *the strix names,* — thought by *Ovid* to be a devourer of children, — *strix* also *strygium* naming; who by writing *of the Old Goths* were called *magas Amanicani*, as writes *Tacitus* (lib. 2 *De moribus*, cap. 1). *Nekromantic* is he who *speaks in secret with the underworld and demons*, whence also the herb *mandragora* is called *Necromantia*, — which the *Germans* call *Aluranas*.

The *Germans* call magi *Zeuberer*, whence *Wolgnisti Sagas* are called; and by that name however these come who — with things arising, wishing — the aid of the demon by *pact tacit or express, some marvellous many things above the strength of nature — with God permitting — either they signify or seem to do or predict, — which since according to the order of nature cannot happen, are commonly held for miracles*.

But from that name and crime are exempt those who use created things in that manner *not knowing and willing, but through error*, — deceived by others, — as if a sick man received *diabolic medicine* which the physician (whom he judged to be a good man) offered, he would not be a magus, since he has just cause of ignorance; — but if the physician invoked the devil in his presence, or used superstitious words or things, the sick would not be excused.

The devil however has various modes of deluding men, whether to their benefit or harm, — hence are distinct the *species of magic*.

*God himself* (Deut 18:10–11) enumerates *nine species* in the Scripture. In the first are ***lustratores***, who lead their sons through fire. In the second, *ariolos or divinators*, who from any inspection of Scripture, or from cast revelation, others about future or absent things presume to teach and inform: for the Hebrew word is from the root *jaadeh*, which in general signifies *to teach*, — sometimes even good divination it denotes (Prov 3:15), but often in the bad part it is accepted for illicit divinations (Deut 18:10; Num 22:14; Ezek 21:6). In the third class are ***augures***, from whom the doubting receive responses — from the root *nach, to respond*. In the fourth are ***calculators*** (*mecalculatores*), who *number the days*, prefer one to another, or lean on lots and augurs: for the Hebrew word *mecalculatores* has its name from *numbering*. In the fifth are ***praestigiatores*** *sedim*, who fascinate the eyes of men. In the sixth are ***venefici***, those who associate themselves — that they be at the choruses and conventicles of the magi. In the seventh are ***pythones***, who invoke spirits and from them solicit occult things, as of old was done in oracles. In the eighth are ***idoli***, who consult the devil, and from his responses draw forth their wisdom. In the ninth class finally are ***necromantici***, who consult the dead. These are the genera of magic which Scripture shows.

Others distinguish into *magic properly said*, which by others is called *incantation*, into *divination*, and into *superstition*.

Most-used is it to constitute *two species* of magic. One is called *goeteia*, the other *pharmakeia*. This comprehends the studies of men, — their *words* and works *by incantation, superstition, and abuse of the creatures of God*. The other adds *the prestiges and marvellous operations of the devil*. *Pharmakeia* is twofold, further: — when *venoms* are prepared and thereby men and animals are harmed, by which means very often violent plague is caused; — the other, when not by *venom* but by *words, characters, herbs*, and other superstitious things, which of themselves have not that efficacy which follows, — but others are harmed, — with *ergeia* or operation of Satan acceding, so also — very seldom that seem to happen by *mere prestige* and occult *fascination*, — as what by magic seems from the sky to be brought, forests transferred, hay-wagons devoured, men into beasts transformed. The other, when in truth something happens, although the mode be *prestigial*, — as when suddenly storms are excited, diseases most-violent inflicted, illicit loves among men kindled, others' things are taken with marvelous celerity, — in which the devil has his occult operation.

To this genus is also referred *Necromancy*, — when either *the dead are consulted*, or *are seen to be excited by the demon*: — has this name from *nekroi* — the dead — and *manteia*, — since to *sepulchers* it is customary to divine.

**In these arts more frequently uses the devil the labor of women than of men**, — just as *sagae and magae* are more numerous than *magi*, — of which the reason chiefly is that Devil, — as *the Lord* also says in the law (Exod 22:18), *not a prestigator but a poisoner shalt thou not suffer to live*. And the *Hebrew* proverb is: *the more women, the more sagae*, — which *Herodotus* (Hist. lib. 4) also noted. And *Cicero*: *of the greater knowledge in venefice* (that is, in magic arts), *the greater is grace* (lib. 13 *nat. hist.* cap. 22); and *Quintilian* (in *Declaratio*): *because ill-fated grace, — for the woman was born a poisoner*, — which some ascribe to the *infirmity of sex*, — on account of which the devil *especially wills women to be watched*; others to *brute cupidity of audience*, which drives the woman to satisfy her cupidities, or to vindicate; others refer to the *providence of God*, — who, as he concedes the faculty to Satan usually into creatures unworthier — as serpents, spinelings, and similar bees — so likewise the *most pestilential* art of magic he permits to be exercised by the *sequior sex*, and among them by those who *transfer their life to pecu-conception*.

But of the same read the *elegant authors* who ex-professor have handled this matter, — *Wier, Bodinus, Godelmannus*, and others.

Our institute is to consult consciences in those *cases* which about *magic* or *magi and veneficas* fall, — for which purpose we make a beginning from the very *first* place.

**Casus I. Whether Christians can with good conscience use magic, or works of magi and sorceresses?**

*Reply.* We do not speak here of *natural magic*, which by natural causes, but not to all obvious, — or through occult qualities, — to none, unless from the effect known, marvelous things it produces. For there is between things natural *sympathy* — as between magnet and iron, since it attracts to itself; there is also *antipathy* — as between some men and cats; there are also *medicaments* which applied to certain species of things, remove venoms; — the venom from the scorpion's sting is drawn out by the scorpion applied to that place; — from a *viper* is a most-effective viperine.

Such then are *illicit magical arts of magic to be discerned*, — of which knowledge for utility's sake it is licit to make use.

But we here treat of *magic in that genus*, — in which *created things of God are usurped* by the virtue of the *devil*, — differently than by *God* they are ordained, — whether to hurt or to procure some evil.

Such magic today many *praise*, and *believe it can be usurped without sin*. Among these are *Cornelius Agrippa* and *Theophrastus Paracelsus* (*Sacralius*), — *Cornelius Agrippa* wrote *four books* on *hidden philosophy*, of which the fourth is on *magical ceremonies*, which he calls *the key of all magical operations*; — although the very *book that key* he denies (lib. 2 *de vanit. scient.* cap. 5), where also he places the *summary of it*. *Paracelsus* not only the *most-famous magi*, — none excepting even the *Egyptians* — the time of *Moses*, commends, but even *the art itself he writes to be from GOD* — and pious, — since Scripture with harsher word he calls it *Hebraeos* (lib. de *morbo invisibilibus*, p. 184). The same many diseases naturally-incurable he affirms could be *by magic cured*, and *that this mode of curing and diverting devils he does not deny — either from him to receive medicaments and benefits*, — one thinks it *pleasant*. The mode of curing by magic those who have been *harmed by magic art* he shows (lib. *de peste ad Sylviacum*), — where also he *approves the ways of the men-of-that-place* to *Virgil* and of a certain *magi Selesiades*, of *calling on the demon and repelling him*, and a *magical mirror in which all things can be seen*, — and similar things approved. *Sacralius' Philosophia sagax* (cap. 4) *makes species* of magic, — from which he teaches that images and forms may be made, — in which by marvellous *characters and figures* the powers of *heaven* can be imprinted, — which all *provide* what otherwise from *natural things* one composed instruments make.
