## Chapter III. Goods of Fortune

*De casibus conscientiae circa bona fortunae — On cases of conscience concerning goods of fortune (wealth, riches).*

*Prooemium.* Goods of fortune are otherwise called *external goods*, — such as riches and wealth. And because these sometimes befall even the impious without study or labor, hence they are called *goods of fortune*, as if by chance falling to man.

Some however are unwilling to call such things *goods*, but rather *commodities of body and external*, — because no good will they place in man beside *virtue*, as the art of living well, which is only in the soul, — as *Augustine* has it (*De civ. Dei* lib. 9 c. 4). *Plato* also (*De legibus* lib. 4) says external goods without virtue not only help nothing, but are even harmful and pernicious, — that these are called *human*, but those which reside in the soul are *divine*, — by which alone divine man becomes blessed.

Yet those external goods are also called goods, since they are needed for the use of common life, and by virtue they become better, since they are its instruments. If however they resist virtue and disturb it, they are mere pests and destructions.

Since therefore man is occupied about these goods, questions occur in which information is needed, that conscience be not wounded by them: which we shall now consider in order, with God as our starter.

### Casus I. Whether by primeval Christian principle a man may possess goods and wealth with good conscience

*Reply.* This question is rendered doubtful by certain sayings of Scripture — as when the Savior says of the rich: *But woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your consolation.* (Luke 6:24); and *Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:* (Matt 6:19); and *Jesus said unto him, If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me.* (Matt 19:21); and what *Paul* writes (1 Tim 6:9): *They that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare of the devil, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.* — *Tertullian* also in his *Apology* c. 39 writes of the first Christians: *Nothing among us is common except our wives, — indistinct are all things among us apart from wives.*

By these sayings the *Anabaptists* partly have abused them, asserting proper possession of goods illicit to Christians; partly the *Papists*, who in the desertion of external goods have placed a good part of Christian felicity and perfection.

But first Scripture testifies, that as all goods, so also riches are *from God*, — for *David* Ps 24:1 says *the earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof*; who is that which hath created it, *Prov 22:2* — *the rich and the poor meet together: the Lord is the maker of them all*, *Sir 11:14* — poverty and wealth are both from God; *whose blessing enriches* (Prov 10:22); *His work is honourable and glorious: and his righteousness endureth for ever.* (Ps 111:3); who set out inheritance to his people, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Israel (Deut 12:8); who *gave his own people the possession of the land of Canaan*, as a possession, — *proper possessions given to the tribes* (Isa 13); *who fixed times and boundaries of the habitation of men* (Acts 17:26); who *made a law that boundaries were not to be transferred* (Deut 19:14; Prov 22:28); and in the Decalogue the seventh and tenth precept of anyone's goods, — as if with a wall he circumvallated them, lest they should sustain damage from injury of others: — *alms* to the poor to be given, — *let us break bread to the hungry* (Isa 58:7), — *and let us receive strangers into our houses* — which cannot be done, if profession of one's own goods were forbidden Christians.

Wherefore *Paul* wills, that *Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.* (Eph 4:28). Besides, *Paul* does not prohibit private possession of goods, but he exhorts those possessing, *that they trust not in uncertain riches* (1 Tim 6:17); wills a bishop to rule his own house well (1 Tim 3:4); wills each one to provide well for his own (1 Tim 5:8); wills each to eat his own bread (2 Thess 3:12) — which all things could not be done by those who live not from a personal store but from a common treasury.

Add examples of the holy: *Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Job, David*, and others, who in great abundance of wealth lived, and yet pleased God.

These are altogether contrary to the *Anabaptists*, which from possession of external goods can remove every scruple for wealthy Christians, — provided the riches be *rightly acquired, well used, and joined with piety*, as *Paul* commends (1 Tim 6:18).

Why in the primitive Church Christians contributed their goods in common (Acts 4:34 and following) — this was not done from an opinion of singular sanctity or perfection, but from love they contributed money and their fields for the sustenance of the brethren, — retaining, however, their own houses, in which they received strangers (Acts 9:8; 10:5,6). No one was forced to divest of his own goods, but it was free even to retain fields and money in one's personal store — as *Peter* said to *Ananias* (Acts 5:4): *While it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power?* Which liberty the *Anabaptists* leave to no one.

The perfection of Christians also is vainly sought in the desertion of one's own goods and voluntary poverty. — For the perfection of the saints derogated nothing to possession of one's own goods, — no mandate certainly do we have of perfection to be acquired in this way. As for what Christ says to that adolescent (Matt 19:21): *If thou wilt be perfect, sell all that thou hast* — this was a *singular* mandate, whereby Christ willed to blunt the boasting of the youth about his full observance of the law, — a *singular example that does not make a law*.

That Christ elsewhere pronounces woe against the rich, this is said to those *who abuse the goods of the world for luxury and pride, for the oppression of the poor and similar sins*. In the same way *Paul* indicates *the peril* which follows from the collection of riches — not as if riches were evil in themselves, but because desire for them is the occasion of many evils. Therefore caution is needed, lest through them we perish, — as also *David* exhorts (Ps 62:11): *If riches abound, set not your heart upon them.*

So Christ prohibits *laying up treasures on earth* (Matt 6:19-21) — not as if the collection of riches were disapprovable, — since *Paul* teaches otherwise (2 Cor 12:14): but avarice and confidence placed in uncertain riches he reproves.

### Casus II. What is the honest use of goods

*Reply.* Since therefore the possession of one's own goods is not per se sin, the goods of fortune with good conscience can be possessed. But not every use is legitimate: they are *rightly used* when a man distributes them according to the ordinance of God. Whence *Solomon* exhorts: *Honor the Lord with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase; so shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine* (Prov 3:9-10). And *David*, when to the building of the temple with a liberal hand he had contributed, said to the Lord: *All things are thine, and of thine own we have given thee* (1 Chr 29:14).

**Rules of just distribution of goods:**

**(1)** *To God*, when a part of our goods he claims for himself for the sustentation of the ministry. — As all rivers are from the sea and to the sea return, so all our goods are from God, and to God they must return.

**(2)** *To the magistrate*, whose we render what is commanded by the Christian magistrate — as *Christ* says (Matt 22:21): *Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's*; and *Paul*: *Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.* (Rom 13:7).

**(3)** *To our children and family*, according to that of *Paul*: *But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.* (1 Tim 5:8).

**(4)** *To the poor, widows, orphans, exiles, sick, and workers laboring in need* — if not alms, at least a loan, according to that of *Christ*: *Give to him that asketh thee, and hoping for nothing again* (Luke 6:35). *And to everyone that asketh thee, give*, says the Savior (Luke 6:30). This is the debt of charity, — which consists (1) in alms, according to that of Isaiah: *Break thy bread to the hungry* (Isa 58:7); (2) *In loan*: for *he that has mercy lends to his neighbor* (Sir 29:1); (3) in relief of the sick or of those enduring violence, — of which *Solomon*: *If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain;* (Prov 24:11); (4) in *hospitality* toward exiles and other poor, especially companions of the faith, according to the precept of the Apostle: *Let brotherly love continue: forget not hospitality* (Heb 13:1-2); (5) in the payment of a wage due to the laborer at the just time — *Thou shalt not defraud the wages of thy diligent and poor brother, whether he is thy brother, or a stranger who dwelleth with thee in thy land within thy gates: but on the same day thou shalt pay him the price of his labor before sunset; because he is poor, and with it he sustains his life; lest he cry against thee to the Lord, and it be counted to thee for sin* (Deut 24:14-15).

To all these giving must be *(1)* willingly — not with wringing of soul, — *out of a hilarious heart give thou; that hilarious giver God loves* (2 Cor 9:7); *(2)* hilariously — *God loves a hilarious giver* (2 Cor 9:7); *For giving in gladness — beauty of God — is in gladness of countenance one who gives* (Sir 35:11); *(3)* simply — without ostentation; so that the left hand know not what the right does (Matt 6:3), — for it is a fool's ostentation to make one's works seen; *(4)* not from another's goods, but from one's own substance, not from things gained in unjust ways, but from those which can come to the use of others — according to the admonition of *Sirach* (14:15).

Thus you may use goods with hilarious soul.

If anything then remains, it can with good conscience be lent to others, especially to those of one's own religion — who can add to their affairs, or for annual interest to be given for lands or estates. — For to do this is not illicit — as the example of the *primitive Church* proves (Exod 22:25; Sir 7:26 and following).

### Casus III. How the soul may not be corrupted by inordinate care of wealth

*Reply.* Because the affections readily are inordinately borne to riches, the soul must be armed against them, lest by desire of them we perish. Sacred Scripture, we have already seen, calls the desire of riches *the root of all evils* (1 Tim 6:10), — which drags into perdition. Wherefore the *Apostle* himself (1 Tim 6:8): *Having food and raiment, let us be therewith content.*

Remedies: **(1)** Recognition of oneself as a pilgrim in this world, — that we have brought nothing into this world, — and neither can we carry anything out (1 Tim 6:7). **(2)** Meditation on the vanity of riches — *Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death.* (Prov 11:4). **(3)** Nature is content with few things. **(4)** Consideration of the many perils that follow riches — envies, enemies, thefts, moral corruption. **(5)** Trust in God's Providence — *But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.* (Matt 6:33).

### Casus IV. Whether it be lawful to take usury (interest) from money lent

*Reply.* Sacred Scripture prohibits usury from the poor: *If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury.* (Exod 22:25); and *Ye shall not lend upon usury to thy brother* (Deut 23:19). *Ezekiel* also (18:8) numbers among the notes of a just man: *he giveth not upon usury, neither taketh any increase.* And *David* (Ps 15:5) among the marks of a citizen of God's tabernacle: *he that putteth not out his money to usury.* — Whence the ancient Church accounted usury among grievous sins.

Yet *usury on the poor* is one thing; and *taking of moderate interest from richer men who improve their own affairs with our money* is quite another. — For to those richer men one may rightly ask something above the principal — as much namely as the laws permit — because these are not so obliged to us in the office of lending; nor ought they to grow rich by our money, — with our resources (which we could increase by that same money) diminished — according to that of the Apostle: *For I mean not that other men be eased, and ye burdened:* (2 Cor 8:13). — Therefore it is not inequitable, if we come to a share of gain which they have acquired by our money.

### Casus V. Whether it is lawful to lend money in such a way as to keep something in place of a pledge, which if the borrower does not return the loan at the appointed time, comes into the power of the lender

*Reply.* This practice is not only very common with common usurers, but is even *approved by the Pontificals*, although otherwise they seem very hostile to all usury. — For they have devised the *mount of piety* (as they call it), whose invention they refer to *Pope Pius II*, and it was approved by the bull of *Leo X* in the Lateran Council.

The mount of piety is called *an accumulated heap of coin, designed for relieving through loan the miseries of the poor, — yet by this law, that any borrower contribute a small money each month, — not indeed (as they say) by way of loan, but as a stipend of the ministers, who for keeping and shaking out pledges, and for holding the accounts of receipts and payments, are appointed*, — as *Sotus* describes (lib. 6 *De just. et jure*, quaest. 1 art. 6).

To this mount are set out certain rules — the second being that *the borrower (though poor) give to the mount suitable pledges: which, when the fixed time for payment of the loan has elapsed, are immediately sold; if the borrower does not pay, that by the price of the pledge the money owed to the mount be paid, and the rest returned to the owner of the pledge* — of which see *Azorius* (part 3, *Instit. mor.* lib. 6 cap. 8).

We however boldly affirm that in this way riches are unjustly accumulated, from whomsoever it be done. For to *receive a pledge from the borrower* is licit, just as a *hypothec* (mortgage). Scripture, however, requires two things about this: **(1)** That we not set for the borrower a term of payment too tight — which many do for their own gain's sake, — namely, that they might seize the pledges more quickly. Against which guile the Lord in the law commands: *If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury.* (Exod 22:25); and *Sirach*: *Have patience with thy neighbor in poor time, and give him alms* (Sir 29:8).

**(2)** Scripture wills that we not seize the pledge of the neighbor rapaciously, especially if it be the pledge of the poor — as clothes and household utensils, of which they can be without for not even one day, — or the instruments of their arts by which they seek food for themselves and theirs, — or the annual revenue given to them by which they live. *Such things it is not indeed lawful to pawn* — much less to seize when payment is not made at the appointed time. *If thou hast received the vestment of thy neighbor as a pledge, thou shalt restore it to him before sunset. For it is the only garment with which he is covered, the clothing of his flesh; nor has he another wherein to sleep: if he cry to me, I will hear him, because I am merciful* (Exod 22:26-27). And with *Ezekiel* it is placed among the requisites of the just man: *If he restore to the debtor his pledge* (Ezek 18:7).

Therefore that contract, whereby pledges after the appointed time come into the possession of the lender when payment fails, — we hold to be usurious, impious, and illicit, — by which wealth is unjustly increased. And the creditor thereby deservedly incurs the penalties of usurers.

### Casus VI. Whether the debasement of currency is a legitimate mode of enriching

*Reply.* Money is not the least bond of human society, whose great use is in contracts, especially of buying and selling — whence *Aristotle* (*Ethics* c. 5) rightly called it *a common measure by which all things are appraised.* Money should be such *according to its intrinsic goodness* — not of copper or bronze, but of gold or silver, — having its due title of alloy, — that is, an equal proportion in the mixture of metals, — and its due weight adjusted to the legal foot, — which is conformable to the emperor's decrees, — and *according to its extrinsic goodness* of just weight and value.

If money is *debased*, it loses both its name and its office; for money (*moneta*) is so called from *warning* (*monendo*), because it warns that no fraud or falsity be committed in it. And manifold damage from such debasement in every estate and kind of life must emerge — as *Suarez* writes (*De just. et jure* lib. 6 disp. 2): *The corruption of coins is an incredible damage to all and each — a daily growing damage.*

Debasement occurs when, whether at command or by permission of a magistrate, the old and good-valued larger coin is resolved into lesser parts, — so that the purity and weight of the monetary constitution is lost, and in place of one Imperial thaler come eight, nine, or ten others — but adulterated, — differing in size and quality from that good weight, — and generated in lighter and smaller sorts of pieces: — by this reason moneyers indeed, and other administrators of this adulteration, become rich quickly; but this way of enriching is worse than usury, and unworthy of a Christian man.

**(1)** Such minters cannot in the truth of the matter say, that they have been made rich *by the blessing of God*. Even if this sin, by God's permitting and by his just judgment punishing other sins, be committed — yet not by his approval or willing does it come to pass. For he himself *abominates deceitful weight and lesser measure, and lengthenings* (Amos 8:5); he himself is not the God of confusion (1 Cor 14:33). Just as from the beginning he *created all things in number, weight, and measure* (Wis 11:20-21), so all things by just number, weight, and measure he wills to be preserved: — which is not done by that monetary confusion. God is a just and just avenger of all injustice — and terrible *That no man go beyond and defraud his brother in any matter: because that the Lord is the avenger of all such, as we also have forewarned you and testified.* (1 Thess 4:6). Therefore especially he commanded a *just measure, just weight, and just balance* (Lev 19:35-36; Deut 25:13-15; Prov 20:10, 23; Ezek 45:10; Hos 12:7; Mic 6:11).

**(2)** Certain it is, that debasement of coin overthrows the fundamental laws of the empire — sanctioned by the common consent and suffrage of the princes, and made stable in the Diets of the year 1442 in the time of Emperor *Frederick III* at *Nuremberg*, of 1559 in the time of *Charles V* at *Augsburg*. — Also the constitutions of emperors and princes wherein monetary valuations and probations are reduced to just moderation, — as the constitution of *Ferdinand I* in 1559, of *Maximilian II* in 1566, 1571, 1576. Against just laws and sanctions of the highest magistrate to attempt something is to *reluctate against God* himself, and to overthrow good order in the commonwealth. Therefore money collected in this way is received *not from God's hand, but from the devil's*. *Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation.* (Rom 13:2).

**(3)** Debasement of money is an unhappy daughter of the pernicious mother *avarice*. — Remove the mother, and the daughter will not exist. Those who receive their goods from God's blessing do not wish to enrich themselves by these means. He wounds conscience who, for his private little gain, from avarice, overthrows good order in the commonwealth, and inflicts damage on many others in domestic matters. — Truest is what *Sirach* wrote: *He that loves gold shall not be justified* (Sir 31:5) — that is, shall not be without sin — and *Paul*: *But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.* (1 Tim 6:9).

**(4)** Experience testifies how manifold and inexcusable inconvenience arises from debasement of money — which is realized only late, when it has already taken root — whence *Emperor Leo* (Novella 26) *has compared it to a slow-growing tumor*. For hence grow the prices of all things; good faith among contractors is wounded, — since in place of good money accepted, a viler one is returned; the very substance of goods, that is, gold and silver, is carried away to foreigners, — leaving us dross; annual revenues are attenuated, — and finally annihilated; hence to widows, orphans, and others who cannot seek support elsewhere than from such revenues, much damage is inflicted; ministers of the church and schools, professors in Academies, and all who live from salaries, — are for the most part defrauded of their salaries; the treasuries of the Republic and of the Church are exhausted; studies of the good arts, especially theological, are deserted, — because with these arts it happens that not many children of opulent parents can live in Academies. — Whence great is the fear of a deficit of foundational theologians who can solidly resist the enemies of truth; — since most students of poorer fortune apply their soul rather to political studies where they may seem to grow rich. Even princes do not thereby grow rich (as at first appears), — because when ordinary revenues come in with cheaper money, but everything needed for the sustenance of the court is bought more dearly, — the treasury, without anyone noticing, is gradually enervated. In domestic economy inestimable damage follows, — commerce is all upset, monetary loans are dropped — if in place of silver money one must await dross, — hence the poor lose their easy subsidy in their handiwork; — patrimonies are attenuated, — scarcely can any patrimony be left as a legacy; — legacies of pious ancestors are reduced to nothing; — wages due to workers cannot be paid, — which thing gives occasion of idleness — *from which many follow evil vices*.

The moneyers themselves and their administrators sin multiply and prepare for themselves most pestilent peril. For while with prepared work they cling to avarice — which *Paul* elegantly calls *idolatry* (1 Tim 6:) — they gather also for themselves the reward of the enemies of God, — namely, dissipation of their own resources (Prov 22:23; 21:6), — from the kingdom of God are excluded because of avarice (Eph 5:5), — are destitute of the love of the neighbor, — for they benefit no one, but bear away the goods of others — *But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?* (1 John 3:17). — They are the cause that prices of things grow; that widows, orphans, ministers of schools and churches are so meagerly sustained; they are secret thieves, harpies of money, who plunder the poor and the rich, — the sighs and groans of all the pious against themselves they raise, by which finally they are dragged down to lower places.

Whoever therefore his own temporal safety loves, this way of enriching he will abandon. — For with the *just judge Basil*, *no one shall find gold and silver in the day of wrath* (Ezek 7:19); nor *dost thou hoard, though the whole world thou gather* — but toward the eventide the shadow shall come. *A vine of a vineyard is thy planting* (Sir 27:2); *The blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it.* (Prov 10:22); but with all these things which are had are wont to be counter to the Lord, — and even more so many fountains and streams of pestilence. — Of which to write more it does not seem needful.

### Casus VII. Whether commerce (mercantile trade) is a legitimate means of acquiring wealth

*Reply.* The *Anabaptists* dispute this, in reliance on these arguments: **(1)** Solomon (Prov 22:16) numbers among evils *he oppresseth the poor to increase his riches — and he giveth to the rich*, — as means of unjust augmenting of gains; **(2)** Christ cast the *buyers and sellers* out of the temple (Matt 21:12); **(3)** Merchants and merchandise are called *chi-mera* (as their pride puffs up).

But not the less notwithstanding, many things stand: that riches acquired through commerce are participated in without sin. *God himself* does not damn commerce, but only sets the mode — *Thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights, a great and a small.* (Deut 25:13). The same we hear from Christ (Luke 19:13; and Apostle Paul in 1 Cor 7:30): *let those who buy, be as though they possessed not*; and (1 Thess 4:6) *let no one overreach or defraud his brother in any matter*. And Christ compares the kingdom of heaven with mercantile activity (Matt 13:45), and with this simile he exhorts to right use of his gifts (Matt 25:14).

The Apostle James also does not condemn mercantile trade, but rather admonishes merchants that *among transactions they be mindful of their mortality — and appoint their affairs according to the will of God* (James 4:13-14). — Holy men used contracts of buying and selling: *Abraham* (Gen 23:16); *Jacob* (Gen 33:19); *Joseph* (Gen 47:16); *Jeremiah* (Jer 32:9); *Joseph of Arimathea* (Mark 15:46). *Solomon* also praises *the woman merchant* (Prov 31:14). And *Paul* baptized *Lydia the purple-seller*, leaving her in her trade as if in her calling.

Add to this the great necessity of commerce in common life, — for since God has not given all things to one region, — merchandise must be brought from elsewhere to us — in which trade moderate gain, as a wage of labors, can be conceded for one's honest sustenance and for one's family.

*What the Anabaptists object to*, — this pertains to the *abuse* of commerce, — for when both buyer and seller are intent only on gain, — with the law of charity neglected, — so that they attempt to impose fraud upon others, — they are surely not without sin. Therefore all guile must be absent from this contract. And when Christ ejected buyers and sellers from the temple, he does not damn the trade itself, — but its exercise in a *sacred place*. And who seek nothing but *gain and accumulation of wealth*, without love of the neighbor, without fear of guile and fallacy, — they do commerce ill.

Pious merchants subordinate gain to the sustenance of themselves and their families. In which sentence *Augustine* writes (on Ps 70): *A merchant greedy of gaining, for damage he blasphemes; for prices of things he lies and swears. But these vices are of men, not of the art itself, which can be done without vices.*

Two things above all vitiate this means of acquiring wealth: **(1)** When gain is the ultimate end of trading, and for that cause a thing is sold at a higher price than it was bought — not to sustain us honestly, or to compensate the labor with due wage: — but we seek immoderate gain, only that we may thereby become rich. — Hence *Chrysostom* writes (on Matt 12): *Whoever obtains a thing so that untouched and unchanged it may be sold and gain be made, — that is that merchant, who is cast out of the temple of God. But if moderate compensation of labors or dangers, which must be endured in transferring the thing from place to place — is sought, — there is no sin: — or when the thing changed for the better is sold, or by another for his high necessity is exacted from a possessor who otherwise would not sell it, — then in place of emerging damage from him who has gained great advantage from the bought thing, — something beyond what the buyer gave to the seller — from the buyer can be exacted.*

**(2)** When *ecclesiastical persons* exercise commerce that they may thereby become rich, — this is altogether illicit. — *No one warring for God entangles himself with secular affairs* (2 Tim 2:4); — clerics ought to be contemners of gain and of earthly wealth, content with their stipends.

### Casus VIII. What of the goods otherwise unjustly acquired

*Reply.* Since possessions unjustly acquired always bring vexation to conscience, — some ask: *when the possessor of unjustly acquired goods is in no way vexed in his conscience about it, — how then can the vexation of his conscience be relieved?*

Many there are who are little touched by the care of this thing, — and although they are not ignorant of that oracle: *Whence hast thou obtained it, none demands: about your heirs however be not solicitous*, provided that they, while they live, possess great treasures. — These are those whose *God is their belly*, — neglectful of their salvation, — having *conscience cauterized*, that is, seared as with a hot iron.

Others have this worm gnawing at the conscience — they feel indeed the *thunderbolts of Scripture* against the avaricious, against the usurers, against the harpies, and unjust depredators of the neighbor — but they do not fear their bite. Yet if it is once revealed to them that these acquisitions have been *unjustly acquired by faith with the sighs and groans of the poor*, — they cleanse their conscience — perhaps in a stronger way that they may destine [the goods] to a pious cause.

And truly some there are who imagine that they can *make satisfaction for their thefts through alms from ill-gotten goods*, — an error which *Catharinus* attributes to the Greeks, as *Lessius* refers (lib. 2 *De just. et jure* c. 9 dub. 12) — and which they bring in defense from what *Christ* says of the *Pharisees* (Luke 11:41): *Verumtamen quod superest, date eleemosynam, et ecce omnia munda sunt vobis* — *Truly however give alms of what remains, and behold, all things are clean unto you.*

But this is not the meaning of Christ's saying — that only alms compensate rapines and frauds of unjust men: but only *the alms of the just, in place of rapines* — since this is a sign of true repentance, it easily cleanses what in the platters and cups seemed unclean: for it is better to give than to receive. — But those who think that they can *satisfy their rapines by alms*, are much deceived, and involve themselves in more and more sins. — For first, the goods of the poor unjustly acquired they retain with themselves, — and thus with the blood and sweat of others they fatten themselves. Then about the sin of the loss they do not yet seriously grieve, — but in their iniquity persist. Further they attempt to deceive God as hypocrites, — as if with this sacrifice of alms they can reconcile him.

For which cause the *Scripture* detests such alms as an abomination before the Lord: *He that offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor, — as one who kills a son in the sight of his father: — the bread of the needy is the life of the poor; he that defrauds them is a man of blood* (Sir 34:24-25).

Then also to those wealthy men who have exacted usury from the poor, *Nehemiah* counsels (Neh 5:7ff.): *You demand usury of your brothers. Restore to them today their fields, — and also their olive orchards and vineyards, and the hundredth part of the money, wheat, wine, and oil, which you were wont to exact of them. Give it back to them for those things. — And they said: We will restore, and require nothing of them: so will we do as thou sayest.*

Thus also *Zacchaeus* said to *Christ* (Luke 19:8): *Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have defrauded any man by false accusation, I restore fourfold.*

In the same sense *Augustine* writes (*Ep. 54*, ad Macedonium): *If a thing another's — on account of which sin is committed — can be restored, and is not restored, then is not repentance being done, but feigned. But if it is truly done, then is not the sin remitted, unless what has been taken away be restored.*

The sum of divine and human right is *to restore the things taken*, if they still exist. — Where however this cannot be done, — as when the goods no longer exist in the taker's power, — then not indeed *external* restitution is necessary (since *no one is obliged to the impossible*), — but *the proposition of restoring* is necessary: — otherwise his repentance is not serious. **Exceptions** are noted: (1) When the debtor knowingly and willingly, not coerced by force or fear, — nor circumvented by guile or fraud, — but spontaneously *remits the debt*, — then he loses the right to the debt, and this becomes a *donation*. (2) When *ignorance of the fact* enters, — as when someone in good faith received something as an inheritance from his father, or in good faith bought or accepted a donation from another. — *Ignorance of law*: as when he does not know that the contract, whose fruit he possesses, is usurious, or that he is bound in right to restitution, — because perhaps by the counsel of a good and honest man he believed he was not obligated to restitution — such is not obliged to restitution as much as was taken, but only as far as he unjustly gained, — as *Azorius* has (part 3 *Institut. moral.* lib. 5 c. 10). (3) When the pledge is not more in the faculty of the taker, — then not exact restitution is necessary (since no one is obliged to the impossible), — but the proposition of restoring is necessary, otherwise his repentance is not sincere. (4) When restitution involves either damage of the neighbor's soul or body, — the demand is not required immediately.

Such restitution seems dishonorable in the eyes of men, but glorious in the eyes of true Christians, whose *proper it is to do good and to hear evil*: to retain another's goods is dishonor and worthy of punishment. Yet even here consolation is offered — that if the ignominy and contempt of men becomes intolerable, one may ask a good man's counsel — either himself, if still alive; or the heirs, if he has died; — through a preacher one may return the money — with the condition however that his name be not revealed, — and only from the preacher be it said, that this money is sent to him from an honorable man, — who owed it to his father. Of which an example is in *Paulus Fagius* (in *Ethica praeceptor.* p. 30).

If, however, when all diligence has been employed, no heirs can be found to whom you may restore another's thing, — then at last let alms be given to the poor — but so much as answers to unjustly acquired goods, and with the condition that no one persuade himself that he satisfies for his rapines with alms. — For *no one is justified for money*, says *Basil*. But that restitution flows from a truly humbled heart, — which recognizes and deplores the sin, — and asks God for the sake of Christ to condone it, — and for which even to rapacious men, — if they seriously repent and restore, — the Lord will pardon.

### Casus IX. Rules for wisely distributing wealth

*Reply.* We have shown above that possession of goods is not sin — whence follows: neither must wealth be cast away, nor all reduced to the beggarly poor. *Men do not despise a thief, if he steal to satisfy his soul when he is hungry;* (Prov 6:30) — much less must goods be sent to monasteries for devotion or merit; for *no one prescribes to a Free God with a bounty from a base intention* (Wis 3:14).

Every honest fruition of goods consists in *giving* — but in giving to those to whom giving is due. For giving can even be done with sin, — as when riches are poured out into gluttony, for gambling of dice or cards, for pride in dress, for useless buildings, when with money are bought traitors or assassins, and whenever riches are spent to our own harm or to the neighbor's.

*Rightly* however we give **(1)** *to God*, when a part of our goods he claims for himself for the sustentation of the ministry. — For as all rivers are from the sea and to the sea return, — so all our goods are from God, and to God they must return. Whence *Solomon* exhorts: *Honor the Lord with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase; so shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine* (Prov 3:9-10). And *David*, when to the building of the temple with a liberal hand he had contributed, said to the Lord: *All things are thine, and of thine own we have given thee* (1 Chr 29:14).

**(2)** *To the magistrate*, whom we render what is commanded by the Christian magistrate — as *Christ* says (Matt 22:21): *Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's*; and the Apostle *Paul*: *Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.* (Rom 13:7).

**(3)** *To our children and family*, according to that of *Paul*: *But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.* (1 Tim 5:8).

**(4)** *To the poor, widows, orphans, exiles, sick, and workers laboring in need* — if not alms, at least a loan, according to that of *Christ*: *Give to him that asketh thee, and hoping for nothing again* (Luke 6:35); and again *and unto everyone that asketh thee, give* (Luke 6:30). This is *the debt of charity*, which consists (a) in alms according to *Isa 58:7*; (b) in loan according to *Sir 29:1*: *He that has mercy lends to his neighbor, and gives*; (c) in relief of the sick or of those enduring violence, according to *Prov 24:11*; (d) in hospitality toward exiles and other poor, especially companions of the faith, according to *Heb 13:1-2*; (e) in the payment of a wage due to the laborer at the just time, according to *Deut 24:14-15*.

To all these giving must be **(a)** willingly — not with wringing of soul: *for a hilarious giver God loves* (2 Cor 9:7); **(b)** hilariously (Sir 35:11); **(c)** simply — without ostentation, so that the left hand know not what the right does (Matt 6:3); **(d)** not from another's goods, but from one's own substance, not from things gained in unjust ways — according to *Sirach* (14:15).

Thus you may with hilarious soul use your goods.

If anything then remains, it can with good conscience be lent to others, especially to those of one's own religion, — who from it can add to their affairs, — or on annual interest for lands or estates. For to do this is not illicit — this is proved by the example of *David* in Exod 22:25 and *Sirach* 7:26 and following.
