## Chapter VII. Cases of Conscience concerning the Office of Preachers of the Church

*De casibus conscientiae circa officium concionatorum ecclesiae.*

### Preamble

Those who are legitimately called and ordained to the ministry of the word — ought so to do all things in their office — for right reason of their vocation and ordination which they have received.

Their office moreover consists in *four members*: (1) In the *propagation of true doctrine*; (2) In the *administration of the sacraments*; (3) In the *reproving of the vices* of hearers by the word — the *elenchtic office*; (4) In the *preservation of the order and discipline of the Church*.

Concerning individual matters many things can be moved, — in which the younger ministers have need of information, — lest they do anything against conscience: — but since concerning others in books elsewhere it has been treated more copiously, — we shall choose the chief points, — of all which now in order we shall speak, — and in this chapter we shall explain the doubts which occur about *the sermons to be held*.

For this head of the ministerial office is one, — and the chief of all, — which pertains to the *pastors and teachers* about whom *Paul* speaks in the same way (Eph 4:11), — that pastors understand that to their office pertains *the doctrine of Christ*.

### Casus I. Whether the minister of the Church can conform his doctrine to the prescription of the magistrate with good conscience

*Reply.* The *unique norm of doctrine* is the *word of God*, in which all the counsel of God is revealed (2 Tim 3:16); whatever cannot make a man perfect toward God is to be despised (2 Tim 3:17). — Wherefore *Peter* commands: *If any man speak, let him speak as the oracles of God* (1 Pet 4:11).

It can however happen — that a *pious magistrate* prescribes a certain form of teaching to the churches of his regions, — not spun from his own brain, but drawn from the Scripture, — collected and approved by learned and religious men, — to this end, — that among so many *heresies* — each of which appeals to Scripture — a certain manner of speaking may be held, — and a *form of sound words* observed.

And here doctrine is comprehended in *public books*, which they call *symbolic*, — because they are as it were the *symbol and tessera of the doctrine*, — which sounds publicly in those churches.

Such books the magistrate can commend to doctors in the churches and schools of his regions, — and mandate that they form sermons according to their prescription.

Thus in the *Nicene Council* under the nod of the most pious Emperor *Constantine* the symbol was drawn up — which is called by the name of the *place*, *Nicene* — of which *Athanasius* in his epistle *ad Epictetum* writes: *A faith set forth by the fathers in synod according to the sacred Scriptures, is sufficient to overthrow every hostile impiety of heresy, and to confirm pious faith in Christ*.

**Symbolic book of our age.** The symbolic book of our age is the *Augustana Confessio* invariata, in the year of Christ 1530 at *Augsburg of the Vindelici* presented to Emperor *Charles V*; — and the book of the *Christian Concord* composed by orthodox Theologians, at the command of the most religious prince, *Augustus Elector of Saxony*, — which, — because it is conformable to sacred Scripture *in every part*, — and produces from their lurking-places the errors of many who name themselves *socii* of the *Augustana Confessio* — ought to be commended to those teaching in the Church before all others: — not indeed as *judge*, — but as *witness* of the doctrine comprehended in Scripture and infallibly explained. — For thus *Augustine* distinguishes between *sacred Scripture* and *other theological writings* (epist. 19 ad Hieronymum): *I alone of these books of Scriptures which are called Canonical — have learned to bear this fear and honor, — that of no of these authors do I believe that anything was written by them in error: — others however I so read, that with whatever holiness and doctrine they excel, — I do not therefore judge to be true, because they themselves so felt, — but because they by those Canonical authors, or through probable reasons, — persuaded me that they do not depart from the truth*.

The *Formula Concordiae* itself also determines this concerning itself, — in the preface, *de compendiaria regula*, etc.

**The status of the symbolic books.** — The commemorated symbols and other writings, of which a little before we made mention (namely the *tria symbola* Apostolic, Nicene, Athanasian, *Augustana Confessio*, its *Apologia*, articles *Smalcaldici*, *both Catechisms of Luther*), do not obtain the *authority of a judge*: — for that dignity is due to the *sacred letters alone*: — but only they *bear testimony* of our religion, — and they *explain* it, — that it may be manifest — in what sense they accepted the sacred letters, — and how they were interpreted by those churches then existing, — and by what reasons they *rejected and condemned* dogmas conflicting with sacred Scripture.

**Different case: an ambiguous prescription is not binding.** — *Another case it is*, — when the magistrate — either wholly given over to *false religion*, — or in some way suspicious of it, — obtrudes libels on the Church — in which Christian doctrine is proposed in *slippery and ambiguous words*, — and nevertheless wills those teaching in the churches and schools to be bound to these as to some *norm of doctrine*: — such ministers of the Church are not held, — but *piously* to examine that libel by the norm of sacred Scripture, — and to point out those errors with solid arguments, — and to seek that they be not compelled to teach anything contrary to Scripture.

In which way of old, — when under *Emperor Charles V* the *Interim* was obtruded on the evangelical churches, — many *Theologians masculinely contradicted*, — even at peril of life, — or loss of office, — although not a few from *too great pusillanimity* consented to Caesar's mandate, — not without scruple of conscience.

For it is *the same* — whether you propose to your hearers doctrine *openly false*, — or *ambiguous and buskin-like* [*cothurno similem*].

Here therefore let the *Apostle*'s saying have place: *That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;* (Eph 4:14).

### Casus II. Whether the minister of the Church for the sake of tranquillity may abstain from *antithesis* and from the condemnation of *false doctors and their doctrine* in sermons with pious conscience

*Reply.* You find among politicals not a few, who not even the mention of true doctrine can bear to be uttered in a sermon, — thinking that disputations concerning religion should be shrouded in silence, — or at least remitted to schools, — that they pertain not to the people: — plainly like of old *Valentinian and Ursacius, Germinius, Auxentius*, and *Demophilus* in the *Rimini Synod* postulated — that individual sentences be not for the future too curiously investigated, — lest dissensions and seditions be moved (as *Sozomen* refers, lib. 4 *H.E.* c. 17).

**Others permit antithesis** — nay call it an *adamantine nail* of true concord (which is the word of *Victorinus Strigel*): — but *doctors of false doctrine* they cannot bear to be refuted *by name* in sermon, — nor their doctrine to be *condemned*. Thus of old in the *Eastern churches* it was sought — that concerning the *divinity of the Son of God* orthodox doctrine be entirely proposed, — and contrary doctrine refuted, — with suppression of the name of *Arius* or of the *Arians*, — to which petition many obeyed (referring *Philip* in *Praelectiones Targinsibus* year 1548). — At the time of *the Interim* there were not lacking those to whom *Caesar* was formidable, — who persuaded, — that *the Pope, bishops, monks* and similar should not be expressly named in sermon, — much less should their doctrine be condemned.

**Others cannot bear it any less**, — than that the *names of their doctors* be expressed, — when we refute their doctrine, — or than the *Calvinist-like* condemnation: — as among other things appears from the *Neustadt admonition* which *Formula Concordiae* opposed cap. 7, — and from *Targeliae antitheses* num. 32: — whence more often it happened that *magistrates were inflamed against doctors of the Church*, — and mandates of inhibition impeded.

**Reply as to why antithesis cannot be omitted.** — For antithesis of true doctrine no one can omit, — since Scripture is *useful for teaching sound doctrine and for refuting contrary* (2 Tim 3:16). — And to the office of a *bishop*, that is, of a minister of the Church, — pertains also *διακρίνειν* [to discern] *precious from vile* (Jer 15:19), — the *clean from unclean* (Ezek 22:26).

Who therefore prohibits ministers of the Church to treat antithesis, — takes a good part of the ecclesiastical ministry. — And although the *more accurate treatment* of controversies pertains chiefly to schools, — necessary however it is — that each preach the refutation to his hearers' comprehension, — that *simpler ones* may not only hold the *foundations of sound doctrine*, — but *refute the errors of adversaries* according to their measure, — lest wholly *hosts* in this genus they be, — if we do not have adversaries' errors from their books thoroughly-known, — we shall deceive both ourselves and others not without blushing.

**Much error in this genus commit those** who condemn our doctrine neither read nor understood. — Of which genus of egregious specimen has *Johannes Ittigius* published in *Orat.*, — that he confesses he has not read the *book of Concord*, — nor ever seen, — in *praelectiones publicis* praelectiones pag. 90 in *vindicatione* — pag. 16, and *utilius* — c. 4, — worst things about that book he has vomited. — Our doctrine of *oral manducation* of *worthy and unworthy*, he calls *two hairs from the horse's tail*. *Two black hairs, pulled from the most beautiful horse's tail, are compared to the beautiful form of a horse, — thus the doctrine of oral manducation of Christ's body, and of manducation of unworthy — nothing profits the institution of the Lord's Supper*. — The doctrine of *majesty of Christ's flesh* he calls *filth of a female nymph, τερατολογήματος* [monstrous-utterance], — a new prostitute in the Church, — Sphinx and Chimera, — in which are all things *Manichaean, and Valentinian, and Arian, and Eutychian, and Nestorian, and Sabellian* — false and inane dogmas. — So lightly certainly we do not judge concerning the doctrine of adversaries not yet known. — For we know that saying (Sir 11:7): *Before thou hearest, do not answer, — and in the midst of discourse do not interrupt: — before thou hast investigated, do not blame anyone; — first investigate, — and before speech-hear-a-response*.

**In antithesis of doctrine also be observed**: — not anything be done from hatred of person, — but all from love of truth, — to which erring ones (if it can be) are to be reduced, — according to the sentence of *Christ* in *homily de anathemate*: *Dogmas of impiety and heretics — one is professed to be argued anathematized, — a man however to be spared, — for his salvation to be prayed*.

**With this refutation also *peace with salt* to be entered** — that is, mildness with pious zeal to be tempered. — For the *Apostle* wills the minister of the Church to be *instructed to every good work* (2 Tim 3:14); — but wills also *seductores to be argued* (Titus 3:10) — in the manner Christ himself, mildest of all men, called *Herod a fox* (Luke 13:32); — *pseudo-prophets ravening wolves* (Matt 7:15); — *scribes and Pharisees hypocrites, whited sepulchres* (Matt 23:27); — *Paul* called *pseudo-apostles deceitful workers* (2 Cor 11:13), — *enemies of the cross of Christ* (Phil 3:18), — and cursed *whoever preaches otherwise* (Gal 1:8), — and prayed for the *disturbers of the Galatian church* that they be cut off (Gal 5:12), — and named specifically *Hymenaeus and Philetus* (2 Tim 2:17), — and *Alexander the coppersmith* (2 Tim 4:14).

To this example did the *Fathers of Constantinople* specifically anathematize *Arius, Eutyches, Macedonius, Pelagius*, and other heretics — and to those who orthodox to feel would not, — to these they said *anathema*, — as it is in Canon 1 of the *Council of Constantinopolitan* first; — and *Augustine* to all heresies of his time struck with anathema (lib. 5 *Hypognosticon* c. 6). — And why should it not be lawful to name those, — whose doctrine we know to be false? — for how otherwise can others be warned against them by the hearers?

**Objections and reply.** — Which objections are made by adversaries are of no great moment, and are refuted in *disputat. de anathemate* cap. 5 thesi 9 and following.

**From abstaining from anathema not follows omission of elenchus.** — From condemnation neither is Church-integrity — according to *Jerome* on ep. 61 *ad Pammach.* — *another people hear, another priests preach*; — but *heresiarchs* are condemned, — and those who to them pertinaciously-adhere, — monstered-to-the-truth-not-yielding, — in the manner *Paul* the *disturbers* of the church of *Galatia* condemned, — the church however he loved — and rightly-formed brethren in her acknowledged (Gal 5:1) — with which also the *Formula Concordiae* explicated its mind concerning condemnations in the *preface*.

**Third: from condemnation of false dogmas the propagators are to be pierced specifically.** — In antithesis and condemnation of false dogmas — the propagators are to be pierced specifically. — We have foundations sufficiently firm: — (1) *God's mandate is* — that those who lead the *people to idolatry — into stones-crush* (Deut 13:11); — and *pseudo-prophets be avoided* (Matt 7:15). — (2) *Now I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them.* (Rom 16:17); — that *those who resist the truth be corrected* (2 Tim 3:17); — in all which places, — not so much erring doctrine — as the *reprehension of false doctors* is enjoined.

By which way *Elijah* stood publicly against *Ahab* for idolatry (1 Kgs 18:17); — *Baalites* (1 Kgs 18:25); — *Isaiah* reproving *the people of Israel*, *Isaiah* arguing *Ephraim* (Isa 28), — arguing *pseudo-prophets* (Isa 56:10, seq.); — *Jeremiah* (Jer 23, 54).

**5. The inhibition of the elenchtic office also promotes impious doctrine**, — with dogs silent — who ought to watch — for the Lord's sheep, — easy is access of the wolf to the sheep.

**6. It has a species also of *Epicureanism*** — as though one religion is not better than another. For if we have some dogma for erroneous, — why do we not permit that publicly to be argued and damned?

**7. And finally not far off it is from *ἀσέβημα* [impiety]** — for it is not of the magistrate — to prescribe to ministers of the Church, — what to teach, — what to refute, — when to speak, — when to be silent. — For, as *Ambrose* to Emperor *Theodosius* said (lib. 5 epist. 26): *Neither is it of the empire, — to deny liberty of teaching, — nor of the priesthood, — to say not what he feels*.

**8. Therefore ministers of the word are not bound to obey mandates prohibiting the elenchus**, — because it is *manifestly against the word of God*, — which a pious man ought to obey more than men: — in the manner in which, — when to *Peter* and other Apostles preaching of the gospel of Christ was prohibited by *Sadducees and heads of people*, — they did not obey, — saying: *But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.* (Acts 4:19).

**Objections from adversaries are of no great moment** — and are refuted in *disputat. de anathemate* — where at large: for even error in doctrine often serpent-like as *cancer* (2 Tim 2:17).

### Casus III. If those *erring in doctrine* by name may be refuted in sermon, — is it not also lawful *those sinning in morals* by name to be pierced

*Reply.* Even if *vices of hearers* in sermons must be gravely castigated, — for here also is part of the *elenchtic office*, — whose author is *the Holy Spirit himself*, who *convinceth world of sin* (John 15:8), — nevertheless it is not lawful to *pierce any delinquent in morals by name*, — or so to depict him in his colors, — that anyone can point him out with a finger: — which especially is most scandalous *in the magistrate's own house*, — as it is prohibited in our churches.

Neither did *Christ* nor the *Prophets* nor the *Apostles* do this, — although they refuted *pseudo-doctors* even *specifically*.

**Great is the difference** between errors in doctrine and sins in morals. — (1) In *doctrinal errors* it treats of the *salvation of the whole church*, lest it be led astray; — in *sins of morals* it treats only of the *conversion of individual sinners*.

**(2) Sins of morals fall under the *external senses*, — and cannot long be hidden**: — errors in doctrine often serpent-like as *cancer* creep (2 Tim 2:17).

**(3) Sins of morals only harm by example**: — errors in doctrine deliberately are sown, — and to others by way of instruction are propagated.

**(4) The *heretic* teaches to *believe evil*: — the *wicked man* does not teach others to *live evilly*.**

**(5) The *heretic* by believing badly *also makes them live badly*** — for *badly is lived*, if *God is not well believed*, as *Augustine* says (lib. 5 *De civ. Dei* c. 10); — but the *wicked man* only by his own example harms his life.

More accurate *animadversion* therefore is needed on *heretics* than on those who *live badly*: — whence also there is *diversity in the elenchus*.

### Casus IV. Whether the minister of the Church can with good conscience entirely omit the *elenchtic office*

*Reply.* In no way. — In the manner in which Scripture is *useful for reproving and correcting* (2 Tim 3:16), — thus the minister of the Church ought to be *Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.* (Titus 1:9).

**They are *shepherds*** — and *feed their sheep* so that — what is weak — they *corroborate*, — what is *sick* they *heal*, — what is *broken* they *bind up*, — what is *pushed out* they *bring back*, — what has *perished* they *seek* (Ezek 34:4).

**Architects they are *in the house of God*** (1 Cor 3:10), — therefore not only should they *build*, — but should also *resist those who* by false doctrine or by corrupt morals *destroy* the edifice, — and restore what has been destroyed. *What is it to be an architect in vain*, as *Bede* says on cap. 5 epist. 1 *ad Petrum*, — *to gather stones which are to be destroyed by others, — to permit*.

**Bishops are *watchmen*** (Ezek 3:17; 33:7), — therefore let them *animadvert* on those who *live impiously*, — and *announce their impiety to them*, — otherwise *their blood God will require from their hand* (Ezek 3:18, seq.).

**And for this cause God himself enjoined ministers of the word:** *Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins.* (Isa 58:1).

**Ill-hear the Prophets:** — *Ye have not gone up into the gaps, neither made up the hedge for the house of Israel to stand in the battle in the day of the LORD.* (Ezek 13:5); — *who deceive the people, saying: peace, and there is no peace* (v. 10); — *who sew cushions under every elbow of the hand, — and make coverings under the head of every age to catch souls* (v. 18); — *who violate the Lord to the people, — for handfuls of barley and morsels of bread, — to slay souls that should not die, — and to save souls that should not live* (v. 19).

**Diverse however are the ways of men.** Some sin *from weakness of the flesh*, — and *easily admit correction*: — these are to be *mildly treated*, — and with the *spirit of gentleness*, — according to the admonition of the Apostle: *And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,* (2 Tim 2:24); — and again: *Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.* (Gal 6:1). — In which sentence writes *Chrysostom* in homily 1 *De incomprehensibili natura DEI*: *With an angry man let us act modestly, — and lovingly, — and humanely dispute: — nothing prevails more than mildness, — nothing more efficacious than modesty*. — *D. Paul* also wills consideration of *sex and age*: *Rebuke not an elder, — but entreat him as a father; — younger, as brethren; — elder-women, as mothers; — young-women, as sisters, — in all chastity* (1 Tim 5:1-2).

**Some however sin *scandalously and enormously*, — and *in sinning are obstinate***, — whence it comes that *vices grow*, — with peril of salvation: — here *asperity* is required, — even without discrimination of age. For as *Gregory* speaks (lib. 7 epist. 1): *Where a senior gives an example of interim to youths, — is to be smitten with severe rebuke*. — Hence is that of the Apostle: *Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear.* (1 Tim 5:20). — And *Cyprian* writes (*de lapsis*): *To tolerate the molestness of pertinacious men is not to love a man, — but to accede: — if any nourishes sinners and impious in wickedness, — and by obsequious deceives, — deceives itself like an unskilful physician, who softly-handles heavy wounds with sparing-hand*.

**In this elenchtic office are to be avoided:**

**(1) That *vengeance* be not sought in the vice-taxation, — but the *emendation of the delinquent, — or the aversion of scandal***. — For in every punishment threefold-view is: — either that he who is punished may be *emended*, — or that his punishment may render others *better*, — or that with *public evils* others may live more securely, — as *Seneca* admonishes (lib. 1 *De clementia* c. 22).

**(2) Before some one's vice is *taxed in sermon*, let the *gradus of admonitions* be premised, — as *Christ* wills** (Matt 18): — that is, — let the delinquent first be admonished *privately* of his delict: — if he does not care, — let one and another of the ministry be adhibited, — and the admonition repeated: — if neither by this reason he is emended, — let him be told to the Church, — that is, — let him be *publicly reprehended*, — if perchance suffused with shame he may wish to return to the fruit.

**(3) Moreover *no delinquent* be *specifically pierced in sermon*, — or so painted, that anyone can understand who is noted**: — which in the *Constitutio Electoralis* art. 3 *curialis* is expressly interdicted.

If however some hearer applies this general rebuke to himself, — the *efficacy of the word* is thence to be recognized, — because *For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.* (Heb 4:12) — and it has such efficacy — both in the *pious*, who by this medium are emended, — as was made in the hearers of *D. Peter* (Acts 2:37), — as in the *impious*, — which happened to the hearers of *D. Stephen* (Acts 7:54).

### Casus V. Whether the minister of the Church for *vehement rebukes* may be summoned to court before the political magistrate

*Reply.* *Pious zeal* in arguing vices even *publicly in sermon* is not to be extinguished, — provided the minister of the Church remains *in generalibus*, — without express nomination of delinquent persons, — or their-description. For it is not becoming ministers of the word to be *mute dogs* (Isa 56:10), — or blind watchmen, — from whose hand *God will require the blood of the dying in his sin* (Ezek 3:18).

**If anyone therefore thinks himself injured by the minister**, — whom by that name before the magistrate he does not doubt to summon to court, — the minister cannot be compelled to *appear and answer*, — partly because *the political magistrate is not the competent judge* of what pertains to the minister's office, — partly because *the minister did not conduct his own cause, — but Christ's, — in the manner in which he is legate*, — and through whom *God himself is said to exhort* (2 Cor 5:20). — Wherefore *Christ said to the Apostles and their successors in ministry: — He that heareth you heareth me; — he that despiseth you despiseth me* (Luke 10:16). — With him therefore let him deal, — who is so impatient of admonitions.

**If however it happen (as often it does)** — that a minister has *κακοζηλίαν* [ill-zeal], — and from *private affects* too much inclines to species-of-personal-attack, — and *without preceding gradus of admonitions* inveighs against some person, — either *by name*, — or *by vivid colors*: — in this indeed he sinned, — and is worthy of correction; — but *the cognition of the cause pertains not to the political magistrate*, — which would not be without contempt of the ministry: — but let the matter be referred *to the ministry*, — or for gravity of excess *to the Consistory*, — that the excess be punished, — and to the ministry its authority nonetheless be left.

### Casus VI. Whether *the magistrate himself* also is to be reproved in sermon

*Reply.* Many there are who cannot bear this, — call it *crimen laesae maiestatis*, — and sedition — by which subjects are moved to *contempt of the magistrate*.

But it should be thought — that even the *magistrate* is taken *from among men*, — who can slip, err, and be deceived; — turn, — they are not men who in the ministry deal with them, — but the *Holy Spirit* whose office is *to convince the world of sin* (John 16:8), — who through the mouth of the ministers deals with others in the world contemned. — *Greater however is the majesty of the Holy Spirit* — than of most powerful kings and princes; — therefore *crimen laesae divinae majestatis* commit those, — who wish to hear *nothing harsher* against the magistrate, — but *only pleasing things*.

**A faithful minister of the Church therefore** — cannot in this genus spare even the magistrate — (who is a *good part of the Church*), — if need be.

**Let this correction however tend not against the magistrate qua magistrate** — for that would tend against the very *ordinance of God*, — which no man ought to overthrow — or bring into contempt among others: — but *against the vices of the magistrate*, — which often more enormously in this order of men are found than in others, — according to the customary little verse:

> *Every vice of the soul so much more conspicuous in itself has crime:*
> *the greater who sins, — the greater is held.*

**Vices of the magistrate are of *two kinds*.** — *Certain* are in the magistrate — *as in a man*, — which he has *in common with others*, — like *homicide*, *adultery*, *revels*, and similar things: — that these must be *taxed in sermon* no one can deny, — unless someone would wish to estimate — that the magistrate has *privilege against the law of God* of sinning freely. — Thus *Nathan* argued *David* for adultery and homicide (2 Sam 12). — *John the Baptist* argued *Herod* for incest (Mark 6:14).

**Other are the *vices in themselves* which are perpetrated against the *office of the magistrate***, — like *harshness and tyranny*. — And here again distinction is needed. Rightly it is said: *Of tyrants many things are to be pardoned*. — Sometimes however tyranny and harshness is manifest, — namely when *exactions* are made from the people, and *new burdens* imposed *without mode and without public necessity*, — in the way in which *Pharaoh* harshly treated the *Israelites in Egypt*, — *Nebuchadnezzar* the same in the *Babylonian captivity*, — or when the magistrate takes the goods of subjects *by species of right unjustly*, — as *Ahab* the *vineyard of Naboth* (1 Kgs 21:5); — and as *certain nobles* do — who *extort corn* from their subjects for a *tiny price*, — obtrude on them *ill-cooked beer*, — make their goods *vendible*, — and other things of this genus. — Such *harshness, tyranny, and injustice openly* — by the ministry of the word is to be *taxed*, — in the manner in which *Moses* did to *Pharaoh*, — *Isaiah and Jeremiah* to *Nebuchadnezzar*, — *Elijah* to *Ahab*, for similar flagitious deeds reprehended.

**Otherwise it stands**, — when *public calamities* befall, — where the magistrate cannot help the republic without *subsidies from subjects*. — There if *new contributions* are exacted from the people, — the magistrate is not to be reprehended; — but the minister of the word ought to admonish the people of the *differences of times*. For some age is *golden*, some also *iron*, — some flourishes and is *grateful to the people*, — some also *withers*, — and to the people is *hard*: — under *David and Solomon* the state of the Church was flourishing, — under *Ahab* not. — The sins of this people are the cause of *non-felicity*, in which the magistrate too is involved.

**As therefore the calamity of the magistrate** — by the beneficence of subjects is to be lifted, — especially when it makes for the *advantage of the Republic*: — so conversely *the rapacity and injustice of the magistrate* — is not to be passed over in silence, — but reproved before others in sermons, — as the *Prophets* frequently — (especially *Habakkuk* c. 1) — gravely argued *the vices of princes*.

Whence *Luther* writes in *comment. in Hebraeos* tom. 5 *Ien. Germ.* fol. 130. 4: *But the captain of the guard left of the door of the poor of the land to be vinedressers and husbandmen.* (2 Kgs 25:12).

**Caution however in this genus** — lest by this elenchus of the magistrate the *reverence and obsequium* — which are due to the magistrate — be diminished: — therefore let those vices indeed be taxed, — but *with common admonition to the people* — that they not therefore *detract the obsequium due to the magistrate*, — but themselves also *recognize themselves as men*, — pray for their *emendation*, — and bear *their own burden patiently*: — and this *for God's sake*, — in whose place the magistrate — even *not altogether the best* — is prefect to them: — in the manner in which *D. Peter* commands to obey servants their lords — *Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear; not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward.* (1 Pet 2:18).

Of other things — which pertain to sermons *usefully and to the edification of hearers* to be formed, — I have sufficiently treated in *Institut. minist.* c. 12-14 sequ., — which here to be repeated I supersede.

## Chapter VIII. Cases of Conscience concerning the Administration of Baptism

*De casibus conscientiae circa administrationem baptismi.*

### Preamble

The second office of the ecclesiastical ministry concerns the *administration of baptism*, — whose necessity is the greater — since it is the *sacrament of initiation* and the *gate to grace* — wherefore many things here occur, — in which much circumspection is needed.

Of most of these we now treat, — and with the assistance of the grace of the Holy Spirit we shall arm the conscience of the minister.

### Casus I. Whether baptism administered by a drunken minister is to be held for true and legitimate, — and is such a minister to be pardoned

*Reply.* The sacraments must be handled *with great devotion and reverence*. There is no doubt. — In the manner therefore in which the minister of the Church ought always to study *sobriety* — which for that cause is put among the *requisites of a bishop* (1 Tim 3:3) — thus above all soberly let him approach the treating of the sacraments, — lest he offer *inevitable scandal* and occasion to *perilous questions*.

If however it happen (as sometimes it does) — that a drunken minister has baptized some infant, — we must see before all — whether he has changed anything in the *substantials of baptism*, — that is, — whether he baptized with *true and natural water in the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit* — and then there is no reason to doubt the truth of this baptism. — For the *virtue of the sacrament does not depend on the dignity, intention, or devotion of the minister*, — but on the *institution of Christ* — which even by evil ministers can be observed.

If however through *drunkenness the minister knows not what he says*, — so that he does not pronounce the words of institution entire, — or clearly enough, — and the bystanders confess that they did not perceive the words themselves, — and therefore doubt whether the infant is truly baptized: — in such case the infant is to be held for *not baptized*, — since it is the same thing to have done nothing at all, — and not to have done legitimately according to Christ's institution.

Therefore without any scruple or fear of iterated baptism, the infant is to be offered to a *sober minister* for baptism, — since according to the rule of *Leo*: *cannot be called iterated what is not known to have been done*.

**Beati Lutherus' judgment on women's baptism.** — In the same manner *Blessed Luther* judged concerning baptism by women, — if through sudden terror and dismay of soul in the extreme grade of necessity they know not what they said or did — when they baptized the infant — and afterwards the infant survived: — without any delay he is to be brought to baptism by an ordinary minister. — For it is a serious matter — the baptism of any man — about whom there is no room for doubt whether he received it according to Christ's institution.

That drunken pastor moreover, at the recognition of the *Consistory*, deserves to be punished, — by severe rebuke, — if he has fallen only once into the vice of drunkenness — and has seriously repented of this his lapse. — If however he has contracted a *habit of drunkenness*, — and thence given evident scandal in administration, — and given occasion to this doubt about the infant's baptism: — either he is to be *removed from office*, — or, — if there is hope of emendation, — transferred to another place, — or even (as the case may require) subject to *pastoral custody*.

### Casus II. What is to be thought of baptism which the minister has administered not in the name of the three persons expressly proposed of the Holy Trinity, — but only in the name of the Trinity or of Christ

*Reply.* That form of baptism must be retained which *Christ himself expressed in the words of institution*: *Baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit* — not on account of some *magical force* which is nothing in the words, — but on account of the *authority of Christ*, — who commanded his disciples to observe all things which he prescribed to them (Matt 28:20).

It can however happen that someone baptizes only *in the name of the Trinity* or *of Christ*: — such baptism the *Pontificals* do not hold for true. — Thus writes *Bellarmine* (lib. 1 *De baptismo* c. 3): *It is certain that baptism must be repeated either absolutely or under condition, — if it be given in the name of Christ, — or of some other person, — without the expression of others*. — Similar things has *Gregory of Valentia* (tom. 4 disp. 4 quaest. 4, *quiles quam* in 4 *Sent.* disp. 4) — writers.

**Zwingli's contrary position rejected.** — Others think it makes no difference which formula one uses, — as *Zwingli* in lib. *De vera et falsa religione* — writes: *concerning baptism there is no necessity of a certain form of words*. — And to this some accommodate the words of Paul (Rom 6:3) — where he writes that we are *baptized into the death of Christ*: — and the Apostles are written to have baptized *in the name of Christ* (Acts 2:38; 10:48; 19:5). — The *Gnostics* baptized *in the name of the unknown father, in truth mother of all, in name of him descending on Jesus*, as *Irenaeus* refers (lib. 1 c. 18). — The *Cataphrygians* and *Paulianists* did not baptize in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, — therefore they are commanded to be rebaptized in the *Nicene Council* can. 19 and in the *Council of Laodicea* can. 8. — Our sentence is: in the praxis of baptism it is by no means to be departed from the *formula prescribed by Christ in institution*; — therefore certain *Arians* are ill-spoken, — because they were baptized *in the name of the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit* (Nicephorus lib. 5 c. 18); — and *Eunomians*, because they baptized *not in the name of the three persons, but into the death of Christ* (Socrates lib. 5 *Hist. eccl.* c. 24).

*Jerome* also teaches (epist. 340 *ad Heuncum*) — that baptism which someone conferred *out of ignorance in the name of God and Holy true Trinity* — seems true to him. — *Ambrose* (lib. 2 *De Spiritu Sancto* c. 3) thinks it sufficient for baptism *invocation of one only person of the divine Trinity, — and especially of Christ*. — All which cannot with piety-preserved be approved, — for the cause indicated above.

**Reply for baptism-form deviations.** — If therefore someone in baptizing does not use the words of institution, — but with wholly foreign — him we determine *not to have administered true baptism*, — because he made no mention — either tacit or express — of the *most sacred Trinity*, — which is the other essential part of baptism.

If however someone baptizes either *in the name of Christ*, or *in the name of the Trinity*, — this indeed *gravely sinned*, and would be worthy of punishment, — because he changed the *form of Christ* — whether temerariously or through *unskilfulness*: — nevertheless we concede this baptism itself to be true, — because in the sense of the words of institution he changed nothing — since the *equivalent phrases* are *to have been baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit*, — and *to have been baptized in the name of the Trinity*, — or *in the name of Christ*, — or *into the death of Christ*.

Wherefore such baptism is not to be repeated, — either absolutely or with condition, — because as to sense in the words of institution nothing was changed, — although the praxis departed from Christ's precept and the *custom of the Apostles*, — by which name such a temerarious minister is to be punished.

**Objection from Rom 6 + Acts 2:38, 10:48, 19:5 solved.** — And that we are said to be *baptized into the death of Christ* — and Apostles read to have baptized *in the name of Christ* in the places above praised, — that does not express the *formula of baptizing*, — but is referred only *historically*, — that Christians were baptized *into the faith, doctrine, and confession of Christ*. — And in this sense *B. Luther* wrote in *lib. De captivitate Babylonica* (in title *De baptismo*): — *whatever the mode in which baptism is treated, — whether in the name of Jesus, or in the name of God is treated, — truly it saves*. — Whereby he does not want anyone to use whatever formula of baptizing which is pleasing to him (as certain among ours interpret) — but that such baptism should not for the *temerity of the minister* be held for invalid, — since as to *sense in the substantials nothing was changed*.

*Brenz* also and *Zwingli* (in Catechism, cap. *De baptismo*): *If it be true that the minister after the recited Catechism-Symbol of faith so demands a divided-in-parts confession of the faith of the one to be baptized: — Do you believe in God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? — Into this therefore confession the ordinand is baptized, — and this itself is a form of confession of Christ, — whence in peace: — although still let the form used by the Church be preserved*, — in the manner *Melanchthon* and *ordinary Chytraeans* also.

### Casus III. Whether the minister of the Church can omit those words in infant baptism — *the remission of sins from the Symbol of faith* — since the infant has not yet sinned actually, — nor can otherwise understand what is done, — nor can distinguish darkness from light nor be otherwise said to be ignorant

*Reply.* The words which in that place have been used — although not in the ecclesiastical constitutions from which the sum of the liturgy is proposed — in which our books of *Agendas* are held, — that in the baptism of *adults* only those words are to be attended, — as chiefly appears from *Agenda* of the *Wirtemberg* churches p. 21, — and in our *Wittenberg* churches — even from these words which are read in parenthesis: *neither among us in the baptism of infants are they used*. — The reason is: — because many recognize no *actual sin* in infants: — whence also commonly on account of *original sin* they die immediately, — since by the Apostle Paul it is written (Rom 5:14): *death reigned even over them who had not sinned according to the similitude of the transgression of Adam*, — that is, even in infants who have not sinned actually.

**But actual sin in infants defended.** — For not all *actual sin* infants lack. — But distinction must be made: — for actual sin properly is that action *with deliberated purpose* which is *contrary to the law of God*, — as with adults who can withdraw. — Actual sin properly is not in infants — because they lack *deliberated purpose*: — because they are destitute — up to the age of discretion — of intellect: — infants are said to not know *the difference between good and evil* (Deut 1:39; Jonah 4:11). — Actual sin however, — such as that in *original sin* is wont to be — whose root never quiescent but always produces its actual movements — cannot be denied to be in infants, though *unknown* to them. — For its indication is *wrath, impatience, reluctant movements* — to which infants even before the years of discretion are subject.

Hence also the ancients respected these things — chiefly those who used those words *sacrament — and remission of sins* in baptismal prayers.

**Then let them also respect these words.** — Then let them respect those words about the *dying to sin* — which in adults after baptism follows. — For not in baptism only is the *remission of original sin* made, — but of all — with which man in his whole life-time can be defiled: — hence baptism is called by the Apostle Peter *the stipulation of good conscience with God* (1 Pet 3:21) — because there is no sin — which can afflict us in conscience — whose remission is not made in baptism.

For these causes those words of the prayer are rather to be retained, — than would be more useful to omit: — but it has obtained among most an *inveterate custom*, — that they be omitted; — of these things I make no law.

### Casus IV. Whether the minister of the Church can with good conscience gratify the *parents*, — if perhaps they would wish their children to be baptized with *generous wine or with rose water*

*Reply.* The *substantial parts* of this sacrament by no means are to be changed. — For it is not fitting that we should be wiser than *Christ*, — who willed the sacrament of *regeneration* to be made with *water* (John 3:5): *unless anyone be born again of water and Spirit, cannot enter kingdom of heaven*: — nor better, — because he himself also *at the Jordan* was baptized like others (Matt 3:16). — Now it is manifest that *water* is the other substantial part of baptism, — and indeed *fountain or river water*, — as the Lord created it, — without mixture of balsam or other liquors.

**No one should change substance for splendor.** Therefore no one, — of whatever rank or condition, — ought to be content with it, — for these reasons:

**(1) Because from that first of all *God* commanded it** in the baptismal formula (Matt 3:11; Mark 1:8; Luke 3:16; John 1:26); — and lest anyone think that only *the waters of Jordan* were consecrated for baptism, — it is noted — that they baptized *disciples also in Aenon near Salim*, — where the waters were many (John 3:23).

**(2) The Apostles baptized with no other than *simple water*** (Acts 8:36; 10:47).

**(3) *Christ himself was baptized with water from Jordan*** — and by this manner consecrated all waters for salvific baptism (Matt 3:16). — Who therefore *not with the same water* with which Christ was baptized? — For no one has more force than that water which is prepared plainly by man.

**(4) *Baptism*, by reason of etymology, is nothing other than immersion or dipping in water** — like the other significations of that word *catachreastic*: — like *baptism of the cross* (Mark 20:23), *baptism of flame*, or of *Holy Spirit* (John 1:16), *And were all baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea;* (1 Cor 10:2).

**(5) Baptism is called *washing of water*** and simply *water* (Eph 5:26; Titus 3:5).

**(6) *The Fathers* also thought the *element of water* in no way to be changed in baptism**, — as *Augustine* (tract. 15 and 80 in John), *Ambrose* (lib. 1 *De initiandis* c. 2), and *Luther* himself writes in *sermon on Deut* tom. 5 *Ien. Germ.*: — *let it be however of person impious and incredulous, — provided the institution of Christ preserves inviolate, — and not with wine, beer, lye or any other thing besides water associated to divine word — otherwise it is not called sacred baptism*.

Against Christ's institution therefore they act (a) who baptize with *another liquor*, — as with wine or beer, — with which they think the *nobility* of the person increased: — nor is *rose water* to be used — since it *deviates from ordinary water*: — as *Beza* to *Thomas Tilius* writes (contra *epist.* 61 *De arguendo, — and yet baptism of someone with edification cannot be made otherwise, I certainly do not, — even if it were pure lye by our judgment, I would judge preferring it, than to seek from some Pontifex — as from Rocher-Grad Montanus, Richardus, and Toletus* lib. 1 *cas. consc.* c. 18, *Valentia* tom. 4 disp. 3 v. 1 — who think one may baptize with lye or broth of meat).

**(b) Who determine baptism must be done only with *water consecrated in the vigils of Passover and Pentecost*, — and prepared with certain rites**, — as it is in *Constitution* p. 105. — But *by Christ's baptism all waters are consecrated*, — says *Augustine* (serm. 27 De temp.); — and the Apostles consecrated *no water*, but used *natural water* as they could have to hand for baptism, — whence the *eunuch* coming to a river said to *Philip*: *Behold, water, — what hinders me to be baptized?* (Acts 8:36).

**And this was also the custom of the primitive Church**, as *Justin Martyr* writes (Apol. 2 pro Christianis): *believers-catechumens are led there — where there is water, which those there wash in be born again*.

**(c) Those who wish their children to be baptized with medicated water** — to whom by no means gratification should be made, — since this at least from *pride* is made — as though their infants born of *noble stock* were of better condition in this genus than others, — since however parents ought to remember — that therefore their children are baptized — because equally as others they are of nature unclean, — and sons of wrath, — because conceived in sins: — which things all ministers of the Church should inculcate to them, — and from *singularity* deter them, — lest for pleasing of men what is against Christ's institution be done.

### Casus V. Whether ministers of the Church sin, — if parents beyond just right delay baptism

*Reply.* The *Calvinists* care little about this, — because they do not think baptism is such a necessary means for salvation, — nor for the ordinary means of confirming faith and regeneration. For they say the children of pious parents are *holy in the womb*, — and born in the *covenant* — concerning which see especially *Calvin* Instit. lib. 4 c. 15 §17, — where he denies the *efficacy of baptism*, — that is, denies that anything depends on baptism: — because they will not have sacraments bound to the confer-ence and efficacy of grace, — as *Zwingli* in *Confessio ad Carolum V* Art. 7 and *Beza* in *Colloquy at Mömpelgard* p. 44 *the elect from mother's womb without-baptism are not lost from the fold, — even if a thousand times baptized: as Beza* there in same colloquy Mömpelgard p. 44 Q. 6.

**And this doctrine is cause** — why *Calvin* (place cited above about baptism, — fol. 638) inveighs into those — who with their infants hasten to baptism, — where if worldly-cares of the age impede, they themselves take no displeasure at the *deferring* of that ordinance of the Lord.

**Against Calvinism: baptism is simpliciter necessary.** — I add — that no one can neglect it without peril of eternal salvation (Eph 2:5) — *in sins conceived we need regeneration*, — in the manner Paul calls baptism the *bath of regeneration* (Titus 3:5).

Hence is that gravest asseveration of Christ (John 3:5): *unless anyone be born again of water and Spirit, cannot enter kingdom of God*. — Whence firmly we conclude — that as long as infants are not yet baptized, so long they remain in their sins, — and outside grace are, excluded from the kingdom of heaven, — into which we are ordinarily received *through baptism*.

**Rightly therefore they do who to infants**, — *as soon as it can be done*, — promote them to baptism. — Gravely on the contrary sin, — who *baptism of infants* — day after day *procrastinate*: — for if their infant dies without baptism, — hardly can the parents excuse themselves of *contempt of baptism*; — for it is a pompous matter — how by that delay they seek that God cannot mete out, — if he wishes to remove infants — even before baptism from this life. — But if they do not attach to the sacred coena, — those pastors of the Church have need to *inculcate* — that the *baptism of infants* has its foundation in *sacred Scripture*.

Some parents indeed excuse themselves through *lay-baptism*, — namely that if the infant is oppressed by a lethal disease, — from the time of the delivery from the mother, — or a little after the birth, — is exposed to *privation of baptism*, — the ordinance of God is exercised by anyone, — which most certainly can be done, — but should be submitted; — since here part of the minister's office is diminished, — and it is not lawful for parents on account of some *private honor, gain, or advantage*, — to themselves and to the infant thus involve in inevitable danger.

### Casus VI. What if the infant is oppressed by disease so much that it is thought — with parents preparing baptism of course-of-time it will die

*Reply.* Two things are here asked: (1) *concerning the infant*; (2) *concerning the parents*.

**Concerning the infant.** — If it is certain that the parents-of-the-infant delayed baptism-of-infant, but by no fault of theirs, some think, the infant is *safe* — as it is in *Lombardus* lib. 4 dist. 4 (which see supr. lib. 2 dist. 25) — where the *Parisian faculty* on those words *In Deo* was held. — But if the parents were of *external negligence*, — some hold the contrary — as *Gerson* in Serm. de Nativitate Virginis Mariae and *Gabriel Biel* in 4 *Sent.* dist. 4 q. 2 art. 3, *Cajetan* in p. 3 *Thom.* ad q. 68 art. 2, and others.

**We hold this sentence.** — Infants dying before baptism, — even if by parents' negligence they were deprived of baptism, — we cannot condemn; — for on the *part of the infants there was no contempt*, — but a *bare privation*: — and if maximally on the part of parents some contempt has acceded, — still the Prophet's saying has place here: *the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father* (Ezek 18:20; Jer 31).

Those infants already in the *mother's womb* through the prayers of the parents and of the Church were *offered to God*, — nor was it their fault that they were not baptized *sufficiently early* after birth, — why therefore should we deny them salvation? — God *most certainly extraordinarily in these can kindle faith*, — in the way he could in *John the Baptist*.

Therefore in the manner in which no one condemns those infants who *in the desert* perished without circumcision — so neither those infants — even by parents' fault omitted — do we wish to condemn.

And in the manner in which the *impiety of parents* does not harm children — who do not follow the same footsteps of impious parents: — so neither may this *negligence of parents*, — where children come into light-of-mind (mental awareness), — be for their harm.

In the manner also concerning the salvation of infants who *in the very birth* by wicked mothers are killed, — doubt is not lawful, — so concerning those, who *by parents' negligence* are deprived of baptism. — For in both places no *fault of the infants themselves* rests: — therefore we hope for the *most abundant mercy* of God — poured out even upon these infants, — lest the defects in parents themselves be imputed to them.

**Concerning parents.** — What concerns the parents, — who by their procrastination impede the baptism of their infants, — diverse causes they can have — why they defer infants' baptism. — Sometimes so great is the mother's *illness*, — that the domestics almost forget the infant, — so that through one and another day they do not think of baptism. — This indeed is great negligence, — but among the *sins of ignorance and infirmity* to be classed; — which is not to be imputed to mothers, — but rather to associates who ought to have been admonished, — that at another time they consider the mother's health, — that they neglect not the *eternal salvation of the infant*. Sometimes *waiting for the time in the Church destined for such acts*, — and if the infant has just valid health, — but suddenly falls (as can happen): — there excuse has place: — since no one *by private daring* ought to change the ordinary time of baptism, — unless *evident peril of death* has come — but all rather in the church in *order* to be done. Sometimes baptism is deferred *for some days*, — only on account of *foreign godparents*, — or *because the things which pertain to the pomp and banquets of baptism are not yet prepared*. — By these gravely, — nay, — doubly sin, — because in a matter of such moment less necessary they prefer to most necessary, — and at that time, — when mothers of all most primarily *of the first curse* on the pains of childbirth ought to be mindful, — of pride and luxury are more curious, — of the *infant's salvation* little solicitous. — Therefore they would rather that their children die, — than that infant baptism be deferred for some hours — and here again distinction is to be made. — For some are of *bad name*, — who more from custom than from serious purpose of soul procrastinate baptism-of-infants, — of parents' wickedness — perhaps most gravely to be admonished, — that they treat the salvation of infant more, — and that hereafter into such a dangerous custom they consent no more. — Some however are of *simple* — who this custom to have entered by chance, — and care little for infant's salvation, — with these some acrimony is needed — that they may understand, — how gravely they sin against God, — to whom they did not sufficiently hasten in offering the good things of theirs; against the infant, whose baptism for causes so light they had impeded; against the Church, — that they have not fulfilled the duty of pious parents, — where they themselves have inflicted scruples on themselves about salvation of their infant, and to *diabolical temptations* opened doors.

Therefore they are to be admonished — that they should not extenuate their sin, — but seriously acknowledge, — deplore, — pray for its remission through faith in Christ, — and hereafter into such procrastination of baptism never again consent, — but rather among others, — as far as in themselves is, — impede it — since — with how great danger it is conjoined — they will now understand.

### Casus VII. Whether the minister of the Church is to baptize infants of *Papist parents*

*Reply.* Not few are those who have *inopportune zeal* in this part, — and without probable reason such infants keep-from baptism, — until the parents *profess our religion*.

**But this manner of converting is *impious*.** — For it is characteristic of the *Papacy* — (as is known) — that by these acts *evangelical parents* are compelled to their church. — More probable and safer is the sentence — which determines, — such parents — who from our churches seek baptism of their infants — even if of our religion they are not confessors, — should not be denied this petition — because: **(1)** it is a sign — that they do not despise our religion, — since they wish to use our rites, — and receive from us their doctrine — of whose return to the bosom of our Church there is nothing to despair. **(2)** Because the minister of the Church is bound to baptize all in the *Church of his nativity*, — even the children of infidels, — if he had been in his own power — as we shall show below by 8 questions. **(3)** Because infants cannot warrant the *fault of parents*, — since false doctrine has not yet depraved understanding. **(4)** Denial of baptism is a species of *excommunication*, — which cannot fall on an infant. **(5)** Exclusion of infant from baptism — with parents still teachable, — from our religion utterly-alien can-render, — since they see it not from them-seeking-it. — For these causes I judge — that the *infants of Cryptopapists* — or even of *Pontifical parents* — should be admitted to our baptism, — provided they in the *received rites of our church* — much less in the *substantials of baptism* — demand no change. — For in these to *adversaries of truth* not even *for one hour* is to be yielded (Gal 2:5).

**Objection resolved.** — Some object, — such parents cannot be present at our baptism, — nor with us commune-in-sacrifice, — because they have not *true faith*. — But I answer to this: — nothing hinders them from our baptism, — of which even *notorious heretics* can be present: — for as *heretical minister* nothing detracts from the truth of baptism, — provided he does not change in the *substance of this sacrament nostro*, — so neither the *error of parent* to the baptism of the infant present.

**(2) The parent's presence is not necessary**, — let rather he be kept-off — who is against infant's baptism.

**(3) Nor is he confessor for the baptized infant** — because not into his faith, — but into the Church's is baptized the infant. — Which in his place the godparents profess.

**(4) If the *prayers of parents* are not sufficiently firm** — so much more validly let the *Church* pray — which is adjoined to the baptized infant in *place of pious parents*.

Sum: — let this have place — the saying of Christ: *he who is not against me, is with me*. — Since therefore those infants are not against us, — why should we not permit them to be *with us*? — Nor can be, that when adolescents shall have grown, — that to *our churches* they should be *re-adjoined* — to whose baptism-communion they were adjoined in their infancy.

### Casus VIII. Whether the minister of the Church may baptize the infants of *infidels*

*Reply.* *Infidel parents* are those, — who live *outside the church*, — as *Jews and Turks*. — Concerning their children, — some receive *no ordination*, — because in 1 Cor 5:12 it is written: *what to me concerning those without to judge?* — Others promiscuously and without distinction of infants of all infidels — as being able to be baptized — teach, — using the Apostle's saying (Acts 2:39): *for the promise is unto you and to your children and to all who are afar off*, — where those *who are afar off* are opposed to those *who are near*, — that is, gentiles at that time far from our churches.

**But neither sentence is true.** — For it is impious surely — that we should have *no care of the salvation* of infants — since we ought all with *the Psalmist* be together with pious people (Ps 87:5) — nor is it commanded — that promiscuously all infants of all sorts be baptized: — since *not to whom you would has all things been given*, — is what is granted (Gal 6:10).

**What however Paul said** (1 Cor 5) — has nothing about *ecclesiastical right*, — or about *communion of word and sacraments* — how far he extends, — but treats of *political conversation*. For when Paul had admonished the *Corinthians* — not to associate with the *manifestly wicked*, — the Corinthians so accepted it, — as if for all *promise* the wicked communion should be avoided, — which they could hardly do, — since they lived in a city — whose inhabitants were still much *pagan*. — Paul therefore explicates his mind, — that of *the Corinthian Christians* he was speaking, — who Christians wished to be, — and yet lived worse than the *pagans*: — these they should shun. — But those who are *outside*, — he said — he did not care much about this, — and could permit the Corinthians as time-serving to *converse with them* in civil-things. — Nothing therefore has this to do with *baptism*, — as though of infidels an *unlawful baptism* were flatly *denied*.

**The other sentence also cannot simply be held.** For — even if it is true, — that even *gentiles born-again* in the front are baptized: — yet nowhere is read — that gentiles were *compelled to baptism*, — or their children snatched from parents and *seized to baptism*; — nor is this anywhere commanded: — nor can this from the words of Peter which are asserted from Acts 2 be gathered: — but there — since the promise of God is conceded even to *gentiles who are far off*, — with those to whom they could not otherwise be — unless *the Lord called them*, — as expressly is added.

**The true sentence is this**: — (1) the children of *infidels from baptism* — by no precept of God are excluded, — but yet more *near* have that right — the children of faithful, — as *born in the Church*, — of whom the Apostle says: *For if the firstfruit be holy, the lump is also holy: and if the root be holy, so are the branches.* (Rom 11:16); — *For the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified by the husband: else were your children unclean; but now are they holy.* (1 Cor 7:14). — Thence they have more-accessible right to baptism, — because they are *treasure of the church*.

**(2) When they are still in the power of their parents**, — outside our family cannot yet be baptized, — because the Lord has not yet called them.

**(3) When they have come into our power** — whether by right of war, — or through purchase, — or donation, — or through captivity, — or by whatever other legitimate manner, — and thus are of *our family made-full-fledged*, — then not only children of infidels, — but also parents are to be baptized: — as *Abraham* not only those born from his blood, — but *emptied ones* — who were not from his stock — circumcised (Gen 17:12) — which the praxis of the Church of all times proves, — and from *Cyprian's book confirmed*, — where in book *De praedest. et lib. arbitrio* c. 12 he writes: *the sons of infidels also are graced with grace of baptism, — with occult providence of God — in the hand of theirs — however-cumulated-through-happen*.

**(4) Distinction between adult and infant infidels to be held**. — Adults previously in the articles of Christian doctrine — rightly are to be instructed, — that they may make public confession before baptism, — of that doctrine into which they are baptized. — Infants however are not held to wait so long — until they learn Christian doctrine — but as our infants, so they also — even in their infancy are to be baptized into the faith of the Church on account of the *peril of mortality*, — and because they by *doctrine or perverse life* cannot yet place *obstacles* to Holy Spirit working in baptism; — if however the infant is of sufficiently firm health, — it is useful — that first he be instructed in the principles of Christian doctrine, — before he is brought to baptism.

**(5) If the parents of the infant have been our captives**, — first their conversion is to be attempted, — and then together with the infant themselves also are to be baptized: — if the parents refuse to receive Christian faith, — then even against their will it is lawful to *snatch and baptize the infant*, — since they are no longer of proper right, — but together with the infant have been reduced into our power. Contrary the *Calvinists* determine, — but without reason: — see *Junius* controversy 4 lib. 4 c. 17. Examples of *baptized Turks and Judaeans* — and their entry into our churches — see in *Consil. Dedekenn.* tom. 1 fol. 393 seq. — Here pertain also certain other cases about baptism of the *supposititious*, — of the *dying*, — of the *monsters*, — of the *ancient-clothed*, — and similar. — Concerning these see *Instit. minist. verbi* c. 8 progress-in.

### Casus IX. Whether one is *secondly* to be baptized, — if of baptized state is doubted, — who then baptism-of-supra survived, — nor sufficiently is known, — whether he was also rightly baptized

*Reply.* That also *laymen in extreme necessity* can baptize, — and the person to be baptized cannot lie unbaptized, — we above proved (c. 3 sect. 9).

**Nor** — that on this matter *scruple be produced* — the *ecclesiastical constitution* of these regions has prescribed a certain manner, — how such baptism is to be confirmed. — If the infant has survived, — it is not necessary to iterate the baptism, — but the infant is to be brought to the temple, — and those who were present at the baptism of the infant are to be interrogated, — whether they know for certain the infant to have been baptized, — and with what words when they baptized: — which if with response they say, — with premised invocation of divine name *in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit*, — there is no need for the minister of the Church to *rebaptize* him, — but with repeated prayers to receive him into the *catalogue of true citizens* of that Church.

Concerning all these things see the *Constitutiones Electorales* tit. *Von der Taufe*.

### Casus X. How the minister of the Church ought to *succour afflicted consciences*, — if any perchance doubt — whether they were ever baptized, — although they were baptized

*Reply.* The *supreme good of the Church is baptism*, — in which we are *adopted into sons of God*, — and into inheritance of kingdom-of-heaven ascribed: — therefore nothing is more necessary — than that each be *most-certain of his baptism*.

To that end, — both godparents as *witnesses of baptism* are adhibited, — and the *names of the baptized* — into a *certain catalogue* — which the *aedituus* has — are inscribed.

It can however happen — that neither godparents nor the *minister who baptized* are any more among the living, — nor the catalogue of the baptized be had, — nor anyone-else at hand who could testify of someone's baptism: — most-certainly moreover his *name* also could not be witnessed, — but to himself in these matters, — with acuminate darts he pierces the man, — that concerning baptism and salvation of his own he begins to doubt, — nay — of that which was baptized, — hardly easily persuaded is placed.

**Two remedies against these temptations of the malignant spirit.** — To these temptations of the malignant spirit — chiefly two are opposed — which take away that doubt.

**First is *invocation of God*** — by which such a man can still call *God his father, — and Christ his brother*, — though *languishing faith*, — likewise — that he does not *contemn* — but *loves the word*, — which of salvation is desirous, — that he feels *sparks of piety* in his own soul. — These all are of the *Holy Spirit* — without whom no man can *call Jesus Lord* (1 Cor 12:3). — But the Holy Spirit is only in the *regenerate*, — in whom he *seals the grace of God*, — *faith and eternal salvation*, — indeed *The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God:* (Rom 8:16). — From these movements of the Holy Spirit therefore we can collect — that we were baptized, — and through baptism into grace by God received: — because the *unbaptized* neither feel these movements — nor have Holy Spirit inhabiting in them.

**The other is *the proper name*** — which anyone at his own baptism was reposed, — of which he is to be admonished — in his adult age, — that in the *book of life* he was inscribed, — and to the *branch of Jesus Christ* inserted. — Whence had he his name, — unless he had been baptized? — since it is not the custom, — elsewhere than in *baptism* to give names to children.

**Memorable history.** On this matter I record a memorable *history* — which *Spangenberg* recites *De Katharina Kapfattirin*, — wife of the deacon *Clemens Schavius of St. Andrew*, — of Eiselben, — who already-in-agony-of-death-constituted, — when she seemed to grow-hard by the reprobate-spirit and imposition-of-various-sects-was, — finally by instinct of Satan concerning her baptism she began to doubt, — since indeed *no one at all was surviving*, — who of her baptism could testify: — parents-therefore-however youths — kept-testifying-that-she-was-baptized-then-under-Papacy-lie, — nevertheless as the Church tearfully-prayed for her, — and finally, — what was her name, — they enquired: — which when she had indicated, — they immediately urged this name, — contending, — that she had a *proper name*, — and *as it were of pia and honest branch*, — even *in the middle of Christians born*, — believing altogether — that also that one is baptized: — which consolation so *penetrated her heart*, — that she ceased to doubt of her baptism, — but freed from these temptations placidly in the Lord fell-asleep.
